## 2026-09-24 — 0.89.82 — the module builds on RHEL 9; the platform roadmap is in the registry

`data/platforms.json` now carries every platform MXFS intends to support, in
order:

| priority | platform | status | kernel |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS | released | 6.8 |
| 2 | RHEL / AlmaLinux / Rocky 9 | development | 5.14 + backports |
| 3 | Debian 13 | development | 6.12 |
| 4 | Proxmox VE 9 | released | 6.17 / 7.0 |
| 5 | Ubuntu 26.04 LTS | development | 7.0 |
| 6 | RHEL / AlmaLinux / Rocky 10 | development | 6.12 + backports |
| 7 | Debian 12 | planned | 6.1 |
| 8 | RHEL / AlmaLinux / Rocky 8 | planned | 4.18 |
| 9 | SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16 | planned | 6.12 |
| 10 | FreeBSD 14 | planned | a port, not a build |
| 11 | macOS 26 Tahoe | planned | a kernel extension (XNU) |

The order is estimated installed base among servers, with RHEL 8 moved below
RHEL 10 and Debian 12 because 4.18 is the widest API gap of the Linux
targets. Proxmox VE 9 is fourth by count and remains the product's reason to
exist. Debian 13, RHEL 10 and SLES 16 share a 6.12 base, so one port serves
the three. For the
RHEL family, the minor release decides a kernel's APIs, not the vendor:
AlmaLinux and Rocky rebuild Red Hat's kernel, so runtime verification runs on
RHEL and build checks run on all three. SLES 15 (6.4 with SUSE's own
backports) is left out. macOS will be a kernel extension: it needs Apple's
kext-signing entitlement, notarization, and on Apple Silicon a one-time
Reduced Security setting on every Mac, and macOS has no built-in iSCSI
initiator, so MXFS either sits on a third-party initiator or ships one.

### The module builds on RHEL 9 (AlmaLinux, Rocky)

RHEL 9 reports kernel 5.14 for every minor release, while Red Hat backports
newer APIs into it and keeps older ones. The shims in `xfs/xfs_platform.h`
were gated on `LINUX_VERSION_CODE`, so on RHEL 9 they redefined what the
kernel already had. On 9.8 (`5.14.0-687.49.1.el9_8`) that stopped the build
at the first header.

- **Kernel APIs are probed, not inferred from a version.** New
  `pal/linux/kcompat_probe.sh` compiles one small test per API against the
  target kernel's own headers, with the flags every module object gets, and
  Kbuild writes the answers to `pal/linux/mxfs_kcompat.h` as `MXFS_HAVE_<API>`.
  Where a declaration is not enough, the probe also requires the symbol in the
  kernel's `Module.symvers`: RHEL 9.8 declares `bio_add_folio` and does not
  export it. The shims that collided are gated on their own probes. On Ubuntu
  6.8 and on both Proxmox kernels, every probe answers as the version gate
  did.
- **What RHEL 9.8 carries, by probe:** `super_set_uuid`, the bdev file API,
  `s_bdev_file`, `bio_add_vmalloc*`, `bio_add_virt_nofail`, `bdev_rw_virt`,
  the atomic-write helpers (without `bdev_validate_blocksize`),
  `super_set_sysfs_name_id`, `generic_atomic_write_valid`, the three-argument
  `generic_fill_statx_atomic_writes`, `iomap_last_written_block` and an
  exported `iomap_write_delalloc_release`, which RHEL now uses in place of
  MXFS's own variant.
- **What RHEL 9.8 keeps from before, and the port for each:**
  - `->update_time(inode, timespec64 *, int)`: a wrapper drops the time
    argument. The body sets the current time itself, which is how the VFS
    computed it.
  - An `int` `filldir_t`, where 0 means "keep going": the shard directory
    actor returns and reads through `mxfs_filldir_ok()`. Under the int
    convention the old `!actor()` test would have read every entry that fit
    as "buffer full".
  - `iomap_page_ops`: the mapping revalidation hook is installed there.
  - No `iomap_iter.private`, no `iomap_dio_ops.bio_set` and a six-argument
    `iomap_dio_rw`: the private context is dropped, it is only ever non-NULL
    for a zoned write, and a zoned filesystem is refused at mount on such a
    kernel. A direct read on a stable-writes device is issued without the
    bounce ops, as XFS did before bouncing existed.
  - `error_remove_page` instead of `error_remove_folio`.
  - `struct scsi_request` still inside `scsi_cmnd`: the compare-and-write
    passthrough puts its CDB in `scsi_req(rq)->cmd` and reads result, sense
    and residual from there. Writing the CDB through `scmd->cmnd`, which is
    unset until dispatch there, would have faulted.
  - `bio_add_folio_nofail` is built on `bio_add_page`, which every supported
    kernel exports.
- **Verified at runtime on AlmaLinux 9.8** (`5.14.0-687.49.1.el9_8`), two
  QEMU guests, packaged RPM (`tests/evidence/alma_rhel9_0.89.82`): DKMS build
  and load; with firewalld active and only 7600/tcp, 7601/udp and 7603/udp
  opened, a two-node mount with no options, cross-node checksums, 500 files
  created on one node and removed from the other (7.5 s and 9.8 s),
  `chk_mxfs` clean, `peer=` with multicast dropped, and a reboot after which
  the module auto-loaded and every checksum matched. With SELinux enforcing
  after a full relabel: mount, cross-node writes, create/remove, symlinks and
  user xattrs with no AVC denial. Files are `unlabeled_t`, though; filed as
  D-SELINUX-HAS-NO-LABELING-RULE-FOR-MXFS-FILES-ARE-UNLABELED_T.
- **A hung node on RHEL 9 is fenced and recovered.** Freezing alma9-2
  (`tests/tcp_peer_freeze_death.sh`, `PREP=alma`): death declared at +60 s.
  The QNAP had dropped the victim's key, so the LU-reset fence ran, admitted
  by fingerprint (RHEL 9.8's libiscsi TMF declarations hash to the audited
  value), and was certified. The journal was replayed, and the survivor wrote
  again at +71 s (`tests/evidence/tcp_peer_freeze_death/20260924T055819`).
  The harness now freezes a guest that is not a libvirt domain through QMP
  `stop`/`cont` on its monitor socket.
- **RHEL 9 is a released platform** in `data/platforms.json`. Its
  `build_check` runs the AlmaLinux and Rocky container builds.
- **Build checks:** `scripts/rhel_kbuild_check.sh` passes against AlmaLinux 9
  and Rocky Linux 9 kernel-devel (both `5.14.0-687.49.1.el9_8`), and the
  existing checks pass on Ubuntu 6.8.0-101 and PVE 6.17.2 / 7.0.14. Each run
  now restarts its container first, because a build whose `docker exec`
  client had died was still compiling in there, competing with the next run.

- **`tools/platforms.py add`** registers a platform as development or planned.
  It refuses `released`: a release claim comes only through `set --status
  released`, which needs a `build_check`, and then `verify`.
- **`priority`** orders the work within a status, and the listing sorts by it.
  `set` also takes `--priority`, `--kernels` and `--packages`.

## 2026-09-24 — 0.89.81 — the vSphere failures were the guests' clock, not MXFS

No module change. Three vSphere-only records (a lone mount that never renewed
its lease, a survivor that declared its peer dead after 836 s and then
returned EIO, and a joiner stuck past its survivor-scan window) had one cause,
now measured: the Ubuntu 24.04 guests on the nested ESXi hosts lose their
kernel jiffies clock.

- **What the guest does.** On vstest2, jiffies jumped 516,630 ticks (~516 s at
  HZ=1000) in 1.4 s of real time, then stood still until real time caught up,
  resuming at uptime ~630.7 s against the ~632 s the jump predicts. Both
  CPUs kept taking timer interrupts, userspace kept running, and uptime
  tracked clyde's clock. Every jiffies-timed sleep in the guest stalls through
  that window, and every MXFS thread sat asleep with a flat wake count. MXFS
  then did what it is built to do: a node whose heartbeat stops landing
  self-fences at lease expiry, and a node whose peer goes silent recovers it.
  In the same run the peer whose clock did not jump dropped the stalled node
  and finished recovery 3 s later. No clocksource warning is logged: a VMware
  guest trusts the TSC and runs no clocksource watchdog. Evidence:
  `tests/evidence/vsphere_lone_mount_stall/20260923T212257`.
- **The EIO was the survivor's own self-fence.** In the original run, the
  node called the survivor had logged nothing for 495 s while its userspace
  answered every second. Its own lease expired and it withdrew at 683 s,
  long before the late death declaration.
- **`tests/vsphere_lone_mount_stall.sh` records the guest's clock.** Each
  sampler tick now carries jiffies, each CPU's local-timer interrupt count
  and each MXFS thread's last CPU and voluntary context switches. The verdict
  reports the longest stretch over which jiffies or any CPU's count stood
  still.
- **0.89.80 builds on 6.8.0-53.** The DKMS build installed and loaded on both
  vSphere guests (`tests/evidence/vsphere_ubuntu_0.89.80`).
- **Ubuntu 24.04 is a released platform.** The packaged `.deb` was verified
  at 0.89.80 on two KVM guests (test3/test4, 6.8.0-101): DKMS build and a
  module loaded from `updates/dkms`, a two-node mount with no options,
  cross-node checksums, 500 files created on one node and removed from the
  other (7.2 s and 8.6 s), `chk_mxfs` clean, `peer=` with multicast blocked,
  and a reboot after which the module auto-loaded and every checksum matched
  from both nodes (`tests/evidence/ubuntu2404_release_0.89.80`). Together
  with the rig's 2/tcp suite, that is what `platforms.py` now requires there.
  A reboot of these guests takes about 3 minutes, and not because of MXFS:
  with the module unloaded, `lvm2-monitor`'s stop still ran 2 min 40 s,
  scanning the iSCSI LUN after its session had logged out.
- **`tools/platforms.py set`** changes a platform's status, `build_check`,
  `verify_env`, `verify_tests` or `notes`, so `data/platforms.json` keeps one
  writer. A promotion to `released` still fails `check` until `verify`
  records the release's version, and it is refused without a `build_check`,
  because `release.sh` runs that string with `eval`.
- **`scripts/release.sh --publish --version V`** publishes the verified build
  in `dist/V/` after the tree has moved on to a later version, and never
  builds: a rebuild from the later tree would be an unverified package
  carrying V's number. 0.89.80 was published this way.
- **`scripts/rhel_kbuild_check.sh`** compiles the module against a RHEL-family
  kernel's headers in a kept AlmaLinux container (`-i almalinux:9` by
  default), since a RHEL kernel's version number does not say which APIs Red
  Hat has backported. Written, not yet run. **`scripts/vnc_screenshot.py`** saves one frame of a
  VNC console, connecting shared so a watching client keeps its session.
- Records removed:
  D-FIRST-MOUNT-HEARTBEAT-LEASE-NEVER-RENEWED-SELF-FENCES-VSPHERE-6.8.0-53,
  D-SURVIVOR-TAKES-836S-TO-DECLARE-HUNG-PEER-DEAD-THEN-CANNOT-FENCE-MOUNT-EIO,
  D-JOIN-MOUNT-STUCK-UNKILLABLE-IN-SURVIVOR-SCAN-PAST-ITS-WINDOW (disproved as
  MXFS defects), and
  D-MODULE-DOES-NOT-BUILD-ON-UBUNTU-6.8.0-53-FALLOC-CONSTANTS-ABSENT (fixed in
  0.89.79; its verification had been recorded but the record never removed).

## 2026-09-23 — 0.89.80 — a hung node no longer freezes a Proxmox cluster

A frozen node on Proxmox VE 9 left its survivor unable to write
indefinitely: death was declared at +60 s, and then no fence could be
certified, so the dead node's journal was never replayed and its locks stayed
frozen. 0.89.79 had passed every Proxmox round, and none of them killed a node.

- **Why the survivor could not fence.** The QNAP drops a frozen initiator's
  registration about 40 s after the freeze, without moving the PR generation
  (READ KEYS sampled every 2 s: the victim's key gone at +41.8 s), before
  death is declared. With the key gone, PREEMPT AND ABORT has nothing to
  name, and the only certifying route is the witnessed LOGICAL UNIT RESET.
  That route failed twice over on Proxmox:
  - it was admitted only on two exact kernel releases, `7.1.0-rc7` and
    `6.8.0-101-generic`, so every Proxmox kernel was refused before issuing
    (`P238-FENCE-LURESET verdict=kernel-unaudited`);
  - its user-mode helper was never packaged. The module upcalled
    `/usr/local/sbin/mxfs_lu_reset_witness.py`, which only the rig's prep
    installed, so on every packaged install the reset was refused with ENOENT
    (`P305-LURESET-NOEXEC rc=-2`) whatever the kernel.
- **Kernels are admitted by the shape of their libiscsi declarations.** New
  `pal/linux/libiscsi_fingerprint.sh` hashes the TMF enum and the eight
  serialization members of `struct iscsi_session`; Kbuild runs it against the
  headers of the kernel being built and compiles the result in. The pin keeps
  its exact rows and also admits a kernel when that fingerprint equals a read
  tree's, the running release is the one the module was built for, and the
  release is not on the new denylist. The log names the admission as
  structural (`P308-LURESET-PIN-FINGERPRINT`): declarations unchanged, bodies
  not read. The read 7.1.0-rc7 tree, 6.8.0-101-generic, 6.17.2-1-pve and
  7.0.14-19-pve all hash to the same value
  (`scripts/pve_libiscsi_crosscheck.sh`); a Proxmox update that leaves those
  declarations alone stays admitted.
- **The helper ships with the module**: `/usr/sbin/mxfs_lu_reset_witness.py`
  in the .deb and .rpm, which now depend on `python3`, and the module's
  default `lu_reset_helper` points there. The rig's prep installs it at the
  same path.
- **Verified on Proxmox** (`tests/tcp_peer_freeze_death.sh`, `PREP=pve`,
  pve9-2 frozen): 4 of 4 laps pass, three on 7.0.14-19-pve and one on
  6.17.2-1-pve — each kernel admitted structurally, the fence certified at
  about +66 s, the slice replayed, recovery complete by +77 s, the survivor
  writing from +73–75 s; `chk_mxfs` clean after recovery; the resumed
  victim's writes bounced off the target with RESERVATION CONFLICT and it
  withdrew without re-registering. The Ubuntu rig passes the same freeze on
  the new build. Record:
  D-PVE-FROZEN-PEER-UNFENCEABLE-LURESET-PIN-REFUSES-PVE-KERNELS-CLUSTER-FROZEN.
- **The blkid udev rule works.** udev rejected `60-mxfs-blkid.rules` at every
  boot ("invalid substitution type") because the shell's `$(...)` and
  `$magic` are udev substitutions too, so filesystem auto-detection never ran.
  Shell dollars are now written `$$`. On both pve9 nodes the previous boot
  logged the rejection and the boot on the fixed rule does not, and `lsblk`
  reports the LUN as `mxfs`. Record:
  D-UDEV-BLKID-RULE-REJECTED-INVALID-SUBSTITUTION-FS-AUTODETECT-NEVER-WORKS.
- **Release verification.** The 2/tcp rig suite passes 30 of 30 on this
  build, and Proxmox VE 9 is verified at 0.89.80 (`platforms.py verify`):
  install and DKMS on both PVE kernels, no-option mount, cross-node checksums,
  create and remote delete, `chk_mxfs` clean, `peer=` with multicast blocked,
  `peers=`, `pvesm` add/remove holding one mount, and a reboot into the default
  kernel with every checksum intact
  (`tests/evidence/pve9_release_0.89.80/`). The remote delete took 30.4 s for
  500 files; that pace is recorded as
  D-TCP-REMOTE-DELETE-OF-PEER-CREATED-FILES-16-PER-SECOND.
- **Tooling.** The freeze test gained a Proxmox mode and a reservation-key
  sampler; `scripts/pve_kbuild_check.sh` prints each build's libiscsi
  fingerprint.

## 2026-09-23 — 0.89.79 — platforms are release criteria

The release criteria had two dimensions, node count and transport, and no
notion of the operating system a release is for. That is how 0.89.77 passed
every gate on the rig's Ubuntu kernel and shipped a .deb that did not build on
Proxmox VE, the product's target.

- **`data/platforms.json`** lists each platform with a status — `released`
  (a release claims it), `development`, `planned` — its kernels, packages,
  build check, verification environment and required tests, and the version
  last verified with its evidence. Today: `pve9` released (verified at
  0.89.78); `ubuntu2404` and `rhel9` in development; `rhel10`, `rhel8` and
  `freebsd14` planned.
- **`tools/platforms.py`** is its reader and writer: `verify <platform>
  --version V --evidence DIR` records a verification (the evidence must
  exist), and `check --version V` fails unless every released platform was
  verified at exactly that version.
- **`scripts/release.sh`** runs every released platform's `build_check`
  before building packages, and `--publish` refuses unless `platforms.py
  check` passes for the version being published.
- **Defects carry a `platform`** (`-P`, default `any`, fail-closed like
  `nodes`/`dlm`), and the gate takes `--at 2/tcp@pve9`. The two RHEL 9
  records are scoped `@rhel9`.
- **The .deb pulls in kernel headers.** Proxmox's `dkms` neither depends on
  nor recommends headers, so an install on a node without them failed its
  DKMS build. The package now depends on
  `proxmox-default-headers | linux-headers-generic | linux-headers-amd64 |
  linux-headers` — the meta-package that tracks the default kernel, so a
  kernel update brings its headers and DKMS rebuilds. The RPM requires
  `kernel-devel`.
- **The .deb builds the module for every installed kernel with headers**, not
  only the running one. The header meta-package installs the default
  kernel's headers, which is not the running kernel on a node that has not
  rebooted since an update, and a fallback kernel keeps a module. It fails if
  any build fails or no kernel has headers, and says so when the running
  kernel is the one without them.
- **Builds on Ubuntu 24.04 kernels before 6.8.0-101.** 6.8.0-53 lacks
  `FALLOC_FL_ALLOCATE_RANGE` and `FALLOC_FL_MODE_MASK`, which Ubuntu
  backported later in the 6.8 series; `xfs/xfs_platform.h` defines each only
  where the kernel headers did not (a version number cannot tell). Verified by
  a DKMS build on vstest1 (6.8.0-53) and on the rig host (6.8.0-101).
  Record: D-MODULE-DOES-NOT-BUILD-ON-UBUNTU-6.8.0-53-FALLOC-CONSTANTS-ABSENT.
- **Rig VMs get ACPI.** The libvirt definitions of test1..test32 and
  pve9-1/pve9-2 had no `<features>` section: `virsh shutdown` was ignored and
  a guest's own poweroff halted without switching the VM off (pve9-1's journal
  reached "System Power Off"; the domain stayed running). New
  `scripts/libvirt_add_acpi.sh` adds `<acpi/><apic/>` to a definition that has
  no `<features>`; applied to all 36 lab domains, effective at each one's next
  start.
- **Lab VM sizing.** pve9-1/pve9-2 raised to 8 vCPUs (the DKMS build took
  ~4.5 min per kernel on 2). New `scripts/vsphere_vm_cpus.sh` resizes vSphere
  VMs through govc with the osimager vCenter credentials, never forcing a
  power-off; vstest1/vstest2 are at 2 vCPUs.
- **The vSphere lab's ESXi hosts are nested VMs in VMware Workstation on the
  rig host**, and were oversubscribed: esxhost1 had 14 vCPUs on threads 0-31
  (both sockets, overlapping esxhost2's cores), esxhost2 14 vCPUs on 8 cores.
  Both are now 8 vCPUs on 8 physical cores of their own socket (`0-7,28-35`,
  `14-21,42-49`). vstest1/vstest2 at 4 vCPUs on those hosts soft-locked on
  every CPU; at 2 vCPUs vstest1 booted clean 5 of 5.
- **The vSphere guest lockups are the nested platform, not MXFS.** With the
  mxfs module file moved out of the module tree (kernel "Not tainted"),
  vstest2 soft-locked anyway under NFS and raw-LUN load: CPU 0 stuck 48 s in
  `smp_call_function_many_cond` waiting on a TLB-flush IPI while CPU 1 ran
  `dd`, and one 12 s load iteration took 379.5 s. Removed from the queue:
  D-VSPHERE-GUEST-SOFT-LOCKUP-IN-USER-PAGE-FAULT-MAS-WALK-WITH-MXFS-LOADED.
  The two earlier records seen only on those guests are scoped `@ubuntu2404`
  and stay open.
- **New harnesses.** `tests/vsphere_lone_mount_stall.sh` (lone mount, or a
  timed two-node join, with every instrument streamed off the guest:
  netconsole, `dmesg -w` over ssh, a per-second sampler, clyde-side uptime
  probes — a hung guest loses its unflushed page cache on reset);
  `tests/vsphere_boot_lockup_ab.sh` (repeated idle boots, lockup counts);
  `tests/vsphere_nfs_control.sh` (the same guests under I/O load with mxfs
  unloadable); `tests/tcp_peer_freeze_death.sh` (freeze one node of a 2/tcp
  rig cluster with `virsh suspend`, and time the survivor's death
  declaration, fence and first write — the suite never froze a node).
- **A frozen peer is recovered on the rig.** First run of
  `tcp_peer_freeze_death.sh` (2/tcp, test2 frozen): disconnect seen at
  +26.7 s, death declared with slot and incarnation at +64.8 s, fence
  certified at +67.2 s, slice replayed and recovery complete at +78.3 s, the
  survivor writing by +76 s. On vSphere the survivor's death worker stopped
  running for ~800 s on a guest proven to lose inter-processor interrupts;
  that record (D-SURVIVOR-TAKES-836S-...) is scoped `@ubuntu2404` and open.

## 2026-09-23 — 0.89.78 — the module builds on Proxmox VE 9's kernels, and no package is built unless it does

0.89.77's .deb failed to install on every Proxmox VE 9 node: its DKMS build of
`mxfs.ko` broke against the Proxmox kernel (6.17.2-1-pve on PVE 9.1.1) and
against PVE 9's current default kernel (7.0.14-19-pve). The rig builds only
against Ubuntu's 6.8, so the release gate never compiled these paths.
Record: D-PVE9-DKMS-BUILD-FAILS-ON-PROXMOX-KERNELS-6.17-AND-7.0-0.89.77.

- **6.16+:** `d_hash_and_lookup()` is VFS-internal; the dirshard mkdir ioctl
  uses `try_lookup_noperm()` there (arguments reversed) and now skips an
  `ERR_PTR` return, which the old call could also produce and the code used as
  a dentry. `destroy_timer_on_stack()` became `timer_destroy_on_stack()`;
  `xfs_platform.h` maps the new name back for older kernels.
- **7.0:** `i_state` is a struct behind accessors. Every MXFS read now goes
  through `mxfs_istate()` (`xfs_platform.h`), which returns the flags as an
  unsigned long on every kernel, so the `%lx` diagnostics print correctly
  instead of passing a struct through varargs (41 reads); the three writes use
  `inode_state_assign_raw()`. The iomap read path uses the
  `iomap_bio_read_folio`/`iomap_bio_readahead` wrappers (the read context is
  now an argument); `mmap_prepare` uses the `vma_flags` descriptor helpers;
  `kernel_bind`/`kernel_connect` take their address through `void *`, which
  converts to both the old `struct sockaddr *` and the new
  `struct sockaddr_unsized *`.
- The 7.0 version gates are proven at the ends that exist here (6.17 old
  form, 7.0 new form); 6.18 and 6.19 were not compiled.
- **`scripts/pve_kbuild_check.sh`** compiles the module, staged exactly as the
  .deb stages it, against Proxmox VE kernel headers in a Debian 13 container
  (the current default kernel, plus any version named). `scripts/release.sh`
  runs it first and builds no package if it fails.
- Verified builds: clyde 6.8.0-101 (rc 0), 6.17.2-1-pve and 7.0.14-19-pve
  (`PVE_KBUILD_OK`, srcversion 1822F50D479D56C14C76006 on both).
- **The packages now declare `target_cache_protected=1`.** 0.89.77's
  `/etc/modprobe.d/mxfs.conf` set only `force_transport=1`, and with the
  module's `fua_disable=1` default every clustered mount was refused
  (`P-DOMAIN-REFUSED`): no one could mount the released package. The rig
  never saw it because its prep loads the option itself. It is the released,
  tested configuration: the storage's write cache survives power loss, or
  target power loss is out of scope. The README states that scope where it
  describes the released configuration. Record:
  D-RELEASE-PACKAGE-CONFIG-REFUSES-EVERY-CLUSTERED-MOUNT-0.89.77.
- **New mount option `peer=ADDR` (repeatable): additional peers on top of
  multicast discovery.** Multicast runs as usual and every discovery, lease
  and nudge datagram is also unicast to each listed address; nobody is
  dropped. It reaches a node the multicast group cannot, such as one on
  another network. `peers=` keeps its meaning — the list is the whole
  cluster, multicast off, everyone else dropped — and is now the exclusive
  form of one shared list: a repeated `peers=` adds to it instead of silently
  replacing the earlier addresses, and `peer=` addresses given with it join
  it. `dlm/static_peers.h` carries an `exclusive` flag and one
  `mxfs_static_peers_send()` used by discovery, lease and both CAW nudges; the
  multicast join and the sender filters apply only to an exclusive list.
  `P-PEERS-MISMATCH` now fires only when this node does not unicast to the
  sender. `/proc/mounts` shows `peers=A/B` or `peer=A,peer=B`. Documented in
  `mxfs(5)` and `docs/discovery.md`.
- **Proxmox storage plugin: one mount, not a stack.** It compared the
  configured `blockdevice` to `/proc/mounts` as a string, so a stable name
  (`/dev/disk/by-path/...`) never matched `/dev/sdX`: the storage read
  inactive while mounted and every activation mounted it again (pve9-1: three
  stacked mounts after `pvesm add`, four after `pvesm remove`). It now compares
  device numbers. Record: D-PVE-PLUGIN-STACKS-MOUNTS-WHEN-BLOCKDEVICE-IS-A-STABLE-NAME.
- The packaged tools report the package version; they reported the
  `mxfs_common.h` fallback, 0.10.0, because nothing passed the version in.
- **Proxmox VE 9 verification of the module fixes** (pve9-1/pve9-2, QNAP LUN,
  `tests/evidence/pve9_release_0.89.78/`): the .deb DKMS-built in 259-272 s
  on 2 vCPUs over the broken 0.89.77; two-node TCP mount, 256 MiB cross-node
  checksums, 500 creates / 111 remote deletes (389 on both), `chk_mxfs` clean;
  `peers=` mount and five refused values; then `proxmox-default-kernel` to
  7.0.14-19-pve, DKMS auto-built, reboot, iSCSI back by itself, the earlier
  file's checksum unchanged and new cross-node writes matching. The rebuilt
  packages then mounted with no hand-set option, `peer=` joined both nodes
  with multicast blocked by iptables, a repeated `peers=` merged into one
  list, and the plugin held exactly one mount (`pve9_release_0.89.78b/`).
- **The 2/tcp suite binds the rig's LUN by WWN, never `/dev/sda`.** On
  test1/test2 `sda` was the LIO bench target on test32, not the QNAP LUN
  `data/rigs.json` names, so every 2/tcp suite since 2026-09-22 ran there. On
  s173 a PREEMPT AND ABORT against the destroyed node deadlocked LIO
  (`core_scsi3_pro_preempt → core_tmr_lun_reset → target_put_cmd_and_wait`),
  the survivor lost its storage and self-fenced as designed, and crash_audit
  failed on the target. `run.sh` now defaults tcp to
  `/dev/disk/by-id/wwn-0x<qnap lun_wwid>` from `data/rigs.json`. Record:
  D-2TCP-SUITE-BINDS-SDA-AND-RUNS-ON-THE-LIO-BENCH-TARGET-NOT-THE-QNAP.
- **No RPM is published.** On AlmaLinux 9.7 (kernel 5.14.0-611.5.1.el9_7) the
  module does not compile: RHEL's 5.14 carries backports that the
  version-gated shims in `xfs/xfs_platform.h` redefine, and lacks APIs they
  call. The RPM is removed from the 0.89.77 release (asset, SHA256SUMS and
  notes) and `scripts/release.sh` builds it but attaches only the .deb files.
  The RPM's `%post` also reported success with no module built. Records:
  D-MODULE-DOES-NOT-BUILD-ON-RHEL9-KERNEL-BACKPORTS-COLLIDE-WITH-VERSION-SHIMS,
  D-RPM-INSTALL-REPORTS-SUCCESS-WHEN-THE-DKMS-BUILD-FAILED.
- **Regression (rig, 6.8):** full 2/tcp suite on the QNAP LUN, s174 on
  EDB0D0BF2AC901EDC1A661E: 30/30 PASS, crash_audit 248 s with the fence
  proving exclusion, replay complete in 77 s and all 165 acknowledged files
  verified (`tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_s174.log`).

## 2026-09-23 — 0.89.77 — release packages for Debian, Proxmox and RPM systems, built so their tools run on the systems they target

- **`scripts/release.sh` builds every release package** into `dist/<version>/`:
  `mxfs_<v>_amd64.deb` (Debian/Ubuntu/Proxmox), `pve-storage-mxfs_<v>_all.deb`
  (Proxmox storage plugin), `mxfs-<v>-1.el8.x86_64.rpm` (RHEL/Alma/Rocky/
  Fedora/SUSE) and `SHA256SUMS`. `--publish` creates the GitHub release with
  them attached, using this version's changelog section as notes.
- **Packages are built in containers of the oldest distribution they target,
  never on the host.** Built on clyde (Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39), `mkfs.mxfs`
  and `chk_mxfs` required GLIBC_2.38 and would not have started on Proxmox 8 /
  Debian 12 (2.36) or RHEL 9 (2.34). Built in Debian 12 the .deb's tools need
  2.34; built in AlmaLinux 8 the RPM's need 2.14, and `mkfs.mxfs` ran there.
- **The RPM now carries what the .deb does.** `packaging/mkrpm.sh` did not
  build or install `mxfs_admin`, did not install the udev blkid rule, and
  listed man pages by name so the `mxfs_admin.8` page would have been an
  unpackaged file. It now builds all four tools, installs the rule and reloads
  udev, lists man pages by glob, and disables the debug subpackage, whose empty
  debugsource list failed the EL8 build outright.
- **The packages select the TCP transport.** Both install
  `/etc/modprobe.d/mxfs.conf` with `options mxfs force_transport=1`. The
  module's own default forms a new cluster on CAW, so an installed package
  previously came up on the configuration that is still in development. A
  config file, so a local edit survives an upgrade.
- **README states the released configuration at the top**: 2 nodes on TCP is
  the only supported configuration, and more than 2 nodes and the CAW
  transport are in development. It had claimed every configuration passed at 1
  to 32 nodes. It also said a forming node probes CAW and falls back to TCP;
  no code does that — `force_transport` is the only selector — and the quick
  start now says how to load the module for TCP.
- The build containers use the host network: docker's bridge network on clyde
  has no outbound TCP, so apt and dnf could not reach a mirror.
- `dist/` is ignored by git.
- **Rig evidence and ccloop run state are no longer published.**
  `tests/evidence/` had grown to 22 GB in 107k files of raw rig capture, past
  what a git host accepts in one push, and `.ccloop/runs/` is local loop state.
  Both are ignored and untracked; they stay on the rig host.
- Profanity quoted from review sessions is paraphrased out of the memory notes,
  the timeout-budget doc and the derule journal; `MODULE_AUTHOR` names the
  copyright holder.

## 2026-09-23 — 0.89.76 — two gates ordered random inode generations and each failed on a coin flip when a number was reused

XFS draws every new incarnation's generation at random
(`xfs_init_new_inode`, `get_random_u32`); `xfs_ifree` bumps the freed image's
generation by exactly one. No order relation between two incarnations'
generations says which is older. Two gates believed otherwise.

- **The eviction-ring consumer no longer poisons a successor it does not own.**
  `mxfs_dlm_evict_inode_cb` flagged, and for an open shell poisoned, any cached
  inode with `i_generation <= freed_gen` ("at or behind the freed
  incarnation"). Measured on 2/tcp (`tests/d0977_open_unlink_tcp.sh` s170f):
  B closed incarnation A of number 2127, the peer freed it and created a
  successor on the same number, B opened the successor (recycling its shell in
  place), then A's free entry reached B from the ring and poisoned the live,
  open shell whenever the successor's random generation fell below A+1
  (victims 2 and 4 of six read -ESTALE; the harness graded it lost data). The
  consumer now acts only on the freed incarnation itself (generation `gen` or
  `gen - 1`) and logs `EVICT-RING-OTHER-INCARN` for any other cached
  incarnation. This resolves the record filed at 0.89.75 as
  D-TCP-OPEN-UNLINK-HELD-FD-READS-EMPTY-AFTER-PEER-UNLINK-S170F; it was not
  caused by the 0.89.75 open-mark change, whose branches are no-ops with two
  nodes mounted.
- **The recycle gate adopts a peer's new incarnation whatever its generation.**
  `xfs_iget_recycle` re-read the platter for a stale shell but adopted the
  image only when `(s32)(disk_gen - incore_gen) > 0`. All 14 decisions captured
  by d0977 laps tracked that order, and the one refusal that met live
  descriptors (s171c arm C, ino 4241) left a fresh open of a valid file on the
  dead incarnation's shell; the grant-time reload found the mismatch under two
  descriptors, poisoned it, and the first read returned -ESTALE. The gate now
  adopts a live platter image of any different incarnation, keeping only the
  same incarnation and the one exact lag a node produces itself: a platter one
  generation below a shell this node freed in core (the ino 1862 autopsy).
  Record: D-TCP-RECYCLE-GATE-ADOPTS-A-PEERS-NEW-INCARNATION-ON-A-COIN-FLIP-S171C.
- **Verification** (2/tcp; ring fix on AB7E3C52F75AFA9D1E836BB and
  09EBACFC4803E44977E9F0C, recycle fix on the latter): d0977 s171a, s171b,
  s172a, s172b, s172c PASS in 83-92 s each (`tests/evidence/d0977_s17*.log`,
  `20260923T03{3632,3759,3924,4939,5114,5247}Z_d0977`); the ring exposure
  (an entry for another incarnation landing while B held the number open)
  occurred in s171b, s172a and s172c with the held read returning the original
  bytes; zero `poisoned=1` flags on any victim; six recycle decisions in s172
  all adopted, five with a platter generation the old rule refused, each
  followed by `P-RELOAD-IDENTICAL`; full 2/tcp suite s172d 29 PASS, 0 FAIL
  (`tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_s172d.log`).
- **Harness.** d0977 arm B now captures the held read's errno, asserts per
  victim that the ring never poisoned B's live shell, counts the exposure,
  and from victim 3 creates a spacer file so a victim lands on a fresh number
  while a master face is still missing (s170f ran six victims on one number
  and never reached the remote face); up to 8 victims, bound 340 s.
  `docs/reuse-barrier.md` §6 states the ring's incarnation contract.

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.75 — an incarnation revocation queued on an inode the iget miss path then freed directly

- **`mxfs_incarn_poison` no longer takes a reference or queues a revocation
  for an inode that is not the cache's inode for its number.** A coordinated
  reload inside `xfs_iget_cache_miss` runs before the radix insert, can poison
  the new inode, and the function's error exit then frees it with
  `__destroy_inode` + `xfs_inode_free`, ignoring `i_count`. The revocation
  worker's reference did not keep the inode alive, and the worker ran on
  freed memory. The field signature was `BUG_ON(I_CLEAR)` at `iput+0x1c5`
  (resolved by disassembling the 6.8.0-101 image) from
  `mxfs_incarn_revoke_work_fn`, which panicked a node during dirent_durability.
  Such an inode was never opened, mapped or given page cache, so the flag
  alone contains it. Reproduced on demand before the fix
  (`tests/revoke_direct_free_repro.sh` s166a: panic in the worker, page fault
  in `d_mark_dontcache` on the freed object). Clean after it (s166b: 8
  injected, 8 recognised as uninserted, no direct free with a revocation
  outstanding, no oops). The D-0941 poison loop still passed 12/12 (s166c),
  dirent_durability passed 10/10 (s166d), and the full 2/tcp suite (s166e)
  failed only the three rows that also failed before the change
  (alloc_witness, chk_clean, guard_census).
- **The natural path is observed, and the defect
  (D-TCP-INCARN-REVOKE-WORKER-IRELE-HITS-IPUT-BUG-NODE-PANIC) leaves the
  queue, FIXED AND VERIFIED.** New workload `tests/incarn_reuse_lookup_stress.sh`,
  no injection. test1 churns create+unlink of 32 names. test2 stats and
  touches them and drops its caches each round, so its lookups take the iget
  miss path against numbers the peer has just reused. Test knob
  `poison_uninserted_legacy` (default 0) restores the old behaviour, so the
  defect and the fix run in the same build.
  - Legacy arm, s167b: test2 panicked in `mxfs_incarn_revoke_work_fn`, with
    `d_prune_aliases` walking a recycled object.
  - Fixed arm, s167e: `P-POISON-UNINSERTED` fired with the whole natural
    stack (`xfs_lookup` → `xfs_iget` → `xfs_iget_cache_miss` →
    `mxfs_dlm_reload_inode` → `P34H-INCARN-POISON src=freshsrc`; the cached
    buffer read FREE, the platter live with a different gen). No revocation
    was queued, no direct free, no `P-REVOKE-*`, no panic, both mounts kept.
  - s167d and s167f met no uninserted poisoning (the race is rare per two
    minutes). s167c aborted in prep because test2 was still booting after
    s167b's panic; the prep refused correctly.
- New probes: `P-POISON-UNINSERTED` (the poison and its caller) and
  `P-REVOKE-DIRECT-FREE` (the miss path freeing an inode a revocation still
  holds). New test knob `dbg_poison_direct_free` (default off) poisons the
  next N inodes the miss path frees directly.
- `tests/dirent_durability_loop.sh` counts the new probes.
- **alloc_witness measures what it claims on the suite's aged filesystem, and
  chk_clean can reach release=CLEAN again.** In every full 2/tcp suite the row
  reported coverage=INSUFFICIENT (own_ag, overlap, breadth), so chk_clean could
  only say release=VACUOUS. The cause: each node's affine AG held more free
  inodes (1379 and 1570, measured) than the row ever created, so no create
  carved a chunk. The counter was fine; the unchanged row passed on a young
  filesystem (s168a). Each node now creates files in a private directory
  until its affine AG carves a chunk, before the counters are cleared
  (bounded by `AW_FILL_MAX`, with its own failure reason). No floor changed.
  Full 2/tcp suite s168b: all 29 run rows PASS, alloc_witness coverage=PASS,
  chk_clean release=CLEAN. The fill measured 2112 and 2496 creates in 62 and
  65 s, about 34 creates/s in an uncontended private directory; that is
  filed as D-TCP-PRIVATE-DIR-CREATE-RATE-34-PER-SECOND. The row now uses 108 s
  of its 120 s budget.
- **The sole-survivor guard census is green.** The three unclassified
  single-node fast paths are read and classified in
  `tests/criteria/sole_survivor_sites.json`:
  - `mxfs_dlm_recycle_grant_check`: instrument.
  - `mxfs_bmbt_tenure_end_evict`: epoch, covered by the join's freeze and
    drop. One unproven window is filed as
    D-BMBT-TENURE-END-EVICT-SKIP-WINDOW-BETWEEN-JOIN-DROP-AND-FLIP.
  - The guard in `mxfs_dlm_open_last_close`: durable. A lone last close
    leaves a published open mark; filed as
    D-OPEN-LAST-CLOSE-SKIPS-THE-CLEAR-WHEN-ALONE-LEAVING-A-DURABLE-OPEN-MARK.

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.73 — the bench target's persistence never activated because LIO never creates its own database directory

- **`tools/lio_bench_target.sh setup` creates `pr/` and `alua/` under the

  `/etc/rtslib-fb-target` with targetcli-fb on this distribution) and refuses
  to continue if it cannot. LIO writes its APTPL table to
  `<dbroot>/pr/aptpl_<unit serial>` with O_CREAT and never creates the
  directory, and nothing in the targetcli-fb packaging does either. With it
  absent, every REGISTER that carries APTPL (the kernel's sd layer sets it on
  all of them) added the registration and THEN failed on the metadata write
  ("Could not update APTPL" in the target's log), so the initiator saw an

  `tests/evidence/20260922T181531Z_aptpl_s160a`), and the key it never got an
  acknowledgement for stayed in the table. MXFS's next mount on that node then
  refused, correctly, on a registration on its own nexus it could not classify
  (P305-PR-SELF-SUCCESSION-REFUSED, register failed -17). Not an MXFS defect;
  the target was under-provisioned. Verified after the fix: a REGISTER with
  APTPL from test1 read back PTPL_A=1 and the target wrote the file. `status`
  lists that directory instead of a hard-coded `/var/target/pr`.
- **`tests/target_restart_pr.sh` reads the fenced victim's key from
  P-PRKEY-FENCED** (hex, by slot index), falling back to the decimal key on the
  P236-FENCE-CERTIFIED line. It had looked for `key=` on the fence-arm line,
  which names the victim and the prover and never the key, so both first laps
  on the bench target (s161a service, s161b host) aborted at that capture
  before the restart — the harness refusing to grade on an empty capture, as
  designed. Verified against a live ring: both sources give the same key.
- **The target-restart tranche of the fence crash matrix is measured, and
  D-FENCE-CRASH-MATRIX-UNTESTED leaves the queue.** On the bench target
  (`liovm`, 0.89.70 module 8DC6EA554D7D201E308BB35 on the nodes, no module
  change since), `tests/target_restart_pr.sh` PASSED 4 of 4:
  service restart s162a (1021 s) and s162c (624 s), target-VM crash and
  reboot s162b (606 s) and s162d (617 s); `tests/evidence/lapq_s162.log`,
  `20260922T183555Z_trpr_service_s162a`, `20260922T185256Z_trpr_host_s162b`,
  `20260922T190302Z_trpr_service_s162c`, `20260922T191327Z_trpr_host_s162d`.
  In every lap: APTPL capable and active with two registrations and the
  write-exclusive all-registrants reservation before the cut; the victim
  destroyed with 32 fsynced files; the survivor's P&A acknowledged, the
  certificate sealed and the recovery claimed and parked before any image;
  before the restart one key (the survivor's), the victim's key absent; after
  it the survivor's key still present, the victim's key STILL absent, the
  reservation held with the same type and scope, the PR generation reset

- **The restart lap reports the outage as the largest gap between consecutive
  poll timestamps**, because the poll in flight when the sessions drop is
  queued through session recovery and completes as the first command into the

- **The lease state word now reads the withdrawn flag as well as the
  authority object.** 0.89.68 built and measured (module
  5C9E1C7956FCF6247901A64, s149a, `SUSPECT_FIRST=1

  withdraws the mount the way the record describes — a forced shutdown
  (`dbg_dialloc_shutdown`), `P-WITHDRAW`, the WITHDRAWN stamp — which poisons
  the session and sets `ctx->withdrawn` but never moves the authority object
  off ADMITTED, so `v5_lease_member_state_cb` answered MEMBER for every
  renewal after the stamp; the peer logged no `P-LEASE-WITHDRAWN-RENEWAL`
  and promoted the SUSPECT entry back to ACTIVE 546 ms after it had read
  the stamp (`P163-WITHDRAW-SEEN` 23849.337, `transitioned to ACTIVE (was
  SUSPECT)` 23849.883). The renewals a withdrawn mount keeps sending exist
  only to hold mastership until its slice is replayed
  (`mxfs_v5_dlm_withdraw`), which is what WITHDRAWN says, so the provider
  now answers WITHDRAWN when `ctx->withdrawn` is set or the authority is
  CLOSED. Queued for s150d. The ordinary arm s149b PASSed on the same build
  (the state word changes nothing where the stamp is read in milliseconds).

- **A grant's completion of a DLM pending entry no longer races the

  `pending_signal_resource` found the entry under `pending_lock`, unlocked,
  and only then called `pending_complete` (which takes the entry's own
  mutex); `fail_all_pending` collected entries under the lock and completed

  (`MXFS_LOCK_ACQUIRE_WAIT_MS`) had just timed out takes `pending_lock` in

  at an attempt's timeout is the ordinary shape of a contended remote
  acquire. Both completion paths now complete the entry before releasing
  `pending_lock` (`pending_lock` → entry lock is the only order anywhere:
  `pending_wait` holds the entry's lock only inside its timed wait), and a

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.68 — a lease renewal says what its sender is, and the withdraw thread starts on the transport that ships

- **The withdraw thread now starts on the TCP transport.** 0.89.67 started it
  before the LAST success return of `mxfs_v5_dlm_init`, which is the CAW
  path's; the TCP path returns earlier, after its membership settle, so on
  the transport under release the thread never existed and no line said so.
  Measured s148b on 0.89.67 (`PUMP_HOLD_MS=700000
  tests/parked_log_waiter_across_closure.sh`,
  tests/evidence/20260922T050229Z_plwait_s148b): `P290-AUTH-CLOSED` landed on
  time with the PR worker's pump held, `via=withdraw-thread` never printed,
  and the filler was still in `xlog_grant_head_wait` 120 s later — the same
  reading as s146e. The control arm s148a on the same build converted via
  `pr-worker` in 26 s, which is why the first lap did not notice. The start
  is now `v5_auth_withdraw_thread_start`, called before both returns, and it
  announces itself as `P290-AUTH-WITHDRAW-THREAD node=... transport=` so a
  mount without the thread is visible; the lap's subject arm requires that
  line on the victim when the module carries it.

- **The lease beacon carries the sender's authority state and incarnation,
  and the receiver takes nothing but mastership retention from a withdrawn
  one** (D-POST-CLOSURE-MEMBERSHIP-RENEWAL-HAS-NO-DEFINED-MEANING-AT-THE-PEER,
  step 3). s146c measured the defect on 0.89.66: a post-closure renewal from
  a withdrawn node promoted the peer's SUSPECT entry back to ACTIVE
  (`transitioned to ACTIVE (was SUSPECT)` 90 ms before `P163-WITHDRAW-SEEN`).
  The wire message (`dlm/lease.h struct mxfs_lease_udp_msg`) had no field
  that could say otherwise, and the epoch argument on the UDP path is the
  literal 0. Now the former `pad` word is `state` — `MXFS_LEASE_STATE_MEMBER`
  while the authority is live, `MXFS_LEASE_STATE_WITHDRAWN` once it is
  CLOSED, 0 from any earlier sender and read exactly as before — and the
  sender's incarnation (the authority's, the disklock epoch) is appended
  after `view_hash`; a packet of the earlier full length is still a complete
  view report (`MXFS_LEASE_UDP_MSG_VIEW_LEN`), the version word is unchanged
  so an older receiver keeps reading the packet it knows. The provider is
  `v5_lease_member_state_cb` (dlm/v5_mount.c), wired on both transports. The
  receiver (`mxfs_lease_process_renewal`): a WITHDRAWN renewal keeps the
  entry and stamps no liveness and promotes nothing, logged once per
  transition as `P-LEASE-WITHDRAWN-RENEWAL`, so the monitor ages the entry to
  SUSPECT and DEAD on its own schedule if no other detector recovers the node
  first, and a corpse can never promote itself; the first renewal naming an
  incarnation binds it to the entry (`P-LEASE-INCARNATION`), and a renewal
  naming another incarnation is not liveness at all
  (`P-LEASE-INCARNATION-MISMATCH`, rate-limited, -ESTALE) — the held
  incarnation must be recovered first, which is the reboot case the record
  named. `tests/post_closure_renewal_at_peer.sh` `SUSPECT_FIRST=1` now grades
  the promotion count at 0 and requires the WITHDRAWN line when the module
  carries the receiver. Compiled, not yet built into a module or run: the
  s148 queue is deploying 0.89.67.

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.67 — a closure's withdrawal gets its own thread, and the old-epoch hold moves below a stacked device that can register

- **A closure's withdrawal now has its own thread, because the PR worker's
  tick was the only thing that converted a closure into the shutdown that
  frees a task parked in the log.** Measured s146e on the 2-node TCP rig at
  0.89.66 (`tests/parked_log_waiter_across_closure.sh`, `PUMP_HOLD_MS=700000`,
  tests/evidence/20260922T041710Z_plwait_s146e): with the PR worker's pump
  held, `P290-AUTH-CLOSED reason=AUTHORITY_LEASE_EXPIRED` landed on time,
  zero withdrawals followed, and a filler parked in `xlog_grant_head_wait`
  was still there 120 s later, its stack unchanged. The control arm s146d,
  same build, freed it at the closure (25 s). A log wait exits on
  `xlog_is_shutdown` or grant space and nothing else, and the PR worker can
  be inside a fence, a reset or a storage stall for as long as the storage
  is unreachable, which is exactly when leases expire. So
  `v5_auth_withdraw_worker_fn` (dlm/v5_mount.c) idles interruptibly at
  100 ms, takes only the withdrawal flag, and shares no lock with the
  fence, the reset or the heartbeat; the PR worker's pump remains as the
  backstop and the take is now an exchange
  (`mxfs_authority_take_withdraw`), so exactly one consumer notifies. The
  withdraw line carries `via=withdraw-thread` or `via=pr-worker`. The
  thread honours the blind-victim knob (`dbg_auth_pump_pause_ms`) so the
  three laps that keep a fenced node from converting anything are
  unchanged; `dbg_auth_withdraw_pause_ms` holds the PR worker's pump alone,
  which is how the thread's contribution is measured. The subject arm of
  the log-waiter lap now predicts the opposite of s146e: freed, by name.
  Not yet verified on the rig.
- **`tests/delayed_write_across_fence.sh` holds the write in a single-path
  dm-multipath map, not in dm-delay.** Its first run (s147c,
  tests/evidence/20260922T044107Z_dlywrite_s147c) could not mount through
  the dm-delay map: `P305-PR-SWAP-NOKEY` then `P305-PR-NEXUS-ALREADY-REGISTERED`
  on a nexus that held nothing, and afterwards the LUN carried only the
  peer's key. The module's REGISTER goes through the stacked device's
  `pr_ops` (`mxfs_pal_scsi_pr_register` -> `dm_pr_register`), and dm-delay's
  `iterate_devices` hands `dm_pr_register` its one backing device three
  times (read, write and flush classes): the first REGISTER succeeds, the
  second answers RESERVATION CONFLICT because the nexus is now registered,
  and dm_pr_register rolls the first back. That is dm-delay's shape, not the
  module's; multipath lists each path once, which is what dm_pr_register was
  built for and what a deployment looks like. The lap now creates
  `multipath 1 queue_if_no_path ... round-robin 0 1 1 <path> 1` over the
  LUN without the mpath- uuid (multipathd ignores it), fails the path with
  `dmsetup message` after the heartbeat is parked, proves the hold from the
  writer's state, the LUN's completed-write count and the dm device's
  blk-mq requeue list (`/sys/kernel/debug/block/dm-N/requeue_list`), and
  reinstates the path under a kernel-log mark after A's recovery, so a
  withdrawal is graded VACUOUS only when it precedes the release. Verified
  by hand on test2 2026-09-22: a direct read through the failed path sat in
  `submit_bio_wait` for 5.3 s until the reinstate. The 0.89.66 entry below
  described the dm-delay version, which never ran a write. Bounds 1400 s
  (block arms), 1850 s (SITE=log).

**The s130 handoff-boundary sweep never reached the peer's dead window.**

victim's authority deadline and the peer's earliest handoff action (62 s dead
window, 2 s sampling, 30 s lease) and measured 0.9-1.6 s four times. The
evidence already on disk says why: in every lap the peer's death line is
preceded by `P163-WITHDRAW-SEEN`. The harness's own writer made the victim's
gate close at the deadline, the closure withdrew the mount, the withdrawal
stamped the slot WITHDRAWN, and the peer fired on the stamp at its next 2 s
pass. "Expired after 14 checks" was the sample count at that instant, not a
threshold (`dead_threshold` is 31 on both nodes; both timeout knobs read 0).
A margin on that chain is one monitor pass and positive by causality, so the
four PASSes are measurements of the cooperative path only.

Verified under unchanged acceptance criteria on every producer of the state: the injector reproducer (s100/s101: census classless=0 dino_none=0, foreign replay complete, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE), a REAL VM kill at 0.89.41 (board row crash_audit PASS, all 263 fsync-acknowledged files back at their md5 after drop_caches, cold chk_mxfs clean with no inobt/AGI freecount disagreement - the record's own on-platter signature absent), and the two durable-write injection arms at 0.89.43 where the replay-side guards refuse a wild agino and a straddling cluster by name and a healthy slice still replays (s115d, s115e, s115f). The last open item, a crash-order matrix around the replay, is exercised by fence_crash_cuts cut 7 (replay-partial: a nonempty durable prefix, a nonempty unissued suffix, no completion durable, then a successor's full recovery, unmount/remount and cold check with churn oracles), PASS on s130-c7 and s133e7, and every remaining crash point of that matrix is enumerated and tracked by D-FENCE-CRASH-MATRIX-UNTESTED, which stays open; the whole fence lineage was re-banked on 0.89.65 today (s145, 6 of 6 PASS). Nothing about this record's defect - a dead peer's committed log slice lost to a terminal refusal - has reproduced on any build since 0.89.28.

- **The authority lease is a node-wide admission condition, and nothing checks that an admitted mutation still owns the RESOURCE it is about to change - so an unexpired lease says yes to a write whose AG grant this node has already published as free, or whose WITHDRAWN record it has already published to its peers.** — DISPROVED by measurement on the 2-node TCP rig: an admitted mutation cannot outlive this node's publication of its AG grants, because put_super cannot reach the publication while one is in flight, for every class the gate names that is reachable on this rig. The lap is tests/admitted_write_parked_across_unmount.sh, which holds ONE admitted submission between the gate's yes and the layer below it (dbg_admit_park, 120 s) and reports which of three orderings it got, by the module's own line stamps. data (buffered writeback's ioend, no descriptor held) s138c, 0.89.59+, tests/evidence/20260921T223659Z_admumnt_s138c: ORDER=barrier - ADMIT-PARK-END at 1283172 ms, P482-UMOUNT-AGREL 39 ms after it; put_super waited 94 s on the parked ioend before publishing; platter R1=R2=R3, a fresh mount decides the same way, cold check clean. log without a descriptor (the create committed and closed, the unmount's own log force parked) s146g, 0.89.66 A46A495ED258EA96F46EDDD, tests/evidence/20260922T042354Z_admumnt_s146g: ORDER=barrier - ADMIT-PARK-END 2249815 ms, AGREL 2249859 ms, 44 ms after; put_super waited 78 s on the parked iclog; the peer then allocated 2000 files, cold check clean, no BUG/Oops/shutdown. dio s130d (20260921T103504Z_admumnt_s130d) and log with fsync s140e (20260922T010626Z_admumnt_s140e): ORDER=vfs-busy - the unmount is refused (rc=32) while the write's descriptor is open, so put_super is never entered; a user direct write or fsync in flight always holds its file, which makes this a structural barrier, and the record's own concern was the descriptor-free classes. meta: the only class inside the departure drain's own account, asserted quiescent at the release point and counted by P483-AGFREE-WINDOW, which has always read zero. dio-zoned: unreachable, no zoned device on this rig. The WITHDRAWN half is bounded by the fence rather than the lease and is measured in D-OLD-EPOCH-IO-BELOW-THE-AUTHORITY-GATE-IS-UNBOUNDED schedule (A): every class parked across a fence and released was refused by the target (dio s130a EBADE, data s138d EBADE, log s138k EIO) with the platter unchanged at R2 and after a later remount at R3. Step 3's first option - after grant publication the only remaining producers are permitted journal-retirement and coordination producers - is established by measurement for the clean-unmount half and by the target's exclusion for the withdrawal half; the capability-on-the-operation alternative is not needed because no barrier is missing.

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.65 — the strand escape TCP actually has, and the one that cannot be reached

**The s143 queue's in-flight lap FAILed all three of its escape assertions,
and the capture shows a mechanism hypothesis H1 did not name.** H1 predicted
the 280-sample strike escape would accumulate too slowly under the 1 s
backoff cap. It accumulated nothing: across the whole 20 s hold the release
pipeline took zero samples on the strand, because every gate upstream of the
sampler treats a standing `i_dlm_acq_inflight` as a live acquirer to protect
— `__mxfs_dlm_bast_notify` parks the BAST (`P-ACQWIN-PARK`, 2 lines) and
`mxfs_dlm_bast_dwork_fn`'s busy check re-arms without running the release.
The instant the injected acquirer exited, the strand was the abandoned shape
and the sess10 arm freed it 1.4 s later. So the record's premise — that the
strike counter is TCP's only strand escape — is false on both shapes: the
abandoned one is freed by `P15-TCP-ORPH-PROCEED` at about the fifth sample,
and the in-flight one is parked before the sampler for exactly the acquirer's
lifetime, which is the daf50d34 design that stopped the double-EX dirent
loss. The comments that said otherwise (the CAW-only gate's "TCP keeps the
same-gen 280-strike escape, so it converges", the 0.89.64 knob comment, the
injector's own line) now say what was measured, and the branch stays as the
census it also is. The in-flight arm of `tests/stranded_grant_escape.sh` now
asserts that design by line order in a window opened at this lap's injection
(the ring outlives a module reload, every lap's file lands on inode 131, and
gens repeat, so ino+gen alone can name an earlier lap's lines): no escape
before the acquirer's END line, the park by name, the abandoned arm after it
and inside 3 s of it, the unlock anchored on the strand's gen. Both arms
re-run on this build: s144a PASS (871 ms), s144b PASS (release 2024 ms after
the exit, negative control 11 ms, no shutdown, BUG or Oops).

- **xfs_inode.h declared i_dlm_orphan_strikes as uint8_t while xfs_mxfs_dlm.c:21294 escalates on '++ip->i_dlm_orphan_strikes >= 280'. A uint8_t promotes to at most 255, so the comparison is provably false, the compiler deleted the branch, and the stranded-grant release it performs has never been able to run. The threshold was deliberately raised from 4 to 280 in an earlier session, on instrumented evidence that 4 was too tight; the field was not widened with it, so the change that was proven necessary silently removed the mechanism.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED for the coding defect, and the stability claim that made it a release blocker is DISPROVED by measurement. The defect: i_dlm_orphan_strikes was uint8_t against a 280 threshold, the compiler deleted the branch and P15H-STRANDED-RELEASE was not a string in mxfs.ko. Fixed 0.89.59 (uint16_t, xfs/xfs_inode.h:239), verified in the binary on every build since: tools/probe_audit.sh --gate P15H-STRANDED-RELEASE P15H-STRIKES exits 0 on 30E71D19B4653FB9A1D5EC4 (0.89.65). The claim: that this counter is TCP's ONLY strand escape, so a stranded grant hangs the node. Measured false on the 2-node TCP rig with the module's own one-shot strand injector (dbg_strand_ino, dbg_strand_hold_ms) and tests/stranded_grant_escape.sh, kernel 6.8.0-101-generic, builds 03D5944DDFCEB6ADC320CDD (0.89.64) and 30E71D19B4653FB9A1D5EC4 (0.89.65): the pipeline discriminates two strand shapes by i_dlm_acq_inflight and neither reaches the strike sampler. ABANDONED (acquirer gone): the sess10 arm P15-TCP-ORPH-PROCEED frees the grant after 500 ms of persistence, at about the 5th pipeline sample - s143a 901 ms, s144a 871 ms, unlock anchored on the strand's own gen (P6U-UNLOCK gen=12), both nodes reading seed,b1,b2, P15H=0. IN FLIGHT (acquirer alive with its count, state NONE, held 20 s): every gate upstream of the sampler parks the BAST for the live acquirer - P-ACQWIN-PARK in __mxfs_dlm_bast_notify (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c:27680-27696) and the busy re-arm in mxfs_dlm_bast_dwork_fn (:25558-25563) - so there were 0 release samples across the whole hold (s143b, s144b), no escape line precedes P-DBG-STRAND-INJECT-END, and the instant the count drops the same abandoned arm frees it: s144b P15-TCP-ORPH-PROCEED 2024 ms after the acquirer's exit, anchored on gen 8, RESULT PASS fails=0 with the negative control (a live grant, ordinary demote 11 ms, neither arm firing) and no BUG, Oops or shutdown on either node. That park is the daf50d34 design - releasing under a live acquirer is the double-EX that lost dirents - so the in-flight strand lasts exactly the acquirer's lifetime, which the slow path's own timeouts bound. Hypothesis H1 on this record (the strikes cannot converge under the 1 s backoff cap) was DISPROVED by s143b: not slow convergence but no samples at all. The 280-strike branch has no reachable shape on TCP; it stays as the census it also is, its comment now says so (0.89.65), and nothing may be argued from it firing or not. The remaining harness assertions for the in-flight arm (line order in a window opened at this lap's injection, the park by name, the release inside 3 s of the exit) encode the measured design. Evidence: tests/evidence/strand_s144a.console, strand_s144b.console, 20260922T024635Z_strand_s144a, 20260922T024759Z_strand_s144b, lapq_s143.log, 20260922T015424Z_strand_s143b.

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.64 — the strand injector learns the in-flight shape

**The stranded grant has two shapes on TCP, and s142a had measured only one
of them.** `dbg_strand_ino` dropped a granted acquire and exited at once, so
`i_dlm_acq_inflight` fell to 0 and the sess10 abandoned-grant arm
(`P15-TCP-ORPH-PROCEED`) freed the grant in 885 ms — the escape the record
had not accounted for. The shape the 280-sample strike escape was written for
is an acquirer still in flight whose ACQUIRING was trampled to NONE, and the
injector could not produce it. `dbg_strand_hold_ms` now makes the acquiring

(`P-DBG-STRAND-INJECT-END` marks the exit). `tests/stranded_grant_escape.sh`
runs either shape by `STRAND_HOLD_MS`, counts every escape by its own
`ino=<n> ` line format rather than a bare probe name the injector's line

converge under the 1 s backoff cap) is measured rather than argued. The s143
queue ran both: the abandoned arm PASS (901 ms, anchored unlock, both nodes
agreeing on the bytes); the in-flight arm's verdict is adjudicated in

## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.63 — a lazytime write that recursed until the node panicked, and a fence retry that disowned its own arm

**The s140 re-run of the corrected lazytime lap did not find the timestamp
loss it was built to find. It found a kernel panic in front of it.** The
subject arm's 4 KiB in-place overwrite on the lazytime mount never returned;
test1's serial capture holds a stack guard page hit in `dd` with the call trace
alternating `xfs_vn_update_time` / `inode_update_time` 169 times, then a fatal
exception. The cause is a name that means two different functions: upstream
7.x's `inode_update_time(inode, type, flags)` sets the timestamps and returns
the I_DIRTY_* flags, and the fork's lazytime branch was written against it; on
every 6.x kernel `inode_update_time(inode, flags)` is the VFS dispatcher that
calls `->update_time` — which XFS installs — so the branch called itself. The
pre-7.0 branch now takes upstream 6.8's own shape (`generic_update_time()`,
which marks I_DIRTY_TIME or I_DIRTY_SYNC and never re-enters `->update_time`,
unless a queried iversion must be bumped, in which case the inode is logged).
Reading the completion half found a second fault the panic had hidden: the
`dirty_inode` hook installed in 0.89.60 carried the pre-5.12 guard, false on
every call since `__mark_inode_dirty` started clearing I_DIRTY_TIME from
`i_state` and passing it in `flags`. Both are verified by the lap that was
written for them (s141a, below).

**The live-prover fault mode 3 hang is a retry gate that reads only the
platter.** After an ambiguous arm (the CAS landed, the prover was told it
failed) the attempt is classified PRECOMMAND and the retry latch is armed; the
worker then asks the descriptor whether the attempt is re-drivable, sees the
durable "may have run" flag, answers "ambiguous — not ours to retry", disarms,
and nothing ever revisits the slot. The flag cannot say whether a command was
issued under it — it is written before the command so a crash reads
conservatively — but the incarnation that wrote it knows. `struct mxfs_v5_dlm`
now records, per slot, the (victim, incarnation, term) under which an attempt of
this incarnation returned having crossed the command boundary; the retry gate
answers a third value for "ours and armed", and the worker re-drives an arm it
never issued under (`P304-FENCE-RETRY-ARMLANDED`, then `P304-FENCE-ARM-STANDING`
from the idempotent arm step) while an arm it may have issued under stays with
the proof resume. The same witness, read under the single-prover guard, refuses
a second command under an arm whose first is unresolved
(`P238-FENCE-BOUNDARY-HELD`). `tests/fence_live_prover_faults.sh` mode 3 now
requires the re-drive and a served mount, and reads "the fence did not
complete" as the FAIL it is.

**A producer for the stranded grant.** `dbg_strand_ino` (one-shot, by inode)
drops the next granted slow-path acquire unconsumed — mirror granted, in-core
NL — which is the shape the 280-sample strike escape exists to free and which
had no known producer. `P15H-STRIKES` logs the census every 70 samples with the
gen it counts on, so the never-measured claim that the TCP gen does not churn is
measured. `tests/stranded_grant_escape.sh` drives it with an ordinary-contention
negative control.

- **On kernels before 7.0 the lazytime branch of xfs_vn_update_time calls inode_update_time(inode, flags), which on those kernels is the VFS dispatcher that calls inode->i_op->update_time — i.e. xfs_vn_update_time itself. The first timestamp update on a lazytime mount recurses until the kernel stack guard page is hit and the node panics. The 7.0+ helper of that name returns the I_DIRTY_* flags; the fork carried the 7.x call under the pre-7.0 signature.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED. Cause proven from the panic itself (test1 serial capture, s140a: 169 alternating frames of xfs_vn_update_time and inode_update_time under a 4 KiB dd, stack guard page hit, fatal exception) and from both kernels' sources: below 7.0 inode_update_time(inode, flags) is the VFS dispatcher that calls ->update_time, so the fork's lazytime branch, written against the 7.x helper of the same name, called itself. Fix (0.89.63, pal/linux/xfs_iops.c): under the pre-7.0 signature the branch takes upstream 6.8's shape — generic_update_time() unless the caller's queried version must be bumped, in which case the inode is logged with XFS_ILOG_CORE. Verified live: tests/lazytime_timestamp_durability.sh s141a on build 06AC7CB42624D7E279F66AF, kernel 6.8.0-101-generic, 2/tcp (tests/evidence/20260922T012118Z_lazyts_s141a, console tests/evidence/lapq_s141_1.console): the subject arm's in-place overwrite plus fsync on the lazytime mount returned rc=0 in under a second (was: never returned, node panicked), the in-core mtime advanced 1790040149 -> 1790040152, no BUG or Oops, RESULT PASS fails=0.
- **After the live-prover armambig injection - the arm CAS lands and is reported to the prover as having FAILED - the prover's own mount stopped answering a bare mountpoint check, and eight minutes later the node still could not release mxfs. The fence never certified, and the node that was doing the fencing is the one that hung.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED. Cause, read in the tree and confirmed by the fix's own lap: after the ambiguous arm scsipr returns before issuing (P304-FENCE-NOARM), the attempt is classified PRECOMMAND and the retry latch is armed; the worker's mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_retryable() then read the durable MAY_HAVE_RUN flag off the descriptor and answered 0 ('ambiguous - needs reconciliation, not retry'), the worker disarmed, and because the PRECOMMAND classification never set the in-memory blocked record the proof resume never revisited the slot either - FENCING with may_have_run on the platter, no latch, no fail-fast block, the victim's grants frozen, and every path operation on the prover that needed one blocked (s133c3: 20 s stat bound, module unreleasable 8 min later; s138m: stat unanswered in 5 s, after settle kind=NONE fence_term=1). The durable arm is written before the command so a crash reads conservatively; it cannot say whether a command was issued under it, but the incarnation that wrote it can. Fix (0.89.63): struct mxfs_v5_dlm keeps, per slot, the (victim, incarnation, term) under which an attempt of this incarnation returned with phase MAY_HAVE_SUBMITTED, set where every fence leg converges in v5_pr_fence_prove_locked; retryable() returns 2 for 'ours and armed' (dlm/disklock.c) and the worker re-drives when that witness does not match (P304-FENCE-RETRY-ARMLANDED; the idempotent arm step now logs P304-FENCE-ARM-STANDING) and disarms when it does; the same witness under the single-prover guard refuses a second command under an unresolved arm (P238-FENCE-BOUNDARY-HELD). Verified: tests/fence_live_prover_faults.sh mode 3 s141c, build 06AC7CB42624D7E279F66AF, 2/tcp, tests/evidence/20260922T012402Z_flpf3_s141c, console tests/evidence/lapq_s141_3.console - the arm landed before the prover was told it failed, the injected attempt recorded command_may_have_run=no and certified nothing, the retry recognised the standing arm as its own (P304-FENCE-RETRY-ARMLANDED 1), the completing command met its own boundary first (P304-FENCE-ARM-STANDING at +15, PREEMPT AND ABORT at +17), the certificate followed the command (+19) on a real receipt (PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1, pr_gen 0x1a44 -> 0x1a45, victim key consumed), a stat on the prover's mount was SERVED (was blocked past 5 s and 20 s), no shutdown, BUG or Oops across the settle window; RESULT PASS fails=0. The harness's mode-3 assertions, which had encoded the hang as the expected outcome, now require the re-drive, a certificate that follows a completed command, and a served path operation.
- **Buffered writes never revalidate their cached extent mapping on this kernel. xfs_iomap_valid() is written, correct, and referenced by nothing the 6.8 build compiles, so the compiler drops it; the validity_cookie it would check is stamped on every mapping and read by nobody.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED. Cause (proven by the compiler, tools/warn_sweep.sh on 0.89.60: 'xfs_iomap_valid defined but not used'): the hook was installed only in the 6.15+ iomap_write_ops, which the pre-6.15 call macro expands away, so on 6.8 nothing referenced it and it was not in the module. Fix (0.89.60, pal/linux/xfs_iomap.c): below 6.15 a static iomap_folio_ops holding .iomap_valid is assigned to iomap->folio_ops beside the validity_cookie in xfs_bmbt_to_iomap, which is the hook this kernel's iomap consults. Verified in the three steps the record demanded. (a) The compiler: the post-fix sweep no longer reports the function unused, and P312-IOMAP-REVALIDATED / P312-IOMAP-STALE are strings in mxfs.ko (tools/probe_audit.sh --gate, build 06AC7CB42624D7E279F66AF). (b) The hook is CALLED: tests/iomap_revalidation_hook_reached.sh arm 1, s138a (DDAEDE2AE6EF6DA6E290F29) and s141b (06AC7CB42624D7E279F66AF), kernel 6.8.0-101-generic, 2/tcp: P312-IOMAP-REVALIDATED fired on an ordinary 64 MiB buffered write. (c) The case the hook exists for: arm 2 (s141b, tests/evidence/20260922T012241Z_iomapreval_s141b, console tests/evidence/lapq_s141_2.console) ran one 256 MiB write() with a second thread fsyncing the same file continuously (4 fsyncs raced it), the schedule having first been proven to make a cached mapping stale on native 6.8 XFS (tests/iomap_stale_loop_control.sh s140x: xfs_iomap_invalid fired 12 times): MXFS's hook refused 3 stale mappings (P312-IOMAP-STALE ino=132 at pos 0, 37617664 and 56623104, cookie 0x1->0x2, 0x5->0x7, 0x9->0xb), the write completed rc=0, and after unmount and remount every one of the 65536 pages read back cold with its own stamp (CHECKED=65536 BAD=0). No BUG or Oops. RESULT PASS fails=0 on both arms.
- **On a lazytime mount xfs_vn_update_time defers the timestamp by setting I_DIRTY_TIME and returning 0. The hook that is supposed to persist it later does not exist on this build: the fork carries the 6.19+ replacement (inode_operations.sync_lazytime), version-gated out, and dropped the hook this kernel actually has (super_operations.dirty_inode) with it.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED. Two faults, both read in the source and both fixed in 0.89.63: (1) the completion hook this kernel has, super_operations->dirty_inode, was installed in 0.89.60 but with the pre-5.12 guard 'flags != I_DIRTY_SYNC || !(i_state & I_DIRTY_TIME)', which is false on every call since 5.12 because __mark_inode_dirty clears I_DIRTY_TIME from i_state and passes it in flags (fs/fs-writeback.c, unchanged on 6.8) — the guard is now 'flags != (I_DIRTY_SYNC | I_DIRTY_TIME)'; (2) the deferral branch itself recursed and panicked the node before the completion could be measured (the record above, fixed in the same version). Verified live by the lap this record specified, tests/lazytime_timestamp_durability.sh s141a, build 06AC7CB42624D7E279F66AF, kernel 6.8.0-101-generic, 2/tcp (tests/evidence/20260922T012118Z_lazyts_s141a, console tests/evidence/lapq_s141_1.console): control arm (no lazytime) base=1790040137 incore=1790040139 after_remount=1790040139; subject arm (lazytime, confirmed in /proc/mounts) base=1790040149 incore=1790040152 after_remount=1790040152 — the acknowledged timestamp survived the unmount and remount on the lazytime mount, which before the fix it could not (the write is an in-place overwrite of allocated blocks so nothing else carries the inode core to the platter). RESULT PASS fails=0.

**Every one of the four s138 laps left unadjudicated by 0.89.61 was a harness
fault, and each is fixed at its cause.** The module is unchanged.

- `tests/lazytime_timestamp_durability.sh:116` died on `arm: unbound
  variable` because `local arm=$1 opts=$2 f=$MNT/lazyts_${LABEL}_${arm}` expands
  every word before any assignment lands, so `$arm` read the caller's unset
  one. Split into two statements.
- `tests/fence_live_prover_faults.sh` graded mode 4 (uncertain) against
  `command_may_have_run=no`, the line modes 1-3 log. Mode 4's whole design is
  that the prover CANNOT say that — the boundary is armed, the response is a
  timeout — and the module says so with `P238-FENCE-UNPROVEN ...
  phase=MAY_HAVE_SUBMITTED command_may_have_run=YES`, which is exactly what
  s138j logged. The assertion graded the inverse of the design. Mode 4 now
  requires that line and requires that the attempt was NOT put on the
  automatic retry series (`P238-FENCE-PENDING` = 0 after the injection).
- `tests/parked_log_waiter_across_closure.sh` (s138e, s138f) ABORTed because
  `PLW-MARK-<label>` was no longer in test1's 1 MiB ring by the end-of-lap
  window: the filler's ~8000 transactions log it out. `tests/lib/rig.sh` gains
  `kmsg_follow_start` (write the mark, start `dmesg --follow` into a file on
  the node, verify the mark is in the file) and `window_into` takes an optional
  node-side file to window from instead of the ring, mark guard unchanged. The

- `tests/admitted_write_parked_across_unmount.sh` (s138l, SITE=log) was
  graded VACUOUS at R1 by the slice arm's guard — "the nonce is already on the
  platter, so nothing was held across the publication" — on a lap whose
  `order=vfs-busy` meant there had been no publication for R1 to be after.
  Under `barrier` the nonce at R1 is likewise what the order means. The guard
  now applies to `order=overlap` only, which is the only order it is about.

All four are re-run as the s140 queue (`tests/evidence/lapq_s140.queue`).

- **The authority gate's buffered-data arm (site 'data') is not wired into the writeback hook this kernel uses, so it is compiled out entirely and buffered writeback is never gated. pal/linux/xfs_aops.c placed the gate in xfs_writeback_submit, which is only referenced by the 6.17+ xfs_writeback_ops; the module is built for 6.8.0-101-generic, which takes the pre-6.17 ops struct (map_blocks / prepare_ioend / discard_folio). Nothing referenced xfs_writeback_submit, so the compiler dropped the function and with it the only place the 'data' class is ever asked whether this incarnation still holds authority.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED. Cause (proven from the object: nm showed pal/linux/xfs_aops.o with no writeback_submit symbol and no reference to mxfs_mount_write_admitted): the gate's data arm sat only in xfs_writeback_submit, which the 6.8 build never references, so the compiler dropped it. Fix (0.89.59): mxfs_ioend_write_admitted() lifted out of the version split and called from xfs_prepare_ioend on pre-6.17 (returning -EIO, iomap's own fail-this-ioend path) and from xfs_writeback_submit on 6.17+. Verified on build DDAEDE2AE6EF6DA6E290F29 (0.89.60), kernel 6.8.0-101-generic, 2/tcp: strings -a mxfs.ko now carries P290-AUTH-REFUSED-DATA once (was 0).
