## 2026-09-22 — 0.89.61 — a lap that graded holes as lost data, and the instruments that told the difference

**The s138 queue's lap 3 FAILed the delalloc dirty-tail check with every
mmap-dirtied page below a moving boundary reading back zero after a remount.
That was not the filesystem.** Native 6.8 XFS, same reproducer, same kernel,
produced the identical verdict on a loop device (`tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_loop_control.sh`
s139a/b: pages 1..19 and 1..13 "lost"), which ruled the fork's shim out before
a line of it was re-read.

**How the loss was followed to its source, since reading found nothing.**
`tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_trace.sh` ran one closing pass under the kernel's
xfs/iomap/filemap tracepoints and `tests/ddtt_follow.py` followed the lost
byte range through it: the first 256 KiB folio was written back once, at the
end of the pass, by the msync. `tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_kprobe.sh` then put
kprobes on `ifs_alloc`, `ifs_set_range_dirty`, `ifs_clear_range_dirty`,
`iomap_dirty_folio`, `__iomap_write_begin`, `iomap_write_end`,
`folio_clear_dirty_for_io`, `iomap_do_writepage`, `iomap_writepage_map`,
`iomap_add_to_ioend` and `folio_end_writeback`, reading the folio's per-block
uptodate and dirty bitmaps at each one: every block of that folio was dirty
going into writeback and every block was added to the ioend and written
(`tests/ddtk_story_summary.py` condenses the story). So the zeros were in the
page cache at submission. The reproducer then stamped its own progress into
the same trace ring: its first store of the closing pass was at page 4039 —
the toucher was still finishing the previous pass's last window at the far end
of the file, and by the time it re-read the writer's position the writer was
at page N. **The odd pages below N were never stored to in the closing pass.
They are the holes the punch left, and the oracle expected data in them.**
Every "lost" set in every run — 1..9, 1..13, 1..23 — ends exactly where the
writer was when the toucher caught up.

**The fix is to the oracle.** `tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_race.c` now records,
page by page, which odd pages the toucher stored to during the closing pass and
writes that manifest beside the data file; `tests/ddtr_verify.py` checks every
even page and only the odd pages the manifest marks, and reports the rest as
`UNTOUCHED`. It also grew an optional live checker (`check`) that `pread`s the
manifest's pages during the pass and marks the kernel trace the instant one
reads back wrong. With the manifest, native XFS passes 3/3 (s139h1-3;
`UNTOUCHED` 7, 0, 3 — the old oracle's "lost" pages) and the 2-node MXFS lap
passes twice (s139j, s139k: P313-DELALLOC-KEEP ×60, 2001 and 2002 toucher pages
verified on the platter, 0 lost).

- **On kernels below 6.12 the compat macro for iomap_write_delalloc_release() punches the ENTIRE unwritten range of a short buffered write in one blind call, with no page-cache scan. Upstream's function exists precisely to skip the sub-ranges that still hold dirty folios; the shim keeps none of that.** — FIXED AND VERIFIED. Cause: the pre-0.89.60 compat macro for iomap_write_delalloc_release punched the whole tail blind; 0.89.60 replaced it with upstream's page-cache scan (xfs/xfs_platform.h) and the P313-DELALLOC-KEEP probe at the keep decision. Verified live on the 2-node TCP rig, 0.89.60 module DDAEDE2AE6EF6DA6E290F29, tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_durability.sh s139j and s139k (tests/evidence/20260922T002956Z_ddtr_s139j, 20260922T003239Z_ddtr_s139k): the scan took the KEEP decision 60 times per run under the deterministic short-write/mmap race, and after unmount+remount 2001 and 2002 mmap-dirtied pages plus every write()-page read back correct, 0 lost. The s138b2 FAIL that preceded this was the reproducer's oracle: it assumed the toucher stores every odd page in the closing pass; the toucher lags the writer at the pass restart and the pages below where it catches up are holes, not lost data. Native 6.8 XFS reproduced the identical false verdict (s139a,b,d-g), kprobes on the folio's per-block state showed every block dirty, submitted and written, and the reproducer's own trace marker showed its first closing-pass store at page 4039. The reproducer now writes a manifest of stored pages and tests/ddtr_verify.py checks against it; with it native XFS passes 3/3 (s139h1-3).

**Two things learned about the rig on the way, recorded so they are not
re-learned.** A loop device cannot host a single-node MXFS mount on 0.89.60
even on the TCP transport: admission needs `fence_capability_override=1` AND
`single_node_exclusive=1` together, and then the page-authority ledger writes
its records with COMPARE AND WRITE, which a loop device does not have
(`P304-CAS-NOCAW`, rc=-95); the first inode lock fails and the mount shuts
itself down. The MXFS side of a single-node question is answered on the real
LUN. And on 6.8 `DELAYSTARTBLOCK` is -1 and `HOLESTARTBLOCK` is -2 in the
`xfs_iomap_found` tracepoint's `startblock` field, not the other way round.

**The rest of the s138 queue** (14 laps, 8 PASS): lap 2 died on an unbound
variable in `tests/lazytime_timestamp_durability.sh:116`; laps 6 and 7 ABORTed
because `PLW-MARK-<label>` was no longer in test1's ring by the time the window
was read (the filler's log volume wraps it); lap 11 (fence live-prover mode 4)
FAILed one assertion; lap 13 (SITE=log unmount) was VACUOUS at `order=vfs-busy`.
None of those is adjudicated here.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.60 — three more things the compiler had already deleted, and the sweep that found them without relinking

**Last version found two branches gcc could prove unreachable. This one asked
the same question of all 131 objects and got three more answers.**

`tools/warn_sweep.sh` is new and exists because the obvious way to ask — build
the tree with `-Wextra` — could not be used. Changing `KCFLAGS` changes every
recorded compile command, so it rebuilds all 131 objects and **relinks
`mxfs.ko`**; a relink while a lap queue is running deploys a different module to
the remaining laps and splits the sweep across two srcversions. Instead the tool
replays each object's own recorded command out of its `.cmd` file, with the
warning flags appended and `-o /dev/null`, so nothing in the tree moves:

    tools/warn_sweep.sh                    # all 131, ~85 s, safe against a live rig
    WARN_FLAGS="-Wtype-limits" tools/warn_sweep.sh

It exits 1 if any `comparison is always true/false` survives, because that class
has now produced two shipped defects.

**The `-Wtype-limits` sweep is complete and its remainder is clean.** All 131
objects, 20 sites, and every one of them is the same benign shape: a
`uint8_t namelen` tested against `MAXNAMELEN` (255), where the type already
enforces the bound and the genuinely invalid value (`0`) is still checked
beside it. Recorded here so the next reader does not re-derive it.

**The `defined but not used` remainder, likewise adjudicated so it is not
re-chased.** After the three fixes below, seven names remain and none is a
defect:

| name | why it is not one |
|---|---|
| `xfs_fs_report_error` | `super_operations.report_error` is a 6.19 hook with no older equivalent, and upstream's only caller of `xfs_healthmon_report_file_ioerror` is this function. Health telemetry for file I/O errors is a facility this kernel does not have — a gap, not a violation of correctness, durability or safety. |
| `caw_unlk_delta_is_registration` | a thin wrapper over `caw_unlk_delta_classify`, which is called; CAW-only either way |
| `out` (`v5_mount.c:5184`) | a dead label, not a function |
| `xfs_inobt_first_free_inode` | inherited libxfs helper |
| `mxfs_ilk_dump_stuck`, `mxfs_dir3_data_superset` | uncalled diagnostics/helpers |
| `_mxfs_ioend_bioset_compat` | compat object, deliberately spare |

Two locals also read `set but not used` — `merge_ours_bytes` and `b_need_adopt`
in `mxfs_dlm_reload_inode_under()`. Both were traced: the declaration comment
claims `b_need_adopt` "feeds the install-point stamp", but both stamp sites sit
on paths where the adopt (or the final keep decision) has already been
committed, so nothing needs to consult it. The comment is stale; no decision was
dropped.

**A third sweep, for copy-paste guards, found nothing and is recorded so it is
not repeated.** `WARN_FLAGS="-Wduplicated-cond -Wduplicated-branches
-Wlogical-op"` over all 131 objects: 25 sites, no defect. The `-Wlogical-op`
hits are all either `ret == -EAGAIN || ret == -EWOULDBLOCK` (the two are the
same value on Linux, and writing both is the idiom), a bound tested against two
macros that happen to be equal (`slot < MXFS_DISKLOCK_HB_SLOTS && slot < 64`),
or a defensive `!node || node == MXFS_RECOV_OWNER_NONE` where the sentinel is
zero. The identical-branch hits are inherited upstream code, except one worth
naming because it is a latent slip rather than an idiom:
`dlm/bootstrap.c:275` logs `P-BOOT-CLAIM` with
`mxfs_pal_log(rc ? MXFS_LOG_WARN : MXFS_LOG_WARN, …)`, so a *successful* boot
claim is logged at WARN. It is a log level and nothing else — left alone
deliberately rather than churned mid-campaign.

---

### Buffered writes never revalidated their mapping

`xfs_iomap_valid()` was written, correct, and referenced by nothing:

    pal/linux/xfs_iomap.c:77: warning: ‘xfs_iomap_valid’ defined but not used

It was installed only in `xfs_iomap_write_ops`, which is a **6.15-and-later**
mechanism. Below that, `xfs_platform.h` supplies a compat `struct
iomap_write_ops` purely so the fork compiles, and the macro that calls
`iomap_file_buffered_write()` expands the argument away, because the older
prototype has nowhere to put it:

    #define mxfs_iomap_file_buffered_write(iocb, from, ops, wops, priv) \
            iomap_file_buffered_write(iocb, from, ops)

The hook this kernel consults is `iomap->folio_ops->iomap_valid`, and
`grep -rn folio_ops pal/ xfs/ include/` found **zero** matches in the tree. So
the mapping-revalidation check did not exist on this build, while
`iomap->validity_cookie` — the sequence number that check compares against —
was stamped on every mapping `xfs_bmbt_to_iomap()` returned and read by nobody.

Upstream added that check mid-cycle because a cached iomap goes stale under a
long-running buffered write when writeback converts the delalloc extent beneath
it. MXFS widens that window rather than narrowing it: a peer node's activity
changes this inode's extent map too.

`xfs_bmbt_to_iomap()` now sets `iomap->folio_ops` beside the cookie, so both
halves of the mechanism travel with the mapping or neither does.

### The delalloc release shim punched out from under dirty folios

    pal/linux/xfs_iomap.c:2251: warning: the address of
        ‘xfs_buffered_write_delalloc_punch’ will always evaluate as ‘true’

That `if (punch)` is inside the compat macro, and reading the macro is what
exposed the rest of it:

    #define iomap_write_delalloc_release(inode, start, end, flags, iomap, punch) \
            do { if (punch) (punch)(inode, start, (end) - (start), iomap); } while (0)

It punched the entire unwritten tail of a short write in one blind call.
Upstream's function exists precisely to *not* do that — its own comment says to
punch everything in the range "except for those that have dirty data still
pending in the page cache - those are going to be written and so must still
retain the delalloc backing for writeback", and, on why the lock is held, that
failing to do this "can leave dirty pages with no space reservation in the
cache." The shim produced that state by construction rather than by racing.

Every other guard was faithful — `IOMAP_DELALLOC`, `IOMAP_F_NEW`, the
`IOMAP_FAULT` early return, `iomap_last_written_block`, the `invalidate_lock`.
The scan itself was the single missing piece, and it is now backported into the
shim, with two deliberate differences stated in the code: the outer
`mapping_seek_hole_data()` loop is gone (it is an optimisation, it is not
exported to modules, and the scan already steps over an absent folio a page at a
time), and the sub-folio pass that punches clean blocks *inside* a dirty folio
is gone (it reads iomap's private folio state, which a module cannot reach;
keeping the reservation spends space and never loses data, and it is what
upstream itself did before that refinement existed).

Routing to the kernel's own `iomap_file_buffered_write_punch_delalloc()` — which
6.8 exports and which does all of this correctly — was rejected: it takes
`invalidate_lock` itself and the caller already holds it on one of its two arms,
and its three-argument punch cannot carry the `iomap` this fork's punch
dereferences for the COW-fork choice.

### A lazytime mount accepted timestamps and then never wrote them

    pal/linux/xfs_iops.c:1638: warning: ‘xfs_vn_sync_lazytime’ defined but not used

— in a file containing **four** `.sync_lazytime = xfs_vn_sync_lazytime`
initialisers, all four inside `#if LINUX_VERSION_CODE >= KERNEL_VERSION(6, 19, 0)`.

`xfs_vn_update_time()` defers on a lazytime mount deliberately: it marks the
inode `I_DIRTY_TIME` and returns 0 without logging anything. Something has to
come back later and write it, and which hook the VFS calls for that moved in
6.19 — `inode_operations->sync_lazytime` replaced
`super_operations->dirty_inode`. The VFS says so itself:

    if (sb->s_op->dirty_inode) {
            sb->s_op->dirty_inode(inode, ...);
    } else if (was_dirty_time && inode->i_op->sync_lazytime) {
            inode->i_op->sync_lazytime(inode);
    }

The fork carried the newer hook and dropped the older one with it —
`grep -rn dirty_inode pal/ xfs/` returned zero matches in the whole tree. So
below 6.19 the deferral had no completion path at all: not at writeback, not at
the last iput, not at sync, not at unmount. The update was acknowledged and
lost.

`xfs_super_operations` now carries a `.dirty_inode` below 6.19 with upstream's
two guards, calling through to `xfs_vn_sync_lazytime()` so the transaction that
persists a lazytime timestamp is written once whichever hook the running kernel
offers.

---

### Three harnesses that were grading the module on their own defects

**The fence live-prover modes 1 and 2 FAILed four assertions each, and the
module was right every time.** They asserted, of a capture taken ~20 s after the
injection, that the victim's key was still registered, that the PR generation
had not moved, that no preempt-and-abort had completed and that no durable
marker said a command may have run. But the module logs, at the injection,
`retry=automatic next_retry_ms=279` — and means it. Mode 1's own window shows
the whole sequence:

    +536.8  P-PR-FENCE-INJECT mode=1 ... nothing was consumed, safe to repeat
    +536.8  P238-FENCE-PENDING ... command_may_have_run=no retry=automatic
    +537.3  P304-FENCE-ARM     ... the submission boundary is DURABLE
    +537.3  P-PR-FENCE preempt-and-aborted ... EXCLUSION PROVED
    +537.3  P236-FENCE-CERTIFIED ... kind=PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1

The retry armed its **own** boundary 531 ms after the injection and certified on
a real receipt. That is the behaviour the ruling asks for, graded FAIL because
the lap cannot outrun a 300 ms retry and was trying to. The assertions now ask
the **order of the module's own lines** — which no delay can erase: the injected
attempt must record that it consumed nothing, and any later completion must be
preceded by a fresh `P304-FENCE-ARM` rather than reusing the arm that was
injected. If the fence did *not* complete, the old "the target is untouched"
assertions still apply and still run.

**`mountpoint -q` was being used as a liveness probe on the one arm designed to
break it.** Mode 5 FAILed `the prover is still alive and mounted` with
`mounted=0`, while its own capture shows `P238-FENCE-BLOCKED-AMBIGUOUS` saying
in terms that "path operations that need those grants now fail fast (EIO)".
`mountpoint` stats the mount root, so the designed containment reads as an
unmounted filesystem. Mode 3 hit the same probe from the other side — the stat
*blocked*, burned the 20 s bound and ABORTed the lap before a single assertion
about the fault was reached. It now reads `/proc/mounts`, which the VFS answers
without touching the filesystem, and probes usability separately as a recorded
NOTE that distinguishes served / refused-fast / **blocked** — the third being
the one worth chasing. This is the project's own standing rule, written down
after `mountpoint -q` read a working quarantine as an unmounted filesystem and
cost six FAILs in one run.

Dry-run against the banked captures, the rewritten assertions grade modes 1, 2
and 5 as PASS and let mode 3 reach its subject. That is a check of the logic,
not a result; the laps are queued.

**And one assertion that could not fail.**
`tests/incarnation_mismatch_probe.sh:476` asserted that
`P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED` never fires. That probe sits below the retirement
return in `mxfs_disklock_recovery_begin` and is not in `mxfs.ko` at all, so the
assertion passed for free — silently, in the direction of good news. It now asks
the module whether the probe exists and, when it does not, prints
`NOT-MEASURED` and says the question is unanswered instead of banking a pass.
The same line's sibling patterns dropped `P234-RECOV-FENCED`, which comes from
the same retired function; the three `P236-FENCE-*` names beside it are live, so
those counts still move.

A line-by-line pass over all six harnesses named in the ledger record found this
is the *only* assertion of the seventeen that an absent probe makes vacuous —
the rest are printed censuses, collection filters and comments, and the two
budget-based verdicts (`hotslot_contention`, `mass_umount_stall_probe`) never
read the probe count at all.

---

**What is verified and what is not.** All three fixes are compile-verified the
same way the defects were found: the whole tree replays clean with zero errors,
and each warning that named the defect is gone — which is what says the code is
in the object rather than only in the source.

**And the module now carries them.** The probe gate was run against the old
module first, deliberately, as the positive control — it has to be able to fail
before a pass from it means anything:

                                 before        after
    P290-AUTH-REFUSED-DATA       MISSING   ->  in mxfs.ko
    P302-FUA-READ-DEADLINE       MISSING   ->  in mxfs.ko
    P15H-STRANDED-RELEASE        MISSING   ->  in mxfs.ko
    P312-IOMAP-REVALIDATED       MISSING   ->  in mxfs.ko
    P313-DELALLOC-KEEP           MISSING   ->  in mxfs.ko

`srcversion F3199FE2112E215C2FBB787 -> DDAEDE2AE6EF6DA6E290F29`. Five branches
the compiler had proved unreachable are now in the thing the nodes load.

**That is not the same as being reached.** A referenced function is still not a
called one, and none of the three has been reproduced live. Each record names
the lap that owes it, and all three laps are new in this version —
`tests/iomap_revalidation_hook_reached.sh`,
`tests/lazytime_timestamp_durability.sh` and
`tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_durability.sh` with its reproducer
`tests/delalloc_dirty_tail_race.c`. Each one refuses to run if the probe it
grades on is not a string in `mxfs.ko`, and the delalloc lap reports VACUOUS
rather than PASS if its subject never occurred.

The rebuild waited: an eleven-lap queue was still running on
`F3199FE2112E215C2FBB787` when this work started, and relinking mid-queue would
have deployed a different module to the remaining laps.
`tools/rebuild_after_queue.sh` is new and is why the wait cost nothing — it
derives its own bound from the sum of the queue's unfinished laps, so a queue
that overruns that is reported as stuck rather than waited on forever.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.59 — a gate arm the compiler deleted, and a lap that drove one class of write through another class's syscall

**Four of the authority gate's five arms were in the module. The fifth was not
in it at all.**

`mxfs_mount_write_admitted()` is what a mutating submission asks before it
reaches the shared LUN, and it has five call sites, one per class: the iclog
write (`log`), direct I/O (`dio`, `dio-zoned`), metadata buffers (`meta`), and
buffered writeback's ioend (`data`). The `data` site lived in
`xfs_writeback_submit()` in `pal/linux/xfs_aops.c` — a function referenced only
by the **6.17-and-later** `iomap_writeback_ops`. This module is built for
`6.8.0-101-generic`, which takes the other arm of the version split, whose ops
struct is `map_blocks` / `prepare_ioend` / `discard_folio`. Nothing referenced
`xfs_writeback_submit`, so the compiler dropped it, and the gate's buffered-data
arm was not merely unreached — it was absent:

    strings -a mxfs.ko | grep -c P290-AUTH-REFUSED-DATA     -> 0
    strings -a mxfs.ko | grep -c P290-AUTH-REFUSED-LOG      -> 1
    strings -a mxfs.ko | grep -c P290-AUTH-REFUSED-DIO      -> 1
    strings -a mxfs.ko | grep -c P290-AUTH-REFUSED-META     -> 1

and `nm pal/linux/xfs_aops.o` listed no reference to `mxfs_mount_write_admitted`
whatsoever — that translation unit called the gate zero times.

What that means on a running cluster is that a node whose authority over the
shared LUN has closed still pushes its dirty pages to that LUN, with nothing
asking, including after a successor has begun replaying the dead incarnation's
journal slice. Every other class of write from that node is refused. This one
was never asked.

The rig had already been telling us. Lap `s132f`
(`admitted_write_parked_across_unmount`, `SITE=data`, 2/tcp) armed the
post-admission park for class `data`, ran a whole unmount, and reported
`P291-AUTH-TAIL tail_admit=1` for site `log` and not one `data` submission at
the gate before exiting VACUOUS. That was read as a harness that had failed to
produce its subject. It was the module reporting, accurately, that the subject
does not exist on this build.

The gate now lives above the version split as `mxfs_ioend_write_admitted()` and
both hooks call it: `xfs_prepare_ioend` before 6.17, returning `-EIO`, which is
iomap's own mechanism for "fail this ioend instead of submitting it" — the
folios are ended and `fsync` sees the error through the mapping's errseq — and
`xfs_writeback_submit` from 6.17, unchanged in behaviour. It is asked only when
the submission was going to happen anyway, so it can neither mask nor replace an
error already in flight. Whichever hook the kernel offers, the same question is
asked in it.

**A third deleted branch, and this one is TCP's only way out of a stranded DLM
grant.** Asking the compiler directly — ten decision-dense objects rebuilt with
`KCFLAGS="-Wtype-limits"`, a flag the ordinary build does not pass — produced
eighteen "comparison is always false due to limited range" warnings. Seventeen
are a `__u8 namelen` tested against `MAXNAMELEN` (256), where the guard's
`== 0` half still works and nothing is lost. The eighteenth is
`xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c:21294`:

    } else if (++ip->i_dlm_orphan_strikes >= 280) {

`i_dlm_orphan_strikes` was `uint8_t`. It promotes to at most 255, so the
escalation could never fire, and the compiler removed it — the built module
carries no `P15H-STRANDED-RELEASE` string at all, while its siblings
`P15H-PEER-STARVE-TIMEOUT` and `P15-REL-ABORT` from the same region are both
present.

The threshold had been deliberately raised from 4 to 280 in an earlier session,
on instrumented evidence that 4 was releasing grants a live consumer was still
mid-consuming. The field was not widened with it, so the change that was proven
necessary silently removed the mechanism it was tuning. The counter three lines
below it in the same struct, `i_dlm_p72_strikes`, is already `uint16_t` for a
threshold of exactly the same shape.

What makes this a TCP defect rather than a curiosity is the comment sitting
twenty lines below, which scopes the *other* escape deliberately: the wall-clock
strand timer is `CAW ONLY`, because on TCP a granted-but-unconsumed mirror is
legitimate for up to the 6 s `ACQUIRE_WAIT` retry gap and a sub-6 s force would
release a live-but-slow grant into a double-EX. "TCP keeps the same-gen
280-strike escape." It does not. On TCP there was no escape at all, and the
history recorded beside the mechanism says what that costs: every release
attempt aborting forever, a hot directory wedged 184 s across two holders with
PR waiters at `rc=-110` and a six-node shutdown cascade, and separately a peer
blocked 360 s that self-fenced with the DLM inode lock unrecoverable.

The field is `uint16_t`. Rebuilding that one object makes the warning disappear
and puts the probe back in the object — the compiler restoring a branch it had
proved unreachable is the before and after.

**Then the same question was asked of every other probe, and it found more.**
`tools/probe_audit.sh` is new: it compares the probe names written as string
literals in the kernel-built sources against `strings -a mxfs.ko`, prints the
`file:line` of every one that did not make it into the binary, and has a
`--gate` form that exits non-zero when a named probe is missing — which is what
a harness's build precondition should be asking. Of 1594 distinct probes in the
source, 1577 are in the module. **Eight of the seventeen absentees are counted
by six harnesses**, which means those harnesses have been grading on a line that
cannot be printed.

Seven of the eight have one cause. `mxfs_disklock_recovery_begin` was retired on
a design ruling — it logs `P238-RECOV-BEGIN-RETIRED` and returns `-EPROTO` at
the top — and the 185 lines after that `return` are unreachable, taking
`P234-RECOV-FENCED`, `-OWNED`, `-UNREADABLE`, `-BEGIN-FAIL`,
`P237-RECOV-INC-MISMATCH`, `-INC-UNOBSERVED` and `-SUPERSEDED` with them. The
retirement line itself is in the module, which is exactly what proves the
function compiles and the rest of it does not. Four harnesses are still asking
the retired function's questions. The module is right here and the harnesses are
wrong; the fix is to point them at the probes the live path emits, never to
re-enable dead code.

**The eighth absentee turned out to be the most interesting thing in this
version, and the compiler had been saying so all along.**
`P302-FUA-READ-DEADLINE` survives the preprocessor and is absent from both the
object and the assembly, while a sibling `pr_warn` from the same loop is present
in all three — and no `if(0)`, always-false local or false `#if` covers it. In
the assembly not just the string but the whole arm is gone: no `$-62` (the
`return -ETIME`), and not even `p_fuadl_n`, the static counter that ratelimits
the log line. GCC deletes `if (budget_ms < 0)` only when it has proved the value
cannot be negative.

It had. `mxfs_pal_io_budget_remaining_ms()` reported an exhausted per-task I/O
budget as `-1` — through a conditional whose other arm is `jiffies_to_msecs()`,
which returns `unsigned int`. The usual arithmetic conversions make the whole
conditional `unsigned int`, so the `-1` became `4294967295` before it was ever
widened into the function's `long`. The sentinel could not be represented, and
so it was never returned.

The damage is the exact inverse of the intent. At the moment the deadline has
passed, the caller sees ~49.7 days remaining, takes the `budget_ms > 0` branch,
and hands that number to `msecs_to_jiffies` as the per-command SCSI timeout —
the largest one the conversion can produce, with retries set to zero because the
deadline was supposed to be the only retry policy in play. Up to twenty-one
attempts, each timing out at a value that in practice never fires. The loop is
bounded by `fua_try >= 20`, which is the only reason this is not an infinite
wait.

The fix is `(d <= 0) ? -1L : (long)jiffies_to_msecs(d)`, and its verification is
the compiler again: recompiling that one object takes the probe count from 0 to
1, because the branch it had proved unreachable is reachable again. A sentinel
that cannot be represented is not a sentinel, and the same shape — a negative
literal sharing a conditional with an unsigned-returning kernel helper — is
worth sweeping for elsewhere.

Four further absentees are accounted for and are not defects, recorded so they
are not re-discovered as such: a deliberate `if (0 && ...)` with a comment
saying so; a local `bool` never assigned true, left behind when a broader
preventer superseded it; an uncalled static function; and a whole file that is
not in the Kbuild object list.

**A guard that cannot fail, because the thing it guards against contains its own
name.** `tests/parked_log_waiter_across_closure.sh` marks the victim's kernel
log, later marks it again at the heartbeat park, and captures its window from
the first mark. `window_into` scopes that capture with `sed -n "/$MARK/,$p"` and
then checks `grep -F "$MARK"` — a guard whose entire purpose is to catch a mark
that was never written or whose ring has since wrapped. The second mark was
spelled as the first with `-PARK` glued on the end, so it *contained* the first,
and the guard matched it and passed.

On `s133b` the window therefore opened at the park mark, fifty-five seconds
after the arm. The pump-hold injector's own confirmation line fell outside it
and counted zero, so the subject arm failed its arming assertion for a reason
that had nothing to do with the pump — and the `P290-AUTH-CLOSED` count taken
from the same late window, on which the lap's whole "no closure happened"
verdict rested, is not established either.

The park mark now has a name that is not a superstring. The injector's
confirmation is read *at the arm*, under a 20 s bound — the pump ticks every
250 ms, so its line lands within seconds or not at all — and its absence is an
ABORT rather than a verdict, because an arm that cannot show it armed has
measured nothing. The end-of-lap count is demoted to corroboration, where a zero
means the ring no longer reaches back to the arm rather than that the pump was
running.

**And the control arm of the same pair was discarded on a measurement that was
never taken.** Its observer builds each count as
`$(grep -ac PAT FILE 2>/dev/null || echo 0)` — but `grep -c` prints `0` *and*
exits 1 when it matches nothing, so the `||` fires as well and the substitution
yields two zeros, which is an arithmetic syntax error. The `POKE_WINDOW` and
`FILL_WINDOW` lines were therefore never printed. `POKE_POST`, three lines away
and counting with `wc -l`, printed normally, and that contrast is what
identified it.

The verdict then read the absent filler-error delta through a `${FERRD:-0}`
default as "the filler completed further transactions without a single error"
and threw the lap away as a drain confound — while the window it was ignoring
showed the authority closing at 26 s, the withdrawal, the self-fence, the
shutdown, and both tasks released. A control arm that had done exactly what a
control must do was discarded because a number that was never measured defaulted
to the value that means "confounded".

The ten count sites now yield exactly one integer in all three cases (match, no
match, missing file), and the extraction refuses the lap outright if a delta is
absent or non-numeric, because every branch below it treats these as
measurements.

What the pair was trying to say, and can say once it has a window worth reading:
with the pump running the authority closed 26 s after the heartbeat park and the
parked filler was freed at the same instant; with the pump held nothing closed
in 120 s and the filler was still parked. If that survives, the withdrawal pump
is load-bearing for a task already asleep in a log wait, and the comment
claiming only the promptness of the withdrawal is lost is wrong.

**A second, independent reason the same class kept coming back vacuous.**
`tests/admitted_write_parked_across_fence.sh` chose its writer program from
`ORACLE`, and `ORACLE` collapses `dio` and `data` into `block` because both read
back from the same probe block on the platter. So `SITE=data` ran the
**O_DIRECT** writer, which enters the gate as the `dio` class and can never
reach buffered writeback's ioend. The `data` park could not fire however the
module behaved, which is what lap `s132e` reported: *no submission of class
'data' was admitted and parked within 60 s*. Where the write is read back from
and which class submits it are two different choices, and the harness now makes
them separately: `data` writes buffered and `fsync`s, which is also what keeps
the writer inside the submission while the park holds it. The control line now
names the operation it actually performed, so it cannot claim an O_DIRECT write
on a lap that issued a buffered one.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.58 — an injector that could not be told which victim it was for, and a lap that could not tell two opposite silences apart

**A node id does not fit in an `int`, and more than half of this rig's do not.**
`mxfs_node_id_t` is `uint32_t`, and `dlm/scsipr.c` declared the fence
injector's victim filter as a signed `int` module parameter. Writing a node id
above `INT_MAX` to it is refused by `kstrtoint` with `-ERANGE`, so the stored
value stays **0** — which is that knob's documented "apply to any victim"
value. The injector therefore degraded silently from the victim-filtered
one-shot the fence-matrix ruling requires into the global one-shot the same
ruling refuses, and it did so without a single line in the log.

Five laps of the live-prover fault matrix aborted on it before injecting
anything, at roughly nine minutes of fleet time each:

    FAIL A armed mode 1 for victim 2585738898 got=ARMED=1 victim=0
    FAIL A armed mode 2 for victim 2431490331 got=ARMED=2 victim=0

The mode parameter beside it read back correctly, which is what makes this
present as an arming bug in the harness rather than a type error in the module.
What caught it is that the arm step **writes the value and then reads it back
and compares** — an arm that only wrote would have run all five laps to a
verdict with the injector catching whichever fence attempt arrived first. The
parameter is now `uint` and its "unset" test is `!= 0` rather than `> 0`,
because the signed representation of a large id does land in an `int` and then
fails a `> 0` test, which is the same global one-shot with no error to notice.

**An empty list of failures is produced by two opposite states, and
`tests/parked_log_waiter_across_closure.sh` was reading it as one of them.** The
arm that holds the withdrawal pump off read zero authority closures and an
empty poker errno list, and reported that nothing had discovered the expiry.
But a poker that issued nothing because it had parked in the same log wait as
the filler, and a poker whose writes were still being **admitted** a hundred
seconds after its lease had expired, both produce exactly that: no errors. The
second is not a vacuous lap — it is the direct refutation of the argument the
withdrawal pump rests on, that every mutating submission refuses on its own. So
the observation window now carries the poker's completed-write count on each
side of the instant the lease had certainly expired, and the poker's own kernel
stack, and a poker still completing writes past that instant is graded as a
failure of the record rather than discarded as silence.

**The same lap was throwing away the subject it had successfully produced.** It
required `xfsaild` to log a hold on the pinned inode before it would grade
anything, and one arm produced the subject perfectly — the filler stopped dead
for twelve seconds with `xlog_grant_head_wait` on its own kernel stack — and
was discarded because that hold never appeared. It had not needed to: the
filler's own 8047 transactions filled the log before the pinned item ever
reached the tail, so the knob was never the thing holding it down. The pin is
one way of producing the subject, not the subject. What it was standing in for
is real and is now asserted directly where it belongs: a filler released by the
log draining rather than by the closure resumes with no error at all, while one
released by the shutdown the closure drives fails its next transaction, so the
release is attributed from the filler's own transaction errors and a lap that
cannot attribute it says so.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.55 — the fence faults a destroyed prover cannot produce, and the drain that was never there

**The six fence crash cuts all destroy the prover, and a whole class of the
matrix needs one that lives.** The banked ruling says so in its own words:
MAY_HAVE_SUBMITTED needs live-prover faults — a definite pre-command failure,
an uncertain submission, a successful target action with the response lost, an
arm CAS that fails or completes ambiguously. None of them is about what the
platter holds after a death; each is about what THIS prover does next with an
answer it cannot trust, and a destroyed prover does nothing next.

The ruling offered one way out: these may be omitted as crash laps once it is
established that pending I/O has drained before a successor acts. **That route
is closed, and the module says so itself.** The post-reset probe bound in
`dlm/scsipr.c` is written against exactly this: waiting a stranded command out
there "would be this barrier doing the pre-reset drain the design ruling
rejected". There is no drain to establish, so the faults have to be injected.

`mxfs.pr_fence_submit_inject` is read at the command-submission boundary inside
`mxfs_scsipr_fence_node()` — the one line in the tree that separates "nothing
was consumed, this is safe to repeat" from "something may have run". Five
modes: a definite pre-command failure; the arm refused; the arm LANDED and
reported as failed; armed with no command issued and a transport timeout
returned; and the command issued, completed at the target, its victim key
really consumed, and its successful response replaced with a timeout while the
prover stays alive. It is one-shot and filtered by victim node, because the
ruling refuses a global one-shot that can catch the wrong attempt. Nothing it
does changes what the target is asked to do except by not asking — only the
answer handed back is replaced.

**Two of the five can be armed into a no-op and they decline loudly rather than
report a substituted answer for a state that never existed.** If the arm
genuinely failed there is no landed arm whose answer can be made ambiguous; if
the real PREEMPT AND ABORT did not succeed there is no completed action whose
response can be lost. Both print `P-PR-FENCE-INJECT-VACUOUS` and let the true
outcome stand, and the lap reports VACUOUS instead of a verdict.

`tests/fence_live_prover_faults.sh` drives them. It refuses a destroyed victim
up front and says why: every mode sits at or after the submission boundary, and
a fence against a victim whose registration is already gone returns
KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN long before that boundary — on this rig a destroyed victim
loses its registration with its iSCSI session, so the injector would never be
reached and the lap would burn its whole budget to report VACUOUS. The sharpest
assertion is the one no crash cut can reach: after a completed command whose
response was lost, no certificate may claim PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN. Key absence
plus a higher PR generation is not a receipt for the command that produced it.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.54 — a queue that starts itself when the one before it finishes, and a running script that must not be touched

**The rig went idle between queues because nothing could launch the next one.**
The lap queue is serial by design — every lap re-preps the whole fleet and
several destroy and reboot a domain — so a second queue may not start until the
first has written its DONE line. Until now that line was read by a person, and
the gap between a queue finishing and the next one being launched was however
long it took someone to look. `tests/lap_queue_chain.sh` closes it: given the
running queue's log and the SUM OF THAT QUEUE'S OWN LAP BOUNDS, it validates
the next queue file up front, waits for a `QUEUE DONE` that is newer than the
newest `QUEUE START` (the log is append-only across runs of one label, so a
stale DONE would otherwise release it immediately into a running fleet), and
then execs the queue. Reaching the bound is a REFUSAL and never a start: the
fleet may still be in use, and two laps at once is the one thing every harness
in that directory is written on the assumption cannot happen.

**It is a new file rather than an option on `lap_queue.sh`, and that is the
point.** The chaining need arises exactly while a queue is RUNNING. Bash parses
a script one command at a time and returns to the file at a saved byte offset,
so inserting lines into a script an instance is executing shifts every later
offset and can make that instance resume mid-file. The option was written into
`lap_queue.sh` first, while it was 20 minutes into a 10-lap, ~3-hour queue; the
running instance was inside the lap loop and had not yet needed to re-read, so
reverting it byte-exactly cost nothing. Had it stood, the damage would have
surfaced three hours later as a queue that never printed `QUEUE DONE` — and a
chained successor that therefore never started. A new file cannot do that to a
running one.

**An apostrophe in a `${var:?message}` swallowed the next line.** The word after
`:?` goes through quote removal like any other word, so the `'` in "the running
queue's log" opened a quote that stayed open until the `'` in the NEXT line's
message closed it — consuming that line's assignment entirely. The script then
died on `AFTER_BOUND: unbound variable` two lines below an assignment the reader
can see. `bash -n` passes, because the quotes do balance eventually; the file
parses, just into something else. Both messages are reworded without
apostrophes, and the reason is written where the arguments are read so the next
edit does not reintroduce it.

**The s131 queue is chained behind s130 and holds the one 2/tcp blocker s130
does not touch** — both arms of `tests/parked_log_waiter_across_closure.sh`,
control and pump-held. Its `PUMP_HOLD_MS` is derived from the lap's own
post-arming timeline (585 s of budgeted work between the arm and the end of the
observation, covered at 700 s), because a hold that expired mid-observation
would let the pump resume, take the withdrawal and free the waiter — the one
reason the arm exists to exclude.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.49 — the partition arm was grading the inverse of the design

**The network-partition arm asserted that nobody may be fenced, against a
module that declares it will fence.** `mxfs.tcp_death_grace_ms` is a live
parameter and its meaning is explicit: a TCP peer that goes silent is SUSPECT,
and it is declared dead only if it fails to reconnect inside that grace. The
grace is 40 s. The arm held its partition for 120 s — three times the tolerance
the module promises — and then asserted zero certificates. It could only ever
assert the inverse of the design, and on its first run (s123a) it scored a
textbook-correct resolution as three FAILs: A preempt-and-aborted B at +40 s,
certified `LU_RESET_WITNESSED_V1`, sealed the manifest and replayed B's slice,
while B self-fenced on repeated RESERVATION CONFLICT and contained itself.
Every one of those is the behaviour the arm exists to require.

The arm now reads the grace off the running module — never a constant copied
into the harness, which would grade one build's behaviour against another
build's promise — and grades the partition it actually held against it. Inside
the grace, nobody may be fenced and B must be writing again after the heal.
Past it, exactly one side must fence the other and owes the whole chain: a
durable certificate, a sealed manifest, the victim's slice replayed to
completion, the victim silent. Neither shape may ever produce two certificates.
The grade is on the OBSERVED outcome and the grace decides which outcomes are
allowed, because the socket needs time to notice the block (12 s, measured) and
a partition close to the grace may legitimately resolve either way.

**A fence that is under way is not yet a certificate, and the arm was reading
its verdict at one fixed instant.** Measured s123a: the capture that concluded
"nobody fenced" ended 24 s BEFORE the certificate it was looking for. The
discriminator is now the START of a fence — the PREEMPT that proves exclusion,
or the durable intent — and once one is seen the partition is HELD while the
pipeline settles. The settle bound is what the pipeline is made of and not a
round number: the victim stops heartbeating once its own I/O bounces (~2 s),
the disklock dead window is 62 s, and the queue, fence, LU reset, certify and
seal took 5 s end to end. 69 s measured, 100 s bound. A settle that times out
is not a slow pass — it is a fence that proved exclusion and never became
durable, which the module's own certify-failure text calls unreplayable by
anyone. The arm's caller bound is re-derived to 900 s for the two bounded waits
it did not have before; it is not the same arm at a longer bound.

**A surviving iSCSI session does not make `iscsiadm -m node --login` a no-op.**
The storage arm assumed it did, in those words. It does not: with the session

login is now attempted only when the LUN does not already answer, every

paths was taken is printed.

**`tests/admitted_write_parked_across_fence.sh`** had two numbers that would
have bitten it on its first run. Its budget counted the wait for the
successor's recovery and the remainder of the hold as additive terms; they are

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.48 — the schedule the authority gate cannot see

**The gate has never been measured on the one ordering that matters, because
nothing could produce it.** Every authority lap in this tree parks a caller
BEFORE `mxfs_mount_write_admitted` and grades the refusal that follows. That
proves the gate refuses. It says nothing about an operation the gate ADMITTED
which had not yet reached the layer below it when a successor fenced this node
and began replaying its journal slice — and if such an operation can still
change what the successor recovered, no second check near the gate closes it,
because another check only moves the pause point.

**`mxfs.dbg_admit_park_site` + `mxfs.dbg_admit_park_ms`** (`pal/linux/xfs_super.c`)
hold the first submission of one named class between the gate's "yes" and the
caller's submission. The gate's answer is computed before the park and returned
after it unaltered: no decision changes, no refusal is removed. The selector is
a name rather than a blanket delay because the gate's five call sites are the
five classes of submission — `log`, `data`, `dio`, `dio-zoned`, `meta` — and
grading them together would make an unordered write indistinguishable from a
late completion of an ordered one. The site names are read from the call sites
themselves; the writeback arm passes `data`, not the `ioend` a reader would
guess. Trailing whitespace in the selector is ignored, because a charp module
parameter written from a shell keeps its newline and a plain comparison would
match nothing while the knob read back as armed.

**`tests/admitted_write_parked_across_fence.sh`** is the lap. B's O_DIRECT
write is admitted and parked FIRST; only then does B stop heartbeating, with
its periodic PR check and its periodic lease evaluation both held off so
nothing withdraws its mount. A declares B dead, fences it, certifies and
replays its slice. When the hold ends, the submission is handed to the block
layer by a node that believes nothing has happened, so the only thing left that
can keep it off the platter is the target's own exclusion.

The verdict is the platter and never the return code: the probe block's
physical extent is taken with FIEMAP while B is healthy, and the block is read
off the raw device with O_DIRECT immediately after A's recovery completes (R1),
after the parked writer returns (R2), and after A is unmounted and mounted
again (R3). R2 != R1 is an old-epoch write landing in a recovered region; R3 !=
R1 is the same arriving by a later replay, which an immediate byte comparison
cannot see. Both verdicts are that a block did NOT change, so a healthy
unfenced B runs the identical write first and MUST move it — a lap whose
control fails has measured its own plumbing and says so.

The journal and metadata arms are REFUSED by this harness rather than graded:
their submission lands in B's journal slice and in shared metadata, which the
probe block does not cover, and reporting "nothing changed" for a write that
landed somewhere the oracle does not look would be worse than not running.

published in exactly one place, on that function's single success return, so

  over a page its own node already owns, no judgement would be consulted, and a

  kernel's own line — not `fsfreeze`'s exit status, which is 0 for a freeze
  whose clustered cover then failed — and declares itself VACUOUS before
  anything is destroyed if it is missing.
- **The injector is the manifest snapshot, not the completion ladder.** Both
  park a descriptor below `IMAGES_REPLAYED`, but the completion ladder's
  failure ends at a deadline that WITHDRAWS the mount, and a withdrawn mount is
  shut down — so the final SB summary write takes its skip branch and never
  acquires the lock at all. `rman_inject=1` fails the prover's snapshot before
  the manifest write: the attempt parks at `SNAPSHOTTING`, the guard stands,
  and the prover's mount stays healthy, which is the only shape in which the
  non-fallible caller is reachable.
- **The unmount's kill bound is the instrument, not a budget.** Every other
  bound here is a performance assertion and reaching one is a failure. This one
  is different in kind: the thing being measured is a wait with no exit but a
  fatal signal, so the lap has to end it itself. It is derived from the
  property being asserted — the stall detector fires at 30 s and the stall must
  be seen twice with the caller still parked — rather than from patience, and
  reaching it is recorded as the defect it is. The parked task's kernel stack
  is captured WHILE it is parked, because after the kill there is nothing to
  read.

A lap where the guard does not stand below `IMAGES_REPLAYED`, or where the
unmount never meets a page in transition, is VACUOUS rather than a pass; and an
unmount that returns before the stall detector ever fired proves nothing about
a permanently refused page, so that is VACUOUS too. When the unmount has to be
killed the prover's domain is recycled on the way out, because a half-torn-down
mount with a DLM acquire parked underneath it is not something the next lap's
preparation can fix.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.46 — the partition and reconnect laps the crash matrix has never had, and the APTPL bit nobody had read

**The fence crash matrix's own ruling says killing both VMs exercises neither a
partition nor a reconnect.** Every lap the matrix has banked so far destroys
the prover while the victim is already down, so all of them grade a total
outage through the whole-cluster bootstrap owner. Three of the matrix's
remaining entries need something none of those laps can give: a prover that
stays ALIVE through the fence, the certification, the seal and the victim's
slice replay, and a victim whose path comes BACK afterwards.

**`tests/fence_partition_reconnect.sh`** is that lap, and it crashes nobody.
Its storage arm drops the victim's iSCSI portal traffic with node-local
iptables — nothing on this host and nothing on the target is touched, and an
exit trap flushes the rules on every path out, including an abort. On a target
that purges a dead session's registration the victim's key then leaves with the
PR generation unchanged, its heartbeat stops because it cannot write it, and
the survivor fences, certifies and replays.

Two things in it are there because the obvious version of the lap would have
lied:

- **The reconnect is driven, not awaited.** `iscsid` tears a dropped session
  down at `replacement_timeout` (120 s) and a partition held long enough to
  cover the 62 s dead window plus the fence is past that. A lap that only
  removed the iptables rules would read "the victim's key never came back" and
  score `iscsid` having given up as safety. So the login is issued explicitly,
  which of the two happened is recorded, and a path that does not come back is
  VACUOUS rather than a pass.
- **The write oracle is timed on completion, never on when the attempt
  started.** An `fsync` that begins before the fence and returns after it is a
  write from the fenced incarnation that landed; scored by its start stamp it
  would be filed on the safe side of the boundary, and with the path gone an
  attempt can block for the whole 180 s SCSI command timeout.

The reservation is sampled every two seconds across the whole lap from the
survivor, so a re-registration is observed as a transition rather than inferred
from two endpoint reads. The verdict on it is the ruling's: a registration
alone restores nothing under plain Write Exclusive, so what must not change is
the RESERVATION — no preempt, no release, no type change, no relaxation back to
all-registrants — and no write from the fenced incarnation may complete, before
or after the path returns.

**The network arm holds a DLM-port partition past the dead window**, which the
existing `fault_netpartition` deliberately never does (it holds 3 s, and says
why in its own header). Its assertions are the safety properties rather than a
prediction: the two nodes may not certify each other, and whichever way the
partition resolves, the loser owes the silence any fenced node owes.

**`tests/pr_aptpl_probe.sh` reads the bit the restart laps rest on.** Supported
and active are different bits and a target answers them separately: `PTPL_C`
says it can persist its PR database through a power loss, `PTPL_A` says a
registration actually turned that on. Capable-but-not-activated is scored FAIL,
not noted, because it is the configuration in which a target restart silently
unfences every victim this cluster ever proved. The probe issues PR IN commands
only — report capabilities, read keys, read reservation — plus an inquiry for
the target's identity, so it is safe against a live mounted cluster and is the
prerequisite of the restart laps rather than one of them.

`tests/fence_partition_sweep.sh` drives the three arms in order under the
bounds each harness derives in its own header. None of them has run yet.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.45 — a standing fence intent made the filesystem unmountable, and the crash cuts were graded against two routes the code no longer takes

**A total outage with a fencing intent standing left no node able to mount at
all.** The whole-cluster bootstrap is the only route to a mount after a total
outage, and it refused: `P-BOOT-KEY-UNCLASSIFIED 1 victim record(s) carry no
identity block — a victim without a key cannot be fenced; bootstrap refused`,
then `P-BOOT-MOUNT-REFUSED rc=-1` and `MXFS DLM init failed — aborting mount of
cluster (envelope) volume`. `MOUNT_RC=32` after 64.6 s on every attempt, both
dead nodes' slices unreplayed on the platter, and the 64 files the victim had
fsynced before its death coming back different.

**The identity block was intact; the CRC over it covers a field somebody else
is allowed to move.** `hb_ident_crc()` mixes `hb->flags` into the identity CRC,
and the writer that installs a fencing intent moves the victim's record to
`RECOVERY_GUARD` without re-binding it — only the retirement paths re-bind. So
the victim's own block, byte for byte what a fence of that victim needs, reads
invalid to the flags-strict `mxfs_hb_identity_valid()`. This exact failure was
found once before and closed by adding `mxfs_hb_guard_identity_valid()`, which
retries the CRC under the states the victim's own writer could have bound it to
— and that fix reached the admission reader only. Every other caller of the
strict predicate restricts `flags` to ACTIVE/WITHDRAWN/RETIRE_PENDING before
asking, so no guard record reaches them; the bootstrap scan takes guard records
as victims deliberately, which left it the one site that could be wrong, and it
was. Fixed by asking the guard-aware predicate there. Nothing is relaxed: slot,
fs_gen, node, epoch and the block itself are still checked, so a block copied
from another record or another incarnation still fails. The refusal also names
the slot and its identity fields now (`P-BOOT-SCAN-NOIDENT`) — the bare count it
printed before cost four laps of reading to attribute.

**Measured, six laps on 2/tcp then two confirming ones.** In sweep `s118d` at
0.89.44 the only variable was the victim slot's flags: cut 1 parks the prover
before the intent is durable, leaves the slot `ACTIVE`, reads `noident=0` and
passes in 612 s; cuts 2-6 park it after, leave `RECOVERY_GUARD`, and all five
read `noident=1` and refuse. With the fix (`s118e`, srcversion
`0EA704DBF87AFF66D6CA9DE`) cuts 2 and 3 both pass with zero failures: the mount
completes, both victims are certified, `P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE` for the
foreign-replayed victim, the adopted slice replayed and the bootstrap complete,
every file identical, no descriptor standing.

**The witnessed LU reset reaches the crash cuts, and it works.** Cut 1 had been
recorded as unrunnable on a target that purges a dead session's registration:
nothing is left for a PREEMPT AND ABORT to name, and the sole-survivor gate
proves admission only, so the attempt refused for want of a retirement basis.
Both victims are now certified `LU_RESET_WITNESSED_V1` on
`retire_basis=completed-target-op`, with the reset issued through the userspace
upcall, the target readmitting it with the PR generation unmoved, and the
post-reset authority barrier held. Neither `P238-GATE-NO-RETIRE-BASIS` nor
`P238-BOOTSUCC-NO-RETIRE-BASIS` ends an attempt: both refuse without touching
the verdict, so it stays `KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN` and falls through to the
witnessed-reset leg.

**The leg needs no caller-side guard against fencing a bystander, because the
storage layer refuses it first.** An LU-scope reset terminates the task set of
every I_T nexus attached to the unit, so "is anybody else using this LUN"
decides whether the operation is a fence or an attack. It is answered in
`mxfs_scsipr_lu_reset_admit` before anything is issued — exactly one
registration matching our own key, the victim's absent, and no third — and a
caller asking under any other census is refused by name. That is why the leg is
as safe from the boot-succession and self-succession fall-throughs as it is from
the gate.

**And the harness was grading two routes the code no longer takes.**

**The witnessed LU reset reaches the crash cuts, and it works.** Cut 1 of the
fence crash matrix (`tests/fence_crash_cuts.sh`, `VICTIM=destroy`) had been
recorded as unrunnable: on a target that purges a dead session's registration
there is no descriptor left for a PREEMPT AND ABORT to name, so the
sole-survivor gate proves admission and nothing else and the attempt refused
with no retirement basis. On 0.89.44 the same lap certifies BOTH victims
`LU_RESET_WITNESSED_V1` on `retire_basis=completed-target-op`, with the reset
issued through the userspace upcall, the target readmitting it with the PR
generation unmoved (`6301` before and after), the post-reset authority barrier
held, and every one of the 64 files the victim fsynced before its death back
byte-identical. Neither `P238-GATE-NO-RETIRE-BASIS` nor
`P238-BOOTSUCC-NO-RETIRE-BASIS` ends the attempt any more: both refuse without
touching the verdict, so it stays `KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN` and falls through to
the witnessed-reset leg.

**The leg needs no caller-side guard against fencing a bystander, because the
storage layer refuses it first.** An LU-scope reset terminates the task set of
every I_T nexus attached to the unit, so the question "is anybody else using
this LUN" decides whether the operation is a fence or an attack. It is answered
in `mxfs_scsipr_lu_reset_admit` before anything is issued — exactly one
registration matching our own key, the victim's absent, and no third — and a
caller that asks under any other census is refused by name
(`OTHER_REGISTRANT`, `MULTI_NEXUS`, `VICTIM_REGISTERED`). That is why the same
leg is safe from the boot-succession and self-succession fall-throughs as it is
from the gate.

**What actually failed the lap was the harness, twice, and both were
assertions measuring a route the code stopped taking.**

*The certificate kind.* The accepted set for a purged victim was
`BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT` or `EXCLUSIVE_WRITE_GATE` — written before kind 24
existed. `LU_RESET_WITNESSED_V1` is a proof of the successor's own term in the
strongest sense the set contains: the successor issues the command itself,
under its own term, and it is the only one of the three that establishes
retirement rather than only admission. What the assertion refuses has not
changed — a certificate that relabels the absence of the victim's key as a
proof — and a certificate naming kind 24 now has to carry its witness: the
reset issued, the target readmitted with the generation continuous, the
authority the replay runs under still live, and the verdict certified on a
completed target operation.

*A1's recovery.* The harness demanded `P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE` for the dead
prover's slice. Every cut destroys the prover while the victim is already down,
so the next mount finds a frozen table with two victims, declares a total
outage and comes up as the whole-cluster bootstrap owner — which ADOPTS one
certified victim's slot as its own log and replays it fully under authority
evaluation instead of foreign-replaying it. No `P163` is owed for that victim,
and demanding one failed a recovery that ran: `P-BOOT-ADOPT slot=0 … rc=0`,
`P-BOOT-ESCROW-K-REPLAY-OK`, `P-BOOT-RECOVERY-COMPLETE`, and the platter left
with no recovery descriptor standing. Adoption alone is still not recovery, so
the bootstrap branch requires the adoption, the adopted slice's replay coming
back OK, and the bootstrap reaching completion, all three — a lap that adopted
a slot and did not replay it fails exactly as before.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.44 — a terminal verdict is a finished judgement, so the survivor can leave

**A guard that protects a judgement has to notice when the judgement is
over.** A dead node's authority-ledger pages are held frozen while its
slice replay is still being judged: the replay compares committed images
against a manifest sealed at fence time, and retiring one of those records
early turns a healthy replay into "authority mutated after the seal" and a
terminal whole-filesystem quarantine. The predicate that decides this read
one thing — has the replay reached IMAGES_REPLAYED. A replay that ends in a
TERMINAL REFUSAL never does: it publishes the quarantine flag and leaves the
stage where it was. So the predicate answered "still judging" for the life
of the filesystem, and every page the victim had authored stayed frozen
forever.

**What that cost was a node that could not be unmounted.** On the two-node
TCP rig, ~250 pages per lap were refused, and a survivor whose `put_super`
needed one of them blocked in `dlm_takeover_page` until the harness
SIGKILLed it at 70 s, with the kernel's own "task umount blocked for more
than 60 seconds". A node that cannot unmount cannot be patched, rebooted
cleanly or removed from the cluster — and it cannot reach the documented way
out either, because `chk_mxfs --accept-quarantine-loss` refuses while any
other slot is still ACTIVE.

**The arms that hung and the arm that did not were doing the same thing.**
Two injected arms reached the identical terminal verdict; one hung on two
laps of two, the other unmounted in 2 s. Counting the refusal probe by the
path it names rather than by whether it fired: 260 pages refused in the
passing arm and zero on-demand refusals, against 250 and 237 pages in the
hanging arms plus 840 and 661 on-demand refusals concentrated on one page
each. The guard was armed identically everywhere. The only difference was
whether the unmount happened to need a page inside the victim's authored
set, which is luck, not a property.

**Retiring the records after a terminal verdict cannot cost a judgement,
and the code already knew it.** No further judgement of that slice is
reachable: recovery takeover and fence takeover both refuse a quarantined
descriptor, the replay-eligibility classifier refuses it by name, the
completion ladder is not re-armed, and the verdict is never rewritten. Nor
can a refusal leave a half-applied platter to walk into: a foreign-slice
replay defers every per-LSN drain and submits once at the end of the pass,
and a refusal fails that batch with no I/O at all — measured on the refusing
lap as `drain_deferred=66`, one `P227-FR-UNWIND`, thirty `P227-FR-BUFFAIL`,
zero images applied. And it cannot spoil another victim's manifest, because
the fence-time collection filters by the victim's own node, epoch and slot.
The takeover's own retirement step already had a branch for a terminally
refused owner, which keeps every record inside the quarantined domain and
re-imports it as a frozen blocker; that branch was simply unreachable from a
dead victim's takeover. The verification lap exercised it on 272 pages with
`cleared=0 kept=1` — nothing inside the domain was deleted.

`v5_recovery_judging_cb` now treats a published terminal verdict as a
completed judgement, in its marker arm and its platter arm alike, and says
so once per victim rather than once per page. What it deliberately does not
do is synthesize stage progress: the stage stays below IMAGES_REPLAYED, the
slice stays refused, the slot stays frozen until an operator accepts the
loss, and every gate that asks about the slice keeps reading the descriptor
rather than the ledger.

Measured on 0.89.44, srcversion 2350134021B88829F43134E, 2/tcp. The arm that
hung: PASS in 123 s, zero failures, umount rc=0 at 2 s, the superblock
summary lock GRANTED at `put_super` where it had never returned before, 272
victim-authored pages taken over, zero takeover refusals of either kind, and
zero "task umount blocked". The terminal verdict itself is unchanged —
`P241-RECOV-TERMINAL`, an FSWIDE quarantine imported, EIO inside the domain.
The other injected arm still PASSes in 124 s and the plain control in 120 s
with its replay complete. No shutdowns and no in-memory corruption on any
lap.

Two further laps of the arm that hung confirm it, on the same build: PASS in
226 s and 223 s, umount rc=0 at 4 s and 2 s, the summary lock granted at
`put_super` on both, 261 and 252 victim-authored pages retired with
`cleared=0` on every one of 526 and 677 page events, and zero takeover
refusals of either kind. Each of the three laps still reproduced the
defect's own setup rather than passing by avoiding it: the injector fired,
the replay refused the substituted image by name and failed with -117, and
the FSWIDE quarantine was imported. Three of three against two of two that
hung before.

The hang needed two conditions, and only the first of them is fixed here.
The second is still live and is now tracked on its own: the retry layer
detects a page transition that has stopped advancing and then, for a caller
its fallible-boundary oracle does not name, resets the stall clock and waits
again with no bound. The hanging laps logged that stall twice and still ran
to SIGKILL. Nothing reaches it today through the path measured above, but
`dlm_takeover_page` has other permanent refusals, and a caller parked behind
one of them has no exit but a fatal signal.

**Also: sshd answering is not boot finished, and the next lap paid for it.**
systemd keeps `/run/nologin` until the boot transaction completes, and its
banner landed in the captured output of the following `prep_cluster`'s
srcversion probe. Two preps of three reported `PREP FAIL: bad nodes:
test2(no usable srcversion — still booting?)` and `ABORT: cluster prep
failed` while both nodes were healthy on the right build, and the laps that
followed passed with zero failures. A prep that says FAIL about a healthy
cluster is how a real prep failure gets waved through, and it leaves the
next lap's build identity unverified. `tests/tcp_death_replay.sh` now waits
for the banner to clear, not just for sshd.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.43 — the replay guards are exercised, and they refuse

**A fault injector can be perfect and still measure nothing.** The two
knobs that substitute a value into the LOG copy of an inode-buffer image —
one plants an agino no allocation group contains, the other moves the
image's block so its cluster crosses an AG boundary — had never once
fired on a real image. Three separate things stood between them and the
guard they exist to reach, and each was found only by running the previous
fix and reading what came back.

**The workload logged nothing to substitute into.** The victim's arm
opened a file, unlinked it and closed the descriptor before moving to the
next one. A closed descriptor frees the inode immediately, so the AGI
unlinked bucket was empty again at every insert — and an empty-bucket
insert writes `NULLAGINO` over `NULLAGINO`, which upstream does not log at
all. Every image the injector was offered was declined "not an
inode-buffer image", because no inode-buffer image existed. The arm now
holds all seventeen descriptors open across every unlink, so each insert
after the first finds a non-empty bucket and logs a `di_next_unlinked`.

**The substituted image was carried past before the kill.** With the
first fix in, the substitution landed and the survivor still replayed to
completion: the whole foreign replay covered two checkpoints and nineteen
buffer images, and the injected block was not among them. Under the
writer's fsync stream xfsaild keeps the log tail within a couple of
checkpoints of the head, so the seconds between the unlinks and the
destroy are enough for the cluster buffer to be flushed and the record
carried past. The arm now pins the tail on one inode item first; the
replay window went to fifty-three checkpoints and four hundred and eleven
images, with the injected block in it.

**And then the relog erased it.** A buffer log item is re-formatted on
every relog, and each format replaces the log vector the one before it
built, so only the LAST format before the checkpoint reaches the log. The
substitution was landing on unlink fourteen of sixteen and being
overwritten by the two that followed. The knob is now armed between the
last two unlinks and the log forced immediately after, so the substituted
format is the one written. The cumulative dirty map means that last image
still carries every inode the run unlinked.

**With all three closed, both guards refuse by name and a healthy slice
still replays.** The wild agino is refused with "di_next_unlinked
2147483646 ... is not NULLAGINO and not a valid agino of AG 1", the
straddling cluster with "straddles an AG boundary; refusing to replay
it"; both fail the slice with `-117` rather than adopting the image, and
neither shuts the survivor's filesystem down. The straddle lap passes
outright in 124 s. The plain control lap replays to completion in 127 s —
and a control lap now explicitly disarms both injectors and the tail pin
on the victim before it starts, because a lap that aborts leaves them set
and the next control would silently inject while reading as a regression.

**One thing this uncovered is not fixed and is in the queue.** On the
agino arm the survivor keeps serving outside the quarantined domain and
never shuts down, but its unmount blocks in `put_super` waiting for an
authority-ledger page the dead victim wrote, and the guard that protects
a recovery victim's records until its replay passes judgement never
clears for a replay that terminally failed. Measured twice at seventy
seconds and killed both times.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.42 — an injector that declines says why

**A silent return was the whole measurement.** Both durable-write
injectors returned without a word from the test every image that is not an
inode buffer fails, so a lap could not tell "the injector was never
called" from "it was called on every image and rejected them all" — two
causes needing opposite fixes, reading identically as `fired=0
declined=0`. Every rejection path now names itself and prints what it
judged: the flags it saw, the logged range it searched, the block. The
next lap answered the question in one run.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.41 — the whole-cluster restart completes on 2-node TCP

**A wait bounded by a lease is unbounded for the one caller that holds no
lease.**  `mxfs_v5_dlm_lu_reset_barrier` asks whether this node's coordination
I/O converged after an LU-scope reset and whether it still holds the authority
it would replay under.  Both of its exits read state that a claimed heartbeat
slot produces: the disklock beat's timestamp, and the slot's authority lease.
A whole-cluster bootstrap owner has no slot by design — it fences at phase 3
before any claim — so its beat timestamp never advances, and its authority
object stays in the not-yet-admitted state, which reports authority as HELD so
that a mount still establishing itself is not refused.  A beat that cannot
advance and a gate that cannot close is a loop with no exit at all.  Measured
on 0.89.40: the owner's kernel log ends at the convergence call immediately
above the loop and has nothing for the remaining ~170 s of a six-minute
capture; the line the barrier writes unconditionally on BOTH outcomes never
appears, which is not ambiguous — it is the proof the loop never terminated.
The mount never returned, and the module could not be unloaded afterwards
because the owner's own record-heartbeat thread was still beating 988 s later.
An unreturnable mount is a release-bar violation in its own right.

**The fix keeps the barrier's shape and changes where it reads.**  The arm is
chosen by the thing that decides it — a slot.  With one, the disklock beat and
the authority lease answer as before.  Without one, the term is the authority
and the bootstrap record write is the beat: a real compare-and-write to the
same LUN through the same command path, so it converges the reset on exactly
the same argument.  The record's abandon window is the instant a peer may take
the term away, so it bounds the wait without inventing a number, and a term
that has already been taken over ends it at once.  Every record write now
stamps the instant it carried — the ISSUE time — so "issued after the reset
AND landed" is one comparison with no ambiguity about a write already in
flight.  Measured: the barrier holds in 1021 ms and 1028 ms on the two
victims, one refresh interval, with the beat landing 472 ms and 460 ms after
the reset was issued.

**The same owner was also sealing an empty manifest, for the same structural
reason.**  The fence-time manifest on TCP is collected from the durable
authority ledger, through a handle the mount opens with its {node,
incarnation, slot} after the claim.  A bootstrap owner has no such handle, so
every test that named it was false and the snapshot fell through to the arm
that records "this transport has no table" — after which the replayer answers
-ENODEV for every tokened image of the victim's dirty slice and the slice is
terminal.  That is the identical failure this function already records against
itself for the CAW transport in 0.47.0, arriving on TCP by the same route: the
only manifest source the transport has was reachable only through state the
claim creates.  The grants are on the platter either way, and the collector
reads every page fresh from both copies with no cache and no mastering,
because it is written for a prover that does not own the pages.  So the
snapshot now opens a handle on the region for its own duration and closes it:
it issues no transition, commits nothing, is never attached to the DLM, and
its slot is deliberately one no slot table can hold, because this owner has
none and recording a plausible number would be a claim we have not made.
Measured: 204 exclusive-holder entries collected per victim across 26426
pages, sealed with the ledger flag set and the empty-manifest flag clear,
where the previous build sealed zero.

**End to end on the configuration this project ships.**  Two nodes crash with
fsync-acknowledged payload in both journal slices and restart together, mounts
fired off one shared wall-clock epoch.  The term election serialises them; the
winner scans, seals, fences and certifies both victims through the witnessed
LU-reset route, adopts one certified slice as its own log, replays the other,
and publishes RECOVERY_COMPLETE in 148 s.  The loser is refused before it has
claimed a slot, started a journal or taken a grant, and mounts in 5 s on its
retry.  Both nodes then read 2/2 fsync-acknowledged payloads with the recorded
md5, and the filesystem checks clean.

**Two harness defects the lap exposed, both fixed rather than relaxed.**  The
concurrent arm asserted that all N mounts succeed in one attempt, which the
design never produces — exactly one mount can hold the term and every other is
refused by design and told to retry.  Dropping the assertion would have
stopped measuring the thing that matters, so the refused nodes are now retried
once, after the first round has fully returned, and a node that fails its
retry fails the lap.  And the arm's vacuity gate counted only the sole-member
fence gate, so it failed a lap that had fenced and certified both victims
through a route that never touches that gate; it now counts every route the
absent-key leg can take, and a lap that fenced nothing still has all four
counters at zero.  The owner's mount budget was re-derived from the parts it
actually pays rather than rounded.

**Recovery on a target that purges a dead node's registration is now verified
on both of its routes, and the defect it left open is disposed of.**  When the
appliance drops a power-cut node's PR registration with its iSCSI session —
this LUN does so 30-46 s after the cut, while death is not declared for ~66 s —
there is nothing left for a PREEMPT AND ABORT to name, so every fence attempt
classified KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN however often it was retried and the dead node's
journal slice could never be replayed.  On such a target that is *every* node
death.  The route out is one witnessed LOGICAL UNIT RESET, whose defined effect
is to terminate the tasks of every I_T nexus attached to the unit and so reaches
the victim's already-accepted writes whatever became of its registration.

The ordinary single-node death was the half still unmeasured, and it now
recovers completely: board row `crash_audit` PASS 130 s against its unchanged
300 s budget, the same row that failed at 196 s on 0.89.28 and produced the
defect's impact evidence.  The premise is proven rather than assumed — the
victim's key is logged absent before the fence begins — and the survivor then
admits the reset as sole registrant, issues exactly one, has it witnessed
(corroborated independently by the SCSI midlayer's own bus-device-reset
notification), holds the barrier on the disklock-slot arm, certifies with the
witnessed-LU-reset profile, and replays the slice 77 s after the kill.  All 263
fsync-acknowledged files read back at their recorded md5, and again after the
page cache is dropped; the namespace resolves, where the failing build returned
a stale file handle for the root inode and EIO for every sampled file; the
filesystem checks clean.  The barrier's own regression suite, unrun since the
arm selection changed, passes all four arms in 105 s against an 810 s budget —
including the one that must refuse: a reset issued and witnessed, the storage
half still converged, and the certificate refused at the barrier because the
authority lapsed, leaving a resumable durable intent and no proving kind.  That
separates an authority refusal from a storage check failing at the same instant,
which is the whole point of measuring it.

This says nothing about the crash-order matrix between issuing the command and
