recording its result; that remains open on its own record.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.40 — the whole-cluster bootstrap now runs on the shipping transport

**A recovery protocol had one call site, and it was in the other transport's
branch.**  `v5_bootstrap_run` — the total-outage path that detects a frozen
heartbeat table, elects a term owner, fences every dead incarnation, replays
their slices and adopts one as its own log — was reached only from the CAW
branch of `mxfs_v5_dlm_init`.  The TCP branch opened the same bootstrap record,
for an owner-liveness view, and went straight to the ordinary slot claim.  So on
2-node TCP, the configuration this project ships, a whole-cluster restart had no
recovery path at all: each returning node claimed an ordinary slot, saw the
other as a live member, and every fence of a dead incarnation was refused by the
sole-member guard.  Each node was the other's reason it could not certify, both
mounts were refused, and both journal slices were left unreplayed with
fsync-acknowledged data in them — permanently, by the kernel's own words.

**The fix is the call, and equally the position.**  It is placed where CAW has
it: after the slot limit is set and **before any ACTIVE claim**.  That ordering
is the whole safety argument.  A node that loses the term election is refused at
`P-BOOT-CLAIM-LOST` before it has claimed a slot, so it has started no journal,
taken no grant, and done no filesystem I/O; its mount simply fails and is
retried.  The invariant — once a term is claimed, no non-owner acquires
write-capable admission — comes from the sequence rather than from cleanup
timing, which is what makes it hold when the loser dies mid-unwind instead of
finishing it.  The lease is not created until after the claim either, so the
winner's fence sees itself as the only live member exactly as it does on CAW,
and the witnessed LU-reset route it needs is reachable.

**Why adopting a dead node's slot does not resurrect it in the TCP authority
ledger.**  The bootstrap takes a certified victim's slot K as its own log, and
TCP — unlike CAW — carries a durable authority ledger underneath.  A ledger
page's authority is keyed by `{auth_node, authority_epoch}` and every transition
must name that exact pair; nothing in the prepare/activate/purge path consults a
heartbeat slot, and the adopting mount opens the ledger under its own epoch,
with the victim's recorded separately in the escrow.  The one slot-indexed piece
of ledger state is the record-level shared-holder and open-holder bitmask, which
is a grant bit and not authority: a stale bit there fails closed — it refuses a
grant, it never double-grants — and the adopter clears its own on its first
exclusive grant of that resource.  The same exposure already exists for any slot
reuse after a total outage, including the sequential restart that recovers
today, so the concurrent path does not widen it.

**Also**: the TCP branch's comment saying the bootstrap record was opened "for
the owner-liveness view only" because "bootstrap is a CAW path" is gone, and the
non-fatal setup refusal now says what it costs — a volume provisioned without
the record still mounts, and `v5_bootstrap_run` logs `P-BOOT-SKIPPED` there, but
a total outage on it has no recovery path.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.39 — the whole-cluster restart has a concurrent schedule, and on TCP it has no recovery path at all

**A whole-cluster restart arm that brings the nodes back TOGETHER.**
`tests/bootstrap_full_restart.sh` has always measured a *sequential* restart:
one remounter comes back alone, recovers everything, and the other nodes are
admitted afterwards.  That schedule makes the remounter the only live member,
which is the exact precondition the sole-survivor fence leg requires, so it
could never reach the case where two nodes return at once.  `MXFS_CONCURRENT=1`
starts every node together, waits until all of them have ssh, `/src` and the
LUN, and then fires their mounts off one shared wall-clock epoch.

The arm reports `nlive` **as the kernel logged it** rather than as the schedule
intended, because two mounts that serialise anyway would answer a different
question while looking like this one: it measures each node's clock against the
host before trusting the shared instant (198 ms worst on this rig), records each
mount's start and return, and fails as VACUOUS if the mounts did not overlap or
if no node reached the absent-key leg.  Its payload changed for the same reason
— `sync -f` is syncfs and can leave a slice owing nothing, so each node writes
per-file fsync'd data plus 200 unsynced fsync'd creates and dies owing a replay.
It also no longer needs a host-side image of the LUN: the shipping appliance has
none, so the offline check runs through the node-side checker.

**What it measured.**  Both mounts overlapped 132 s and both were refused.  Each
node claimed an ordinary heartbeat slot, saw the other as a live member, and
every fence of a dead incarnation landed on `P238-FENCE-GATE-NOTSOLE nlive=2` —
21 times across the two nodes, with zero LU resets asked and zero certificates
minted.  Both slices went unreplayed through replay round 53, 54, 55 … until the
admission barrier's own `bound_ms=122000` expired.  Both nodes' fsync-acknowledged
files are in those slices, and the refusal is terminal by the kernel's own words.
Nothing crashed, hung or corrupted; the filesystem is simply unmountable, with
acknowledged data unreachable, and each node is the other's reason it cannot
certify.

**The cause, which the lap proves by what it does NOT contain.**  MXFS has a
whole-cluster bootstrap built for exactly this shape — survivor scan, term claim,
sealed victim manifest, fence and certify every victim, adopt one slot as its own
log, replay the rest, publish RECOVERY_COMPLETE, admit the others only then — and
it is a **CAW-only path**.  `v5_bootstrap_run` has one call site, in the CAW
branch before the ordinary slot claim; the TCP branch opens the bootstrap record
for an owner-liveness view and goes straight to claiming a slot.  The runner logs
a verdict on every path it can take, including the one silent early return, and
neither line appears in either node's capture: `P-BOOT-STATE IDLE`, then a claimed
slot 13 ms later.  So on the shipping transport there is no whole-cluster recovery
path, and a concurrent restart deadlocks symmetrically.

No fix is landed here.  The measurement, the cause and the reviewed fix direction
are on the record this blocks; what must be audited before any of it is wired is
whether adopting a victim's journal slot can resurrect that victim's shared
mastership in the TCP authority ledger, whose PR holders are slot-indexed where
its exclusive authority is keyed by node and incarnation.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.38 — two harnesses that measured a producer rather than the thing under test

**The metadata authority arm was counted against a clean AIL.**  The first lap
of that arm read zero post-detach metadata submissions, which says only that
the producer was empty: `tests/auth_lease_unmount_tail.sh` ends its
pre-workload with `sync -f`, and a clean AIL gives the teardown no metadata to
submit.  The unmount stage now stages dirty metadata in the SAME command as
the `umount`, so nothing pushes the AIL in between — 400 creates and 200
unlinks with no sync, leaving inode clusters, the AGI, the AGF and the
free-space btrees dirty at the detach.  The count is reported, not asserted;
what it buys is that a zero further down is about the gate.

Reading the teardown while wiring it found the actual reason, and it is not
the one that lap was read to show.  `put_super`'s final SB summary sync runs
`xfs_log_quiesce` **only when the cluster SB lock was granted**
(`pal/linux/xfs_super.c:1824`), and that quiesce pushes the AIL to empty
before the seal and before the detach at `:2430`.  So a refused lock leaves
MORE dirty at the detach, not less — the opposite of what was concluded from
`P-SB-SUMMARY-LOCK-FAIL` — and on an ordinary unmount the post-detach AIL push
in `xfs_unmountfs_finish` finds nothing however dirty the filesystem was.
Staging dirty metadata cannot reach that arm, because the quiesce drains
exactly what was staged.

So the harness gains `META=1`, which arms a producer that was already in the
tree under another record's name: `dbg_sb_late_dirty` logs the root inode core
*after* the seal and *after* the quiesce (`xfs_super.c:1885-1905`), so its
inode item is still in the AIL at the detach and `xfs_ail_push_all_sync`
submits its cluster buffer with `m_mxfs_dlm` already NULL.  The arm asserts the
injection fired before it asserts on anything it produced, and counts the
gate's lines from the lap's own kernel-log mark rather than the module-wide
total.

**Two measurement defects the arms exposed on their first run.**  The dmesg
mark was named for the label, so three arms run back to back under one label
shared a window across the module reload between them, and the gated arm
counted the blind arm's park, its injections and its blind line as its own.
The mark now names the lap.  And the gated arm asserted that the LOG write was
refused: with the late-dirty producer armed, `xfsaild` pushes inside
`xfs_unmount_flush_inodes`, which runs before `xfs_log_unmount`, so the
metadata arm refuses first and the log cover is never attempted.  That arm now
asserts the refusal it is actually asking about and prints both counts.

**A cut that ends by destroying both nodes left the next lap to pay for it.**
`tests/fence_crash_cuts.sh` waited for its nodes to boot but never started one
that was SHUT OFF, and cut 7 destroys both on purpose — the cold-restart
boundary is its subject.  The next lap then spent its whole 200 s boot-wait
polling a node nobody had asked to boot, and went into prep with it still
down.  `waitboot` now starts a non-running domain before polling it, which is
what the sibling harness has always done.

**And cut 7's post-recovery section had never run.**  The mount probe prints
the whole assignment, `mounted=1` or `mounted=0` — which is also what its own
capture regex requires — and the guard compared that against the bare word
`mounted`.  No mounted node could satisfy it.  A lap that recovered cleanly on
a cold restart, certified the dead prover by LU reset, replayed both slices and
carried `fails=0` was reported FAIL on that line, and with it went new work
after the recovery, the unmount/remount recycle, the churn oracle read through
a second mount, and the offline consistency check — the four things that say
the completed replay is on the platter rather than in a cache.

**Disposed: the metadata arm no longer falls open on the detached DLM pointer.**
FIXED AND VERIFIED.  The patch landed in 0.89.26 (`pal/linux/xfs_buf.c:9794`,
ask the mount's authority object rather than the DLM reference); what was
missing was any lap that could exercise it, for the reason above.  Measured
here on one build across three arms, same buffer and same producer in each —
`daddr=128 len=32 ops=xfs_inode comm=xfsaild/sda`, the root inode cluster.
Clean: `P291-AUTH-TAIL-ADMIT site=meta` — admitted, and the lease is what said
so.  Blind: `P291-AUTH-TAIL-BLIND site=meta` — the pre-fix answer, admitted
because the DLM reference was absent, with the tail parked 45 s past the lease.
Gated: `P290-AUTH-REFUSED-META ... REFUSED (-EIO) and no bio is issued`,
alongside `P290-AUTH-CLOSED reason=AUTHORITY_LEASE_EXPIRED overdue_ms=19664` —
and `UMOUNT rc=0 secs=50 still=0`, so the refused write did not become a hung
task.  No submission reached the gate without an authority object in any arm.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.37 — the inode-buffer replay guard can now be reached, by substituting at the durable write instead of at the check

0.89.35 gave `xlog_recover_do_inode_buffer` three conditions it never had: the
AG comes from the buffer's own daddr and not from the bytes it is meant to
constrain, the image must lie wholly inside that one AG, and every logged
`di_next_unlinked` must be NULLAGINO or a valid agino of that AG.  A real
death and a real foreign replay then measured that nothing regressed.

What that could not measure is the guard.  It fires only on a value this build
will never write, so running the code cannot reach it, and a check nothing has
ever provoked is unexercised rather than verified.  Injecting at the check
would only prove the branch compiles.

So the substitution happens where the image becomes durable.  Two module
parameters change the bytes copied into the LOG VECTOR and leave the buffer
that goes to the platter alone: `dbg_recov_inject_agino` plants an agino no AG
of the filesystem contains into a logged `di_next_unlinked`, and
`dbg_recov_inject_straddle` moves a logged image's daddr so the cluster it
names crosses an AG boundary.  The log then carries exactly what a corrupt or
foreign producer could have left behind, and every check between the producer
and the refusal is untouched.

Both are one-shot and both clear themselves ONLY when the substitution
actually lands, so an arming that finds no inode-buffer image stays armed and
says so on its own line.  An injector that can be armed into a no-op would
otherwise report a refusal it never provoked.

`tests/tcp_death_replay.sh` gains the arms that use them — `TDR_VICTIM_AGINO`
and `TDR_VICTIM_STRADDLE`, armed on the VICTIM in the seconds before the kill,
where every other injection in that harness is armed on the survivor.  The
survivor's replay must then refuse the image BY NAME, fail with -117 rather
than adopt it, and leave its own filesystem running; a plain lap, whose replay
must COMPLETE, is the control without which a refusal count says only that
something refused.  One substitution per lap: two at once and neither refusal
is attributable.

Also: `tests/fence_crash_cuts.sh` counted a silent victim's containment with a
narrower pattern set than the one it captures.  Lap s108a read contain=0 and
FAILed while the victim's own kernel log carried `P131-SELF-FENCE
[AUTHORITY_LEASE_EXPIRED]` and every fsync after it returned rc=1 — a
containment that was working, failed for being announced under a name the
count did not list.  The count now reads the same set the capture collects.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.36 — the death fence comes off the heartbeat thread, so the post-reset barrier can go back to proving what it was built to prove

A node that issues a LOGICAL UNIT RESET terminates its own tasks on that unit
too.  The post-reset barrier exists to establish that this node's authority
survived that, and it did so by waiting for a heartbeat issued after the reset
to LAND — one fact carrying both halves of the question: the stranded beat has
been resolved, and the lease is being renewed.

0.89.34 made that wait issue the beat itself.  The reason was real — the
production caller was the heartbeat thread, so the barrier was waiting for a
beat only it could produce, and the measured result was a 30241 ms wait against
a 30000 ms lease, the authority closing at its deadline, and the surviving node
shutting its filesystem down.  But waiting for the heartbeat SERVICE is how the
barrier established the service was alive and renewing.  Beating for yourself
establishes that one compare-and-write completed.  A node whose heartbeat
thread was parked, wedged or dead could then mint a durable retirement
certificate and start a replay that outlives its lease with nothing renewing
it, while its peers were entitled to fence it and replay the same slice.

The fault was never in the barrier.  It was in the call graph: peer death is
declared from the MONITOR stage of the heartbeat loop, and the whole fence —
durable intent, task-management function, barrier, certificate, replay
election — ran inside that dispatch, burning the very lease the loop exists to
renew.

So the work moves.  The monitor now records the death and hands the slot to the
per-mount PR worker, a thread that already exists because fence retries and the
reservation-health check must both be off the heartbeat thread.  The handover is
published with a full-barrier exchange, single producer and single consumer; a
slot whose handover is still pending, or a mount whose worker failed to start,
runs inline and says so loudly rather than dropping a death.  With the heartbeat
thread free to beat for the whole of the wait, the barrier goes back to
observing a beat it did not produce, and it has no fallback to issuing one: a
heartbeat that dies under the wait fails closed, the lease closes at its own
deadline, and no replay byte and no recovery commit is written.

Measured on the shipping 2/tcp rig, both directions, same harnesses one change
apart.  tests/lu_reset_fence.sh: PASS, 0 failed assertions, 102 s.  Its lapsed
arm parks the heartbeat thread for 45 s under a 30 s lease and drives the fence
from another thread; it is back to REFUSING (barrier-refused, no proving kind,
no retirement basis, the attempt recorded as MAY_HAVE_SUBMITTED, the module
closing its own authority lease), which is the behaviour 0.89.34 had reversed
into eight failed assertions.  The certify arm still certifies.  Board
crash_audit at 2/tcp: PASS 135/300 s — the monitor-stage heartbeat stall that
motivated 0.89.34 has not returned.

## 2026-09-21 — 0.89.35 — replay now judges the unlinked pointer it adopts, instead of only checking it is not zero

Foreign replay patches `di_next_unlinked` out of a log image into an inode
cluster on the shared LUN.  Until now the only thing asked of that four-byte
value was that it not be zero.  Everything else about it was adopted on
trust: whether it named an inode this filesystem has, whether it named one in
the same allocation group as the cluster it was being written into, or
whether the cluster image was even a whole number of inodes.

An unlinked-list pointer is an AGINO.  It names an inode in the SAME
allocation group, or it is NULLAGINO for the end of the chain — and the
in-memory code asserts exactly that on every insert and every remove.  The
replay path asked for none of it, so a wild value was written to the platter
and the damage surfaced later, in whoever next walked the chain, with nothing
left to say where it came from.

Three conditions now have to hold before any byte moves.

The AG is derived from the buffer's own block number, never from the first
dinode's embedded identity — deriving the bound from the same untrusted bytes
the bound exists to constrain proves nothing.  The buffer must lie wholly
inside that one AG: a cluster straddling an AG boundary has no single correct
agino range, so there is no honest way to validate it and it is refused rather
than guessed at.  And each logged value must be NULLAGINO or an agino that
falls inside that AG's inode range and clear of its static metadata.

The third condition is the one the offset arithmetic already assumed: the
buffer must be a whole multiple of the inode size, because the loop indexes
inode `i` at `i * sb_inodesize` and a remainder means the last inode runs off
the end of the buffer.

One thing is deliberately NOT checked, and refusing on it would have been a
regression.  A logged inode buffer is allowed to be a different size from this
kernel's inode cluster size — the log may have been written by a kernel with
unclustered inode buffers, or with a different cluster size — and the write
path already handles that by keeping the odd-sized buffer out of the cache.
A geometry check keyed on the cluster size would have refused replays that are
legitimate, which is the same shape of failure this validation exists to
prevent.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.34 — the witnessed LU reset is now the production answer to a purged registration, and two string knobs stop lying about being cleared

The LU-reset audited-kernel pin can be pointed at a substitute release, so
that its refusal is exercisable on a rig that runs exactly one kernel.  The
knob is a `charp` module parameter, and a sysfs store hands such a parameter
the bytes that were written — newline included.  `echo '' > .../knob`
therefore left it holding `"\n"` rather than nothing, and `"\n"` is a release
no pin can carry.

The measured consequence: a lap armed the injector for its refusal arm,
cleared it, and every later fence attempt on that node refused
`kernel-unaudited` with an empty release.  The arm that had to issue a real
LOGICAL UNIT RESET never reached admission at all (`admit_run=0`), so the
certificate it exists to mint was not merely unwritten — the reset was never
issued, and the whole clause went unmeasured while the log read as though the
operator had cleared the knob.

The effective-release accessor now trims surrounding whitespace before it
decides anything, and reads an all-whitespace value as OFF.  A kernel release
contains no whitespace, so trimming can only recover the value that was meant.
The one-way property of the knob is unchanged: a trimmed value the pin ACCEPTS
is still rejected loudly and the running kernel used instead, because a knob
that could name an audited release would be a way to mint a durable
certificate on a kernel nobody read.

### The route is wired into the fence path

`mxfs_scsipr_fence_by_lu_reset()` had exactly one caller — the debugfs probe
that exists to measure it.  The whole four-arm contract is now measured clean
on the shipping LUN (`tests/lu_reset_fence.sh`, label s105a: the peer arm
refuses and issues nothing, the pin arm refuses before admission is even asked,
the control arm mints kind 24 at phase VERIFIED with all three retirement
fields and leaves the reservation and every registration byte-identical across
the reset, and the lapsed arm issues a real reset, refuses to certify, and
leaves the intent resumable).  So it is now asked from the place that needs it.

That place is the sole-survivor leg of `v5_recover_dead_node()`, at the point
where the retirement proof comes back NONE.  Everything reaching it is about a
victim whose descriptor the target has already purged: there is nothing left
for a PREEMPT AND ABORT to name, and the gate's own `sark=0` preempt aborts no
task set belonging to the victim, so the leg could only log why it was refusing
and give up — which on a purging target is every single-node death, and with it
every one of that node's fsync-acknowledged writes.

A LOGICAL UNIT RESET is defined on the unit rather than on a nexus, so it
reaches work whose originating session is gone.  It is asked ONLY under the
conditions that already guard the gate — this node provably the only live
member, the victim's key absent — because an LU-scope reset takes the in-flight
work of every other initiator with it; "nobody else is live" is what keeps the
operation from being an attack on a bystander, and the storage layer re-checks
the same fact from the target's side and refuses otherwise.

A certified result replaces the verdict.  A REFUSED one is adopted too, but
only once the command boundary was crossed: the reset happened, so the
attempt's phase is `MAY_HAVE_SUBMITTED` and that has to reach the unproven arm
rather than the `PRECOMMAND` phase the key attempt left behind.  A refusal that
issued nothing changes nothing and is left alone.

### The post-reset barrier waited for a heartbeat on the thread that owed it

Wiring the route in exposed a self-deadlock in the barrier, and it cost the
surviving node its filesystem.  Peer death is declared from the MONITOR stage
of the heartbeat loop and the fence runs inside that dispatch, so the
production caller of the barrier IS the heartbeat thread.  The barrier proved
its authority half by polling for a heartbeat issued after the reset to land —
a beat only the thread blocked in it could issue.

Measured on the 2/tcp rig (crash_audit, run 20260921T000602Z): the reset was
issued at 11319.139 and WITNESSED at 11319.196 with the command path answering
22 ms later, and then not one beat landed for 30.2 s.  MXFS's own stall
detector caught it — `P278-HB-STALL stage=MONITOR hb_pid=9566` with the
heartbeat task's stack inside `mxfs_v5_dlm_lu_reset_barrier`, and
`P-HB-MONSLOW monitor_ms=30487`.  The lease expired at exactly its 30 s
deadline, authority closed, and the survivor shut down.  Nothing was wrong with
the SCSI side: the reset's Unit Attention was consumed and the path was healthy
throughout.

The barrier now ISSUES the beat instead of waiting for one, through the new
`mxfs_disklock_beat_now()`.  It is the same proof: the beat goes through the
same single-outstanding compare-and-write under the same mutex, so it still
cannot land until the beat the reset stranded has been resolved, and it still
renews the lease from an anchor taken before it was issued.  What it no longer
does is depend on another thread's schedule.  A beat that lands ends the wait;
one that does not renews nothing, and the lease closes the wait itself — the
exit conditions are unchanged, and no bound was invented.

`mxfs_disklock_beat_now()` deliberately does not drive the heartbeat stage
machine and runs neither the self-fence nor the conflict callback: those are
the heartbeat loop's cycle policy, and it sees the same condition on its next
cycle.  The heartbeat PAYLOAD is now built in one place, `hb_payload_fill()`,
shared by both issuers — a second copy would diverge silently, because a field
left zeroed reads to a peer as "an older build wrote this" rather than as a
bug.

### The helper path had the same newline defect, and it is not test-only

`lu_reset_helper` is how a deployment names the witness helper, and the way a
path is written into a sysfs file is `echo /path > .../lu_reset_helper` — which
stores the newline too.  Nothing exists at the stored path, every upcall
returns NOT_RUN, and on a target that purges a dead node's registration NOT_RUN
is the difference between a recoverable death and a journal slice nobody can
ever replay.  The refusal names the helper, and the name it prints looks
correct.  `tests/lu_reset_witness_probe.sh` restores the path exactly that way
after its no-helper arm, so the trap was already armed in the tree.

The path is now trimmed into a local copy before anything looks it up, and that
copy is what `argv[0]` and both log lines use — so the value that ran and the
value that was reported cannot drift apart if the parameter is rewritten
mid-call.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.33 — a witnessed LOGICAL UNIT RESET is now a durable retirement proof, and it is the only thing that can retire a purged registration's work

When the target has already purged a dead node's registration there is nothing
left for a PREEMPT AND ABORT to NAME.  Every fence attempt against that node
classifies KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN however often it is retried, no certificate can
be minted, and its journal slice can never be replayed.  On the shipping LUN
that is not a corner case: the target purges a registration together with its
iSCSI session, 30-46 s after a power cut, while death is not declared for
about 66 s — so an ordinary single-node death lands in it every time.

The route out is an operation whose own defined effect reaches work that no
registration names any more.  A LOGICAL UNIT RESET terminates the tasks in the
task set of every I_T nexus attached to the logical unit, and the victim's
already-accepted writes are in one of them whether or not its descriptor
survived.  `MXFS_FENCE_KIND_LU_RESET_WITNESSED_V1` (24) is that proof profile,
with `MXFS_RETIRE_CLAIM_LU_RESET_WITNESSED_ALL_TASKS` for what is claimed and
`MXFS_RETIRE_OBS_SOLE_REGISTRANT_VICTIM_ABSENT` for what was observed; the
basis stays a completed target operation, because that is what ran.

`mxfs_scsipr_fence_by_lu_reset()` is its ONE producer, and it mints only when
every clause of the contract held, in order:

- ADMISSION.  An excluding Write Exclusive form in force, the registration
  table read COMPLETE holding exactly one descriptor, that descriptor proved
  to be our own nexus by an idempotent RESERVE, the census bracketed by an
  unmoved PR generation, and the victim's key absent.  The sole-registrant
  half is not decoration: the reset's scope is the whole unit, and this is
  what says no other initiator's registered work is there to be destroyed.
- THE AUDITED-KERNEL PIN, read BEFORE the command boundary.  The witness has
  no correlator on the wire — libiscsi does not validate the Initiator Task
  Tag on a task-management response — and its per-operation meaning comes from
  an enforced one-TMF-per-session serialization instead.  A tag keeps working
  when concurrency is added; a serialization invariant degrades silently into
  an inference if a later version ever allows two in flight, with no change to
  the value the caller reads.  So the release is pinned to the ones the
  invariant was actually read on, and each row records HOW it was read: bodies
  for 7.1.0-rc7, and for the fleet's 6.8.0-101-generic a structural
  cross-check of its shipped `include/scsi/libiscsi.h` against that tree,
  named as exactly that and not as a body-level audit.  The pin is read before
  issuing because spending a bystander's in-flight I/O on a witness this build
  could not have used is pure damage.
- THE OPERATION, witnessed: one reset, the target's task-management response
  received, the transport incarnation unchanged across the call.  An
  INDETERMINATE verdict is never a witness, and it is never collapsed into a
  refusal either — it means the reset MAY have been performed, so treating it
  as "nothing happened" would license a retry under a state nobody has
  established.
- THE POST-RESET BARRIER, both halves.  The reset terminated the issuer's own
  tasks too, so the command path is re-established by a controlled probe, the
  whole admission assertion set is re-run, the PR generation is checked
  unmoved, and this node's own storage authority is proved to have survived by
  waiting for a heartbeat issued after the reset to land.

EVERY REFUSAL AFTER THE RESET IS A REFUSAL AND NEVER A RETRY.  The reset
happened; what did not happen is the proof that this node may act on it.  The
result is a non-proving kind, no replay byte and no recovery-commit byte
follow, and the durable intent stays on the platter for a later authority
holder to resume.  A witnessed reset plus a lapsed lease is exactly the state
that must leave a resumable intent and no certificate.

All three retirement fields are set together in one place, because the
consumer demotes any proving kind back to KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN when the basis
is NONE — a half-filled certificate is not a weaker one, it is none at all.

Also in this version:

- `tests/setup/prep_node.sh` installs the node-local witness helper at the
  module parameter's own default path before the module loads.  The helper is
  node-local by design: a fence that upcalled into the build host's NFS export
  would make one node's storage recovery depend on another machine being
  reachable, at exactly the moment the cluster is already degraded.
- `mxfs_pal_kernel_release()`, so a witness resting on a kernel-internal
  invariant can be pinned to the releases that invariant was read on.
- A refusal-only injector for the pin (`lu_reset_krel_probe`).  It honours
  only a release the pin REJECTS: a knob that could name an audited release
  would be a way to mint a durable certificate on a kernel nobody read, and an
  injector must be able to make a check fail, never to make it pass.
- `tests/lu_reset_fence.sh`, four arms on one build against the shipping LUN —
  one per clause of the contract, each removing exactly one fact and requiring
  the refusal, with the arm that issues a real reset as the control, because a
  fence that refused everything would pass every refusal arm and retire
  nobody's work.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.32 — a node that has just reset the logical unit now has to prove its own authority survived before it replays anything

An LU-scope reset terminates the tasks of every I_T nexus attached to the unit,
and the issuer's nexus is one of them.  So the node that issues one to retire a
dead peer's accepted work comes out the other side with its own commands
stranded — including the heartbeat write that is the only thing renewing its
30 s storage-authority lease.  A node that keeps replaying a dead peer's
journal slice after that lease has lapsed is a second authority over that
slice, because its peers, seeing an expired heartbeat, are entitled to give the
same slice to somebody else.  That is the integrity case the whole retirement
obligation exists to prevent, and until now nothing stood between the reset and
the first replay byte.

The barrier that now does is a POST-reset convergence barrier.  It is
deliberately neither of the two shapes that suggest themselves:

- Not a pre-reset drain.  Waiting for in-flight I/O to finish before issuing
  the reset is waiting for exactly the commands the reset exists to terminate,
  and the gate must never be able to block the reset itself, an abort, an error
  handler retry or transport recovery.
- Not a completion filter.  A command submitted before the reset may have
  COMPLETED after an error-handler retry; discarding that completion because of
  when it was submitted does not produce a safe filesystem retry, it produces
  an I/O error and a shutdown.

`mxfs_scsipr_lu_reset_converge()` establishes the storage half, in order and
each part enforced by the target:

- THE COMMAND PATH CAME BACK, proved by a controlled probe issued as the first
  command after the reset.  A reset leaves a UNIT ATTENTION pending on every
  nexus and the first command to arrive is answered with it instead of being
  executed, so whatever that command is, its result describes the reset and not
  itself.  Making it a PERSISTENT RESERVE IN means the condition is consumed by
  something whose only job is to be consumed — never the heartbeat renewal,
  never a replay write, never the recovery commit.  Its bound is a refusal, not
  a longer wait.
- THE WHOLE ADMISSION ASSERTION SET STILL HOLDS.  The admission function itself
  is re-run rather than a cheaper second set of rules being invented for the
  same question.
- THE PR GENERATION DID NOT MOVE ACROSS THE RESET.  This is the check for the
  hazard peculiar to a target that purges registrations together with the iSCSI
  session: the reset can be followed by error-handler transport recovery, the
  session comes back new, our registration goes with the old one, and a health
  worker's re-REGISTER then restores an admission set that reads identically
  while describing a registration that did not exist throughout.  A reset does
  not bump the generation; every PERSISTENT RESERVE OUT does.

`mxfs_v5_dlm_lu_reset_barrier()` adds the half that is not a property of the
LUN: it waits for a heartbeat ISSUED AFTER THE RESET TO LAND.  That one fact
carries both remaining obligations.  It is convergence — the heartbeat sector
is written through a single-outstanding synchronous compare-and-write, so a
fresh beat cannot land until the beat the reset stranded has been resolved, and
observing the new one is observing the old one finish without draining
anything.  And it is authority — a beat that lands renews the lease from an
anchor taken before it was issued.  The wait needs no invented bound, because
the lease already is one: the only ways out are the beat landing or the
authority gate closing itself at the deadline.  A number chosen here would
either be shorter than the lease, refusing a node that still holds authority,
or longer, which is the assertion of liveness that was rejected.  A refusal
does not mean retry: no replay byte and no recovery-commit byte are written,
and the durable reset intent is left resumable by a later authority holder.

Measured on the shipping 2/tcp rig, `tests/lu_reset_barrier.sh` lap s103b,
25 of 25 in one lap, 110 s, evidence `tests/evidence/20260920T232550Z_lrb_s103b`.
With A the sole registrant the barrier HELD in 2523 ms, probe 1 ms, generation
6078 unchanged across it.  With A's heartbeat thread paused 12 s — under the
lease, so authority never lapses — it still held and it WAITED 12598 ms, which
is what separates a barrier waiting for a beat issued after the call from one
reading the last beat's timestamp: both hold on a healthy cluster, and only the
first can report that number.  With the pause set past the lease it REFUSED
after 28228 ms, with its storage half still reporting converged so the refusal
is attributable to authority, and with the module naming the closure itself.
No reset was issued on any arm, the reservation stanza was byte-identical
across the holding arms, no registration appeared or vanished, and there was no
BUG or Oops.

Asked through a per-mount debugfs trigger, `lu_reset_barrier`, which runs the
production functions rather than a copy: the probe takes its own admission
first and feeds that admission's generation in, exactly as the production
sequence does, because a generation the caller invented would make the
continuity check pass by construction.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.31 — the module now decides for itself whether an LU-scope reset is the right tool, and the target enforces the answer

The witnessed LOGICAL UNIT RESET landed in 0.89.30 with nothing calling it.  Its
scope is the logical unit, so it terminates the tasks of every I_T nexus
attached to that unit — which is exactly why it reaches a dead node's accepted
work after the target has purged the registration PREEMPT AND ABORT would have
named, and exactly why it must not be issued whenever a precisely-scoped
operation would do instead.

`mxfs_scsipr_lu_reset_admit()` decides that, and every part of the decision is
enforced by the target rather than asserted by a deployment:

- READ RESERVATION must show a reservation in force whose type refuses
  media-access writes from non-registrants.
- The registration table, read COMPLETE and never truncated, must hold exactly
  ONE descriptor, and it must carry our key.  One descriptor per I_T nexus, so
  this also refuses a multipath sibling whose in-flight work the reset would
  strand.
- That descriptor is proved to be OURS rather than a re-use of our key value by
  a matching-scope/type RESERVE: only an I_T nexus registered with the key in the
  command completes it GOOD.  It is issued only after a matching reservation was
  already seen in force, so it can never create one — a gate that silently
  re-armed the cluster's exclusion would hide the interval in which
  non-registrants could write.
- The census is bracketed: the same complete view with the same PR generation
  before and after that RESERVE.  A registration that appeared while the gate was
  deciding refuses the admission.

A registered VICTIM is refused before the generic "somebody else is registered"
refusal, because the useful refusal is the one that tells the caller which
operation to run instead: the key preempt is the fence for a victim whose
registration is still in the table.

Measured on the shipping 2-node TCP rig, 22 of 22, one lap, 65 s
(`tests/lu_reset_admit_gate.sh` s102b, evidence
`tests/evidence/20260920T225946Z_lrag_s102b`): both nodes mounted and no victim
named — refused, reason `another-initiator-is-registered`; both mounted and the
peer's own per-nexus key named — refused, reason
`victim-is-registered-preempt-and-abort-applies`; the peer unmounted so its
registration is gone — ADMITTED with own_n=1, other_n=0 and the all-registrants
reservation still in force.  The gate costs 2 ms when it refuses early and 9 ms
for the full admitted path.  Zero LOGICAL UNIT RESETs were issued in the lap,
the reservation stanza was byte-identical across it, the only registration that
left was the peer's own unmount, and none appeared.

The refusal arms would all have passed on a gate that refused everything, so the
lap ends with the arm that MUST be admitted, on the same build against the same
LUN.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.30 — the module can now ask the target to retire a dead node's work, and check the answer

MXFS has had no way to issue a task-management function, so once the target
purged a dead node's registration there was no operation left that retired the
work it had already accepted — and since the deployment clause was withdrawn,
no certificate could be minted without one. On the shipping LUN that is every
node death: the registration is gone ~32 s after the power cut and the first
fence attempt is made at ~63 s. The survivor's every fence then classified
`KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN`, the dead node's journal slice was never replayed, and
the root inode being the dead node's made the whole namespace unreachable on
the only live node.

A LOGICAL UNIT RESET has no such dependency: its scope is the logical unit, so
it reaches work whose originating session is gone. This release builds the
first half of that route — the operation and the witness, not yet the fence
that consumes them.

`mxfs_pal_lu_reset_witness()` (`pal/linux/lureset.c`) generates a 64-bit nonce,
executes a node-local helper, and judges the report the helper writes back
through `/proc/fs/mxfs/lu_reset_report` — a channel that exists only while an
invocation is outstanding, accepts one report per nonce, and discards a report
naming any other. A file on disk would have been stale, substitutable and
replayable; this is none of those. The verdict is WITNESSED only when the
helper crossed the command boundary, the ioctl returned success and the
transport incarnation was unchanged across the call. Everything else is
REFUSED (nothing issued) or INDETERMINATE — and INDETERMINATE is never read as
"no reset happened", because killing the helper does not cancel an ioctl the
kernel is already executing. A result code that will not parse stops the
witness rather than defaulting to the zero that would have let it stand.

The reset itself is performed by `tools/mxfs_lu_reset_witness.py`, which
resolves the logical unit by its VPD designator and refuses any other device,
forbids escalation (without that, a success could come from a target, bus or
host reset — a different operation with a different scope), and never retries.

Two defects were found and fixed in getting there, and the first is the sort
that does not announce itself. A kernel upcall's child inherits the helper
thread's file table, in which descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are CLOSED. The helper
died writing its report to a `sys.stdout` that was `None`, so forty-five
seconds of every invocation were spent waiting for a process that had already
exited — but far worse, its first `os.open()` would have been handed
descriptor 0 and its second descriptor 1, and the first thing this program
opens is the block device it is about to reset. A later write to what the
runtime still called standard output would have landed inside the LUN. The
helper now fills those three descriptors from `/dev/null` before opening
anything, and writes the channel before the console.

The second was in the probe, not the product: each arm's kernel-log window
opened at a marker named for the arm, `sed` opens a range at its FIRST match,
and the nodes are not rebooted between laps — so the second lap read the
first lap's verdicts. It reported a 14 s lap with a 47261 ms wall time and the
previous lap's nonce, which is the only reason it was caught. Markers are now
unique per lap.

Verified by `tests/lu_reset_witness_probe.sh` (lap s101c,
`tests/evidence/20260920T223732Z_lurw_s101c`), 16 of 16 on the shipping 2/tcp
rig: the control arm reached WITNESSED with the nonce bound and the whole
upcall — exec, interpreter startup, sysfs snapshots, the task-management
function and the report — in 79 ms; a designator no device carries was REFUSED
with nothing issued; a helper path that does not exist was NOT_RUN with
nothing issued; an unsolicited report was refused by the channel; the
registrations and the reservation were byte-identical across the resets; and
the issuing node logged no BUG, no Oops and no filesystem shutdown.

What this does NOT yet do: nothing calls it. The fence ladder still ends in
refusal, the certificate kind that would carry this witness is not allocated,
and the sole-initiator admission gate and the local-I/O generation barrier the
route needs are not built. The defect stays open and the 2/tcp release stays
blocked.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.28 — the flag that disqualified every unlink was set once, at allocation, and never cleared

A dirty peer's log slice was terminally refused by the survivor's foreign
replay — `ATOMIC-SKIP`, `-117`, the victim's AGs quarantined cluster-wide and
the domain needing operator repair — on every death with an unlink in flight.
The replayer's own census had been naming the cause for four sessions and
nobody had read it: `dino_none=2 dino_agsib=2`, two classless inode-cluster
images, both with the contemporaneous AG sibling in the same transaction.
That is precisely the shape the producer was written to authorize, so the
question was never "which class should these be" but "why does the predicate
that grants it never fire".

It never fired because it excluded `XFS_BLI_INODE_ALLOC_BUF`, and that flag is
sticky. `xfs_trans_inode_alloc_buf` sets it when a cluster is first
initialised and nothing ever clears it — the formatter clears only
`XFS_BLI_INODE_BUF`. Every later `di_next_unlinked` update to that cached
cluster buffer therefore still reads as an allocation. A producer probe
counted 14 unauthorized images and zero authorized ones, each of them
`bli_flags=0x5a` with `comm=unlink`: an allocation flag on an unlink.

The exclusion was also guarding a class that cannot exist here. On v5 an
allocating transaction marks the cluster image ordered, so it is never
physically logged — only the logical `xfs_icreate_log` item is — and the
formatter sets the wire flag `XFS_BLF_INODE_BUF` unconditionally under
`xfs_has_v3inodes()`, so replay of anything reaching the wire from this
producer applies nothing but `di_next_unlinked`. The in-core allocation flag
carries buffer-item ordering and lifetime meaning, not the later image's
recovery meaning; reading it as an authority discriminator was a category
error.

- **The producer drops only that term.** `mxfs_buf_iunlink_ag_authorized` now
  excludes `XFS_BLI_STALE` and `XFS_BLI_STALE_INODE` — the second added
  explicitly rather than left to a transitive invariant — and gates on
  `xfs_has_v3inodes()` instead of `xfs_has_crc()`, so it uses the same feature
  predicate as the formatter it is reasoning about. Clearing the flag after
  the allocating transaction commits was considered and rejected: the item is
  buffer-scoped and outlives the transaction, and a durable commit record is
  not the ordered initialisation reaching the platter.
- **The replay side gains the mirror refusal.** A class-AG DINODE token is
  MALFORMED if it lacks `XFS_BLF_INODE_BUF` *or* carries `XFS_BLF_CANCEL`. A
  staled cluster emits a cancellation, whose replay suppresses every image of
  the block rather than applying `di_next_unlinked`; the AG grant vouches for
  the unlinked-list mutation, not for a whole-block suppression.
- **Measured as one A/B on one harness, four laps, both nodes verified on the
  srcversion under test.** Before, on 0.89.27, two laps byte-identical:
  `ATOMIC-SKIP` ×2, `P241-RECOV-TERMINAL` ×3, `-117`, `quarantined=0x2`,
  census `classless=2 dino_none=2 dino_agsib=2`. After: zero of every one of
  those, census `classless=0 dino_none=0 dino_agsib=0 ag=8 wapply=8`, the
  `len=32 blft=8` image carrying `class=1 st=1`, `foreign replay of slot 1
  complete`, and `P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE — slice replayed, shared purges done,
  dead slot zeroed`. The producer-only build and the build with the cancel
  guard give the same answer, so the guard is confirmed a no-op on healthy
  traffic.
- **What the byte-level safety rests on is structural, not sampled.**
  `xlog_recover_do_inode_buffer` writes exactly `*buffer_nextp =
  *logged_nextp` at `offsetof(xfs_dinode, di_next_unlinked)` per inode plus
  the recalculated inode CRC, and nothing else — so only `di_next_unlinked`
  and the CRCs that follow from it can move. The class-AG binding check
  derives the AG from the log item's own block number, never from the image's
  embedded dinode identity, which is untrusted bytes.
- **The harness predicate that hid this was itself wrong.**
  `tests/authtail_mount_unwind.sh` gated its whole verdict on counting
  `P163-RECOVERED` — the monitor's *no-replay* completion path, the opposite
  reading, and a line the replay path never prints. Four consecutive laps read
  VACUOUS while their journals carried `foreign replay of slot N complete`. It
  now counts the replayer's own completion line.

Still owed on this path, and not claimed here: the hard-crash arm has not been
re-measured against the fix, because fencing now refuses before replay is ever
reached on a target that purges a dead node's registration with its session;
and `xlog_recover_do_inode_buffer` still checks only that a replayed
`di_next_unlinked` is nonzero, not that it is `NULLAGINO` or a valid same-AG
agino.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.23 — an old build is kept off the LUN by the format, not by an assertion that everyone upgraded

0.89.16 retired fence kind 16 and 0.89.18 revoked kind 17, and a corrected
reader refuses both wherever a certificate authorises replay. That repairs the
reader. It does nothing about the node that still MINTS those classes, and the
direction that corrupts was never the old node reading a new record — kind 23
is a code point it has never heard of. It was an old node JOINING beside a
corrected one and minting kind 16 from a basis that had been retired: the
corrected build refuses that certificate, the old build honours its own, and
replays a peer's slice on a retirement claim nobody proved.

Those two releases changed what a durable recovery descriptor MEANS without
moving the protocol generation, which is the one thing the descriptor's own
coexistence argument forbids — a reader that predates the change replays first
and classifies afterwards, so nothing on the old side fails closed, because
from its point of view nothing changed.

- **`MXFS_PROTO_GEN` moves 21 → 22.** No new on-disk region and no layout
  change; the generation is stamped by `mkfs_mxfs`, or written into an
  existing volume by `chk_mxfs --upgrade-protogate`. Two independent gates
  then cover the two states an old node can be in: not yet mounted, where the
  exact-match C7 gate refuses it with `-EPROTONOSUPPORT`; and already live,
  where the generation travelling in the heartbeat feature block makes the
  monitor fence it and makes a joiner that meets it withdraw.
- **`tests/proto_gen_cutover.sh` measures the exclusion with the binary that
  was actually running** — the arm deliberately deploys nothing, so the module
  already loaded on the nodes plays the pre-cutover build. Lap s90a, 22 s,
  fails=0. The control comes first and is what makes the refusal mean
  something: the deployed module mounts the volume, `rc=0`, and the kernel
  itself prints `proto_gen=21`. `chk_mxfs -U` then moves the envelope 21 → 22
  and sets `INCOMPAT_MXFS_PROTOGATE` on 24 superblock copies. The same
  unchanged modules are then refused on BOTH nodes: `rc=32`, `C7 gate:
  filesystem cluster_proto_gen=22 but this kernel speaks 21`, zero `Starting
  recovery` lines and no BUG/Oops — the excluded node changes nothing on its
  way out.
- **Every generation in that lap is a number the running kernel printed, and
  that is not a stylistic choice.** `srcversion` cannot tell these two builds
  apart: `modpost` folds only same-directory dependencies into it, so a change
  to `include/mxfs/mxfs_super.h` leaves it byte-identical — measured
  `A2ABA0E3B98727EFE11B6B9` on both sides of this bump. Any deployment check
  of the form "the node's srcversion equals the tree's, so it is running this
  build" is unsound for a change confined to `include/`. The C7 refusal names
  both the volume's generation and the loaded module's, which is the build
  identity srcversion could not give.
- **The shipping configuration still works across the cutover**: prep
  re-formed 2/tcp in 55 s, both nodes mounted and converged at
  `active_count=2`, and both logged `proto_gen=22`.
- The decision, and why a generation bump rather than a new format region, is
  recorded in `docs/rulings/fence-certificate-proof-profiles-and-legacy-revocation.md`
  under "How step four is enforced". What it does not claim is also written
  there: it excludes an old implementation from a volume that has been stamped
  at generation 22, and says nothing about a volume nobody re-stamped. The
  cutover is the stamp, not the release.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.22 — the preempt-and-abort race is refused by the target, not silently accepted

No module change in this entry. What changed is that an assumption the fencing
path has always rested on is now measured on the appliance that ships, instead
of being read out of SPC-4 and a comment.

The ordinary fence mints its retirement claim on the grounds that the victim's
registration was in the table at the classifying READ KEYS and the PREEMPT AND
ABORT named it. The registration can leave between that read and the target's
own scope selection, and until now nothing established what the target does
then — so an execution that covered the victim and one that raced its departure
were indistinguishable after the fact, and the claim was minted either way.

- **`tests/pr_absent_sark_probe.sh`** measures it and nothing else. It runs on
  an idle cluster with no mxfs mount, builds the PR state by hand from both
  initiators — test1 registered, test2 registered, Write Exclusive - All
  Registrants held, which is the reservation the module holds — and issues
  three PREEMPT AND ABORT commands that differ only in the service-action key.
  It touches no LBA and puts the table back empty when it is done.
- **The answer is RESERVATION CONFLICT, twice, with the PR generation
  unchanged.** A service-action key that was never registered: `rc=24`,
  generation `0x175e → 0x175e`, both registrations still present. A key that
  was registered and then removed — the transition the fence actually races:
  `rc=24`, generation `0x175e → 0x175e`, nothing removed.
- **The control arm is what makes those two mean anything.** The same command,
  the same reservation key, the same type, with the service-action key present:
  ACCEPTED, `rc=0`, the named registration removed, generation `0x175f →
  0x1760`. The apparatus can produce an acceptance in the same lap, so the two
  refusals are about the absent key and not about a broken probe.
- **So the two executions are distinguished by the target's own status.** The
  conflict already arrives in the module as `-EBUSY` —
  `mxfs_pal_scsi_pr_preempt` maps status `0x18`, `scsipr_preempt_locked` logs
  it as "key not registered; no registration removed and no task set aborted by
  us", and `mxfs_scsipr_fence_node` classifies it `MXFS_FENCE_KIND_RACE_LOST`,
  which carries no claim at all. The claim-minting block is reached only on the
  accepted execution. The raced one is unreachable as a silent success rather
  than merely unwitnessed.
- The measurement is recorded against the rig in `data/rigs.json` and the
  comment in `dlm/scsipr.c` that used to point at an open defect now states
  what was measured. It is a qualified observation of this target, firmware
  revision and session topology — never a promise about an arbitrary SPC
  target — and it says nothing about a registration removed *during* the
  command's execution, which no initiator can schedule.

Queue: `D-PREEMPT-AND-ABORT-CLAIM-RESTS-ON-AN-UNHONOURED-PRE-READ` removed as
disproved, with that lap as the evidence.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.21 — two places that could not see the authority they were subject to: a gate reading a pointer its own teardown detaches, and a lock wait no closure could reach

Module srcversion `2128AAC34DA07491962F81C`.

Three builds were made during the session and the laps below name theirs,
because only the second half of the work separates them. `9C1BADD4E8D0DB6A039D23E`
carries the mount-owned authority object and the teardown-tail arms;
`80F2DC6A2B2932D3C46A9CD` adds terminal authority cancellation to the acquire
machinery, calling into the disklock directly; `2128AAC34DA07491962F81C` routes
that same call through a callback so `dlm/` still links user-mode, and changes
no behaviour.

0.89.20 gave a mount an authority lease it holds to a deadline, and put the
check at the point of use in every producer that can mutate the shared LUN.
Every one of those checks read `mp->m_mxfs_dlm` and treated a NULL as "not a
clustered mount, nothing to own". `put_super` sets that pointer to NULL and
then joins the heartbeat thread — and only after both does `xfs_unmountfs`
write the log cover and the unmount record. So for the whole teardown tail the
gate answered its own question, on a node that had by then stopped proving
liveness to anybody.

- **The hole, reproduced on this build with the fix switched off for exactly
  one line.** `tests/auth_lease_unmount_tail.sh` parks `put_super` immediately
  after the detach and the heartbeat join — the one place where authority can
  only run down — for longer than the 30 s lease, which is an ordering no
  workload reaches because the tail is normally one to four seconds.
  `dbg_auth_tail_blind=1` restores the pre-fix answer for the detached case
  and nothing else, so the before and the after are measured on ONE build with
  no other difference between them to explain the result.

  `blind` arm (`tests/evidence/20260920T173020Z_authtail_s88b_blind`, PASS
  fails=0 wall=103s): `P291-AUTH-TAIL-BLIND site=log comm=umount`, counters
  `tail_blind=1 tail_refuse=0`, `P290-AUTH-CLOSED` count **0** — the lease was
  never consulted, so it never even closed — and `umount` returned **0** after
  39 s. The node wrote its own "I left cleanly" record 35 s after its last
  heartbeat, while its peer was entitled to declare it dead, fence it and
  replay its slice.

  `gated` arm (`20260920T173211Z_authtail_s88c_gated`, PASS fails=0 wall=102s),
  same build, same ordering, same node: `P290-AUTH-REFUSED-LOG bno=356
  count=1024`, `P290-AUTH-CLOSED … deadline_ms=467735 now_ms=476263
  overdue_ms=8528 last_ok_ms=437736` — a deadline 29999 ms past the beat that
  anchored it, and the refusal 8.5 s past the deadline, inside the parked tail.
  Counters `tail_refuse=1 tail_admit=0 tail_blind=0`. The log is left dirty for
  recovery, which is the correct outcome, and the `umount` still **completed**
  (rc=0, 37 s): a refused write must not become a hung task.

  `clean` arm (`20260920T172907Z_authtail_s88a_clean`, PASS fails=0 wall=66s)
  is the positive control, and it is the reason the zeros above mean anything:
  with no injection the tail is **admitted**, `tail_admit=1`, and the unmount
  takes 1 s. Exactly one submission crosses the detach on an ordinary unmount —
  the unmount record's iclog — and until now that one was admitted with no
  lease consulted at all. In every arm `no_authority=0` and neither node logged
  a BUG or an Oops, and the peer was still serving at the end.

- **The fix: the authority object outlives everything that could hold it.**
  `struct mxfs_authority` is now a separate reference-counted allocation
  carrying the one copy of `{state, deadline, anchor, incarnation}`. The mount
  allocates it *before* `mxfs_v5_dlm_init` — before the first instant a
  clustered mutation is possible — and drops its reference in `xfs_mount_free`,
  after every producer, workqueue, timer and I/O completion of that incarnation
  is gone. The disklock context borrows a reference for as long as it lives and
  writes its renewals and closures through to it. There is no second copy to
  publish, so no reader can see a state from one update and a deadline from
  another.

  "Clustered" is now a property of the mount (`m_mxfs_clustered`), decided once
  and never cleared, rather than the liveness of a pointer. A clustered mount
  that reaches the gate with no authority object is **refused** and counted;
  that count is asserted zero on every arm.

  A revocation decided while teardown is already under way also goes to the
  authority object rather than through the DLM context, so detaching the
  operational context cannot suppress a decision that invalidates the remaining
  lease.

- **Why the clean-unmount record gets no exemption.** The counter-argument is
  that refusing it makes departures dirty. The design consult (Astra, ruling in
  `docs/rulings/local-authority-lease-and-the-limits-of-a-software-gate.md`, and
  the corrections it issued this session) is the other way round: a stale
  "I left cleanly" record is *more* dangerous than an ordinary stale write
  because it suppresses recovery. A node that can no longer prove authority
  must not write one, and an unclean departure handled by recovery is the
  correct outcome — the same argument that already refuses an iclog.

- **The refactor did not cost the containment it was built on.** Moving the
  lease state out of the disklock context is the kind of change that can
  quietly break the thing it serves, so both of the laps that established the
  0.89.20 behaviour were re-run on this build.
  `tests/fence_late_detection.sh` — the original defect, a fenced node that has
  noticed nothing writing to an unreserved LUN — PASS fails=0 wall=167s
  (`tests/evidence/20260920T173431Z_lated_s88d`): the platter reads back
  `b a s e l i n e`, all three probes return EIO in 0-1 ms, the closure reason
  is `AUTHORITY_LEASE_EXPIRED` with `overdue_ms=14871`, zero LUN-dependent
  detectors fired at any point, and the healthy control on the same node
  succeeded before the arm. `tests/auth_lease_resurrection.sh resume` — a
  heartbeat that starts working again is not a grant — PASS fails=0 wall=265s
  (`20260920T173722Z_authres_resume_s88e`): `P290-AUTH-HB-STOP`, no reservation
  repair attempted under a closed lease, and a write after the resume still
  EIO.

  And the healthy cluster is untouched: `./run.sh 2 tcp cache_coherency
  posix_multi crash_consistency dirent_durability sustained_load` is 5/5 PASS,
  every one of them well inside its budget — `cache_coherency` 534/534 checks
  in 9 s of 60, `posix_multi` 140/140 in 4 s of 30, `crash_consistency` 104/104
  in 11 s of 90, `dirent_durability` 30 rounds with `durable_loss=0` in 61 s of
  240, `sustained_load` 60 ops at 48 ms each in 5 s of 180. A gate that is
  consulted on every mutating submission has to cost nothing when the answer is
  yes, and it does.

- **What this does not close, stated plainly.** Making the incarnation's
  authority un-detachable stops epoch E from borrowing the authority of a
  pointer that is simply absent. It says nothing about a command E submitted
  *below* the gate before it closed, which can still execute after a successor
  has begun replaying E's slice; that residue is its own queue entry and no
  lease length fixes it. It also does not model per-resource entitlement: the
  lease is a necessary admission condition, not a universal write capability,
  and rights already surrendered — an AG grant published as free, a WITHDRAWN
  record published to peers — are not restored by a deadline that has not yet
  passed.

### The second half: a lock wait that no closure could reach

The lease's gate is at the point of use, so it catches an operation that is
about to submit. A task already parked inside a DLM lock request submits
nothing and asks nothing, and until now nothing ever told it that its mount had
lost the right to complete what it was waiting for.

- **Measured first, and the number is not the one that was on file.**
  `tests/tcp_lockreq_blackhole.sh` gained a lease arm: it finds an inode this
  node does not master, drops that one `LOCK_REQ` so the master creates no queue
  entry and answers nothing, confirms the waiter is genuinely blocked and the
  drop has fired, and only **then** parks the heartbeat so authority expires
  under it. Request outstanding first, authority lost second — an ordering no
  workload reaches, because the acquire is seconds and the lease is thirty.

  On `9C1BADD4E8D0DB6A039D23E`
  (`tests/evidence/20260920T175325Z_lockreqbh_s88f`), with `WORKLOAD=held_fd`,
  whose read goes through an fd opened before the fault and therefore carries no
  fallible registration: `closed_at=+85s`, `waiter_exit=+157s` — **72 seconds**.
  And the samples say something sharper than a slow reaction:

  ```
  +82s  alive=1 closed=0 shut=0
  +85s  alive=1 closed=1 shut=1     <- lease closed AND filesystem shut down
  ...
  +157s alive=0 closed=1 shut=1     <- 72 s later
  ```

  Both stop signals were already present in the same three-second sample, and
  the loop saw neither. It ended at its own retry budget.

- **Why it could not see them.** `dlm_lock_impl()` opens with
  `if (ctx->shutting_down) return -ESHUTDOWN;`, which reads like a general "is
  this mount going away" guard. `ctx->dlm->shutting_down` is assigned in exactly
  one place — `mxfs_v5_dlm_shutdown_defer_release()`, which runs at **unmount**.
  The withdrawal path never sets it, and its own comment says so out loud:
  "conflicting acquires ride their 60 s budgets through the few-second window."

  The wait is not one long sleep either. `pending_wait()` is a condvar timed
  wait of about a second and `mxfs_dlm_lock()` drives 60 retries around it, so
  for 72 seconds this loop returned to a testable point roughly once a second
  and had nothing to test.

- **The fix: terminal authority cancellation in the acquire machinery.** The
  DLM context now answers "has this incarnation's authority closed?" at acquire
  admission, at the top of every retry iteration, and in the membership-settle
  wait, returning `-ESHUTDOWN`. That code is deliberate rather than new: it is
  exactly what the function already returns for `shutting_down`, so every
  caller's unwind already treats it as terminal shutdown rather than as
  something to retry. Checked, not assumed — `v5_dlm_inode_lock`'s `-EEXIST`
  wait loop retries only on `-EEXIST`, and it already answers `-ESHUTDOWN` when
  the context is withdrawn.

  No fallibility class is exempt. That distinction — which spares a caller
  inside a dirty transaction, and was itself the fix for a measured shutdown
  storm — is right while authority is open and a *peer's* recovery is blocked,
  because the transaction might still complete. With this node's own authority
  closed it cannot, and keeping the acquire alive cannot give that back. An
  otherwise healthy node whose lease expired is not thereby authorised: health
  is not authority.

  It goes through a callback on the DLM context rather than calling the
  disklock directly, because `dlm/` also builds user-mode and the `tauth`
  binaries link `dlm.o` without `disklock.o`.

- **Verified, with the control that makes it mean something.** Same harness,
  same ordering, same workload, on `80F2DC6A2B2932D3C46A9CD`:
  `20260920T180536Z_lockreqbh_s88h`, PASS fails=0 wall=162s — `closed_at=+55s`,
  `waiter_exit=+55s`, **delta 0 s** against a 10 s bound, and the wait ended
  *after* the closure rather than before it, which is a separate assertion
  because a wait that ends early ended by some other mechanism. The stack
  assertions hold too: the blocked task was in `mxfs_dlm_ilock_begin`, it was
  getattr's acquire, and it was **not** the `open()` call site that had already
  been fixed — so the caller measured is the one this record is about.

  The control is `20260920T180917Z_lockreqbh_s88i`, PASS fails=0 wall=271s: the
  identical lap with authority left **open**. W blocks exactly as before, and
  when the requests flow again it reads the file and gets the right bytes. The
  unchanged path is unchanged, and the non-fallible caller did not acquire a new
  way to fail.

  Re-confirmed on the shipped build `2128AAC34DA07491962F81C`,
  `20260920T181536Z_lockreqbh_s88j`, PASS fails=0 wall=223s, delta 3 s — so the
  banked evidence for the behaviour that ships was taken on the binary that
  ships, not inherited from the one before it.

  And the healthy cluster is unaffected by a check that now runs on every
  acquire: `./run.sh 2 tcp cache_coherency posix_multi crash_consistency
  dirent_durability sustained_load` is 5/5 PASS on that build — 534/534 checks
  in 9 s of 60, 140/140 in 4 s of 30, 104/104 in 10 s of 90,
  `dirent_durability` 30 rounds with `durable_loss=0` in 62 s of 240, and
  `sustained_load` 60 ops at 54 ms each in 4 s of 180.

- **What it does not do, said plainly.** A grant that arrives and is accepted
  between two checks is still installed; it is the mutating-submission gate, not
  this, that stops it being used. Closure-aware grant acceptance, closure races
  against wait registration, and the other blocking waits the design consult
  named — journal grants, log forces, buffer waits, teardown — are each their own
  measurement and are recorded as such. The CAW transport's acquire has separate
  waits and is untouched; that is a different release.

  The design consult (Astra, `docs/rulings/terminal-authority-cancellation-in-the-acquire-machinery.md`)
  also narrowed the original finding, and the correction is worth keeping: this
  loop is *withdrawal-insensitive*, not demonstrably an indefinite sleep. That
  is why polling at the top of a bounded loop is a legitimate way to bound it,
  and why "wake the waiters" was the wrong prescription for this path — though
  not necessarily for the others.

- **Two harness corrections that the fix forced, both split by cause rather
  than relaxed.** The call-site assertions read a sampler on a 60-second
  cadence; a wait that now ends in three seconds leaves that sampler empty, so
  four assertions failed on a lap where everything under test passed. They now
  read whichever capture was taken while the task was genuinely blocked — the
  pre-close probe in the lease arm, the sampler elsewhere. And "W reads the file
  again afterwards" cannot hold in an arm that withdraws W's mount on purpose,
  so that arm asserts the reason instead: the filesystem was shut down by the
  closure, and W did not quietly recover and read stale bytes. An assertion
  removed without a replacement is an assertion relaxed.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.20 — a fenced node that has not noticed writes to the platter, and the fix is a lease it holds rather than a fence it is told about

Module srcversion `C4939B7C250423F851EA415`.

The laps below name the build each was measured on, because three were made
during the session and only test-only injections separate them: `B65B76C6…`
carried the lease and its gates, `E9DD2E48…` added `dbg_hb_skip_auth_check`,
and `C4939B7C…` added `dbg_hb_completion_delay_ms`. No lease, gate or refusal
differs between them. The headline fence lap passes on `B65B76C6…` (`s87h`,
`s87l`) and again on `E9DD2E48…` (`s87q`); `C4939B7C…` carries `s87t`.

- **The defect, measured, with the bytes read back off the LUN.** A node that
  has been PREEMPT AND ABORTed is contained by NOTICING: a data write bounces
  with SCSI RESERVATION CONFLICT and three of those launch a PR IN inspection,
  or a periodic PR IN finds its own key gone. Both need the LUN to answer. A
  node issuing nothing, whose audit tick has not come round — 60 s for an
  auditor, which in a two-node cluster the victim usually is — is fenced and
  knows nothing. If the prover then dies, the appliance purges the last
  registration and releases the reservation with it, and an unreserved LUN
  refuses nobody.

  `tests/fence_late_detection.sh` drives exactly that ordering and nothing
  else: the victim runs no workload, and two injections hold off its two
  detectors without touching a single gate, refusal or write path. Measured on
  0.89.19/0.89.20 (`tests/evidence/20260920T151252Z_lated_s87e`,
  `20260920T153004Z_lated_s87f`): a real completed target operation removed the
  victim's key and moved the appliance's PR generation (`0x16e0 -> 0x16e1` in
  the first lap, `0x16e5 -> 0x16e6` in the second — a purge does not move it,
  a PROUT does, which is how the lap knows the fence was real); the
  prover was power-cut; 30 s later the LUN held `0 registered` keys and `there
  is NO reservation held`; the victim logged ZERO detection lines at every
  checkpoint. It then wrote. A buffered write plus `fsync` returned **0 in
  1 ms**, an `O_DIRECT` 4 KiB `pwrite` returned **0 in 1 ms**, and reading the
  probe file's physical block straight off `/dev/sda` with `iflag=direct` —
  no filesystem anywhere in the read path — returned
  `f e n c e d - d i r e c t - w r`. Nothing crashed. The containment simply
  was not there.

  The block was located by capturing the file's FIEMAP extent while the
  filesystem was still healthy, because a successful `fsync` is not evidence
  that anything reached the LUN and the only thing that settles it is reading
  the device without the mount.

- **The fix is an authority LEASE, and the shape came from a design consult**
  (`docs/rulings/local-authority-lease-and-the-limits-of-a-software-gate.md`).
  Authority is something this node HOLDS UNTIL A DEADLINE, not something it
  discovers it has lost: `ADMITTED(deadline) -> CLOSED`, sticky, left only by a
  fresh coordinated admission under a new incarnation. Three details are what
  make it sound rather than merely plausible, and two of them corrected the
  obvious implementation:

  - **The deadline is anchored before the heartbeat is ISSUED**, never at its
    completion. A beat can become visible at the target, have its completion
    delayed, be aged out by peers meanwhile, and only then be stamped "now" —
    which would make local authority look *younger* than the authority peers
    can see.
  - **A renewal is accepted only while the previous authority is still valid.**
    A heartbeat CAS succeeds perfectly well against a target that has released
    its reservation and stopped refusing anyone, which is precisely the state
    this defect leaves behind, so a beat issued after the lease lapsed renews
    nothing and closes the epoch instead.
  - **The lease is checked where authority is USED, not only in a timer.** A
    timer and a heartbeat thread can be stalled along with the rest of the VM.
    The check is two atomic loads and a compare on the fast path, it closes the
    epoch itself from whatever context finds it expired, and it reaches no
    lock, no allocation and above all no LUN — a node that cannot get to its
    storage must still be able to contain itself.

  Gates are on the four producers that can mutate the LUN: metadata buffer
  submission (`P290-AUTH-REFUSED-META`, which is also every `xfsaild` push and
  the delayed-write queue), the journal (`P290-AUTH-REFUSED-LOG`), buffered
  writeback (`P290-AUTH-REFUSED-DATA`) and direct I/O
  (`P290-AUTH-REFUSED-DIO`). Each refuses through the error completion its own
  layer already has, so references are released and waiters wake instead of
  hanging. The journal gets no exemption: an "essential log write" carve-out
  would reopen the hazard, and a dirty log is the correct outcome for a node
  that has stopped being allowed to write.

  Coordination I/O is gated too, because it bypasses the filesystem entirely.
  The heartbeat checks the lease before sending another beat (so a thread that
  was parked does not resume by refreshing a slot it no longer owns), and the
  reservation-health tick is skipped once authority is gone — its repair arm
  RESERVEs and its fenced-self arm can re-REGISTER, either of which would be an
  expired incarnation undoing its own fence.

- **The lease is 30 s, and the number is derived from two directions rather
  than taken as a ratio of the 62 s death window.** For availability it must
  outlast a heartbeat cycle plus scheduling and completion delays: a cycle is
  2 s and a cycle over 4 s already logs `P-HB-SLOW` as an anomaly, so 30 s is
  fifteen cycles. For safety it must expire before a peer can complete a
  conflicting handoff, and a peer's observation cannot begin before our beat
  landed, which is after we anchored — leaving 32 s of budget for the pump's
  own lateness (one 250 ms tick, and zero for a submission, which evaluates the
  deadline itself) and for guest clock error (±500 ppm is 62 ms across the
  window). **The 31.7 s left over is not a proof.** Completing a Linux request
  with an error does not establish that the corresponding SCSI command can
  never execute later, and no choice of lease length changes that; the residue
  is tracked as its own obligation.

- **Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, both halves, with a control.** Same
  harness, same assertions, FAIL before and PASS after:

  | lap | evidence | result |
  |---|---|---|
  | before | `20260920T151252Z_lated_s87e` | FAIL fails=4 — fenced bytes on the platter |
  | before | `20260920T153004Z_lated_s87f` | FAIL fails=4 — same, with the control passing |
  | after, submission path only | `20260920T155004Z_lated_s87h` | **PASS fails=0** |
  | after, periodic evaluator live | `20260920T160858Z_lated_s87l` | **PASS fails=0** |
  | after, re-run on the final build | `20260920T163402Z_lated_s87q` | **PASS fails=0** |
  | closed-authority unmount | `20260920T160332Z_authum_s87j` | **PASS fails=0** |

  In both passing laps all three writes are refused `EIO` in 0 ms, the platter
  reads back `b a s e l i n e`, the closure reason is
  `AUTHORITY_LEASE_EXPIRED`, and **no LUN-dependent detector fired anywhere in
  the lap** — so the containment cannot be credited to the paths that were
  already known to work. `s87h`/`s87l` were measured on `B65B76C67058FAEC2A7478F`, before the
  injection below was added; `s87q` re-runs the same lap on the shipped
  srcversion. `s87h` is the stronger of the three: a new injection
  (`dbg_auth_pump_pause_ms`) parks the periodic evaluation entirely, so the
  only thing left that could discover the expiry was the write itself. That
  matters because a fix that needs a worker thread to have been scheduled is
  detection again under a new name.

  Every lap also runs a CONTROL first: the identical probe on a healthy,
  mounted, unfenced node, which must SUCCEED. Every assertion in this harness
  is that a write fails, and a harness that has quietly broken its own probe
  satisfies all of them.

- **Nothing can bring a closed lease back, and that is measured rather than
  asserted.** `CLOSED` being terminal is what the whole fix rests on, and five
  ways it could quietly stop being terminal are written into the code as
  invariants. `tests/auth_lease_resurrection.sh` exercises four of them, all
  **PASS fails=0**:

  - `resume` (`20260920T162402Z_authres_resume_s87m`): the heartbeat thread
    comes back from a stall, finds the lease closed and STOPS —
    `P290-AUTH-HB-STOP`, "stopping the heartbeat rather than refreshing a slot
    this node no longer owns" — and a write issued *after* the heartbeat is
    working again is still refused `EIO`.
  - `staleanchor` (`20260920T162610Z_authres_staleanchor_s87n`): a renewal whose
    beat was ISSUED after authority had already lapsed closes the epoch instead
    of extending it. The evidence is exact —
    `overdue_ms=18129 last_ok_ms=856939` with `last_ok_ms` equal to `now_ms`,
    so the beat really did land on the target and was refused as a renewal
    anyway: *"a heartbeat landed, but it was ISSUED after this node's authority
    had already lapsed, so it renews nothing"*.

    That guard is defence in depth — no live path reaches it, because the
    pre-issue check stops the heartbeat first — so reaching it needed a new
    one-shot injection, `dbg_hb_skip_auth_check`, which removes the primary
    check for exactly one cycle and lets a stale-anchored renewal actually
    arrive. A guard nothing can exercise is a guard nobody knows works.

  Both arms also confirm the reservation-health tick does not run under a
