  closed lease (zero `P305-RESV-REPAIRED`), which is what stops an expired
  incarnation re-REGISTERing or re-RESERVEing its way out of its own fence.

  - `resvgone` (`20260920T163848Z_authres_resvgone_s87r`): the case whose
    absence would have mattered most. The victim really was fenced (registrants
    2 → 1), the prover was then destroyed, and the appliance purged the last
    registration and released the reservation with it — `keys=0`, `there is NO
    reservation held`. A heartbeat CAS against that LUN **succeeds**, because
    nothing is left to refuse anyone; it is precisely the state the original
    defect left behind. The returning heartbeat found the lease closed and
    stopped anyway, no LUN-dependent detector fired, and a write after the
    resume was still `EIO`. Containment there comes from the node's own lease
    and from nothing else.

  - `latecompletion` (`20260920T164812Z_authres_latecompletion_s87t`): the
    invariant the design consult corrected, and the one with no evidence at all
    until now. A new one-shot injection lets the beat REACH THE TARGET and then
    withholds its completion, which is the ordering that matters: peers can see
    that beat and age it while this node waits. The assertion is direct rather
    than circumstantial — `issued_ms=265959`, `delivered_ms=312039`,
    `deadline_ms=295959`, which is `issued + 30000` **exactly**. A deadline
    anchored at completion would have read `342039` and handed this node 46 s of
    authority it never proved. `last_ok_ms` is the late completion timestamp and
    the deadline is visibly divorced from it, which is the whole point.

  One named case remains unmeasured — deferred work crossing an epoch boundary,
  which needs the work to carry its originating epoch and is a change rather
  than a test — along with the remote handoff boundary itself, which the 30 s
  lease is derived against but which nothing has measured. Both stay in the
  queue.

- **A refused log write must not become a hang, so that was measured
  separately.** `tests/auth_lease_unmount.sh` lets the lease lapse, waits out
  the injected park so a sleeping thread cannot be blamed, and then bounds the
  unmount and the module removal. Both complete — `umount` in 1 s, `rmmod` in
  0 s — and the node is still serving afterwards. A mount that can be contained
  but not taken down would have traded one release blocker for another.

- **Three harness defects found on the way, two of which were destroying
  laps.** `field()` was anchored at `^`, so an arm printing `SEEN=1 PAUSED=1`
  read the first field and handed the second an empty string — which the
  verdict helper correctly refused to grade, aborting a lap whose injection had
  in fact worked. Sixteen `tests/*.sh` carried the same copy; all are fixed.
  `sg_persist` reports an unreserved LUN as "there is **NO** reservation held",
  and a case-sensitive filter threw that line away on the remote side, so a
  purge poll spent its whole 120 s bound waiting for a string that had already
  been deleted from the capture — on a lap where the LUN had gone permissive
  40 s in. And the lap left the prover powered off on every early exit, so the
  next lap spent 152 s polling a VM that was never going to answer.

- **The ledger: one off, three on, and the one that came off was the only
  `integrity` bar in the 2/tcp release queue.** The record is disposed FIXED AND
  VERIFIED on the evidence above. Three went on, and each is something this fix
  does not claim rather than something it introduced: a command already
  submitted below the gate may still execute, and nothing here bounds how long
  (`D-OLD-EPOCH-IO-BELOW-THE-AUTHORITY-GATE-IS-UNBOUNDED`); five ways the lease
  could be resurrected or bypassed are written into the code as invariants and
  none has been exercised, while the remote half of the safety argument assumes
  a 62 s handoff boundary nothing has measured
  (`D-AUTHORITY-LEASE-RESURRECTION-CASES-ARE-UNVERIFIED`); and a DLM request
  already parked in a lock wait when the lease expires is not woken
  (`D-A-REVOKED-MOUNTS-BLOCKED-DLM-WAITERS-ARE-NOT-ABORTED`), which the design
  consult named as a second defect in its own right. The 2/tcp release queue
  goes 4 → 6, and its bar profile goes from one `integrity` plus three `verify`
  to six `verify`.

- **The defect ledger now refuses an id over 80 characters.** Ids are minted
  from the summary, so a summary that opens with a paragraph minted a
  125-character id that nobody can type, grep for, or read in a one-line queue
  listing. `add` and `rename` now refuse and ask for a name rather than
  truncating — truncation is not available, because evidence directories,
  memories and CHANGELOG entries already refer to records by name. The twelve
  over-length ids were renamed, and the two citations of them in `docs/` and
  `tests/` were repointed.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.19 — the partial-replay cut fires, and what it shows is that no crash cut can finish on a target that purges the victim's registration

Module srcversion `F76B8A511E923434ACD9E5E`.  (This entry first recorded
`8460A55EE55987F2C4881A8`, an intermediate build from partway through the
session; the tree that shipped 0.89.19 builds the srcversion above, and it is
what every lap run against 0.89.19 loaded.)

- **The partial-replay cut was measuring nothing, and said so.** Its first lap
  reported VACUOUS before anything was destroyed: the whole foreign replay had
  queued ONE buffer (`P-DRAIN-PEAK queued_buffers=1`), so a prefix of 8 left no
  suffix and the module declined the cut rather than grade a lap that had
  quietly become its own control.

  The cause is that the harness's dirty-death oracle `sync -f`s its 64 files.
  That is right for an oracle and wrong as a replay workload: after the sync
  every one of those effects is already on home storage and the replay owes
  nothing for them. The only live workload in the silent-victim arm was one
  file appended to every 500 ms — one dirty inode, one buffer. What a replay
  owes is the victim's committed but not yet checkpointed work at the instant
  it is fenced, so the victim now runs continuous METADATA churn: batches of
  creates, renames and unlinks with the directory fsynced at the end of each,
  running right up to the fence.

  The churn is also the oracle, and a better one than the files were. A batch
  is logged only after its directory fsync returns, so the acknowledged batches
  are exactly the results the filesystem promised, and the suffix the cut
  withheld lies inside that set — where re-reading files that were durable
  before the crash could never tell a completed recovery from a skipped one.
  Measured: 177 batches acknowledged, then 57 consecutive refusals once the
  fence landed, the acknowledged set a contiguous prefix with no batch
  succeeding after one failed.

- **The cut then fired exactly as designed.** 2 buffers durable on home storage
  and 12 required ones never issued; the sealed descriptor FENCED with kind
  `PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1` and the prover named; the execution lease held, so
  the replay was authorised before it ran; the victim's key absent, consumed by
  the PREEMPT AND ABORT; no completion marker durable; the victim's slot
  neither published, retired nor zeroed; and the platter byte-identical at the
  cut and at the quiescent read afterwards.

- **And then neither node could mount.** The peer's mount and the dead prover's
  own next boot both returned 32. Both journals say why, for the dead prover's
  slot: `P238-BOOTSUCC-NO-RETIRE-BASIS obs=no-mxfs-successor-observed` and
  `P238-GATE-NO-RETIRE-BASIS obs=no-mxfs-successor-observed`, with the fence
  classifying `KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN` under a bounded automatic retry series.
  That is the refusal working: since the deployment clause was withdrawn in
  code, the only accepted retirement basis is a completed target operation, and
  on this appliance a power-cut node's registration is purged 30-46 s after the
  cut while death is not declared for ~66 s — so there is nothing left for a
  PREEMPT AND ABORT to name. The same lap measured that gap again from the
  other side: at the cut, the victim's key was already gone with the PR
  generation unchanged, before the prover had written its fence intent.

  What follows is the part that matters for the crash matrix. **Every cut in
  that matrix destroys the prover**, so every one of them now ends with a
  registration the target has purged and a successor that cannot certify it.
  This is not a new defect — it is the measured reach of one already in the
  queue — but it does mean the highest-severity record's remaining work sits
  behind it.

- **So cut 1 was re-run, and it fails.** The crash matrix's banked twelve
  passes were measured on 0.89.10, a build that still had the deployment clause
  withdrawn in 0.89.16 — and every one of those laps recovered a node whose
  registration the appliance had already purged, which is exactly what the
  withdrawal removed. The simplest cut in the matrix, the identical lap that
  passed then, now ends `FAIL ... fails=10 wall=626s`: the victim was not
  certified by its successor, the peer's mount returned 32 and the dead prover's
  own rejoin returned 32 (`tests/evidence/20260920T135544Z_fcut1_s86c_cut1`).
  The lap also caught the gap from the other side — at the cut the victim's key
  was already absent with the PR generation unchanged, before the prover had
  written its fence intent, and the prover's own classification of that first
  fence was `KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN`. A version string on banked evidence does not
  say what the lap depended on; when a change withdraws a mechanism, the laps
  that recovered through it stop describing the build.

- **`chk_mxfs --bootstrap`**: print the whole-cluster bootstrap record and
  exit. Read-only, O_DIRECT and without `O_EXCL`, deliberately, because the
  moment an operator needs that record is the moment a mount is being refused
  because a term is claimed — and the ordinary check cannot run then, since
  another node may still hold the device. A buffered read of a shared device
  would answer from whatever this node's page cache captured first, which on a
  volume another node is writing is an image of the past presented as the
  present.

- **The takeover refusal now records the antecedents it refused.** A lap that
  only shows this build refusing an absent owner key proves nothing on its own:
  if none of the three deleted branches' conditions held, the build that still
  had them would have refused the same history, by falling off the end of the
  same chain — so the lap would exercise the refusal without ever reproducing
  the defect, while reading like a regression test for it.
  `P-BOOT-TAKEOVER-FENCE-UNPROVEN` now carries `would_have_minted=` naming
  which antecedent holds, in the order the deleted chain tested them, plus the
  three inputs it was computed from. `tests/bootstrap_takeover_2n.sh` grades
  that field and reports an arm whose answer is `none` as NOT REPRODUCING
  rather than crediting it.

- **The whole-cluster bootstrap does not run on TCP, and two release blockers
  were filed against it as if it did.** The two-node cold restart — both slices
  dirty, both nodes destroyed, one node back — is the shape that path exists
  for, and measured (`tests/evidence/20260920T140746Z_btk_s86d`) it does not
  take it: the mount read the record, claimed an **ordinary** heartbeat slot
  12 ms later, and then spent 122 s in the admission barrier running 116 inline
  replay rounds that each refused both slices ("the dead node is not provably
  excluded from the LUN") before refusing the mount.

  Between the record read and the slot claim there was no scan line of any
  kind, so "the scan concluded not a total outage" and "the scan never ran"
  were the same observation. `P-BOOT-SCAN-VERDICT` now prints victims, moved,
  unread, noident and the decision on every path, and `P-BOOT-SKIPPED` covers
  the early return that means the subsystem was never consulted. The lap was
  re-run with both in the build and **neither printed** — which is what
  identified the cause. `v5_bootstrap_run()` has exactly one call site,
  `dlm/v5_mount.c:16211`; the TCP arm of `mxfs_v5_dlm_init` ends `return ctx`
  at `:15990`, and everything from `:15993` ("CAW transport requires disklock
  region") is the CAW arm. The tree had said so all along, at `:15653`: *the
  TCP transport carries its own durable authority ledger and no PR-fence
  bootstrap; the record is opened for the owner-liveness view only … (bootstrap
  is a CAW path)*.

  So the bootstrap-owner records are CAW-reach, not TCP, and both are narrowed
  with that evidence — which disposes of nothing and only records which release
  they block. What TCP still does with the record is worth keeping: it opens
  it, reads it pre-register, can set a takeover or resume pending that nothing
  there consumes, and **refuses the mount** for any state that is not IDLE or
  RECOVERY_COMPLETE. A volume a CAW mount left CLAIMED is therefore unmountable
  on TCP with no in-product route at all — `chk_mxfs --clear-bootstrap` accepts
  only a REFUSED record, never a CLAIMED one. A volume that has only ever been
  TCP-mounted never leaves the IDLE that mkfs writes.

- **The ordering the live-loser evidence does not cover is now reachable on
  purpose.** `dbg_resv_health_pause_ms` holds off a node's proactive
  reservation-health check, and `tests/fence_late_detection.sh` removes the
  reactive one by giving the victim no workload at all. The victim is then
  fenced by a real completed PREEMPT AND ABORT against a present key, has
  noticed nothing, and waits while the prover dies and the target purges the
  last registration and the reservation with it — and only then writes. Both a
  data write and a metadata create must be refused. The injection is at the
  DETECTOR, not at the refusal: no gate is weakened, no certificate forged and
  the write path is untouched, so a pass says containment does not depend on
  having noticed, and a failure says it does.

- **Three instruments were lying, and two of them would have failed a correct
  build.** `tools/disklock_hb_dump.py` had no name for fence kind 23, the kind
  every current certificate carries, so it printed `23(23)` and a harness
  comparing against the NAME scored a correct certificate as wrong — which is
  exactly what happened. Kind 22 was missing too. And the post-recovery section
  of the crash-cut harness ran its "the filesystem accepts and persists new
  work" check on a node whose mount had been REFUSED: `/mnt/shared` is an
  ordinary directory when nothing is mounted over it, so the check created 16
  files on the local root filesystem, read them back and PASSED. The mountpoint
  is now the precondition of that whole section.

- **Design rulings banked**: `docs/rulings/bootstrap-takeover-closure-and-the-recovery-dead-end.md`
  separates the bootstrap record's three claims, sets the non-vacuity
  conditions for the takeover lap, withdraws the forged-record reader test as
  meaningless (the reseal check classifies a value the current attempt
  produced, so it is a mint barrier, not a durable reader), and rules that a
  persistent recovery dead end after an ordinary fault is a recovery failure in
  its own right — while ruling out resealing the owner's record REFUSED as the
  repair, because an absent registration does not prove the owner is dead and
  that write would be an unproved concurrent-writer path.

  `docs/rulings/early-revocation-ownership-epoch-split.md` takes up the route
  that would reduce how often the refusal fires: fence while the victim's
  registration still exists. It is implementable as an opportunistic, verified
  revocation of a *storage incarnation* — two state machines, machine
  membership and storage incarnation, with "alive but revoked" as a real
  supported state and a readmission transition that does not require falsely
  declaring the machine dead. It is not implementable by moving the PREEMPT AND
  ABORT earlier: there is no safety-derived interval, the measured 30 s is not a
  guaranteed minimum retention, and the interval must stay out of the safety
  argument entirely. And it does not repair the dead end, because there are two
  retirement obligations and a certificate for the original victim does not
  retire the *prover* that then issued replay writes of its own.

- **What the live-loser lap does and does not establish, which is now a
  defect.** The alive-but-silent victim did everything containment asks of it:
  reservation conflicts on the data path, a PR IN that confirmed its own key
  was gone, a clean self-withdrawal, no shutdown — and, the strongest part, it
  stayed withdrawn after the target later became permissive. But that is
  preservation of a latch **already established**. It says nothing about a
  victim still running when the last reservation disappears. Reading the two
  detection paths rather than assuming them: the reactive one counts SCSI
  RESERVATION CONFLICTs and fires at three, and the proactive one is a periodic
  PR IN where SELF_GONE outranks ABSENT — but its cadence is 5 s only for the
  elected maintainer and **60 s for an auditor**, which in a two-node cluster
  the victim often is. So a victim that issues nothing while the prover dies and
  the appliance purges its registration and the reservation can resume into an
  unreserved LUN, where nothing bounces, with neither detector having run.
  Filed, unmeasured, with the five orderings to inject and what makes each of
  them vacuous.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.18 — the slot binding is enforced a gate earlier than anyone had asserted, and the crash-matrix entry that was next turns out to be a cut already measured

Module srcversion `CCE67219122A8BC75E8BA98`. The binding results below were
measured on `36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343`, before the code change in this version —
nothing in the module moved for them, which is the point: they are findings
about code that was already right and about instruments that were not.

- **The last kind that could certify replay without a retirement proof is
  revoked.** `SINGLE_NODE_EXCLUSIVE` (kind 17) rested on an operator's
  module-load assertion that no other initiator can write the block device,
  plus single-node membership. Both halves are about ADMISSION — which
  INITIATORS may be given permission to write — and the victim of a recovery is
  a previous INCARNATION, whose already-accepted commands the target may still
  be finishing. A replay authorised against those lands as an unordered logical
  write into metadata the replay is rewriting. So the assertion was supplying a
  fact it had never observed, and the design ruling on it is one sentence: *an
  operator parameter may select an operating mode; it must not create a
  retirement witness.*

  It is revoked in the single classifier every reader and the certificate
  constructor both ask, so there is no intermediate state in which one reader
  still honours it. Eight sites moved together: the classifier
  (`dlm/scsipr.c`), the constructor's last exemption (`dlm/disklock.c` — that
  gate now has no exception at all, which is the only shape in which it is a
  choke point), `mxfs_fence_kind_proves_exclusion()`, both producers in
  `dlm/v5_mount.c` (the no-PR leg and the unproven-leg conversion), the
  retirement gate beside them, and the replay-time recheck, which used to
  re-qualify the premise and now refuses outright — re-checking a premise that
  was never sufficient is not a gate.

  The eighth is the one that mattered most and was nearly missed. The
  untagged-replay authority read `desc.fence_kind` **directly**, never asking
  the classifier, so it would still have honoured an older build's durable
  kind 17 after every other path revoked it — and what it authorises is
  applying untagged images, replay's widest permission. It is now constant
  false and says so in the log when it meets such a record.

  The availability cost is real and is the same trade the absent-registration
  kinds already took: a single-node deployment asserting exclusive access can no
  longer replay a previous incarnation's dirty slice. Setting the parameter will
  not unblock a recovery, and the three places that told an operator otherwise —
  the parameter's own description, the `recovery_blocked` debugfs ACTION text,
  and `chk_mxfs`'s remedy — now say what actually clears it: bring the victim
  back so its registration exists and a PREEMPT AND ABORT has something to name.

  Measured on the 2-node TCP rig, and the pair of laps is the point. The
  **mint barrier**: with `single_node_exclusive=1` read back in force on the
  prover and the victim power-cut, the fence refused exactly as it does with the
  assertion absent — 3 refusals, zero certificates of any kind, the gate not
  even attempted, no single-node certificate leg, no kind-17 certificate
  (`tests/fence_gate_basis.sh`, new `snexcl` arm). The **all-reader row**: a
  forged durable kind 17 driven through the consuming side is refused naming the
  revocation, 121 refusals, zero replays, the record byte-identical afterwards
  (`tests/fence_kind_matrix.sh single17`, `fails=0`, which also moves that arm
  from the matrix's supported side to its revoked side). And the **regression
  guard**, because "nothing certifies any more" is also what a build that
  certifies nothing looks like: a real PREEMPT AND ABORT against a registered
  victim still earns `PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1` with
  `retire_basis=completed-target-op`, the slice is replayed, and all 32 fsynced
  files come back byte-identical from the survivor (`tests/fence_strong_basis.sh`,
  `fails=0`).

- **A forged certificate pointed at the wrong slot is refused before its class
  is ever read.** The four binding arms ask whether a fence KIND plus the
  descriptor's existing fields actually binds a certificate to the recovery it
  authorises. Three of them refuse at the claim gate and name the missing or
  wrong field. `bind_slot` refuses much earlier, in
  `recov_outcome_structural()` (`dlm/disklock.c:1868`), which compares the
  heartbeat slot the sector was READ FROM against the descriptor's own
  `victim_slot` and returns `-EPROTO`, "misplaced/copied record: names another
  slot". The consuming side turns that into a fail-closed filesystem-wide
  quarantine and denies admission in 1 s. That comparison has to exist for a
  reason worth restating: the descriptor CRC binds the *sector's*
  `{fs_gen, node_id, epoch}`, and those bytes travel with a byte-copied record,
  so `victim_slot` is the only thing tying a record to the slot it was found in.
  The arm's discriminator is `proven23`, which forges the same kind, the same
  reservation type and the same correct CRC with `victim_slot` equal to its own
  slot: it passes this gate and is stopped later at the claim. One gate, one
  field, isolated by the pair.

  `bind_fsgen` answers the same question with something stronger than a field
  comparison. `recov_desc_of()` verifies the descriptor CRC against the identity
  in the record HEADER (`dlm/disklock.c:1631`); the claim gate recomputes the
  same CRC from the descriptor's OWN `victim_fs_gen`/`victim_node`/
  `victim_epoch` (`:8164`). One seal cannot satisfy both unless they agree, so
  the victim identity triple is **unforgeable at any checksum**, not merely
  checked. On the rig: 121 refusals, zero replays, the mount held shut after the
  full 124 s admission bound, and the certificate on the platter byte-identical
  afterwards.

- **Two faults in the instrument, and both were grading laps that never
  happened.** `mount(8)` prints "already mounted or mount point busy" for every
  `-EBUSY` the syscall returns, and two different things return it here: a
  leftover holder of the mountpoint, where the kernel never saw a mount at all,
  and the admission barrier itself refusing after spending its whole bound. The
  vacuity gate keyed on the message alone and exited *before* taking the kernel
  window, so a 123 s refusal — the measurement — was thrown away and reported as
  a lap that did not happen. The window is now taken first and the discriminator
  is the kernel's own record of having started a mount in this lap's window.
  Separately, a lap that ended early restored the platter but left the reader
  unmounted, because the remount lived at the bottom of the happy path; the next
  arm then aborted on its "the reader is mounted" precondition, so one early
  exit cost two laps. Both the sector and the fleet are now put back on every
  exit.

- **The matrix gains a cut inside the replay, where the ranking says the
  corruption is.** Every cut it had was around the PROOF. The consult ranked
  replay ordering first among the remaining gaps that can actually corrupt: a
  durable prefix replayed twice performs a non-idempotent allocation, free or
  link update twice, and a completion marker that advances over an unapplied
  suffix makes a successor skip work and then discard the only copy of it.

  Reaching that state turned out not to be a matter of picking a cut number.
  **A foreign-slice replay does not write incrementally.** Every image it
  applies is held in core and submitted ONCE at the end of the pass, because a
  mid-pass write can put an intermediate image of a block on the platter ahead
  of the head transaction that overlays it, fail the write verifier, and get
  the whole slice refused. There is also no durable progress cursor anywhere in
  `dlm/` or `xfs/` — replay is LSN-gated and idempotent instead. So the only
  place a durable prefix can coexist with an unissued required suffix is
  *inside* that final submission, which is exactly where a real crash leaves
  it, since the submission is many separate writes and nothing makes them
  atomic.

  Cut 7 splits the list there: the first `dbg_replay_cut_prefix` buffers are
  submitted, waited for and flushed, the remainder are left unissued, and the
  pass parks so the node can be destroyed. Nothing downstream runs, so no
  completion marker advances, no slice is retired or zeroed, and the source
  journal is intact. It refuses a vacuous cut loudly — a prefix that would take
  the whole list leaves no suffix, and "everything was applied" is the ordinary
  success this lap exists to differ from — and it is filtered by victim slot
  **and incarnation**, which needed a new `l_mxfs_victim_epoch` on the shadow
  log: a slot number is reused by whoever claims it next, so a one-shot
  filtered on the slot alone can fire on a different victim than the lap set it
  for.

  Two stale predictions in `tests/fence_crash_cuts.sh` were found while wiring
  it up, both of which would have failed a correct certificate. It still
  predicted `PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE`, the code point retired in 0.89.16 — a
  completed operation has earned `PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1` since — and its kind
  parser was `[A-Z_]*`, which truncates that name at the version digit. The
  banked cut sweeps ran on 0.89.10, before either change. The destroyed-victim
  arm is now noted as unable to reach a certificate at all on a purging target,
  since the absent-registration kinds it rested on are revoked; that refusal is
  `tests/fence_gate_basis.sh`'s subject, not this harness's.

- **The crash matrix's next entry was a cut it already had.** The record's own
  next step proposed arming the lost-response injection and then killing the
  prover, so that a successor would meet the ambiguous descriptor. It is cut 4
  under another name: both histories leave the same durable attempt descriptor,
  the same *completed* PREEMPT AND ABORT at the target, no outstanding instance
  of that command, and a destroyed prover whose differing volatile belief
  nobody can observe. A design consult made that closure conditional on four
  equivalence checks, and all four hold from the code and the version history:
  the injection substitutes its result only after a GOOD completion
  (`pal/linux/kern.c:3865`), so no error handling or reconnection is induced;
  the ambiguous leg persists nothing durable — `v5_fence_block_ambiguous()`
  (`dlm/v5_mount.c:7490`) sets only in-memory state, and the durable
  `mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_mark_blocked()` is reached solely from the
  "submitted NO command" branch (`:10028`); arming the injection is a
  module-parameter write and issues no SCSI traffic; and the banked cut-4 laps
  ran on 0.89.10, after the takeover marker conversion landed in 0.89.9.

  What the same consult would *not* accept is the argument that the
  late-command hazard is unreachable here. "The target purges registrations on
  session loss" plus "two nodes" gives no happens-before edge between the target
  finishing the predecessor's teardown and the successor activating new
  authority; a successor's fresh command against the victim does not retire a
  pending command from the *predecessor's* nexus; and a restarted incarnation of
  the prover is itself a successor without needing a third node. The obligation
  is also narrower than it looked — not "no old command may execute late" but
  "no old command may affect a later valid incarnation" — which makes victim-key
  reuse the thing that has to be proved. The ruling, the ranked list of what
  actually gates an integrity-and-stability release, and the entries that should
  stop being separate laps are in
  `docs/rulings/fence-matrix-remaining-gates-and-partial-replay.md`.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.17 — a build may not mint a certificate it would refuse to read, and the revoked classes are now reachable on purpose

Module srcversion `36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343`. The previous version made a fence
KIND the durable identifier of a proof contract, routed every consuming reader
through one classifier, and revoked the classes whose contracts had been
rejected. What it could not do was show the refusal firing: a build only ever
mints the kinds it still supports, so a durable certificate of a revoked class
is a state the software cannot reach by running. That state is exactly what an
older build left on the platter, and it is the whole subject of the defect.
This version reaches it two ways and grades what happens.

- **The certificate constructor asks the same question the readers ask.**
  `mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_certify()` gated on
  `mxfs_fence_kind_proves_exclusion()` — a second, hand-maintained list of code
  points, which still admits 19, 20 and 21, the classes consumption revokes.
  It now calls `mxfs_fence_durable_kind_supported()`. Nothing reachable today
  passes it a revoked kind, so this changes no behaviour on any path a lap can
  drive; it removes the *shape*, which is the one the design ruling names —
  delete every authorisation decision equivalent to `kind == 16 || kind == 19`.
  The asymmetry is why it is worth doing. Two lists drift, and they drift in a
  direction that cannot be undone: a build that MINTS a kind it would REFUSE to
  read seals a descriptor nothing will ever act on, and a sealed descriptor
  answers `-EEXIST` to every later prover, so that slice could never be
  certified by anybody again. Minting is now a subset of consumption by
  construction. `mxfs_fence_kind_proves_exclusion()` stays, documented for what
  it is: "did this attempt, just now, prove anything", a question about a fresh
  result in the caller's stack, never an authorisation gate and never upstream
  of a durable write.

- **`tools/recov_forge` can write a certificate.** It could already put a
  recovery-guard record in an unused heartbeat slot with the CRC and identity
  binding recomputed; it could not fill in the certificate fields, so every
  record it made read as an intent. `--fence-kind` (with `--fence-resv`,
  `--fence-key`, `--fence-prover`, `--fence-prover-epoch`, `--fence-term`) and
  `--desc-version` now produce a complete replay authorisation of any class,
  including classes no build will ever mint again and one from a build that
  does not exist. `--fence-kind` implies stage FENCED unless a stage is given,
  because a certificate below that stage is refused at the stage gate and the
  arm would grade the wrong thing.

  Two faults in that tool were found by using it. Its help said `--stage 2`
  meant FENCED; 2 has been SNAPSHOTTING since that stage was inserted and
  FENCED is 3. And it set FUA in every CDB, which **the shipping LUN rejects**
  — `sg_raw` on the rig: `88 08 …` gives ILLEGAL REQUEST / invalid field in
  CDB, `88 00 …` returns the sector, `88 10 …` (DPO) is rejected too — so not
  one command it issued against that target had ever completed. The kernel's
  own passthrough has handled this for a long time by latching the rejection
  and falling back; every userspace tool that builds its own CDB is a separate
  implementation and inherits none of that. The tool now mirrors the kernel:
  drop FUA, retry once, latch it, and say on stderr what was given up, because
  a non-FUA read is answered wherever the target likes rather than forced from
  the platter.

- **`tests/fence_kind_matrix.sh` drives eight classes through the consuming
  side.** Per arm: forge the class into an unused slot on the real LUN, have a
  node mount into it, and require that the claim is REFUSED naming the class in
  words, that the refusal names the kind actually on the platter, that nothing
  is replayed on either node, and that **the certificate is not relabelled** —
  if a refused class could acquire a supported one by being read, the
  retirement would be undone by the readers enforcing it.

  Two arms carry kinds this build still SUPPORTS — 17 and 23 — with the prover
  incarnation blanked. They are the reason the matrix means anything. A refusal
  is easy to get for the wrong reason, and a matrix that only counts refusals
  cannot tell a working classifier from a gate rejecting everything for an
  unrelated cause. Those two must refuse for the missing field and name no
  revoked class, which is a positive measurement of the classifier passing a
  kind through. No arm presents a fully valid certificate, deliberately: an
  accepted one would authorise replaying a journal slice belonging to a live
  filesystem, and the arm that proves acceptance works is a real fence on a
  real victim.

**Verified on the 2-node TCP rig. Eleven laps, every one `fails=0`.**

The eight forged classes, on `36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343`, each its own
`tests/evidence/20260920T11*_fkm_s84b_*` directory:

| arm | on the platter | what the reader said | mount |
|---|---|---|---|
| `retired16` | kind 16 | `RETIRED code point 16: it had two producers…` | rc=32 at 124 s |
| `revoked19` | kind 19 | `REVOKED kind 19: it rested on 'the old task set died…'` | rc=32 at 124 s |
| `gate20` | kind 20, single-holder resv | `REVOKED absent-registration kind…` | rc=32 at 124 s |
| `boot21` | kind 21 | `REVOKED absent-registration kind…` | rc=32 at 124 s |
| `unknown99` | kind 99 | `the record carries no fence kind this build can classify` | rc=32 at 123 s |
| `oldversion` | descriptor version 4 | no class named — refused at the shape gate | rc=32 at **2 s** |
| `single17` | kind 17, no prover | `certificate names no prover incarnation` | rc=32 at 123 s |
| `proven23` | kind 23, no prover | `certificate names no prover incarnation` | rc=32 at 124 s |

Every arm: zero recovery completions on either node, the certificate on the
platter byte-identical after the refusal, no `BUG`, `Oops` or filesystem
shutdown, and the survivor serving throughout.

And the injected pair, which reach the same refusal through the kernel's own
fence path rather than through a forgery —
`tests/fence_strong_basis.sh s84a legacy16` (429 s,
`tests/evidence/20260920T105022Z_fsb_s84a_legacy16`) and `s84b legacy19`
(429 s, `…T105732Z_fsb_s84b_legacy19`): the fence runs for real, proves
exclusion, and the kind is substituted at the durable write, so the record on
the platter carries a revoked contract over an outcome that was genuinely
proved. Both refused at the claim gate, named the class, replayed nothing.

**The path that must still work was proved still working on the new build**,
because "everything is refused now" is also what a build that certifies nothing
looks like: `tests/fence_strong_basis.sh s84d proven` (138 s,
`tests/evidence/20260920T114813Z_fsb_s84d_proven`) — certified 65 s after the
victim went silent, `kind=PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1`,
`retire_basis=completed-target-op`, zero certificates under the retired code
point, the slice replayed, and all 32 files the victim fsynced read back from
the SURVIVOR byte-identical. That lap is what says the constructor's new gate
did not close the one door that has to stay open.

**Two things this measured that are not improvements, and both are now records
of their own.**

A mount that meets a certificate it cannot classify is **bounded, not hung**:
rc=32 at 123-124 s on every classifying arm, against the barrier's own printed
deadline — `P-BARRIER-GHOST-EXTEND undeclared=1 window_ms=62000
bound_ms=122000`. A guard slot with no live heartbeat is an undeclared death,
which buys the barrier's one-time extension. The contrast in the table is worth
keeping: a descriptor whose VERSION cannot be validated is refused in 2 s. The
barrier waits for a certificate it understands and rejects, because a prover
might still appear, and does not wait for one it cannot parse.

But the refusal is permanent, and **no operator route out of it is finished**.
`chk_mxfs --accept-quarantine-loss` says so in its own header — it implements
steps 1 to 4 of its ruling and stops before the destructive ones — and it keys
on a quarantined outcome record, which a revoked certificate is not. So a fleet
upgrading with such a record on the platter has every node refuse to mount it,
with no way out but mkfs. That is availability, not integrity: nothing is
corrupted and nothing hangs. It does not gate the 2-node TCP release and it is
in the queue with the measurement attached.

**Two records leave the queue with this version.** The proof-provenance
defect itself — a corrected build honouring a certificate minted under rejected
rules — is fixed and verified by the eleven laps above. And the record that
said the legacy refusal for kinds 20 and 21 "has never been exercised" is
answered by the `gate20` and `boot21` arms: it asked for a two-build lap or an
offline image driven through a usermode predicate, and got the real LUN, the
real mount path and the real classifier instead. Neither was closed by
inspection; the state was produced and run.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.16 — the deployment could assert the fact the target would not report, and now nothing may: the qualification is withdrawn in code

Module srcversion 58E59BC3EDFEB799DD889C8. A certificate that authorises
replaying a dead node's journal slice needs two separate facts. ADMISSION —
the dead incarnation cannot obtain permission for a NEW write — is what a
registration table and a reservation establish. RETIREMENT — the target has
finished with the commands it ALREADY TOOK from that incarnation's nexus — is a
property of the target, and no SPC command reports it after the fact. 0.89.13
made the second one mandatory; 0.89.13 and 0.89.15 also let the DEPLOYMENT
supply it, by asserting the ordering for the exact target, firmware level and
LUN it had been qualified against. This version removes that second way in.

- **A deployment clause is no longer a retirement basis, and the removal is in
  the code rather than in a configuration file.** An environmental assertion is
  not a witness: the module cannot detect a target that breaks it, and the
  clause this project shipped had exactly four probe laps behind it, each
  observing no late write inside a 180 s window sampled at 50 ms. That
  characterises one appliance under one workload; it cannot exclude a command
  the target retained without it ever becoming observable. A replay authorised
  against such a command lands as an unordered logical write into metadata the
  replay is rewriting — silent corruption, against a refusal that costs only
  availability. `mxfs_scsipr_retire_proof()` now returns NONE for every clause,
  the certificate constructor refuses any replay-authorising kind whose basis is
  not a completed target operation, and no module parameter, elapsed interval,
  retry or operator override re-enables it.

- **A configured contract is REJECTED out loud, not ignored.** The parameter is
  still read for one reason: a deployment that qualified its LUN and set the
  string must be told the qualification is no longer accepted, rather than left
  to infer it from a refusal that never mentions it.
  `P303-RETIRE-CONTRACT-REJECTED` names the value verbatim, on its own line
  because carrying it inside the refusal's reason buffer would have made it the
  part that truncated away. `data/rigs.json` keeps the withdrawn string and the
  measurements behind it as history, under a key nothing ships.

- **Legacy authority does not survive the upgrade.** The on-disk descriptor
  records the fence KIND but not the basis the prover used, so a certificate
  written by an earlier build cannot be asked what it stood on. It does not have
  to be: `BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT` and `EXCLUSIVE_WRITE_GATE` are reachable only
  from the victim's registration already being absent, which leaves nothing for
  a PREEMPT AND ABORT to name, so neither could ever have been minted on a
  completed target operation. Both are now refused where a certificate is
  consumed as well as where one is minted.

- **What is left that still certifies**, unchanged: a completed PREEMPT AND
  ABORT that named a registration still present on the target. Its abort scope
  is the one the standard defines for it, and it is a witness rather than an
  assertion.

**The availability this costs, stated plainly.** On a target that purges a
registration with its iSCSI session — which is what the rig does, 30-46 s after
a power cut, while death is not declared for ~66 s — a node that dies can no
longer have its journal slice replayed at all, so it cannot rejoin and the
survivor cannot reach metadata in its domain. That is a real loss and it is
filed as its own record. It is not a defect in this change: the route it closes
was authorised by an assertion nobody could check.

**Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, four laps, every one `fails=0`.** Both paths
that could reach a certificate from an absent registration were run twice, once
with the module holding the exact string that used to certify and once holding
nothing:

- `tests/fence_retire_basis.sh` (boot succession, kind 21) — `declared`
  (`tests/evidence/20260920T085505Z_frb_s83b_declared`, wall 459 s) and `none`
  (`20260920T090255Z_frb_s83c_none`, 464 s). Four refusals each, ZERO
  certificates, the victim's mount refused with rc=32, the victim not mounted.
- `tests/fence_gate_basis.sh` (sole-survivor exclusive-write gate, kind 20) —
  `declared` (`20260920T091135Z_fgb_s83d_declared`, 445 s) and `none`
  (`20260920T091903Z_fgb_s83e_none`, 448 s). Three refusals each, zero
  certificates of any kind, and `gate_try=0`: an exclusion that cannot be
  certified is not even attempted, so no single-holder reservation is installed
  that nothing would be left to release.

**And the path that must still work was proved still working**, because
"nothing is certified any more" is also what a build that certifies nothing at
all looks like. `tests/fence_strong_basis.sh` is new and runs the other
direction: the victim is NOT power-cut, its heartbeat thread is parked while
its session, mount and PR registration stay up, so the prover declares it dead
with its registration STILL IN THE TARGET'S TABLE — the one case the surviving
basis is written for, and one a power cut can never produce on a target that
purges a registration with its session. `s83h`, `fails=0`, wall 286 s
(`tests/evidence/20260920T094141Z_fsb_s83h`): the prover certified 67 s after
the silence, `kind=PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE`, `retire_basis=completed-target-op`,
`claim=preempt-abort-named-the-victim-registration`; the victim's journal slice
was replayed; and all 32 files it had fsynced before the fence were read back
from the SURVIVOR byte-identical. No certificate of an absent-registration kind,
no refusal, no BUG or Oops, no LU reset.

Each lap additionally required the refusal to be TERMINAL AND BOUNDED rather
than a hang — the returning node's mount returns a real failure inside its own
bound and never a timeout kill, and the prover's slot reaches
`P238-FENCE-BLOCKED` after a bounded series (attempts=22, series_ms=121584)
with `P304-FENCE-BLOCKED-DURABLE` on the platter, after which path operations
needing the dead node's grants fail fast with EIO instead of waiting — that the
surviving node stays mounted and keeps serving its own domain, that no BUG,
Oops or filesystem shutdown appeared on either node, and that MXFS issued no
LOGICAL UNIT RESET (it has no path to one, and a bystander initiator is
destroyed by one: measured in `tests/lu_reset_probe.sh` as D state in
`blk_io_schedule` with no error, no timeout and no retry).

**Two instrument defects were caught on the way and corrected rather than
believed**: a kernel-log window taken with no mark dumped the whole ring and
counted a LU reset the PREVIOUS session's probe had issued five hours earlier;
and a survivor-liveness check that created a directory in the mount root was
grading the dead node's domain, which is refused by design — it now writes into
a directory the survivor took before the cut, and reports the outcome as a
finding while grading only that the operation returned rather than hung.

**The harnesses lost the arms that no longer distinguish anything.**
`fence_retire_basis.sh` and `fence_gate_basis.sh` were built around one arm that
certified and several that refused for different reasons about the contract's
fields. With no clause accepted, a wrong firmware, a withdrawn clause and a
forced replacement observation all produce the identical refusal, so both
harnesses are now two arms — `declared` and `none` — and both refuse. Both also
abort if `data/rigs.json` ever declares an active contract again.

The design consult that ruled this (Astra, session 83) is recorded with the
routes it ranks in
`docs/rulings/retirement-witness-routes-lu-reset-early-preempt-or-refuse.md`,
and what a refusal means for an operator is in
`docs/retirement-witness-and-what-refusal-means.md`.

### And a second change under the same version: a fence kind is now a proof contract, and one that had two producers is retired

Module srcversion `D4C0B9A325D300FBDA8F9FD`. This is the first step of a
second design-consult ruling (Astra, session 83), banked at
`docs/rulings/fence-certificate-proof-profiles-and-legacy-revocation.md`. It
narrows an earlier prescription rather than repeating it: a replay-authorising
certificate does **not** need a new on-disk proof block, because a versioned
fence KIND can carry the proof contract — but tightening what an existing kind
means cannot repair the instances already written under it.

- **`PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE` (16) is retired and `PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1` (23)
  takes its place.** Not renamed — retired. The counterexample is in this tree:
  the fence path wrote kind 16 after a PREEMPT AND ABORT that named a present
  registration, completed and verified its post-state, and the bootstrap-owner
  takeover wrote *the same value* after reading its own PR ledger, with no
  operation run in that attempt at all. A reader handed the record cannot tell
  the two apart, so the code point cannot be classified into a proof contract
  and no amount of tightening makes an old 16 mean the sound thing. The fresh
  value is produced only by the completed-operation path, and its meaning will
  never be widened or reassigned: if its rules are ever found unsound,
  consumption of *that value* is disabled and a new one is allocated.

- **Every reader that did not mint the certificate now asks one function.**
  `mxfs_fence_durable_kind_supported(record_family, kind, &why)` is the single
  place that answers "can this build classify this durable record into a proof
  contract it still supports?", and the recovery-descriptor consumer, the
  bootstrap-owner acceptance check and the mount-time takeover check all go
  through it. That matters more than the answer: the previous shape was three
  separate `kind == 16 || kind == 19` tests, so a revoked class could be
  honoured by whichever reader nobody remembered to update. Refusal is the
  default for anything unclassifiable, including a kind this build has never
  heard of, and each refusal names the revoked class rather than saying "no".

- **`SELF_SUCCESSION_DONE` (19) is revoked at consumption, not only at mint.**
  The previous version stopped minting it, because its reasoning — "the old
  task set died with the old session" — does not survive examination: a REGISTER
  AND IGNORE that replaces a key on the *same* nexus forces no session outcome,
  so the old nexus may still be live with its earlier tasks active. Records
  already carrying it were still being honoured by three readers. Nothing here
  needs each instance shown to be unsound; what is missing is a supported,
  sound interpretation, and that is the test.

- **The bootstrap takeover no longer manufactures a certificate from its own
  bookkeeping.** Three branches used to answer "the victim's key is absent from
  the target" with a fence kind: the node's PR ledger saying FENCED, the ledger
  saying RETIRED, and a boot boundary showing this boot's key had replaced the
  old one on our own nexus. None ran an operation. A ledger status is this
  cluster's record that some incarnation *believed* a removal happened — never
  a target-side fact about the work it had already accepted. All three are
  gone; the takeover keeps only the branch that actually issues the PREEMPT AND
  ABORT and requires the completed profile back, and otherwise refuses with a
  message that says what it would have accepted. Reusing a prior proof is not
  ruled out in principle — a durable certificate of an earlier completed
  operation, revalidated through the same classifier, would be legitimate
  evidence. These labels are not that.

**Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, three laps, every one `fails=0`**, all on
`D4C0B9A325D300FBDA8F9FD`:

- `tests/fence_strong_basis.sh s83j` (140 s,
  `tests/evidence/20260920T095727Z_fsb_s83j`) — the fence certified 65 s after
  the victim went silent, `kind=PREEMPT_ABORT_PROVEN_V1`, zero certificates
  under the retired code point, the slice replayed, all 32 fsynced files read
  back from the survivor byte-identical. The certificate is minted, sealed and
  then consumed through the new classifier, so this lap exercises both ends.
- `tests/fence_retire_basis.sh s83k declared` (456 s) and
  `tests/fence_gate_basis.sh s83l none` (444 s) — the withdrawal laps re-run
  unchanged on the new build: zero certificates, `gate_try=0`, mount refused at
  rc=32 inside its bound, survivor still serving, no BUG, Oops, filesystem
  shutdown or LU reset on either node.

**What this does NOT yet claim, which is why the record stays open.** The
bootstrap-owner producer and reader changes are not exercised by any lap on
this rig — a bootstrap takeover needs a whole-cluster restart, and the harness
that drives one (`tests/bootstrap_seal_fence.sh`) is a 32-node CAW shape. The
ruling names the arm that would do it: use the *old* bootstrap path to write
kind 16 from both FENCED and RETIRED ledger state, then require the corrected
readers to refuse those records with no replay writes and no relabelling. The
operator's single-node topology assertion (kind 17) is deliberately untouched
here and is carried unchanged; it is the next step of the same ruling and has
its own record.

**A second availability withdrawal, stated plainly.** On a target that purges a
registration with its iSCSI session, a bootstrap takeover whose victim's key is
already gone now refuses, exactly as boot succession does. That is the same
trade as the clause withdrawal — the recovery route costs availability, and
authorising it from a ledger label costs integrity — and it is recorded against
the same availability defect.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.15 — a deployment's contract is a conditional, and the code now has to establish its premise instead of matching a string

Module srcversion 8DD801C7A88FEF5E39B9BDE. This finishes the two fence kinds
that authorised replay from a registration's absence, and then corrects the
ground the 0.89.13 package stood on — a design consult, asked while verifying
the fix, showed the fix itself resting on an inference nobody could make.
Ruling banked at `docs/rulings/retirement-proof-obligation-and-observed-transition-classes.md`;
it supersedes the previous one where they differ.

- **A fence kind that certifies from a key's absence now refuses unless the
  deployment's clause covers the transition that was actually observed.** The
  shipped clause said: *for this LUN, every command the target accepted from a
  **lost nexus** completed or aborted before that nexus's registration
  disappears.* That is an implication, and matching the vendor, product,
  firmware and LUN establishes only that the deployment asserted it — never
  that **this** registration disappeared **because the nexus was lost**. No
  initiator can establish that: the target does not report why a registration
  left its table. So the same clause was authorising replay after any absence,
  including one that MXFS itself caused by replacing the key — the exact case
  the previous version refuses outright under its own kind. The clause is now
  written about the thing that can be observed
  (`unreplaced-registration-absence-retires-before-purge`), the prover
  classifies what it observed, and a clause covers exactly one observation.

- **The observed transition is recorded as a fact, separately from the claim
  made about it.** `no-mxfs-successor-observed`, `mxfs-replacement-same-boot`,
  `mxfs-replacement-different-boot`, `victim-registration-present` — and
  `unknown`, which every clause refuses rather than treating as the covered
  one. None of them is a retirement claim on its own. In particular a boot
  boundary is not a target-side ordering witness: an iSCSI connection, an iSCSI
  session, a SCSI I_T nexus and an MXFS boot identity are four identifiers with
  four different lifetimes, and an initiator instance outside the restarted
  component can outlive all of them. The certificate's log line now names the
  basis, the claim and the observation, so what a certificate stood on is one
  grep rather than an inference from its kind.

- **The obligation is enforced where every path already crosses.** Proving
  exclusion answers whether the victim can be given permission for a NEW write.
  It says nothing about the writes the target already accepted, and a replay
  against those lands as an unordered logical write into metadata the replay is
  rewriting. So the certificate constructor now refuses a replay-authorising
  kind that arrives with no retirement basis, whichever classification path
  reached it, and the prover treats a missing proof as a classification outcome
  rather than a publication failure it would retry forever. The one kind
  admitted without a basis is the operator's single-node topology assertion; it
  logs that it was admitted, and it is now an open defect in its own right
  instead of an unexamined exemption.

- **The lost-certificate republish re-derives its proof instead of assuming
  it.** 0.89.14 republishes a gate certificate whose write was lost, reading
  the reservation back rather than re-proving it. The admission half is what
  that read establishes; the retirement half was never carried in the blocked
  record, so it is established again from the standing clause and the ledger.
  If either has changed, the republish is refused and the verdict stays
  blocked.

- **The old clause is still recognised, and always refused.** A deployment that
  never re-qualified must find out, not be certified from a premise nobody
  established — the refusal names the clause and says why it can never apply.
  `data/rigs.json` re-asserts the rig's qualification under the new wording,
  with what the four probe laps actually measured (power cuts: nexus losses
  with no MXFS replacement) and what the clause additionally requires (no agent
  outside the cluster issuing persistent-reservation commands against this
  LUN), stated rather than assumed.

**Measured, `tests/fence_gate_basis.sh`, six arms, every one `fails=0`:**
`qualified` 290 s — the gate certifies, names `retire_basis=qualified-contract`
with its claim and observation, the victim's slice is replayed and all 32
fsynced files come back byte-identical. `none` 443 s, `wrongfw` 450 s,
`oldclause` 450 s — three refusals, zero certificates of any kind, the peer
refused its mount (`MOUNT_RC=32`), and the gate **not even attempted**: an
exclusion that cannot be certified is never taken, because a single-holder
Write Exclusive with no recovery to release it locks the returning incarnation
out of the LUN entirely. `sameboot` 453 s and `diffboot` 452 s — the two
replacement observations refused, each naming what it observed and that the
clause's premise does not hold. No shutdown, BUG or Oops on either node in any
lap.

The replacement arms force the observation through a test-only knob, and say so
in the log and in the lap's own assertions: this target purges a registration
within ~34 s while a node needs ~150 s to return, so a returning incarnation
always registers a fresh key and those two transitions cannot be produced here
by timing. An unexercised refusal is one nobody has seen fire.

**Regression, all `fails=0` on the shipped build:** `fence_retire_basis`
qualified 340 s — boot succession still certifies under the corrected clause
and records the basis it rested on, which is exactly what rewording the clause
could have broken; `fence_rejoin_barrier` 349 s; `fence_cert_publish` spent
299 s; and `fence_lost_response` 763 s, whose three phases are the hardest
regression in this area — an operation needing the unrecovered slice's grants
refused with EIO in 0 s instead of hanging, nothing certified across 240 s
while the victim was still alive in its original incarnation, and the slice
replayed with all 64 fsynced files byte-identical once the boot boundary
supplied the proof.

**Two harness defects fixed on the way, both of which had already manufactured
a verdict.** A lap that exited early between the power cut and the restart left
the victim powered off, and the *next* lap spent its entire budget polling a
corpse and then power-cycling it — the restoration is now on an exit trap and
the boot wait asks the hypervisor before it polls ssh. And the refusal's reason
was composed context-first into a 220-byte buffer, so the sentence the lap
graded on was truncated away while the refusal itself was correct; a reason
that can be truncated now leads with its finding.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.14 — a prover publishes the proof it still holds instead of asking a question its own fence has made unanswerable, and a rejoining node is admitted on recovery being COMPLETE rather than on the manifest being sealed

Module srcversion A61384738B9AFD449E985DD. This closes the post-submit
ambiguity work. Three of the defects fixed here were found by running the
harnesses, not by reading the code, and one of the four "failures" that started
the session turned out to be the harness asserting something it had itself made
impossible.

- **A survivor's own exclusive-write gate locked the returning peer out of the
  heartbeat that would have proved it dead.** The sole-survivor gate is a
  single-holder Write Exclusive reservation under the survivor's key, so no
  other initiator may write the LUN. When the survivor proved exclusion and
  then failed to publish the certificate, its recovery never completed and the
  gate was never converted back — and the returning victim could not publish
  its PR key (`reservation conflict`, `P-PRKEY-PUBLISHED … rc=-52 … refusing`,
  `TCP SCSI PR register failed — aborting mount`), so it never claimed a slot,
  never heartbeated, and could never become the "host live under a later boot"
  that boot succession waits for. Measured: the survivor asked seven times and
  got `P238-BOOTSUCC-HOST-NOT-LIVE` seven times; the cluster stayed at one node
  permanently. **A liveness route whose precondition is an action the node's own
  exclusion forbids is not slow, it is dead.**

- **The answer was still standing on the target, so it is read rather than
  re-derived.** The survivor's own completed PREEMPT AND ABORT installed that
  gate and the gate is still held under its own key: what was lost is the
  certificate WRITE, not the exclusion. The revisit now re-reads the
  reservation (PERSISTENT RESERVE IN only — no command is issued, nothing
  changes) and republishes the kind this attempt actually proved, guarded on
  remembering that it proved the gate, on the reservation still being the
  single-holder form under our key, and never for a victim key that is our own.
  Anything else leaves the blocked verdict standing. This is publication of a
  proof already held, never a fresh proof.

- **The revisit gate could fire exactly once, because the function that read it
  destroyed what it read.** The acquire path records a generic "no certificate"
  verdict on its fall-through, overwriting the specific "proved, certificate
  unconfirmed" verdict the gate keys on — and an attempt that proves through the
  gate submits no command needing a durable boundary, so the other arm of the
  condition was never set either. Measured before: one revisit, then five
  further visits 30 s apart that printed the holder state and did nothing.
  After: seven. A generic verdict may no longer erase the specific one it is the
  consequence of.

- **A slice blocked with an unpublished proof now tells its waiters to fail
  fast.** That marking existed only for the ambiguous case; the unpublished case
  left acquires sitting on a budget that never expires, so the survivor could
  not unmount or unload — the prep that followed such a lap reported
  `did not release mxfs` and had to power-cycle the node. It certifies nothing,
  grants nothing, clears nothing and does not re-arm retry.

- **The liveness observation is an event again, not a 30 s sample.** 0.89.13
  made the revisit react to the victim's host returning under a different boot,
  but left that fact being ASKED only where the acquire path reaches the slot —
  a ~30 s cadence, against a returning peer's 30 s mount barrier. One lap passed
  and three failed on that coin flip. Both questions are in-core, so the
  always-on worker now asks them at its own 250 ms tick and reads the platter
  only once the observation has flipped. Measured: noticing to sealed is now
  **5.1 s** (`P238-FENCE-RESUME-BOOTLIVE-FAST` 5172.1 → `P236-FENCE-CERTIFIED`
  5174.8 → `P236-FENCE-SEALED` 5177.2). Proving was never the slow part.

- **The PREEMPT AND ABORT is submitted with no midlayer retry.** It is a
  state-changing command, and the retry count is the number of times the block
  layer may re-issue the CDB on its own after error handling, invisibly to the
  caller. The damaging schedule is a lockout: the target exceeds the timeout
  while draining the victim's task set, error handling aborts, the midlayer
  re-issues, the FIRST execution already removed the victim's registration so
  the SECOND returns RESERVATION CONFLICT — and the caller, seeing only the
  second result, refuses to certify an exclusion that was achieved, with the
  victim key now consumed. One execution attempt per call leaves the honest
  state instead. The bounded unit-attention reissue is kept: a unit attention is
  reported INSTEAD of executing the command, so it is not a second execution.

- **"Sealed" is not what admits a rejoining node — "recovered" is, and that is
  now measured rather than argued.** Sealing freezes the LIST of the dead node's
  journal work; it does not perform it, and the window between them is about
  8.6 s on this rig — too short to steer a returning peer into. `tests/
  fence_rejoin_barrier.sh` holds it open on purpose (`dbg_replay_hold_ms`, which
  parks the foreign-replay worker AFTER the execution lease is claimed and
  BEFORE the slice is replayed, in workqueue context so the heartbeat is
  untouched). **`RESULT: PASS fails=0`**, twice: with the slice sealed, claimed
  and unreplayed the peer asked for its filesystem and was REFUSED
  (`MOUNT_RC=32`, and the hold provably still in force when the attempt
  returned), and once the hold released the slice replayed in 6 s, the peer
  mounted (`MOUNT_RC=0`) and all 32 files it fsynced before the cut came back
  byte-identical.

- **A successor issuing its own PREEMPT AND ABORT against a victim whose
  predecessor may still have one in flight is not a defect**, and the guard
  that was proposed for it would have created a lockout. With distinct keys
  naming the same victim, whichever transition takes effect first leaves the
  other finding no matching key; the late command cannot redirect its preemption
  to the successor because it does not name it. What makes this safe is that the
  inherited marker is HISTORY rather than a submission by the successor, and
  that an absent key is never read as the dead term's success. Routing an
  inherited ambiguity to the read-only path instead would strand a successor
  with the victim still registered, no independent proof, and no command it is
  allowed to issue. The recovery lease cannot authorise replay without the
  certificate gate, which is what makes the takeover's ignored prove-return
  harmless — checked, not assumed.

- **Ownership is re-validated at the proof commit, and already was.** A CAS
  protects a validated expected image; it does not validate that image. The
  certificate's authority token is issued once when the fencing intent is laid
  and carried unchanged to the commit, which re-reads the descriptor, checks it
  against that captured token — prover incarnation, owner, fence term, victim
  incarnation, recovery generation — and CASes against the validated image. A
  takeover moves the term and the owner, so a stale proof cannot be published
  under adopted authority.

- **Two harness defects, both of which produced false product verdicts.** The
  spent-window arm armed an injector that fails EVERY certificate write, then
  asserted the peer gets its filesystem back — which the same injector made
  unreachable rather than merely unmet (`left=64` at the end of the lap). Four
  consecutive laps read as product failures. The injected fault is now cleared
  at the point the transient ends, which is what the arm always meant. And the
  power-cycle wait treated a successful root login as readiness, but pam permits
  root while `/run/nologin` still exists, so every later command came back with
  the banner concatenated onto its output and the node was failed for "no usable
  srcversion — still booting?" immediately after being reset. Three laps thrown
  away in one session; nine preps ran clean afterwards.

- **Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, nine laps, every one `fails=0`, all on build
  A61384738B9AFD449E985DD.** `fence_cert_publish` spent (`294s`, evidence
  `20260920T043947Z_fcp_s81f_spent`), retry (`294s`), lost (`293s`);
  `fence_lost_response` twice (`701s`, `705s` — phase C green repeatedly, not
  once, which is what the ledger record required); `fence_rejoin_barrier`
  (`349s`); `fence_retire_basis` qualified (`328s`), none (`446s`), wrongfw
  (`445s`). No node shut its filesystem down and no BUG or Oops appeared in any
  lap.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.13 — a fence kind that proves only ADMISSION now refuses to certify until something establishes RETIREMENT, and the default is refusal

Module srcversion AD57DB3E758A380E43DD5FE. 0.89.12 wrote down the premise the
boot-succession certificate rests on. A design consult on that package was blunt
about what it had achieved: documenting an unwitnessed dependency is not fixing
it, and a check in a test harness does not constrain a mounted filesystem. The
production path is now gated.

- **The boot-succession certificate is what authorises replaying a dead node's
  journal slice, and it was minted from identity plus admission alone.** Its
  four facts — the victim's frozen (host, boot), that host live again under a
  different boot, no record of the victim's boot still advancing, and a Write
  Exclusive form reservation with the victim's key absent — all say the same
  thing: the dead incarnation cannot obtain permission for a NEW write. None of
  them says the target has finished with the writes it ALREADY ACCEPTED from
  that incarnation's nexus, and a command that executes after the certificate
  lands under the replay as an unordered write into metadata the replay is
  rewriting. No SPC command reports that retirement after the fact, so the
  premise cannot be witnessed from the initiator — which is exactly why it may
  not be assumed. **`v5_boot_succession_consume` now requires a retirement basis
  and refuses without one**: the attempt stays KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN,
  `P238-BOOTSUCC-NO-RETIRE-BASIS` names what was missing, nothing is replayed,
  and the returning victim does not get its filesystem back. That lost
  availability is the intended price. A deployment whose storage guarantee
  nobody established is not a complete configuration for this recovery route,
  and refusing is the only outcome that cannot corrupt.

- **The basis is a per-LUN deployment contract, scoped to the hardware it was
  qualified on — never a global "trust the target" switch.**
  `target_retire_contract=<vendor>:<product>:<revision>:<lun designator>:<clause>`
  is compared against what the LUN itself reports through INQUIRY and its device
  identification VPD page (`mxfs_pal_scsi_target_id`, new in the PAL: the kernel
  reads the scan-time inquiry data and `scsi_vpd_lun_id`, user mode issues the
  two INQUIRYs and mirrors the same designator preference so one contract
  resolves identically in both builds). **The product revision is in the
  contract deliberately**: a firmware upgrade stops the module matching, so a
  qualification has to be re-measured instead of silently inheriting. The only
  clause this build accepts asserts the ORDERING that a fence keyed on
  registration absence actually needs — every command accepted from the lost
  nexus completed or aborted, with its effects ordered before subsequent I/O,
  *before* that nexus's registration disappears. "The target eventually retires
  tasks" is not a usable assertion.

- **A contract is an environmental assertion, never a witness, and the
  certificate now says which it rested on.** The `P238-FENCE-BOOT-SUCCESSION`
  line carries `retire_basis=qualified-contract` and the identity it matched.
  The distinction is kept in the code as well (`enum mxfs_retire_basis`:
  a completed, correctly scoped target operation is a different claim from a
  deployment's assertion) because the module cannot detect a target that
  violates a contract — what it can do, and now does, is refuse where no
  assertion has been made at all.

- **Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, three arms, all on build
  AD57DB3E758A380E43DD5FE** (`tests/fence_retire_basis.sh`, evidence
  `20260920T015134Z_frb_s80c_qualified`, `…015638Z_frb_s80c_none`,
  `…020403Z_frb_s80c_wrongfw`). Each arm power-cuts the peer after it has
  fsynced 32 files, holds the sole-survivor exclusive-write gate off so boot
  succession is the operative path, and brings the victim back under a new boot.
  *Qualified*: **`RESULT: PASS fails=0 wall=304s`** — one certificate, it names
  `retire_basis=qualified-contract`, the victim mounts (`MOUNT_RC=0`) and all 32
  files come back byte-identical. *No contract*: **`PASS fails=0 wall=445s`** —
  five refusals, **zero certificates**, `MOUNT_RC=32`, the victim's slice not
  replayed. *Contract naming another firmware*: **`PASS fails=0 wall=445s`** —
  four refusals, zero certificates, `MOUNT_RC=32`, and the refusal names the
  firmware level as what did not match. No node shut its filesystem down and no
  BUG or Oops appeared in any arm.

- **The rig's own declaration is what production selects**, so the measurement
  and the thing the module trusts cannot drift apart. `data/rigs.json` carries
  `qnap.task_retirement_contract` beside the evidence that backs it; `run.sh`
  ships it to every node's insmod and `tests/setup/prep_node.sh` resolves it for
  the harnesses that re-prep a rebooted victim directly. A rig that declares
  nothing ships nothing and the module refuses — the honest outcome, not a prep
  failure.

- **The measurement behind the QNAP's declaration is now four laps, and it is
  written down as characterisation rather than as proof.** `s75t` (nslot 32),
  `s76r1` (32), `s76r3` (16) and `s80r4` (64) each power-cut a node writing
  rising O_DIRECT counters and watched the window from the survivor: quiescent
  at the cut, `LATE_ROWS=0`, unchanged for the remaining ~160 s, with the
  registration purge arriving tens of seconds AFTER that quiescence. What that
  establishes is bounded, and `data/rigs.json` now says so beside the
  declaration: no late change was OBSERVED in the monitored blocks over a 180 s
  window sampled at 50 ms, which is not the same as every accepted command
  having retired at the cut, and reads see logical contents rather than the
  platter. A fifth attempt aborted before measuring anything because the victim
  was still booting from the previous lap — `stage=capture`, `No route to
  host` — which is the probe refusing rather than guessing.

- **A module parameter whose value contains a space arrives truncated unless the
  argv element carries literal quotes.** The kernel joins insmod's argv into one
  string and splits it on whitespace, so
  `target_retire_contract="QNAP:iSCSI Storage:…"` — quotes eaten by the shell —
  reached the module as `QNAP:iSCSI`, which then refused every certificate over
  a product mismatch it had invented itself. Caught by the harness's own
  non-vacuity gate, which reads the parameter back out of sysfs and refuses to
  grade a lap whose module does not hold the arm's contract.

- **Two more replay-authorising kinds rest on the same unwitnessed premise, and
  that is now a ledger record rather than a comment.** The sole-survivor
  exclusive-write gate issues a `sark=0` PREEMPT AND ABORT, which aborts the task
  sets of the registrations it removes — and it is reached precisely when the
  victim's registration is already gone, so in its own reachability case it
  aborts nothing of the victim's. Self succession claims that "the old task set
  died with the old session", which holds for full iSCSI session reinstatement
  and not for connection recovery with task reassignment, and nothing in the
  code establishes which ran. Both are accepted by
  `mxfs_fence_kind_proves_exclusion`, whose own contract requires that the
  victim have no surviving in-flight task set. The basis interface they need now
  exists; wiring it in, and measuring each case, is tracked as its own defect.

## 2026-09-20 — 0.89.12 — a fence certificate needs admission AND retirement, and every kind in this tree proved only the first; the target's retirement boundary is now measured instead of assumed

Module srcversion FA068320F44253861244DB5. Two kernel changes: a read-only
resume for a fencing attempt this node's own incarnation left ambiguous, and
the boot-succession certificate naming the premise it rests on. The rest is
measurement, two design rulings, and the harness corrections they forced.

- **A node that lost the response to its own PREEMPT AND ABORT locked the
  cluster down permanently, and the cause was reachability rather than a
  missing proof.** The ambiguous slot was never revisited by anything: it is
  deliberately not armed for retry (re-issuing a command against a victim key
  whose predecessor may still be in flight is the hazard the phase distinction
  exists for), takeover is closed because the attempt's holder is alive — it is
  us — and every other proof mechanism is reachable only from the absent-key
  classification, which an unanswered command never becomes. So even after a
  proof became available, nothing looked. Measured before the fix: the victim's
  slice was never replayed, and **the returning victim could not mount its own
  filesystem** — 32 inline replay rounds, `P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED … fencing
  ATTEMPT only`, then `MXFS mount ABORTED … after 30038 ms`, `MOUNT_RC=32`.
  The fix revisits the slot when the attempt's holder is proven to be this
  node's own current incarnation, issuing **no state-changing command**: the
  sole-survivor gate is unreachable from it, and it asks only the questions
  whose answers do not depend on what the lost command did. A pass that finds
  no proof changes nothing durable — it returns before the point where falling
  through would have armed a retry. Measured after, same reproducer and rig
  (`flr_s75d`, build `69464CFA4A52B09AA73A844`): the boot boundary is taken as
  the proof and named as such (`P236-FENCE-CERTIFIED … kind=BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT
  … prover=… term=1`), **the peer returns and mounts (`MOUNT_RC=0`)**, all 64
  files it fsynced before the fence come back byte-identical, and no fencing
  descriptor is left standing — five phase-C failures down to one, and that one
  was the harness sampling the replay before it had happened. With that
  corrected and the revisit bounded, the confirming lap on build
  `FA068320F44253861244DB5` is clean end to end: **`RESULT: PASS label=s75e
  fails=0 wall=693s`**, phase A 0, phase B 0, phase C 0. Blocking while the
  victim is still alive in its original incarnation is unchanged and still
  correct: phase B stayed at zero failures across every build.

- **The revisit is rate-bounded, because the measurement said it had to be.**
  The first build asked on every claim retry — 68 passes in one 790 s lap,
  each costing a READ KEYS and a READ RESERVATION — while its rate-limited log
  line suggested three. It now asks at most once per 15 s per slot, which stays
  well inside the returning peer's mount barrier; a bound that outran that
  barrier would turn a fixed liveness defect back into a lockout.

- **A certificate rests on two separate facts, and the tree witnessed one.**
  ADMISSION — the dead incarnation cannot obtain permission for a new write.
  RETIREMENT — the writes the target has *already accepted* from it can no
  longer take effect. A Write Exclusive reservation held by our key gives the
  first. Nothing in the fencing path gives the second, and the certificate is
  what authorises replaying the victim's journal slice — so a command still
  executable from the old nexus lands *under* that replay, as an unordered
  logical write into metadata the replay is rewriting. The design consult that
  established this is banked at
  `docs/rulings/fence-ambiguous-drain-and-proof-resume.md`.

- **The sole-survivor exclusive-write gate is not the answer to a lost PREEMPT
  AND ABORT response, and the lost-response harness had been asserting that it
  was.** The gate's PREEMPT AND ABORT carries `sark=0`, so it aborts the task
  sets of *the registrants it removes*; a victim whose registration the
  unanswered predecessor already removed is not among them. Confirmed in a
  target implementation's source: `scst_pr_abort_reg` aborts through
  `SCST_PR_ABORT_ALL` for that registrant's own session and LUN, and
  `__scst_abort_task_set` walks only that session's list filtered by `tgt_dev`
  — one I_T_L nexus. Key absence is not a drain certificate either: a key goes
