## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.17 — no verdict from an unvalidated measurement: the rig capture contract, its library, the chokepoint's status record and the lint

Work on D-A-TEST-HARNESS-CAN-REPORT-A-VERDICT-ABOUT-MXFS (the record stays
open; see the end of this entry).  No kernel code changed.

The class, met again this session before anything was built for it: after a
death-chain lap had rebooted test2 without its NFS source mount, the new
lone-mount crash harness ran its platter probe on test2, the probe printed
nothing, the harness printed "home dinodes before recovery: w=? bt=?" and
went on to a verdict (s54j); in the peer arm the recoverer's node-preparation
script was unreachable on the same node, so every recovery assertion FAILed
about the filesystem (s54k).  The shared helper `rs() { timeout N $SSH host
cmd 2>/dev/null | filt; }` in 134 harnesses discards the remote command's
stderr and returns filt's status, so a measurement that never happened and a
clean system both read as zero, and 538 assertion sites count from such
captures.

The design consult (2026-09-18) ruled: the shared library is the integrity
fix, the chokepoint's status record is a diagnostic aid, the lint is the
migration control, and the safety property is "no verdict from an
unvalidated measurement", not "no empty file after an ssh failure".  Merging
remote stderr into stdout class-wide was rejected (122 sites in 37 harnesses
parse the helper's last line, and error text can contain any string a loose
grep recognizes), and so was a chokepoint-only marker (an old `grep -c`
still turns it into a clean zero).  Design record:
docs/harness-capture-contract.md.

- tests/lib/rig.sh: `rsx` acquires a measurement with the caller's timeout
  observed, the remote stderr kept in its own file under `$OUT/rs_stderr/`,
  and one `MXFS-RS-STATUS v=1 host= rc= err=` record appended on any
  non-zero status (remote, ssh, sshpass, timeout); `capture_require <file>
  <anchored shape> <what>` is the boundary, a statement in the parent shell
  (an exit inside `$(...)` does not stop a harness, which is why no counting
  helper validates); `ensure_src_or_abort` checks the share and the tools on
  a node; `mxfs_dev_resolve` sets the device with an explicit precedence and
  aborts on any other basis.  Failure is ABORT (2), never FAIL, VACUOUS or
  PASS.
- tools/mxfs_sshpass.sh appends the same status record for legacy callers
  when `MXFS_RS_STATUS=1` (opt-in: a remote `grep -c` with no matches exits
  1, and a legacy parse would not expect the line).
- scripts/harness_lint.py prints the residue: assertions fed by a count over
  a capture no guard proved, and a local `rs()` shadowing the library.
  Before this work 277 in 50 harnesses; now 266 in 50 (the three adopted
  harnesses' flows are guarded; nothing else changed).
- tests/lone_rsync_bench.sh takes the LUN from MXFS_DEV (it hardcoded the
  CAW rig's multipath device, one of the 21 such harnesses the record
  counts).

Adopted so far (every counted flow): tests/lone_mount_crash_replay.sh,
tests/d0531_stale_slice_recovery.sh, and tests/rig_lib_contract.sh, the
contract tests of the library against a real node with real commands
(nothing mocked).  Verified on the 2-node TCP rig:

- Contract (s54v, 12 s): a completed measurement with a legitimate zero
  count passes; empty output, malformed non-empty output, a valid-looking
  line followed by a non-zero exit, a timeout before any output and a
  timeout after a valid-looking line all ABORT; a success with noisy stderr
  leaves stdout byte for byte and keeps the stderr in its file; an
  unreachable host aborts with rc 255; a missing capture aborts; the device
  resolver uses MXFS_DEV, aborts on an absent device, aborts with no basis,
  uses the transport default only with MXFS_TRANSPORT set, and aborts rather
  than defaulting when the node cannot be asked.
- Rejection, on real harnesses at the real acquisition point
  (`MXFS_FAULT_UMOUNT_SRC=<node>:<stage>`, a real lazy unmount of the share
  immediately before the named acquisition): d0531 with the share removed
  on test2 before the platter probe (s54w) ran its whole first stage, killed
  the victim, then ABORTed with the probe's own error in the evidence
  ("python3: can't open file '/src/mxfs/tools/slice_image.py'", rc=2, the
  stderr file named) and no ROW; the crash harness with the share removed on

  "RESERVATION: UNKNOWN ... did not answer PERSISTENT RESERVE IN" and exits

  registrants, two keys.
- Healthy path: the D-0531 control arm (s54z) passed through every boundary

The record stays OPEN: shared infrastructure landed, migration partial —
3 harnesses adopted, 266 unguarded counted assertions in 50 harnesses

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.16 — a mount that has never had a peer takes real inode grants, so the images it logs can be replayed after its death

D-LONE-MOUNT-DIRECTORY-BLOCK-IMAGE-SHIPS-AUTH-NOT-HELD-SO-ITS-CRASH-SLICE-IS-REFUSED-AND-AG0-QUARANTINED
is disposed FIXED AND VERIFIED.

The defect (found 2026-09-18 by tests/d0531_stale_slice_recovery.sh, lap
s53f, both arms identical): a node mounted alone on a fresh filesystem did
mkdir + 40 creates + fsync and was destroyed within a second.  Its next
incarnation, still alone, fenced the dead one and replayed its slice as a
foreign slice; the transaction's directory-block image (the directory after
its shortform-to-block conversion) carried authority class NONE / status
AUTH_NOT_HELD while its six AG images were VALID, so the replay atomically
skipped the whole transaction, published a terminal refusal, quarantined AG 0
cluster-wide and admitted the mount with every root lookup answering EIO.
Forty fsynced files and their directory were unreachable.

The cause, proven by instrument before any change (new harness
tests/lone_dir_block_authority.sh, the same workload with no crash, s54a and
s54b on 0.87.15): on the lone mount the capture point recorded 45 non-durable
authority captures of the directory's block — outcome NONE, DLM mode NL,
not even on the deferred-publish list — and with a peer mounted it recorded
zero, because the directory had taken a real EX grant at its first modify.
The inode DLM entry returned at the top for a mount that was single-node and
had never had a peer (`mxfs_v5_dlm_never_multi`, 0.83.3), before the
unpublished-directory divert that claims the durable grant; the same
predicate gated the lock exit, try and demote, the recycled-create re-arm,
both publish workers, the directory hold, and the four create-time and
stale-shell sites in the inode cache.  0.83.3 had argued the exemption from
live coherency: such a mount's caches hold only its own images and "no
successor writer can exist for anything it logs".  After a death the
replayer of its slice is exactly that successor writer, and it authorizes an
inode-owned image only against the grant the owner held at capture.  The AG
path has had no such exemption since 0.41.0.

The design consult (2026-09-18) ruled for removing the exemption uniformly
over two alternatives: a narrow divert for only the block-logging inode
classes (a second set of lifecycle predicates that must all agree, and every
missed one recreates the defect), and a replay-side "never had a peer"
certificate (a second authority regime in recovery, with a transition
hazard when the first peer joins while unreplayed NONE images still exist).
The corrected invariant: being alone permits omitting coordination with live
peers; it never permits omitting the durable authority a future incarnation
or foreign replayer needs.  So `mxfs_v5_dlm_never_multi()` and every site
keyed on it are gone (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c, xfs/xfs_icache.c, dlm/v5_mount.c,
dlm/v5_mount.h): a lone mount runs the ordinary ownership protocol against a
master that is itself, exactly as a sole survivor has since 0.83.3 — a new
inode gets its local unpublished-EX tenure and its place on the
deferred-publish list (no eager publish-on-create; the accepted cost model
is unchanged), a directory publishes at its first EX modify, a file owning
metadata outside its core publishes before its first such image, and the
exit runs the release drain.  `ever_multi` stays for the sole-survivor
predicate; `is_single_node` stays for peer-signalling shortcuts only.  The
recovery side is untouched and still fails closed.

Verified on 2 nodes / TCP, srcversion 0FCDC94EE691B01E8B942F4:

- tests/lone_dir_block_authority.sh s54c: zero non-durable captures of the
  witness directory's block on the lone mount (45 before the fix) and zero
  with a peer; the directory block's first log still printed once per arm.
- New harness tests/lone_mount_crash_replay.sh, two inode-owned witnesses on
  a lone fresh mount (mkdir + 40 creates; a file fallocated as 48 disjoint
  64 KiB extents, an extent map in a bmap-btree block), fsync, destroy
  within two seconds, the home dinodes of both witnesses read FREE from the
  platter by the other node (the work lived only in the log).  Same-node
  return (s54d 275 s, s54f 274 s): the returning incarnation fenced the dead
  one and replayed its slice; the replay summary for the witness transaction
  shows seven buffer images, seven tokened, one inode-class, zero classless,
  seven applied, zero skipped (the s53f shape was seven images, one
  classless, one skipped, transaction refused); across the slice one
  directory-block image and 36 bmap-btree images applied as inode-class
  VALID, 49 transactions with zero skipped images, zero image refusals, no
  quarantine, mount admitted, 40 files with the fsynced bytes, the recovered
  directory accepted a create and a mkdir, test2 joined and read all 41
  files and the extent map cold, offline check clean.  Recovery by the OTHER
  node, itself mounting alone for the first time (s54e 271 s): the same
  result.  (s54d and s54e/s54f each carried one harness verdict bug — a
  refusal grep that matched the fence protocol's own "refusing the claim"
  stage lines, then an extent counter that read filefrag's discontiguous-run
  summary — corrected in the harness; the filesystem evidence is the same in
  every lap.)  Under the corrected verdicts: same-node return s54o PASS
  272 s, recovery by the other node s54p PASS 271 s, and s54t PASS 288 s
  with a third witness, a file carrying a 3000-byte xattr, whose attribute
  leaf image replayed inode-class VALID and read back in full on both nodes
  — the three inode-owned image classes a lone mount can log (directory
  block, bmap-btree block, attribute leaf) all replay.
- tests/tcp_2node_death_chain.sh s54i (two nodes, dirty death of the peer,
  survivor replays): PASS, 353 acked writes, replay 73 s, recovery complete,
  exclusive-write gate restored, one registration after the restore, lap
  117 s.
- tests/d0952_sole_create_rejoin_coherency.sh, the two membership
  transitions the fix touches.  Lone arm s54l (both unmounted, test1 mounts
  alone with no memory of a peer, 200 creates + 100 recycles + links,
  symlinks and renames under its now-real grants, test2 mounts for the
  first time in test1's life): CLEAN — test2 saw 200/200, both directions
  of overwrite read back 200/200 with zero stale and zero errors, no
  shutdown, cold check clean, 57 s.  Sole-survivor arm s54m (the 0.83.3
  regression): CLEAN, same counts, cold check clean, 50 s.

The cost, measured rather than assumed (tests/lone_rsync_bench.sh s54r, the
8714-file tree on test1 mounted alone, this build): the rsync did not finish
in its 60 s bound — 4666 files, about 13 ms per file, every one of them
taking a durable authority page (P-TAUTH-PAGE-MINE per file).  The same
rsync with both nodes mounted (s54s) reached 3266 files in 60 s, so the lone
mount now pays the multi-node per-file cost and no more, but that cost is
itself far past the 2× native ceiling and was already the subject of
D-TCP-LEDGER-SMALLFILE-WORKLOAD-PACE-RULE0-0349, which now carries this
measurement and the trigger seen in the probes: the "unpublished inode owns
metadata outside its core" divert fires for a regular file whose attribute
fork was set up empty at create (extents format, zero extents), which owns
no block.  That is a pace defect in the queue, not a reason to log an
unreplayable image.

The two harnesses take the transport from MXFS_TRANSPORT and never reformat
the LUN under a peer still mounted on the old filesystem (a node fenced that
way withdraws and its module cannot be unloaded; s54a needed a VM reboot);
tests/lone_rsync_bench.sh takes the LUN from MXFS_DEV instead of the CAW
rig's hardcoded multipath device.  Budgets in
tests/criteria/TIMEOUT_BUDGETS.md; design in docs/sole-survivor-sweep.md
and docs/join-transition.md.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.15 — the clean-departure key lifecycle is verified on the 2-node TCP release configuration, including the two-node return after a prover departs with an attempt it cannot certify

D-CLEAN-RELEASE-THEN-UNREGISTER-FAIL-LEAVES-UNFENCEABLE-STALE-REGISTRANT-0356
is disposed: FIXED AND VERIFIED for the shape it was opened on, and the
second shape folded into it on 2026-09-11 is disproved as a defect of this
record on the current build.  No kernel code changed for this entry; the
change is the verification instruments and their reach, and the record's
disposition.  Three findings, kept apart:

1. The release/unregister mechanism.  The record was opened on a clean
   unmount that released its heartbeat slot EMPTY and then failed to
   unregister its PR key: an initiator with write privilege that no peer
   could fence and that refused its own host's next mount.  The design that
   replaced it (0.58.0 to 0.61.6: a RETIRE_PENDING release image that keeps
   the identity block and the key, settlement only on a fencing-grade proof
   of absence, expiry to WITHDRAWN and a certified preempt-and-abort while
   the key is present, the departing node's own WITHDRAWN re-stamp on a
   failed unregister, the departure I/O gate) had its closing evidence, the
   release/unregister crash-cut state table, harvested clean at 32 nodes on
   CAW on 2026-09-02 and never recorded.  Measured today on 2 nodes / TCP,
   srcversion 8C88197C64B31AB03AF342A (chain s53a, tests/evidence/
   d0356_*_s53a.log), each cut a real VM destroy with put_super parked at the
   cut, the sector decoded by an O_DIRECT read from the peer and READ KEYS
   taken from the peer: cut 1 (before the release CAS) ACTIVE naming the key,
   fenced through the sole-survivor gate, recovered, EMPTY after, key absent,
   victim remount admitted, 115 s; cuts 2 and 3 (after the CAS, before and
   after its flush) RETIRE_PENDING naming the key, key present, expired to
   WITHDRAWN after the grace, certified PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE on that key,
   recovered, EMPTY after, no settlement while the key was present, remount
   admitted, 81 s each; cut 5 (after a successful unregister) settled EMPTY
   by the peer's retire worker in 1 s on a proven-absent key with no fence,
   the peer's own SEEN line naming the key it read from the image, 39 s; the
   injected unregister failure re-stamped WITHDRAWN (P301, P303 rc=0), was
   fenced at 0 s, recovered in 6 s, remounted without a predecessor-key
   refusal, and its clean control retired the key with zero fence, 36 s; the
   same failure with the re-stamp skipped expired after the 30 s grace and
   was fenced, 81 s.  No kernel fault or shutdown in any arm.

2. The "release never completed" shape (sess578, 0.81.2).  A node holding a
   standing fencing attempt against a peer whose key the target had already
   purged unmounted with rc=0 but left its slot ACTIVE and the attempt
   standing.  The record attributed it to a retire-worker retry budget; the
   journal shows those three lines were the PR worker's latch firings refused
   by the node's own parked prover, and no such budget exists.  Re-measured
   today with the same harness and hold (tests/evidence/d0932rp_s53b.log):
   after the hold the resumed prover tried the sole-survivor exclusive-write
   gate (added for the TCP transport in 0.85.1, absent from the 0.81.2
   journal), certified EXCLUSIVE_WRITE_GATE, replayed and published the dead
   peer's slice, restored WE-AR, and only then shut the DLM down and released
   RETIRE_PENDING; unmount 70.7 s of which 60 s was the injected hold, no
   attempt left standing.

3. The two-node residual, measured for the first time
   (tests/d0356_stranded_prover_return.sh, lap s53d, tests/evidence/
   20260918T170833Z_d0356spr_s53d): the departing prover is made genuinely
   unable to certify by the existing gate-refusal knob, so its attempt keeps
   answering KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN as it would against a target error.  Its
   unmount waited 110 s on grants the dead victim still held (the root inode
   and the superblock summary lock) until the recovery-blocked cutoff
   answered EIO (P240-RBLK-EIO-ABORT, P-SB-SUMMARY-FINAL-FAIL lock_rc=-112),
   then put_super judged the departure DIRTY (no unmount record) and retained
   the ACTIVE record and the key by design, the attempt standing under its
   own tuple.  The victim then cold-returned alone with nothing repaired by
   hand: it fenced the departed prover by ordinary preempt-and-abort on its
   still-present key, noted the incarnation dead, took the attempt naming its
   own previous incarnation over at term 2, certified BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT
   for it, replayed and published both slices, mounted in 93.4 s, read the
   witness files both incarnations had synced before the deaths, and left no
   descriptor on the platter; the prover rejoined in 2.8 s with no
   predecessor-key refusal and read both witnesses; no fault or shutdown on
   either host.  This is the designed fail-safe for an attempt that cannot be
   certified at departure, and its liveness on two nodes is now measured
   rather than argued.  The harness's own first run scored one assertion
   wrong (a zero grep count also triggered its fallback and printed "0 0");

   the lap repeated clean (s53e, tests/evidence/20260918T171956Z_d0356spr_s53e:
   fails=0, unmount 110 s, lone mount 93.4 s, rejoin 2.9 s, the same fence,

Instruments: tests/d0356_stranded_prover_return.sh (new);
tests/depart_crash_cuts.sh and tests/pr_unregister_fail_restamp.sh take the

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.14 — the AG-metadata track token is returned at both choke points of a log item's life, the completion epilogue is exercised by injection, and unmount takes a per-AG census

D-STALE-AGMETA-BTREE-BUFFER-LEAKS-XFS-BUF-TO-MODULE-UNLOAD-SLAB-WARNING-0924
is disposed: fixed and verified by exhaustive finalization of the tracking
obligation; the single event on 0.75.63 that opened it stays unattributed.
What the record was opened for — six xfs_buf objects reported at every
module unload, "unbounded for the life of the module" — was disproved on
2026-09-17 (one stranded object echoed by slab-cache merging, caches now
SLAB_NO_MERGE, positive control in tests/d0924_zombie_cache_ab.sh).  What
remained was one measured token strand on a build that predates every
closure since, and the record's own closing condition: name the route, or
establish that the class is closed.

The class is the set of ways a tracked buf log item's life can end.
xfs_buf_item_free has one caller, xfs_buf_item_relse, which already
returned the token on every no-I/O retirement (XFS_BLI_NO_IODONE: put,
stale, release-clean, shutdown/abort, the overlay's no-I/O retire arms,
retire-no-bli).  The one deferred case, XFS_BLI_IODONE_FOLLOWS, is
__xfs_buf_ioend calling bp->b_iodone on the next line, and after that call
the code only checked whether the token was still armed and printed.  It
now returns it as well (mxfs_ag_meta_reclaim, why=ioend-unconsumed) — the
same reference the callback would have dropped, at the same point, under
the completion path's own reference (xfs_buf_ioend relse's or completes
only after __xfs_buf_ioend returns), so the use-after-free hazard the
record flagged for reclaiming inside xfs_buf_item_done, before the
callback, does not arise.  No token ABA across that window: the write
holds the buffer lock until the completion's relse, a new dirty epoch arms
only from xfs_trans_log_buf under the transaction's buffer lock, and
neither the callback nor the reclaim unlocks or hands the buffer off, so a
token that reads armed after the callback is this epoch's.  No path resets
bli_flags wholesale and buffer teardown never detaches a live log item, so
every tracked item's life ends at one of the two choke points.  Design
consult (Astra, 2026-09-18) accepted "fixed and verified by exhaustive
finalization; historical trigger unattributed" on three conditions, each
now met: an exclusion argument against ABA (above), the new epilogue
exercised rather than shipped unreached, and conservation checked per AG,
not only module-wide.

Two instruments for those conditions.  dbg_agmeta_iodone_skip=N (test
only, 0 in production) makes the callback leave the next N tokens armed;
mxfs_dlm_ag_force_release_all prints P-AGMETA-UNMOUNT-CENSUS (and a
P-AGMETA-PENDING-AT-UNMOUNT line per non-zero AG) after the drains and
device flush, the one quiescent point at which every AG's pending count
must be zero.

Measured on the 2-node TCP rig, build 8C88197C64B31AB03AF342A (heal-only
build E4EBCBD1D0BAAED545FF487 for the first chain), MXFS_DEV=/dev/sda:
completion route, injected (tests/evidence/d0924_inject_stream_s52d.txt,
d0924stomp_s52d.console): P-AGMETA-IODONE-SKIP 8, P-AGMETA-IODONE-MISSED
8, why=ioend-unconsumed 8, then acquires 78 = returns_iodone 64 +
returns_reclaim 14, outstanding 0, tripwire silent, PASS.  Stale route,
workload (agleak_s52b/s52c, agmeta_stale_leak_2node.sh): releases=2,
reclaim_lines=6, p3_max_us=0, stuckmeta=0, PASS both laps.  Churn with
16202-16212 foreign b_iodone installs and zero stomps
(d0924stomp_s52b/s52c): acquires 745 = 715 + 30 and 725 = 693 + 32 on
rank 1, 45 = 45 and 30 = 30 on rank 2, PASS.  Shutdown inside the churn
(agshut_s52b): tripwire silent, no object in the mxfs_buf slab at unload,
no buffer left in an AG cache, rejoin without operator action; the
harness's non-vacuity check for the put route scored 0 because that route
is not reachable from a shutdown on this tree (the CIL abort retires the
item through unpin, fail_unsubmitted and the completion), as the record
had already measured — put is closed by construction at the funnel, by
the same reclaim call the stale and completion routes exercise, and that
is stated here rather than claimed as measured.  Unload with
SLAB_NO_MERGE (unload_s52b/s52c/s52d): zero slab-leak lines both nodes,
P-AGMETA-UNMOUNT-CENSUS ags=24 nonzero_ags=0 pending_total=0 on both
nodes at both censused unmounts, zero BUG/Oops/WARNING/hung-task lines in
every window.  The first injection lap (s52c) lost its eight lines to
kernel-ring rotation before the sweep, with the counters already
consistent with eight returns; the s52d lap streamed the ring from before
the arming marker and kept them.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.13 — the inode allocator's DEMAND escalation now reaches the holder on the TCP transport, and a demanded candidate cools for the release fence instead of the silent ring

D-DIR-REUSE-COHERENCY-2NODE-TCP-BARRIER-TIMEOUT-ROUND2-BOTH-NODES-0939 is
fixed and verified on the 2-node TCP rig.  The filed failure (both nodes
BARRIER_TIMEOUT in round 2, 2026-09-05) was the pace consequence of the
AG-metadata hold leak fixed in 0.75.63; what remained was the stall that
kept every later PASS one slow lap from the same failure: on 0.87.12 each
round of dir_reuse_coherency cost rank 1's stat of the shared directory a
2.3 s wait in PR behind rank 2's directory EX (23 acquire deadlines and
eight first-timeout stack dumps per lap on rank 1, none on rank 2), and
the row completed 13 rounds in its 100 s time box.

Root, read from both nodes' kernel logs: after rank 1's rm -rf, rank 2's
first create of the next round had to allocate from the only free chunk,
whose numbers rank 1 had just freed and still held as cached EX grants.
The allocator's non-queued reserve probes were all denied
(MXFS_ERR_DEADLOCK, 52 in one round), it fell into its failed-sweep
backoff with rs->demand set — and on the TCP transport that escalation was
inert: mxfs_v5_dlm_inode_reserve_try passed NOQUEUE alone on the TCP
branch and dropped the demand argument, so the master never BASTed the
holder and rank 1 released the corpses only on its own lazy path, 2.3 s
later.  All of that time rank 2 held the parent directory EX with the
create transaction pinned, and rank 1's stat waited behind it past the
1 s per-attempt acquire deadline.  The TCP engine has honoured DEMAND
since 0.75.42; this caller never asked for it.

Two changes, both in the allocation-side interlock (docs/reuse-barrier.md):
the TCP branch of the reserve wrapper now carries MXFS_LKF_DEMAND exactly
as the AG probe wrapper does; and a candidate refused by a probe that
carried DEMAND cools for the peer's release fence (MXFS_DEMAND_COOL_MS
40-80 ms, a named class distinct from the publication-pending one) instead
of the silent ring's 500-1000 ms, because the very next queued EX on such a
number handed off in ~10 ms and a negative cache a hundred times longer
than the release it asked for was the rest of the stall.  Design consult
(Astra, 2026-09-18) rated shipping these two together and named the
hazards: DEMAND must stay a request for release, never permission to
preempt an active reservation (it is — the holder's BAST defers under the
transaction pin exactly as a queued request's does), repeated BASTs must
coalesce on the holder (they do, through the existing bast_pending re-arm),
and the master-side deny must not wait for the release (it does not).
Carrying DEMAND from the first inode probe rather than after a failed
sweep was rated a reasonable further policy, to be landed and measured
separately.

Measured, fresh prep, build 6E3F75294ED5EF9F39FE57A, three consecutive
laps of ./run.sh 2 tcp dir_reuse_coherency (tests/evidence/
drc_2tcp_s52_lap{1,2,3}.log): 3/3 PASS, 17/18/17 rounds in the 100 s time
box against 13 before, P36-RETRY 0/0/0 on both nodes against 23 on rank 1
before, P36-STACK 0 against 8, P-LKTIMEOUT-REMOTE 0 against 23,
P-DEMAND-BAST 152-171 per lap on each node (the escalation now fires),
rank 2's longest directory EX tenure 339-565 ms against 2345 ms, zero
BUG/Oops/WARNING/hung-task lines on either node.  What remains measured
and is not a defect: rank 2 still runs 55-72 failed sweeps per lap because
the first sweep is silent by design, and its directory tenure still
reaches ~0.5 s from that sweep's 500-1000 ms cooldown; first-probe DEMAND
for inode reservations would remove that and is the separately-measured
follow-up the consult asked for.

The row now carries its own stall evidence.  tests/suite/lib.sh appends a
test's SUITE_MEASURED_EXTRA terms to the RESULT line's measured= payload,
and dir_reuse_coherency.sh stamps a start marker and reports rounds,
P36-RETRY, P36-STACK, P-LKTIMEOUT-REMOTE/HOLDER and P-DIALLOC-SWEEP-RETRY
counts scoped to its own run, so a lap that passes while stalling reports
the stall instead of a bare PASS.  The record's other open item, the board
reason string preferring a BARRIER_TIMEOUT record over the BUDGET_EXHAUSTED
one that named the real event, was already fixed in run.sh (superseded
records are carried in measured=) and is verified present.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.12 — a terminal replay refusal now lifts the sole-survivor exclusive-write gate, so the returned victim can rejoin a two-node cluster

D-SOLE-SURVIVOR-GATE-NEVER-RESTORED-AFTER-A-TERMINAL-REFUSAL-SO-THE-RETURNED-
VICTIM-CANNOT-REJOIN is fixed and verified on the 2-node TCP rig.  When a
sole survivor fences a dead peer whose registration the target has already
purged, it installs the exclusive-write gate (single-holder Write Exclusive
under its own key, certificate kind 20) and replays under it.  If that replay
ends in a durable TERMINAL verdict (the slice is refused, the victim's domain
quarantined cluster-wide, the slot frozen until operator action), 0.82.6
released the recovery's gate dependant — and nothing then called the restore.
The restore was driven only from the recovery-complete publication and from
the PR worker re-driving a restore already marked due, and the platter sweep
rightly exempts a quarantined descriptor, so nothing owed the gate and
nothing lifted it.  WE(1) stayed on the LUN for the survivor's lifetime; the
returned victim, a new incarnation with a new key, could REGISTER but its
PR-ledger publish is a write, so it was refused (P-PRKEY-PUBLISHED rc=-52,
'TCP SCSI PR register failed') on every mount.  A two-node cluster stayed at
one node until the survivor unmounted (s610h, 0.84.24).

A durable terminal verdict is a recorded block, and a recorded block drives
the restore exactly as a publication does.  Both terminal-refusal publication
wrappers now call `v5_gate_terminal_release`: the dependant is cleared, the
restore is marked due under the gate lock BEFORE the inline attempt (so
progress never depends on this call reaching the conversion — the PR worker
re-drives a due restore every 2 s), and the same checked primitive runs:
pins, dependants, the platter sweep, then the conversion.  Design consult
(Astra, 2026-09-18) rated that shape first and named the hazard it must
carry: the gate was installed because the victim's key was ALREADY absent,
and absence proves nothing about a revived old incarnation that re-registers
under WE(1) — REGISTER is always admitted, only writes are excluded — which
WE-AR would authorise at once.  So the owed sweep now also reports every
quarantined gate-kind descriptor with its certificate's victim key, and the
restore re-checks each key with a fresh synchronous bracket and converts only
on a proven ABSENT (`P-PR-GATE-RESTORE-VICTIM-PRESENT` otherwise, re-driven).
The consult's other condition — the joiner must install the terminal
refusal synchronously, never on a later monitor pass — was already met and
is now measured: the returned victim imports the verdict inside its mount
barrier before the mount completes and validates it again at registration.

Measured on test1/test2 over TCP with `tests/d_intents_2tcp_open_efi.sh`
`MODE=terminal_rejoin` (new arm: the survivor's completion is switched off so
the open-EFI replay is terminally refused, as the pre-0.85.0 control was):

- Control on 0.87.11 (srcversion FD2459C3B1F8F0B3DB40930,
  tests/evidence/20260918T150424Z_intents2tcp_s51term_ctl): gate installed
  (P-PR-GATE-ISSUE, the QNAP target had purged the victim's key), verdict
  durable, dependant cleared, RESTORE=0, the returned victim refused at its
  publish (rc=-52), not mounted.
- Fix (srcversion 5B38D667EF67EDC233482D7,
  tests/evidence/20260918T150917Z_intents2tcp_s51term_fix): terminal verdict
  at 1101.423 s, dependant cleared, P-PR-GATE-TERMINAL-RELEASE, the victim
  key re-checked ABSENT by proof at 1101.442 s, WE-AR restored at 1101.444 s
  (`P-PR-GATE-RESTORE site=refused-terminal`, 20 ms after the verdict).  The
  returned victim saw WE-AR, published rc=0, mounted (prep_rc=0) in 5.0 s,
  imported the verdict before 'Ending clean mount' and scanned it again at
  registration; its create in its former directory failed EIO
  (P240-QUAR-NSOP-REFUSE) while a create at the root succeeded; the survivor
  stayed mounted with no shutdown; no BUG, Oops or WARNING on either node.
- Repeat (20260918T151554Z_intents2tcp_s51term_fix2): the same shape on a
  fresh filesystem, every assertion again — gate installed, terminal
  release, restore from the terminal site, victim mounted in 5.0 s, verdict
  imported, its old directory refused EIO, the root create succeeded.
- Regression on the ordinary path, `MODE=complete`
  (20260918T152158Z_intents2tcp_s51complete): the gate installed at
  1854.51 s, the obligation engine completed the case, the dependant cleared
  `why=published` at 1866.65 s and the restore landed from the
  recovery-complete site at 1866.87 s (the modified sweep found no terminal
  slot to re-check); the returned victim created in its former directory
  (rc=0), every assertion passed.

The victim-key re-check has not been exercised by a lap in which a
terminally refused victim's key was registered again at restore time; what
is measured is that the check runs (P-PR-KEY-STATE-SYNC state=ABSENT
why=absent-proven on every restore from the terminal site) and that a
proven ABSENT lets the conversion proceed.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.11 — a same-second remount of both TCP nodes no longer refuses the second mount: a disturbed own-key bracket is bracketed again, and the mount thread holds admission on a PRESENT key instead of fencing it

D-TCP-REMOUNT-REFUSED-WHEN-A-PEERS-PROUT-LANDS-INSIDE-THE-OWN-KEY-PROOF-
BRACKET-0965 is fixed and verified on the 2-node TCP rig.  The chk_clean board
row unmounts both nodes, audits, and remounts both in the same second, and on
0.84.24 the second node's mount was refused about the instant the first
node's REGISTER landed, leaving it unmounted for every later row.  Two
interleavings of the same race were found, and each was answered with a
mount refusal where the state was in fact sound.

The first: a node remounting in the same boot settles its predecessor's
RETIRE_PENDING record by proving its own registration in one READ KEYS A /
READ RESERVATION / READ KEYS B bracket.  The peer's REGISTER PROUT landing
inside that bracket moves the PR generation, the bracket is INCOHERENT (no
proof either way, and the probe said so: 'no absence proof from this
view'), and `mxfs_scsipr_own_registration_proven` handed that single
disturbed answer to the settle path, which turned it into
P305-RETIRE-OWN-UNPROVEN rc=-71 and 'TCP mount REFUSED (-16)'.  It now
brackets again — bounded (`dbg_pr_own_proof_brackets`, default 4, 1 restores
the single bracket for an A/B), a growing pause between attempts, stopping
at the first coherent bracket (P-PR-OWN-PROOF-REBRACKET).  A coherent
bracket that lacks our key or the fencing reservation still refuses.

The second: the peer's mount thread meets the predecessor's RETIRE_PENDING
record while the successor has just re-registered the identical per-boot
key, so the key reads PRESENT.  The mount thread used to withdraw a PRESENT
key at once ('settle NOW rather than admit and wait'), which stamped the
record WITHDRAWN 817 ms after first sight, froze the predecessor as a
victim and PREEMPT-AND-ABORTed the key — removing the live successor's
registration and refusing its mount (P303-FENCECAP-SELFABSENT).  The target
cannot tell 'the departure never unregistered' from 'the successor
registered the same key'.  What safety requires is only that the mount
does not go writable beside the registration, so `hb_retire_settle` on the
mount thread now holds admission (P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD, the barrier
re-sweeps) for a first-sight grace, P304-RETIRE-PRESENT-GRACE, and the
successor settles its own record within a second.  Design consult (Astra,
2026-09-18): expiry authorises recovery and proves nothing; the grace
starts at first sight and is never reset by a barrier round.  The mount
thread's grace is its own constant, MXFS_DISKLOCK_RETIRE_MOUNT_GRACE_MS
(10 s), not the monitor's 30 s: measured, a full 30 s mount-thread grace
expired at 29.3 s of the admission barrier's 30 s bound and the fence and
clean-slice replay that follow a genuine withdraw took 12 s more.  A
successor settles 40 ms after REGISTER unloaded and 8 s with a 1.5 s delay
injected into every READ KEYS, so 10 s covers it with a wide margin and
leaves two thirds of the bound for the recovery.

Measured (srcversion FD2459C3B1F8F0B3DB40930, test1/test2 on the TCP
transport; `dbg_pr_read_keys_delay_ms` widens A's bracket so the race is
deterministic):

- Controls.  0.87.10, `tests/d0965_remount_bracket_race.sh`
  (tests/evidence/20260918T134606Z_d0965race_s49ctl): 2 of 2 laps A's mount
  refused rc=32, B withdrew and fenced A's live re-registration.  The fixed
  build with `dbg_pr_own_proof_brackets=1` (s50ctl_v1): lap 1 the
  incoherent bracket was again answered with the refusal.
- Race, variant 1 (B staggered 2 s, 20260918T142850Z_d0965race_s50fix2_v1):
  3 of 3 laps INCOHERENT=1, REBRACKET=1, UNPROVEN=0, REFUSED=0, the record
  settled, A mounted rc=0 in 13.8 / 24.2 / 14.6 s, B rc=0.
- Race, variant 2 (B staggered 1 s, 20260918T142654Z_d0965race_s50fix2_v2):
  3 of 3 laps B held the grace (P304-RETIRE-PRESENT-GRACE=1), no withdraw,
  no SELFABSENT, both mounts rc=0, a file written on A read on B.
- Negative, `tests/d0965_stalled_record_mount_thread.sh`
  (20260918T142424Z_d0965stall_s50neg2): a record whose departure failed to
  unregister and never re-stamped (`dbg_pr_unregister_fail` +
  `dbg_retire_skip_restamp`) is still withdrawn by a lone remounting mount
  thread — after 10.4 s, not at once and not 30 s — its key fenced
  (P236-FENCE-CERTIFIED), the mount admitted; the clean control lap logged
  neither a grace nor a withdraw.
- Negative, `tests/d0965_successor_killed_after_register.sh`
  (20260918T145025Z_d0965kill_s51kill3): a successor that REGISTERED and was
  virsh-destroyed before settling its record.  The peer, mounting 0.7 s
  after the kill, held the grace, withdrew at 10.5 s, fenced the corpse's
  registration (a 1 s key poll on the peer shows the key gone at 12.1 s —
  the fence, not the target: the iSCSI target kept the dead session's
  registration for the whole grace), mounted in 22.7 s; the victim rebooted,
  re-prepped and rejoined without a refusal.

No shutdown or corruption line in any lap.  Harness lessons that cost laps:
a fixed sleep before the virsh destroy killed the successor before its
REGISTER (the kill now keys on A's own P-PRKEY-REGISTERED line); waiting on
the dead node's ssh blocked 96 s, long enough that the arm never ran (the
mount client runs under setsid and is killed with the VM); a rebooted node
has no /src until the NFS tree is mounted, which read as a prep failure.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.10 — the recycle-time unpaired holder end: the last three owed verifications, and the recycle no longer discards a live peer BAST

D-RECYCLE-DEFERRED-FREE-CORPSE-ILOCK-END-UNPAIRED-EX-HOLDER-UNDERFLOW-0532
was fixed at its cause in 0.64.16 (the recycle releases the ILOCK it took
without a DLM begin raw, so nothing consumes a holder count it never
incremented), the internal nowait sites were paired in 0.64.27 and the two
user-reachable ones refused in 0.87.1, and `p71_underflows` has read zero in
every run since.  The record stayed open on four verifications.  Two were
already done: the io_uring/peer-conflict arm ran under 0.87.7 (two arms,
4500 direct I/Os each, images identical), and the reuse laps were written.
This version closes the other two and answers the design consult's hazards
(Astra, 2026-09-18) with measurements rather than churn.

The relog arm (`tests/d0532_relog_live_holder.sh`) could not be run before
now for two instrument reasons.  The peer's session was triggered before it
had logged in, so its write landed after the quiet-age release of the
holder's EX and no BAST ever reached the drain (s49a/s49b: `P70-BP qsrc=5
held_ms=1002`, the peer's write in 98 ms); the session now announces READY
before it blocks.  And the regular-file early-out ahead of the durable loop
skips the loop whenever the drain's own AIL flush has landed the inode,
which on a regular file is every time, so the parked-drain and forced
re-log knobs sat behind a branch that was never taken; the early-out now
falls through while `dbg_relog_force_ino` is armed.  Measured on the 2-node
TCP rig, 4 laps across two builds (s49c 59B10B17…, s49d 9D023C60…): the
drain parks, the forced re-log runs its nowait ILOCK, commit and raw unlock
with `ex_before=0 ex_after=0 pr 0/0`, `p71_underflows=0`, and the genuine
IOLOCK_EXCL holder is admitted only after the release
(`P-IOLOCK-HOLD` ~60 ms after `P146V-RELOG-HOLDERS`, order=serialized 4/4).
That is by design and it is the closure argument the consult asked for: a
user task with nothing pinned asking for a file in state BAST or DEMOTING
parks in the demote-wait (`file_yield_on_demote`, 0.75.40); the only
admissions during a drain are this inode's direct-I/O completions and
folio-holding writeback submitters (`mxfs_ilock_admit_ioend`); the drain
waits out the direct I/O at its entry with no holder present and
`iomap_dio_complete` drops the completion's ILOCK before `inode_dio_end`,
so no completion holder outlives that wait; and the page flush-and-wait
before the loop leaves no dirty folio while every new writer is parked, so
no writeback submitter can be admitted between the last zero-holder check
and the re-log.  The harness header records the measured shape.

The recycle's clearing of a pending BAST (item c) is answered by an
invariant, found by trying to break it.  The consult ruled that a cached
EX that survives a deferred free is the same DLM grant the new incarnation
is served from, so a peer's BAST delivered to the corpse before its drain
ran is an obligation on the grant and may not be discarded because the
inode incarnation changed.  The directed schedule it asked for
(`tests/d0532_pending_bast_recycle.sh`, new one-shot knob
`dbg_bast_defer_ino`/`dbg_bast_defer_ms` parks the BAST work item before it
touches the in-core state) cannot reach the recycle: the work item holds
an inode reference for its whole life, so while a delivered BAST is
outstanding the last iput cannot happen and the inode is never inactivated,
never freed, never reclaimable, never recycled.  Measured 9/9 laps (s49b,
s49c, s49d): `rm` and `sync` completed ~50 ms into a 700 ms park, the
corpse still read `nlink=0 imode=0100644` at `P-BAST-DEFER-END`, the drain
released 4 ms later, `P-INACT-CERT` and `P128-INACT-DEFER` followed 10 ms
after that, the create got a fresh number every lap, and the peer was
served by the one parked BAST (no `P36-RETRY`, one `P7B-BASTNOTIFY`).  An
audit of all 14 sites that record a pending BAST shows each either arms a
work item under an `igrab` reference, parks the signal on a live holder
whose lock end arms it, or sets it on an inode already being evicted.  The
recycle now classifies what it meets: a signal on a grant already NL is
the stale one the clear exists for (`recycle_bast_stale`); a signal on a
live grant is kept, flag and BAST state both, so the queued work drains
and the new incarnation's first acquire parks behind the hand-off
(`recycle_bast_kept`, `P-RECYCLE-BAST-KEEP`; `recycle_bast_keep=0` restores
the clear, `recycle_bast_dropped`).  The kept path was not reached on this
build and `recycle_bast_kept` reading non-zero anywhere is the tripwire
that the invariant broke.  Under peer churn
(`tests/d0532_reuse_lap.sh PEER=test2`, the reuse arm now needs the peer:
a lone creator takes no grant, so nothing is deferred and nothing recycles)
2800 laps met 5273 recycles with a cached grant, 0 phantoms, 58 no-inode
BASTs on reclaimable corpses, 0 live signals, `p71_underflows=0`; the
shape witness is the exact `recycle_grant_cached` counter, because the
`P139` line budget was spent by the first 200-lap run and read 0 for the
next 2000.  A BAST that lands during the recycle's raw ILOCK window meets
an inode in a transient lifecycle class and is parked and requeued
(`mxfs_noino_lifecycle_park`), not dropped.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `9D023C6028C6935FB10A0D9`: relog arm
s49d, pending-BAST schedule s49d 3/3, reuse lap s49d 300 laps / 573
recycles clean; no splat, no shutdown, both nodes mounted throughout.


When a peer dies, the survivor replays the peer's journal slice through its
own buffer cache: every logged block is read into the cache, the image
applied and written home, and the cached copy stays, clean and `XBF_DONE`.
No inode tenure on the survivor read those images, so the tenure-end
eviction of 0.87.6 never sees them, and the acquire-time eviction is keyed
on the acquired inode's number.  After the peer returns, frees the file's
blocks and rebuilds a tree over the same addresses under a different inode
number, the survivor's first access is served the recovery image from its
cache with no read — the 0.87.6 shape from a producer outside the grant
discipline.  Measured on the 2-node TCP rig (`tests/recov_bmbt_reuse.sh`):
the victim built a 20000-extent file and was killed mid-write; the
survivor's replay populated 158 extent-tree images and two AG-btree images
in its cache (`recov_bmbt_cached=158`); with the freed inode number reused
by the new file the survivor's acquire evicted all 158 by owner
(`P67-BMBT-EVICT-ENTER nthisino=158`) and nothing was served stale; with a
different inode number and the retirement off, the survivor's read of the
new file was served two of the dead file's extent-tree images from its
cache with no read (`P-RECOV-CACHE-HIT daddr=4332096` and `4375176`,
`xfs_bmbt`).

Recovery now retires the images it populated before it publishes.  While
the recovery task replays, every buffer it reads is tagged at the read
(`b_mxfs_recov_image`), whether the replay then rewrites the image or skips
it as already newer, and recovery readahead is off for a foreign replay so
every recovery read is that synchronous, attributable one; the tag is
dropped only by the retirement or by another task's fresh read, never by an
I/O completion.  After the replayed images are flushed home and before the
`IMAGES_REPLAYED` milestone is published (after which the dead holds are
purged and access resumes), `mxfs_recov_image_evict` walks the cache and
clears `XBF_DONE` on every clean tagged image of an extent-allocated class —
extent-tree, directory, da, attr and symlink blocks, the AG btrees, and any
block whose verifier the list does not know — with the tenure-end evict's
idiom: never staled, re-checked under the buffer lock, local work refused.
Inode clusters, AG headers, the superblock and dquots are explicit
exemptions: they live at fixed addresses, a stale image of one is what every
previous tenure of this node leaves behind, and their acquire-time reloads
refresh them (counted, `recov_other_cached`).  A tagged image that cannot be
locked in 30 s or still carries local work makes the recovery return a
retryable error exactly as a home-flush failure does: nothing is published
and the next election replays the slice and retires again (`recov_busy`,
`recov_localwork`; `dbg_recov_evict_fail_after` injects it once).  A cache
hit on a tagged image outside recovery counts `recov_cache_hit` and must
read zero; the recovery's own re-reads of what it populated are counted
apart.  `recov_evict=0` keeps the census and skips the retirement.  Shape
per the consult (Astra): provenance by producer rather than by write, sticky
through the recovery, the fence before publication, exemptions explicit,
unknown verifiers fail closed.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build C78E0BB3060F6760E65DDE4 (the reuse
lap needs 0.87.8 underneath it: without the replayed dinode on the platter
the victim cannot even delete its file after rejoining).  Fix laps: the
survivor's replay populated 156 and 165 extent-tree images and 4 and 2
AG-btree images, retired all 160 and 167 before publication
(`P-RECOV-IMAGE-EVICT ... evicted=160 local=0 busy=0`), and after the
victim's rebuild under a different inode number served none from its cache
(`recov_cache_hit=0`, `bmbt_lookup_bad=0`, no CRC line), read the victim's
digest, wrote 64 blocks, and both nodes' final images matched the writers'
block lists; cold check clean.  Retry arm (`RETRYFAIL=20`): the injected
failure fired after 20 of the 162 selected images were retired
(`evicted=20 busy=1 — NOT all retired; slice NOT published, will retry`),
the second attempt 37 s later retired all 162 and published, the same
checks clean.  Control (`recov_evict=0`): 155 extent-tree images left
cached, and the survivor's `md5sum` of the rebuilt file was served two of
them from its cache with no read (`P-RECOV-CACHE-HIT daddr=4332096` and
`4375176`, `xfs_bmbt`); this lap's two served images matched the rebuilt
tree, so nothing else failed.  The recovery task's own re-reads of what it
populated (10171 on the 107-checkpoint lap) are counted apart.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.8 — a dead peer's dinode images replayed by the survivor never reached the platter: the inode-cluster write's authority mask dropped them

When a peer dies the survivor replays its journal slice.  Every inode log
item in the slice passes the node-independent changecount gate and is
applied into the survivor's cached inode cluster, which is queued for the
home flush; the buffer images (extent-tree leaves, directory blocks, AG
btrees) are applied the same way.  But every inode-cluster write on a
clustered mount goes through `mxfs_submit_partial_inode_write`
(`pal/linux/xfs_buf.c`), the authority mask that publishes only the slots
this node logged this round or holds with a write grant, and a slot the
recovery patched is neither: no inode item of this node's is attached, no
in-core inode exists for it.  The mask dropped the replayed dinode as an
un-owned passenger, and with the rest of the cluster free it refused the
whole write with no I/O while completing the buffer as landed, so the home
flush milestone reported the images flushed.  The dead peer's leaves and AG
images landed; its inode cores did not.  Measured on the 2-node TCP rig
(`tests/recov_bmbt_reuse.sh`): the victim built a 20000-extent file and was
killed mid-write; the survivor applied all 7 dinode images of the slice
(`P77-FRINODE verdict=APPLY`, the last at changecount 64509, 32253
extents), then `P218-CLUSTER-PASSENGER daddr=4332104 slot=0 ino=8388736
nocore=1 skipped=1` and `P218-WRITE-REFUSED daddr=4332104 slots=1`, then
`P226-FR-HOMEFLUSH ... flushed home`.  The rejoined victim's `rm` read the
platter dinode still at its pre-death flush (19271 extents, changecount
38546) against leaves stamped with the last replayed checkpoint and holding
19387 records at that point (`P-BMBT-OVERCOUNT`), cancelled a dirty
transaction and shut the node down; the same three lines on the previous
control lap.  This is the mechanism behind the older 32-node record of an
inobt-allocated inode with a free core after survivors replayed two victims
(D-0517's `P-ALLOC-FREE-CORE`): a creation whose AG images landed and whose
core did not.  The 0.83.3 death laps did not meet it because their files
had landed long before the kill, so every inode item was skipped as
already on disk and no cluster write was owed.

The recovery is the authority for those slots: the dead node held them at
death (the token verdict says so) and its grants stay frozen until the
recovery completes, so no successor image can exist.  The buffer now
records the slots a log recovery patched (`b_mxfs_recov_slots`, set by the
inode-item replay at the dinode it applied and by the inode-buffer replay
at every unlinked pointer it copied, for a foreign, adopted or own-slice
recovery alike), and the partial cluster writer treats a set bit exactly as
a slot logged this round: written, never masked, never refused
(`P218-RECOV-OWNED`).  Slots the recovery did not touch keep the mask.  The
bits are cleared when a write of the buffer completes and when a stale
buffer is reused; a failed recovery write stales the buffer as before.
`recov_slots_own=0` is the same-build control.  Two instruments stay:
`P77-FRINODE` prints every inode-item verdict of an untrusted replay with
both sides' changecount and extent count (budgeted, unbounded under
`instr`), and the extent-read overcount that shuts a node down now names
the leaf, the in-core count and a platter read of the dinode
(`P-BMBT-OVERCOUNT`).  The reuse harness fails a lap on a refused cluster
write or a victim shutdown over the recovered file, and ends with the cold
structural check.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build C78E0BB3060F6760E65DDE4, with
`tests/recov_bmbt_reuse.sh` (victim builds a 20000-extent file, is killed
mid-write, rejoins, deletes it and rebuilds over the freed addresses under a
different inode number; the survivor then reads and writes the new file;
both nodes check the final image against the writers' block lists; both
unmount for a cold `chk_mxfs`).  Two fix laps clean on every check: the
survivor applied 107 and 9 dinode images of the slices, each cluster write
carried the recovery-owned slot (`P218-RECOV-OWNED daddr=4332104
slots=0x1`) and none was refused, the rejoined victim's delete and rebuild
went through, the survivor's read matched the victim's digest, its 64 writes
completed, both final images matched the block lists (lost=0 stray=0
short=0), no shutdown on either node, the quiesced volume clean with zero
half-applied inodes (walls 201 s and 206 s).  The retry arm passed the same
checks with two recovery attempts (7 images applied on the first, the same
7 skipped on the second as already on the platter, two owned writes).  The
control with the ownership knob off (`recov_slots_own=0`) shows the
assertion instead of the torn platter: every recovery attempt's cluster
write computed an empty I/O over the owned slot (`P218-RECOV-REFUSED
daddr=4332104 slots=0x1 logged=0x0 skip=0xfffffffe pr_skip=0x1`), the
replay failed and stayed unpublished, and the survivor retried every ~35 s
without publishing; the torn platter itself was reproduced twice on the
previous builds (the `P218-WRITE-REFUSED` and `P-BMBT-OVERCOUNT` lines
above).  Regression on the same build: the death/rejoin lap
(`tests/d0287_2node_death_rejoin.sh`, the holder paused in its release drain
across the peer's death, recovery published in 79 s, the rejoined peer's
read waited out the pause and matched the holder's digest, no shutdown,
328 s) and the three direct-write extent laps
(`tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh` aligned, extending, and the deep
65536-block span: 14510/14939, 13852/14522 and 2058/2013 writes per node,
zero failures, zero shutdowns, walls 90-91 s).

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.7 — an inode grant was released while this node's direct I/O on the inode was still in flight

The release pipeline decided that nobody was using an inode by counting its
DLM holders, and an asynchronous direct read or write is not one for most of
its life: io_uring drops the IOLOCK ride when submission returns
`-EIOCBQUEUED`, with the bios still outstanding (`i_dio_count > 0`).  A BAST
in that window committed the release and handed the grant to the peer, whose
tenure then overlapped bios this node was still landing — a peer read could
run before this node's write hit the platter, a peer write could be overwritten
by this node's late bio, and a direct read here could return a mix across a
peer's write.  Measured on the 2-node TCP rig with a detector at the release
commit (`P-REL-DIO-INFLIGHT`, `rel_dio_inflight`): 16 releases per lap
committed with `i_dio_count=1` under io_uring O_DIRECT reads and overwrites on
test1 with test2 conflicting.  Nothing in the pipeline called
`inode_dio_wait`.

The release now orders: close admission (the BAST state parks new rides) → no
ordinary holder at entry → wait for the inode's direct I/O → drain → terminal
check → NL store.  In `mxfs_dlm_bast_process`, when no holder was present at
entry, `inode_dio_wait` runs before the log force and the AIL drain, so a
completion's commits — an unwritten conversion or a size update that may still
be in the CIL when the wait returns — are covered by the drain that follows
(`rel_dio_waited`, `rel_dio_wait_max_us`, `P971-REL-DIO-WAIT`).  It waits only
from a quiescent entry: a holder still admitted may be mid-submission and about
to park on its own nested ILOCK, so waiting on it would deadlock, and the
holders gate aborts and re-arms as before.  Under the inode spinlock and before
the NL store, a non-zero count now keeps the grant and the BAST state and
re-fires the pipeline at once instead of committing (`rel_dio_defer`,
`P971-REL-DIO-DEFER`); the post-store detector stays as telemetry that must
read zero.  The direct write's completion takes ILOCK_EXCL after its ride is
gone — an unwritten conversion or a size update — while the pipeline is
waiting for exactly that completion.  iomap runs such a completion on the
direct-I/O completion workqueue, a kernel thread, and the cached-grant fast
path admits a kernel thread under the still-EX mode as a counted holder, so
the holders gate before the NL store aborts and re-arms if it still holds;
that is the path measured (`dioend_kthread`, `dioend_in_drain`).  For a
completion in task context, which iomap does not produce today, the whole of
`xfs_dio_write_end_io` is bracketed in a per-task registry keyed on task and
inode (`xfs_diotask_enter/exit`), and `mxfs_ilock_admit_ioend` admits a
registered task as this inode's own nested EX holder under the still-granted
mirror, the same way as the ioend worker and never as a general writeback
privilege (`dioend_admit`).  An O_DSYNC write's sync tail runs after
`inode_dio_end` in iomap and acquires fresh.  Polled direct I/O is refused on a clustered mount
(`-EOPNOTSUPP`, `dio_hipri_refused`): `inode_dio_wait` drives no polling and
the ring that would poll can be parked behind the release, so the mode is
unsupported rather than half-supported.  The wait is unbounded, like the
page-writeback wait: a bio the device still owns is not over because a clock
ran out, and the grant stays this node's until it is; the drain watch names a
stall.  `rel_dio_wait=0` restores the old release for A/B.  Shape per the
consult (Astra): the terminal check is the fail-closed guard, not the
synchronisation.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `82F4ABB2C34644DE8507482`, with
`tests/d0532_nowait_iomap_probe.sh PEER=test2 test1 500`: io_uring O_DIRECT
reads, overwrites, O_DSYNC overwrites, writes into preallocated unwritten
blocks, extending writes and polled reads on test1, 500 each, with test2
looping conflicting O_DIRECT reads and whole-block writes of the same file,
then both nodes' images compared.  Two fix arms from one deployment
(`tests/evidence/20260918T055404Z_d0532nw_fix971b_peer1` and
`..._fix971b_peer2`): `rel_dio_inflight=0` in every phase, the release waited
for outstanding direct I/O 35/8/3/1/3/5 and 37/14/4/7/3/2 times across the
control-mode, read, overwrite, O_DSYNC, unwritten and extending phases (longest
wait 3.5 ms), `rel_dio_defer=0`, every one of the 4500 I/Os per arm
succeeded, the polled reads were refused 500/500, `p71_underflows=0`, no
splat, no shutdown, and both nodes read the identical 4 MiB image with no
torn block.  In every write phase completions began while the inode's
release was in progress (`dioend_in_drain` 3/1/3/5 and 4/7/3/3, all on the
completion workqueue: `dioend_kthread=500` per phase) and the waits ended,
which is the progress path; `dioend_task` equals the refused-nowait count in
each phase — the size-zero error completion of a refused first attempt, run
under the submitter's still-held ride — and `dioend_admit=0`, so the registry
admission was not needed.  The control on the same build between the two fix
arms, `rel_dio_wait=0` on both nodes
(`tests/evidence/20260918T055428Z_d0532nw_ctl971b_peer`): 13 and 17 releases
committed with direct I/O in flight in the control-mode and read phases,
`rel_dio_waited=0`, the lap failed on that count with every I/O still
succeeding and the images still identical — the precondition, not yet the
torn read, at this I/O size.  Regression on the fix build, the
0.87.2–0.87.6 lap set (`tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh`, two nodes
alternating O_DIRECT writes to one file; `tests/d0970_survivor_demote_leak.sh`):
aligned 90 s 14284/14491 writes, mixed sector writes 15052/15509, one-leaf
extending 13418/14355 with all 256 written blocks accounted (`lost=0 stray=0
short=0`), survivor 200 writes with the peer's write landing 467 ms after them,
300 s 48213/49567, and the 65536-block span 2362/2184 with all 4397 written
blocks accounted; every write succeeded on every lap, no shutdown, `crc=0`,
and both nodes read the identical image each time.  Not exercised: a device
stall under the wait (the wait is unbounded and the grant stays pinned by
construction), and a task-context completion with filesystem work, which
iomap does not produce.


## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.6 — a node kept a deleted file's extent-tree blocks in its cache and served one for the file that reused the address

Every extent-tree (bmbt) block a node caches was read under a grant on the
owning inode, and freeing a block of that tree needs an EX grant, which needs
this node's grant released first.  Nothing retired the cached image when the
tenure ended: the reload at the next acquire evicts the cached bmbt blocks the
acquired inode owns, and a block freed from another inode's tree still carries
that other owner.  Measured on the 2-node TCP rig with the probe added at the
btree lookup's refusal path: node B had cached the leaves of a 20000-extent
file under its write tenures, node A deleted the file and built a new one whose
tree reused two of those addresses, and B's first acquire of the new inode
found 107 cached bmbt buffers owned by nobody it held (`P67-BMBT-EVICT-ENTER
ino=132 nseen_bmbt=107 nthisino=0`); 2 ms later its lookups were served the
old images from the cache with no read (`P975-BMBT-LOOKUP-BAD daddr=120
cached_owner=131 ... disk_owner=132 same_image=0`, and again at daddr 3744),
the owner check refused both, and two writes failed `EFSCORRUPTED`.  The owner
check is the only thing that stood between that cache hit and a stale extent
map: the deleted inode number reallocated with its new tree at the same
address would have matched.

The end of a tenure now ends the life of the inode's cached extent-tree
images.  Before the wire unlock of every release, EX or PR, file or directory
(and before the grant leaves through inode reclaim), `mxfs_bmbt_tenure_end_evict`
walks the buffer cache for bmbt blocks whose payload owner is the inode —
data and attr fork alike, both carry the inode as owner — plus any bmbt read
still in flight, whose owner is not yet readable, and clears `XBF_DONE` on
every clean one under its lock after re-checking ops, owner and state, so the
next read goes to disk and re-verifies.  It is a barrier, not a best effort:
a buffer whose lock cannot be taken within 30 s, or that still carries local
work at the end of the tenure, is counted (`bmbt_rel_busy`,
`bmbt_rel_localwork`, with `P975-REL-LOCALWORK` naming the block) and the
release is wedged rather than unlocked, as the other unprovable releases are.
`bmbt_rel_evicted` counts what it dropped; `tenure_end_evict=0` restores the
old behaviour for A/B.  Two audit findings closed in the same change: the
regular-file release's extent-tree durability loop and the scan it runs
applied only to a btree-format data fork, so an inode whose attr fork is the
btree one was released with that tree's blocks unchecked; both now take
either fork.  The consult on the shape (Astra) also named what this does not
cover — buffers that log recovery of a dead peer's slice leaves in the cache
were never read under a tenure — and that is filed as its own record.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `B867315A52D0356C8D92DE1`, with the
pair of laps that reproduced the defect run back to back on one mount
(`tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh NOCAT=1 EXTEND=1 EXTSPAN=1048576
PREFILL=20000`, 90 s each; the first ends by deleting its 4 GiB file, the
second builds a new one over the freed addresses).  With the eviction on,
from a fresh mount: the second lap's acquire on the peer still found 101
cached bmbt buffers of the deleted file and none owned by the new inode,
and not one lookup was refused — `lookup_bad=0`, every write on both nodes
succeeded (450 and 426 contended writes after the 20000 prefilled),
identical images, `lost=0 stray=0 short=0`; the tenure ends dropped 43024
and 43025 images per node in that lap (`bmbt_rel_evicted`, about 100 per
release) with `bmbt_rel_busy=0 bmbt_rel_localwork=0`.  The control on the
same build, `tenure_end_evict=0` on both nodes from a fresh mount: the second
lap refused a cached leaf again (`P975-BMBT-LOOKUP-BAD daddr=120
cached_owner=131 cached_nrecs=176 disk_owner=132 same_image=0`),
`lookup_bad=1`, one write failed, `bmbt_rel_evicted=0`.  The 0.87.2–0.87.5
lap set on the fix build: aligned 90 s 14880/15214 writes and 300 s
50785/50140, mixed 15310/15752, one-leaf extending twice (14052/14589 and
14094/14164, `iomap_iread_pr` about 1600 per node, `bmbt_rel_evicted` about
1850 and the reload's own eviction down to 1 and 0, since the tenure end had
already retired the leaf), the 65536-block span with both writers running
(1758/1667, `lost=0 stray=0`), the io_uring peer probe `P71=0` in every
phase, and the sole-survivor lap (200/200, `end_unpaired_single=0`, peer
write 431 ms after) — every lap `lookup_bad=0 bmbt_rel_busy=0
bmbt_rel_localwork=0 crc=0`, no wedge.  The harness also now fails a lap in
which a writer completed no write, which the preamble read of a gigabyte
span had produced while the lap still passed.  Evidence:
`tests/evidence/20260918T044501Z_dwcd_x976fix1`, `…044755Z_dwcd_x976fix2`,
`…045207Z_dwcd_x976ctl1`, `…045501Z_dwcd_x976ctl2` (control),
`…045824Z_dwcd_r976_aligned`, `…050017Z_dwcd_r976_mix`,
`…050210Z_d0532nw_r976_peer`, `…050227Z_dwcd_r976_ext1`,
`…050503Z_dwcd_r976_long`, `…051025Z_dwcd_r976_ext2`,
`…051217Z_svdl_r976_surv`, `…051237Z_dwcd_r976_deep`.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.5 — a release could hand over a regular file whose extent tree was not yet on disk

A directory's release loops until every bmbt block of its extent tree that
carries local work is written home, and shuts down rather than unlock when it
cannot.  A regular file's release had no such step.  Its AIL wait covers only
the inode's own log item; the bmbt blocks were landed only by the inode flush's
destage hook, which holds at most 64 owned blocks and silently drops the rest;
and a clean inode skips that flush entirely.  One node wrote 20000 random 4 KiB
direct blocks into a 4 GiB sparse file (a two-level tree of about 97 bmbt
blocks) and released it: the release flush logged `held=64 capped=33`, the
peer followed the published root to a block that was not a bmbt block on disk
(3644 CRC failures, 361 failed writes), and every later reload on the first
node still found that block in its AIL with committed content never written
home — which its xfsaild then wrote much later, over whatever the peer had
written there since.

The regular-file EX release now runs the directory's check-and-flush pair
(`mxfs_dir_bmbt_scan`) at the end of its durable block, reached by both the
flush loop and the clean-inode early-out, before the device flush and the
unlock: every owned bmbt buffer that is dirty, in the AIL, pinned, queued, or
logged since it was last written — with no `XBF_DONE` requirement — is written
and waited for, repeated until the check finds nothing.  If that cannot be done
within 30 s the release is wedged (`mxfs_inode_wedge`: the wire CAS refused,
the grant pinned on disk, the mount shut down) instead of unlocked.  The mode
store to NL earlier in the release has already closed the fast path, so no
local operation can add work between the last check and the unlock; the
release path has no EX-to-PR downgrade, and a PR holder logs no extent changes.
The scan's flush half also never writes a stale (freed) buffer now: its free is
retired by the log force, and its payload is dead.  Counters:
`reg_bmbt_rel_flushed`, `reg_bmbt_rel_wedge`, `bmbt_scan_stale_skip`, and the
detectors `iflush_bmbt_capped` and `iflush_bmbt_notdone_needs` in the flush
hook, whose 64-block batch no longer carries the release's correctness.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `8E4C6A2CC5EAC566F5438FD`, with the same
lap that measured the defect (`tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh`,
`EXTEND=1 EXTSPAN=1048576 PREFILL=20000`, 90 s), twice: once with each
writer's preamble read of the file and once without it (`NOCAT=1`).  Zero CRC
failures and zero not-a-bmbt-block verdicts on either node in either lap
(before: 1590 and 3291 failures in two laps); the release scan had to write in
1 release of the first lap and in 1 and 3 releases per node of the second
(`reg_bmbt_rel_flushed`), never wedged, while the flush hook's batch cap was
hit 15265 and 15268 times in the second lap without consequence.  Every write
succeeded: 20000 prefilled plus 428 and 425 contended writes per node in the
`NOCAT` lap, the two nodes read the same 4 GiB image
(md5 `9d9427fa…`, torn=0), and the extending-write check found every one of
the 20654 written blocks holding its writer's byte with every other block of
the 1048557 still zero (`lost=0 stray=0 short=0`; 22494 of 1048573 in the
first lap).  Evidence: `tests/evidence/20260918T040220Z_dwcd_fin_huge` and
`20260918T041101Z_dwcd_fin_hugenc`.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.4 — a regular file's stale extent-tree leaf survived a reload, failing a node's writes and letting its inode flushes write the leaf over the peer's

A node that re-acquires an inode after a peer held it exclusive reloads the
dinode, and with it the root of a btree-format extent map, from disk.  The
reload then evicts this node's cached bmbt blocks so the next extent load reads
the peer's leaves — but only for directories.  A regular file's stale leaves
survived.  Two nodes extending one sparse file with aligned `O_DIRECT` writes
(a one-leaf btree) showed both consequences on the 2-node TCP rig:

- test2's extent loads walked the peer's root into its own pre-reload
  15-record leaf (`P59-IREAD-MISMATCH loaded=15 if_nextents=17..232`), so 3620
  of its 3635 writes failed `EFSCORRUPTED`.
- Its inode flushes — driven by the timestamp updates, while every load failed
  — ran `mxfs_iflush_force_bmbt_durable`, which destages every cached bmbt block
  the inode owns, clean ones included, on the premise that the in-core map is
  authoritative.  That leaf went to disk over the peer's committed one while the
  same flush published the peer's extent count (`P63-TORN-FLUSH if_nextents=N
  leafsum=15`, 1818 times): a torn on-disk dinode/leaf pair after every test2
  release, repaired only because the peer happened to release last.  A merged
  timeline of both nodes' leaf writes to one address shows test2 always writing
  15 records while test1 wrote 17, 21, 28, 33, 37, 41 and on.

Three changes, measured one at a time:

1. The reload's eviction (the owner walk and the evict-by-root companion) now
   runs for every btree-format data fork, not only a directory's; nothing in
   either helper is specific to directories.  `reload_evict_file_bmbt=0`
   restores the directory-only behaviour for A/B.
2. The inode flush no longer destages a clean cached bmbt block while the fork's
   extents are unread.  An unread fork was adopted from disk and has not changed
   here since, so a clean cached block is at best what is already on disk and at
   worst a pre-reload image of a leaf a peer has rewritten.  Blocks that carry
   local modifications are still destaged and counted, since an unread fork
   holding local bmbt work would mean the reload did not retire this node's
   previous tenure.  The torn-flush detector no longer judges an unread fork, on
   which its leaf sum is zero by construction.  Counters: `iflush_unread_clean_skip`,
   `iflush_unread_local`, and `bmbt_write_unread`, an uncapped count at the
   bmbt write chokepoint of any block written while its owner's extents are
   unread.
3. The eviction walk's 64-entry hold array is a batch size, no longer a limit.
   On a file with 20000 extents (about 97 bmbt blocks) the walk left 21773 and
   26941 owned blocks cached in one lap, and one node's extent loads then read
   stale leaves (579 mismatches, every write on that node failed).  When the
   walk sees more than it can hold it drops its holds, sizes the array to what
   it saw and walks again (`bmbt_evict_capped` counts anything still left).

Three detectors read "a one-record in-inode root" as "a single leaf", which
holds only for a level-1 root: a level-2 root with one pointer names an
interior node over many leaves.  On a two-level file tree the torn-flush
detector reported 42 false tears and the insert detector printed on every
extent insert (5791 lines in 90 s, unratelimited).  Both now require
`bb_level == 1`.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `8E4C6A2CC5EAC566F5438FD`.  The
one-leaf lap (`EXTEND=1`, 256-block span, 90 s) twice: 13455 and 14290, then
12573 and 13396 writes per node, none failed, `iread_mismatch=0
torn_flush=0 bmbt_write_unread=0` on both nodes, test2's leaf writes tracking
test1's (1818/1833 and 1724/1753 leaf writes), every written block holding
its writer's byte and the images identical (`lost=0 stray=0`).  The A/B
control with `reload_evict_file_bmbt=0` on the same build reproduced the
failed writes — test1 0 succeeded, 8397 failed, 8398 extent loads — while the
flush guard alone held the disk clean: 1797 clean blocks skipped under an
unread fork, `bmbt_write_unread=0 torn_flush=0`.  The 65536-block span lap
and the two 20000-extent laps of the 0.87.5 entry (a two-level, ~97-block
tree; `bmbt_evict_capped=0`, no false tears) pass with the same counters at
zero.  Evidence: `tests/evidence/20260918T035403Z_dwcd_fin_ext1`,
`…035552Z_dwcd_fin_ext2`, `…035742Z_dwcd_fin_armB` (control),
`…035930Z_dwcd_fin_deep`.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.3 — a buffered read that had to load a file's extent map asked the cluster for EX under its own shared lock and hung both nodes

`xfs_ilock_for_iomap` open-coded the upstream extent-load rule — take
`ILOCK_EXCL` when the extents are not yet read — without the MXFS tag that asks
the cluster for PR instead, and without the re-check after the acquire that the
shared data-map helper carries.  On a clustered mount `ILOCK_EXCL` is a cluster
EX, and every caller that starts at a shared mapping already holds its IOLOCK
shared, a counted PR on the same inode.  With a peer extending the file by
direct writes, a buffered `cat` on test1 wedged in readahead asking EX under its
own PR (`P73-WAITSTALL req=EX mode=PR pr=1 acq_comm=cat`), the release that
peer needed waited for that PR, and the peer's `open()` queued behind it; no
writer on either node made progress for 90 s, 2 of 2 laps.

A shared request now goes through `xfs_ilock_data_map_shared`, so the extent
load takes the local lock exclusive but asks the cluster only for PR, which
already excludes every cluster writer, and the fork is re-checked after the
acquire, whose own reload can unload it.  Explicitly exclusive requests are
unchanged.  One consequence handled in the same change: a shared request can
now come back as local-exclusive-but-cluster-PR, so the direct-write mapping's
"relock if the inode turned copy-on-write" test asks for a true EX rather than
comparing against plain `ILOCK_SHARED`.  `iomap_iread_pr` counts the mappings
whose load asked for PR.

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `8E4C6A2CC5EAC566F5438FD`, with the lap
that hung (`tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh EXTEND=1`, 90 s), twice:
the reader's preamble completed and both writers ran the whole window (13455
and 14290, then 12573 and 13396 writes per node, none failed),
`waitstall=0`, and the extent loads that would have asked for EX asked for PR
instead (`iomap_iread_pr` 1583/1578 and 1514/1510 per node).  The same held
on the 65536-block and the two 20000-extent laps of the entries above
(`iomap_iread_pr` 736, 528 and 425 on the reading node, `waitstall=0`).
Evidence: `tests/evidence/20260918T035403Z_dwcd_fin_ext1` and
`…035552Z_dwcd_fin_ext2`.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.2 — two nodes overwriting one file with direct writes shut both nodes down, and a sole survivor's direct writes, closes and directory operations left unpaired lock ends

Two nodes each overwriting the same file with plain aligned `O_DIRECT` writes
shut both filesystems down in about 70 s on the 2-node TCP rig.  An aligned
direct write takes the IOLOCK shared, which on a cached PR grant is a counted
PR hold, and `xfs_file_write_checks` then updates the timestamps under
`ILOCK_EXCL`, which asks the cluster for EX while that same task's PR is still
counted.  With both nodes in that state the master denies each conversion
(`P-CONVBLK-DENY held_mode=PR req_mode=EX`, `-EDEADLK`); the requester's
self-demote cannot release a PR its own task holds (`P15-REL-ABORT pr=1`), and
after 65 one-second retry laps `mxfs_dlm_ilock_begin` declares an `EDEADLK
retry livelock` and forces a shutdown.  Stacks captured on both nodes at 40 s
put every writer in `xfs_vn_update_time -> xfs_ilock -> mxfs_dlm_ilock_begin`
under its own shared ride.  Measured before the change: test1 74 writes
succeeded and 24282 failed, test2 101 and 25099, both mounts dead.

On a clustered mount the write checks now never reach the timestamp update
under a shared ride: they drop it and retake the IOLOCK exclusive, so the
update's EX nests on the EX the ride holds, and the aligned and atomic writers
demote back to shared for the transfer itself.  The demote moves the holder
count from EX to PR and keeps the grant at EX.  The retake is counted
(`write_checks_excl`).

That change made every clustered direct write demote, which exposed the same
mismatch in three places on a sole survivor — a node that is single-node now
but has had a peer, whose lock begin therefore counts holders like any member
while these three still skipped on "single-node":

- `mxfs_dlm_ilock_demote` returned without moving the count, so each shared
  unlock afterwards ended a PR nobody held: 200 of 200 direct writes on a
  survivor.
- `mxfs_dlm_ilock_try` returned success without counting, so every nowait
  IOLOCK a survivor took — `xfs_file_release`'s trylock at each `close()` —
  was an unpaired end that consumed whatever EX count another task held on
  the inode: 200 of 200.
- `mxfs_dlm_dir_hold_ex` did not count the directory pin its paired end
  releases: each `mkdir` and `rmdir` on a survivor left one.

All three now skip only where begin skips, on a mount that has never had a
peer.  New detectors count what they caught: `end_unpaired_single` (ends on a
survivor that found no holder, with `P71-SURVIVOR-UNPAIRED` naming the site)
and `demote_survivor` (demotes taken on a survivor).

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, build `8E4C6A2CC5EAC566F5438FD`, in one
chain.  The lap that shut both nodes down (`tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh`,
aligned 4 KiB overwrites from both nodes): 14818 and 14999 writes per node
in 90 s, then 49890 and 49513 in 300 s, every one succeeded, every one
retaken exclusive before its timestamp update (`write_checks_excl` equal to
the write count), no conversion livelock, no shutdown, both nodes reading
the same untorn image; the mixed lap adding unaligned 512-byte writes, 15316
and 15888 writes, likewise.  The io_uring peer-conflict probe
(`tests/d0532_nowait_iomap_probe.sh PEER=test2`): `P71=0` in every phase
with identical untorn images.  The sole-survivor lap
(`tests/d0970_survivor_demote_leak.sh`): 200 of 200 direct writes on the
survivor with `demote_survivor=200 end_unpaired_single=0`, its mkdir/rmdir
phase `end_unpaired_single=0`, and the returning peer's first write landed
460 ms after the survivor's writes with identical images.  Evidence:
`tests/evidence/20260918T034355Z_dwcd_fin_aligned`, `…034749Z_dwcd_fin_long`,
`…034544Z_dwcd_fin_mix`, `…034733Z_d0532nw_fin_peer`,
`…034335Z_svdl_fin_surv`.

## 2026-09-18 — 0.87.1 — io_uring could strip a direct I/O's cluster holder count mid-transfer, and the check meant to catch that class could not see it

An ILOCK taken with `xfs_ilock_nowait` enters no cluster DLM begin, while
`xfs_iunlock` always runs the DLM end, so such a lock released by plain
`xfs_iunlock` is an unpaired end.  With no other holder that end underflows
(`P71-UNDERFLOW`); with one it quietly consumes that holder's count, and the
release pipeline — which gives the grant away when both counts read zero —
then sees zero under a live holder.  Every internal site of this shape was
