paired earlier.  Two more were not, and both are reachable from userspace.

`xfs_ilock_for_iomap` takes the ILOCK nowait under `IOMAP_NOWAIT`, and all
five of its callers release it with `xfs_iunlock`.  MXFS never sets
`FMODE_NOWAIT`, so `RWF_NOWAIT` is refused at the syscall, but io_uring treats
any file opened `O_NONBLOCK` as nowait-capable and issues its first attempt of
a read or write with `IOCB_NOWAIT`, which iomap turns into `IOMAP_NOWAIT`.  The
direct-I/O path already holds the IOLOCK — a counted PR — so the mapping's end
took that count, and the transfer ran with the inode's holder count at zero:
a peer's BAST in that window could release the grant under an in-flight read
or write.  Measured on the 2-node TCP rig with a raw io_uring driver, 200
operations per phase: 184 underflows for O_DIRECT reads and 79 (print-capped)
for O_DIRECT overwrites, zero for the same operations without `O_NONBLOCK`.  On
a clustered mount the nowait mapping is now refused with `-EAGAIN` before
anything is taken.  That is the documented `IOMAP_NOWAIT` answer; the first
mapping of the request has submitted nothing, and io_uring reissues from a
worker through the blocking, counted arm.  A counted DLM try inside the helper
would keep the nowait fast path, but it would have to prove a non-blocking end
path and correct handling of a failure on a later mapping of a multi-extent
direct I/O; MXFS does not advertise nowait I/O, so that optimisation is not
worth those risks.  After the change: 184 and 88 refusals, zero underflows,
every operation completed.

`mxfs_dirdump`, the diagnostic behind a lookup of `.mxfs_dirdump1`, released
its per-block nowait ILOCK the same way: 5 blocks, 5 underflows.  It now
releases raw, which is what a dump that is documented to touch no DLM state
should do; afterwards 5 blocks and none.

The mechanical check for this class, `tests/audit_ilock_nowait_pairs.sh`,
scanned a fixed list of files that did not include `xfs_dir2_readdir.c`, and
reported a helper that returns holding a nowait ILOCK as "caller-released"
information rather than a failure — which is how `xfs_ilock_for_iomap`
escaped.  It now scans every source file the last build compiled and fails
any such helper unless the function carries an explicit contract: an IOLOCK-only
helper (the three `xfs_ilock_iocb*` rides, which now also warn if handed an
ILOCK flag) or a nowait arm reachable only on a mount without a cluster DLM.
Result: 105 files, 19 sites, 0 failures.

`P71-UNDERFLOW` prints at most 300 lines per load, so a window after that
budget is spent reads zero whatever happens; `p71_underflows` is now an exact,
resettable counter beside it.  `iomap_nowait_refused` counts the new refusal,
so a harness can prove the path ran — io_uring retries an `-EAGAIN` from a
worker, so a completed operation proves nothing.  A detector,
`P-REL-DIO-INFLIGHT` / `rel_dio_inflight`, counts grant releases committed
while the inode still has direct I/O in flight: nothing in the release
pipeline waits for `i_dio_count`, and under peer conflicts it counted 16.

The verification lap under peer grant conflicts could not complete, and not
because of this change.  Two nodes overwriting one file with aligned
`O_DIRECT` writes deadlock on the upgrade from the PR their shared IOLOCK
admitted to the EX their timestamp update needs, and after 65 one-second
retry laps both filesystems shut down — reproduced with plain `dd` and zero
nowait refusals, so on the ordinary blocking path.  It and the in-flight
release are queued as their own defects.

New harnesses: `tests/d0532_nowait_iomap_probe.sh` (with
`tests/d0532_uring_nowait.c`, `tests/d0532_peer_conflict.sh` and
`tests/d0532_img_check.py`) and `tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh`.

## 2026-09-17 — 0.87.0 — the defect ledger could silently lose a record, its release bar had no writer, and no script could ask whether the queue was clear

The queue that measures progress toward a release had three defects of its own,
all in the writer, and all of them silent.

`data/defects.json` is one JSON document rewritten whole.  `save` truncated the
file in place and there was no lock anywhere, so the read-modify-write window
spanned from `load` to the end of the rewrite.  Two concurrent `remove` calls
each read the same snapshot, each wrote their own, and the later write restored
the record the earlier one had taken out — both printing `removed`, both exiting
0, in a file that carries no dates.  Nothing afterwards showed that it had
happened.  Measured on a copy of the real 858 KB ledger: two paired removes,
one record back, no diagnostic.  A concurrent reader was exposed too, because
`json.load` raises on a truncated document and the rewrite takes about 6 ms.
Writers now hold an exclusive lock on `data/.defects.lock` across the whole
read-modify-write, and `save` writes a temporary file and renames it, so a
reader sees the before state or the after state and never a partial one.  Read
paths deliberately take no lock — the atomic rename makes them safe, and making
the one command every session runs able to block would be a worse trade.  The
wait is bounded at 30 seconds, which is several thousand times what a write
costs: a holder that has not finished by then is wedged rather than busy, and
saying so beats hanging inside a tool.  `load` now also names the file and the
parse error instead of raising a traceback, matching the board's reader.

`--release` keeps every record whose `impact` is not `noblock`, which is the
filter that turns 20 open 2/tcp defects into 16 release blockers.  But `impact`
appeared in no field table and no subcommand wrote it, while three places read
it: the filter, the per-bar tally under a listing, and the full record display.
So the four records currently marked `noblock` could only have been placed there
by hand, and no session could adjudicate a record's release bar through the tool
at all — the blocking set was frozen wherever it had been left.  `add` and
`update` now take `-I/--impact` with the values `integrity`, `stability`,
`verify` and `noblock`, and setting one requires `--impact-why` saying what was
measured.  An absent bar still blocks, exactly as an unexamined reach does:
deciding a record is harmless is a judgement someone makes and signs, never a
default.  Setting the bar to `noblock` disposes of nothing — the defect stays
open, stays in the queue, and still has to be fixed; it records only which
release it holds up.

Every list path exited 0 whether it printed sixteen records or none, so nothing
could test the release gate without parsing prose — and the empty set is exactly
the answer a gate exists to detect.  `--gate` makes the emptiness of the
filtered queue the exit status: 1 while anything is left, 0 when nothing is.  It
is opt-in so that no existing caller starts failing merely because its queue is
not empty, and it composes with `--json`.

`tests/test_defects_ledger.py` pins all three against sandboxed copies of the
real ledger, and asserts at the end that the real one was never written.  It
covers the lost update over twenty paired-remove trials, mutual exclusion while
the lock is held by another process, the absence of torn reads under twelve
concurrent writers, the refusal of a bar with no reason, a `noblock` record
leaving `--release` while remaining in the plain queue, and both exit codes.
The first version of the exit-code case filtered on a configuration that still
matched five records and asserted the blocked branch twice while reporting that
it had covered the clear one; it now fails loudly if the set it calls empty is
not.

Also added `tools/workflow_journal.py`, which extracts agent return values from
a Claude Code workflow journal.  A ten-agent run returned 382 kB and the
notification carrying it truncated all but the first 30 kB; the journal on disk
holds every return value in full, and reading it mechanically beats having a
model decide which evidence survives.

## 2026-09-17 — 0.86.3 — the one seat in bp->b_iodone now has a single door, and walking through it 16227 times eliminated the leading suspect for the AG-metadata token leak

An AG-metadata buffer that is logged takes a one-shot token: an extra buffer
reference and an increment of the allocation group's pending count, which the
DLM release pipeline waits on before the AG grant can be handed to a peer.
Exactly one of two things is supposed to consume it — the write completion
installed in bp->b_iodone, or an explicit reclaim on a detach that will never
write back.  If neither does, the buffer stays pinned and hashed in its AG
cache where the unmount drain cannot see it, and the AG's pending count never
returns to zero, so every later release of that AG spins its full 2 s bound.
That has been observed once, under free-space btree churn, and the route was
never named.

The leading suspect was the b_iodone slot itself.  It holds one function
pointer, it is not chained, and the tracker was guarding only one direction:
it warns when it finds somebody else's callback already in the slot, while
every other writer of the slot assigns unconditionally.  A foreign writer
landing between the track and the writeback would make the completion run
their callback, and nothing would consume the token — with no probe firing at
the time, because the tripwire only fires a whole dirty epoch later, by which
point the route is gone.

So the slot now has one door.  mxfs_buf_iodone_install() is the only way any
writer other than the tracker sets b_iodone, and it counts what passes
through: agmeta_iodone_installs counts every foreign write, and
agmeta_iodone_stomps counts those landing on a buffer whose AG-meta token is
still armed, with a budgeted log line naming the call site.  The denominator
is not decoration.  "stomps=0" alone is equally consistent with "no writer
ever lands on an AG-meta buffer" and "this probe is never called", and those
are opposite conclusions about whether a route has been eliminated.

tests/d0924_iodone_stomp.sh builds the workload the suspicion actually needs
rather than the one that was convenient.  Reading the tree says the writers
are disjoint — the tracker matches AGF/AGI/AGFL and the btree b_ops, the other
writers tag inode and dquot buffers — but a buffer can change what it is
between lives, and a freed btree block whose space comes back as an inode
chunk is how one xfs_buf meets both writers.  Each round therefore creates
2000 files (inode chunk allocation, so inobt and finobt split and inode
cluster buffers are tagged), punches 1024 alternate blocks out of an 8 MiB
file so the free-space trees grow and SPLIT rather than only collapse, then
deletes everything so those blocks are recycled into the next round, with a
peer touch between rounds so the AG changes hands over the churned metadata.

Measured on the 2-node TCP rig, build 7A4E0259C06C3BC5A9DCE8F, 4 rounds:
16227 foreign writes of the slot on the churning node and ZERO of them landed
on a buffer whose token was armed, with no tripwire on either node (taint bit
9 clear, which is the reliable per-boot detector — the WARN is WARN_ON_ONCE,
so counting its log lines measures the budget rather than the events).  The
b_iodone route is eliminated for that workload, and eliminated with a
denominator rather than by a silent zero.

Two things this does not claim.  It does not name the route that stranded the
token, which is still the one thing that record owes.  And it is not a fix:
nothing here changes behaviour, the helper assigns exactly what the five call
sites assigned before it.

## 2026-09-17 — 0.86.2 — the node allowed to restore the fencing reservation is the one most likely to be gone, so the survivors now queue behind it instead of each concluding "not me"

Fencing rests on a Write Exclusive - All Registrants reservation on the shared
LUN.  It is re-checked after mount by a per-mount worker: the node holding the
lowest live heartbeat slot is elected maintainer and re-reads it every 5 s,
everyone else audits on a slow jittered interval, and losing it is reported as
a safety event rather than repaired quietly.  Only the maintainer repaired,
because re-reserving writes a cluster-wide invariant and must not be raced by
32 nodes at once.

"Only the maintainer may repair" is not the same statement as "the maintainer
will repair", and on the 2-node TCP rig the difference is the whole defect.
The maintainer is the LOWEST live slot, so when that node is the one that goes
away its PR worker exits with it, and its slot keeps reading live until a
successor proves the clean release — which needs somebody to mount.  Measured
on 0.86.1: slot 0 unmounted cleanly, the reservation was released out of band
two seconds later, and the survivor reported `state=ABSENT role=auditor` and
declined to fix it.  The LU stayed unreserved until slot 0 came BACK and its
own admission re-established the reservation.  Nothing bounded that window, and
an unreserved LU is one where the next peer death cannot be fenced at all —
which is the interval in which fencing is the thing carrying the filesystem.

The election is now a head start rather than an exclusive right.  A new
mxfs_disklock_live_slot_rank() reports how many live slots sit below this node
— 0 is the elected node, N is the N-th stand-in — using the same liveness
predicate as the election itself, in the same place, because a rank derived
from a second drifting copy of "is that slot live" would put two nodes at rank
0.  A stand-in that has watched the reservation stay absent for longer than the
maintainer's head start (15 s, three of its own cycles) plus one step per rank
(5 s) performs the repair itself, and says so: the repair line now carries
role=auditor-takeover rank=N and states that the elected node being gone or
inert is a second thing to find out.  A node that has seen a safety event also
stops sleeping out its full audit interval, re-looking at a rank-staggered
interval instead, so the deadline is reachable without every auditor
converging on the target at once.

Three things it deliberately does not do, because each trades a detection hole
for a worse one.  It triggers on ABSENT alone: UNKNOWN is an unanswered
question rather than an observed loss and must never buy repair authority, and
a foreign reservation of the wrong type still excludes, so a blind RESERVE is
not a type conversion.  It requires an unbroken run of ABSENT, so a
half-answering target cannot accumulate a deadline out of mixed verdicts.  And
the repair remains RESERVE by a node that has just verified its own key is
present — never REGISTER, because a node that re-registered to fix "my key has
vanished" would be undoing its own fence.

Measured as a matched pair on the 2-node TCP rig, same harness both arms.
Control on 0.86.1: ABSENT reported by the survivor at t+83 s, no repair, the LU
still carrying no reservation when the harness finished.  Fixed: the stand-in
repaired 20.50 s after it first saw ABSENT — the designed 15 s grace plus one
5 s rank step — at t+62 s of wall clock, exactly one repairer, and the
reservation in force at the end.  With the maintainer left up instead, it still
repairs at t+6 s as role=maintainer rank=0 and no takeover fires, so the head
start is intact.  A third arm removed a mounted node's own registration out of
band: it withdrew 4 s later through the existing self-gone inspection, its peer
was unaffected, and both nodes ended with zero kernel splats.

Two harness defects were fixed to get those numbers, and both had been
reporting confidently about MXFS while observing nothing.
tests/pr_reservation_ownership_probe.sh and tests/resv_health_detect.sh
hardcoded the multipath rig's /dev/mapper/mpatha, which does not exist on the
TCP rig; sg_persist errored, the parser found no reservation stanza, and the
probe printed "RESERVATION: NONE HELD" — an assertion about MXFS's state — from
a capture of an error message.  Both now take the device from a node's own live
mount, and the probe reports UNKNOWN and exits non-zero when the target did not
answer a PERSISTENT RESERVE IN at all.  The detect harness also gained a
derived time bound, which it never had: previously a repair that simply never
happened could only be caught indirectly.  Its "the elected maintainer reported
it" assertion became "the repair names the role that performed it", since a
stand-in repair is now a legitimate outcome and attribution was what that
assertion was protecting.

tests/resv_selfgone_withdraw.sh is new: it covers the half of this record that
was measured in the field but never exercised — the reservation staying in
force while this node's own registration is removed.

## 2026-09-17 — 0.86.1 — the takeover pass's two failure outcomes are now exercised, not read, and one of the fixes the record asked for turned out to be wrong

A page is taken over by prepare + activate + purge + import.  The accounting
that says which of those outcomes counts as a transferred page was corrected
earlier the same day — a refused activate and a failed import each return a
negative now, instead of the page being counted and `return 1` running outside
the `if (activate == 0)` that guarded the ownership work.  That correction was
made by reading the code, and reading is not evidence: `takeover_pages_done` is
also the progress signal every request parked on a page in transition waits on,
so a pass that transferred nothing while reporting progress is a hang, and the
claim that it can no longer happen had to be driven rather than argued.

Two one-shot, page-exact fault knobs on the authority ledger make both outcomes
reachable: one refuses the activation of a named page, one fails the scan a
named page's import walks.  They sit beside the fault knobs the ledger already
had (torn write, refused grant, commit failure, activate hold), are zeroed by
the memset in mxfs_tauth_ledger_open like every other field, and are never
written by the module — only by the usermode test.

tests/tauth/dlm_ledger_test case 13 injects BOTH in ONE pass over a dead
authority's 13 pages, with the survivor left as the sole member so every
candidate is certain to take the local activate-purge-import branch.  Measured:
the pass answers -EAGAIN rather than a page count, and progress advances by 11
of 13 — neither failure is counted.  The refused page is still the dead
authority's on the platter; the un-imported page is already durably ours.  Then
each is recovered the way it actually has to be, by an ordinary lock rather than
by another sweep: the refused page's PREPARED image is consumed by the
requester, and the un-imported page is re-imported by the requester, because
publishing a page as ours marks it for re-import.

THAT LAST PART CORRECTED AN ASSERTION OF MY OWN.  The first version of the case
asserted that a later bulk pass would pick the refused page up.  It does not,
and should not: the page is PREPARED to this node, and the pass deliberately
skips a page whose target is live, because that target consumes it at its next
request.  The assertion was wrong, not the code, and it is worth recording that
the failing assertion is what surfaced the real recovery path.

ONE OF THE RECORD'S OWN NEXT STEPS IS WRONG AND IS NOT IMPLEMENTED.  It asked
that the FREEZE_REQ receive path assert the page is ours the way the on-demand
acquire path does, on the grounds that the two callers disagree about whether
rc == 1 can be trusted.  They do not disagree; they ask different questions.
The acquire path needs the page for its OWN request, so it requires ours-ness.
The FREEZE_REQ handler asks whether the transition its sender requested was
performed, and rc == 1 deliberately covers both "activated, purged and imported
here" and "durably PREPARED to a remote owner that consumes it at its next
request" — the function's own contract says so.  Adding the check would
reclassify a legitimate remote-prepare as a failure, and the NOT_OWNER it would
then send names the DEAD authority, which is worse than the current silence.
What is genuinely true is that one success value spans two outcomes; the
residual case (a sender left unanswered while the page goes to a third node)
needs three nodes to arise and so is outside a 2-node TCP release.

Verified with no regression on the 2-node TCP rig, build B061C6BF3FB4BEB138B326A
(confirmed running on the node, not inferred): tests/tcp_death_replay.sh s40reg
PASS, acked=18, replay 73 s, wall 116 s, zero BUG/Oops/corruption/shutdown lines
on either node, taint 12288 (out-of-tree and unsigned only), and the new probes
silent as they should be on a healthy lap.  All seven tests/tauth suites pass.
Evidence: tests/evidence/20260917T204506Z_tcpdr_s40reg.
## 2026-09-17 — 0.86.0 — a dead peer's authority-page takeover leaves the recovery barrier, and the two things the held reservation was quietly covering for are now paid explicitly

After a peer dies the survivor fences it, seals and replays its journal slice,
purges its ledger and table records, and then — still inside the recovery
completion — transferred every authority-ledger page the dead incarnation
owned, one page at a time.  Only after that did it publish
P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE and give back the single-holder Write Exclusive
reservation.  The rebooted victim cannot re-register while that reservation is
in force, so it waited out the whole pass: measured here at 2691 pages and
42.8 s, and on an aged filesystem at 7984 pages and 103-107 s.

The barrier never needed it.  What recovery owes the cluster is that the dead
incarnation can no longer write or grant authority and that every request to a
page it owned has a safe live path — and the fence, the replay and the two
purges establish all of that before the takeover is reached.  Transferring the
pages is eager cleanup and first-access prewarming on top.  It now runs on the
existing departure worker, with its own request flag rather than the ordinary
departure queue, because that queue dedupes by {node, incarnation} and the
completion's call has never been subject to it: reusing it would have dropped
the takeover entirely whenever a GOODBYE or clean-release departure of the same
incarnation had already run, turning a pace defect into pages nobody ever takes
over.

WHAT THE HELD RESERVATION WAS COVERING FOR.  A pass that outlives the
reservation runs while membership moves, and two things that were free under it
are not free any more.

The first is certification.  Both bulk passes tested "am I the node the cluster
certifies to write authority transitions" ONCE, at entry.  That was sufficient
only because the reservation kept the victim out for the pass's whole duration.
Backgrounded, the returning peer can claim a lower heartbeat slot mid-pass and
become that node while the old pass keeps preparing, activating and purging.
Certification is now rechecked between pages; on loss the pass stops between
pages, reports P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-DECERTIFIED and the count it did not reach, and
answers -EAGAIN.  Nothing is lost by stopping, and that is the load-bearing
part: every mount queues an orphan sweep at its own settle, so the node that
took certification is the node that finishes the work.  This is placement, not
fencing — the departed incarnation is dead by proof and every ledger write is a
conditional commit against an exact base token, so a late write could not
corrupt anything; it would only be the wrong node writing.

The second is identity, and it is the one that could have lost data.  When a
takeover activates a page it publishes that page as this node's and marks it for
re-import, and only THEN retires the departed owner's records on it.  Those are
not one transaction: in between, the ordinary grant path can serve a request on
that page and write a record.  The retirement matched on the node id alone and
never looked at the incarnation — so any record carrying the departed node id
under a LIVE incarnation was retired, and the import that followed rebuilt the
page without it.  That is a lock revoked while its holder still believes it
holds it, with no error on any node.

"Node ids are random per mount, so this cannot happen" is not true here: a
resumed term deliberately adopts its predecessor's node id so that every record
it writes carries the identity the term's descriptors name, and a pinned id does
the same.  The clearest evidence is in the tree already — a departure whose
incarnation shares this mount's own node id sets a flag that SKIPS the id-keyed
bulk purges, for exactly this reason, and then ran a pass that performed the same
id-keyed retirement page by page.  The hole the flag exists to close was open one
call deeper the whole time.  The per-page purge now names the departed
incarnation and retires only exact matches; a record of that id under another
incarnation, or under an incarnation the caller cannot match, is spared, counted
in purge_inc_spared and named by P-TAUTH-PURGE-INC-SPARED, because unknown
provenance is not evidence that removal is safe.  The whole-ledger purge still
names a node id alone, deliberately and now in writing: its callers run it inside
the barrier with the departed node fenced, or skip it entirely when the id is
this mount's own.

MEASURED, matched pair on the 2-node TCP rig, ONE build (sv
E0970E5371DE62670F7994D), the same 6000-create residue on the same LUN, the two
shapes selected by dl_recovery_takeover_inline so the control is not a different
tree:

  control (inline)  cand=2691  handoff_ms=42843  ledger_ms=12910  replay->P163 56.47s  gate back after 30s
  fixed   (worker)  cand=2703  handoff_ms=0      ledger_ms=12319  replay->P163 14.92s  gate back after 0s

Both arms verified all 18 acknowledged files by md5, including cold after
drop_caches=2 and after a cold remount, with zero BUG/Oops/shutdown lines on
either node.  In the fixed arm the deferred pass is visible doing the work on
the worker (P-DEPART-WORK-RECOVERY-TAKEOVER queued_ms=32), it moved 225 pages,
10 more of the victim's pages were served ahead of it by the on-demand path,
and it then stopped between pages because the lap's own cold remount of the
survivor began — leaving 2477, which the next incarnation took over
(P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-RUN rc=2953).  Nothing was skipped and every page is
accounted for.  Evidence: tests/evidence/20260917T201734Z_d0962offpath_s40c6,
tests/evidence/20260917T202457Z_d0962offpath_s40f6.

WHAT IS NOT FIXED, STATED PLAINLY.  14.92 s of barrier remains, and 12.3 s of it
is the whole-ledger purge, which is a serial per-page durable pass of the same
shape at 4.6 ms a page.  That one belongs inside the barrier — the held-failure
gate must see its result before the dead slot is republished, or a slot-indexed
shared bit aliases to the slot's next occupant — so it is a separate problem with
a separate cause, and it is now a separate record in the defect queue with this
measurement attached.  It is not dispositioned here and its cost is not credited
to this change.

The two new guards are proven by injection, not by reading, and both without a
rig: tests/tauth/ledger_test case 17 puts EX for {5,100} and EX for {5,101} on
one page and purges naming inc 100 — the second survives, and the same call with
inc = 0 retires it, which is what makes the case non-vacuous rather than a test
that would pass against the old code too.  tests/tauth/dlm_ledger_test case 12
decertifies a running bulk pass at an exact page boundary and asserts -EAGAIN,
one decertification, pages still under the dead authority, and that a later
certified pass drains them.  On the rig both guards were silent
(P-TAUTH-PURGE-INC-SPARED 0, P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-DECERTIFIED 0), which is the
correct result for a healthy lap and is reported as such rather than as
coverage: the rig has not yet been made to rejoin a peer INSIDE the backgrounded
pass, and dl_takeover_pause_ms exists to do it.

Also in the harness, from failures this run produced.  It picked the pass to
report with `tail -1` on P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER, and the lap ends with a cold remount
whose new incarnation takes over its OWN predecessor's pages — a second, larger
line in the same window.  The fixed arm was therefore reporting cand=2953 and
total_ms=29197 from the wrong pass while the recovery pass was cand=2703; the
line is now scoped to the victim named on the completion's own timing line, and
the interrupted-pass line counts too.  Its single "replay->P163 under 5 s"
assertion conflated the two in-barrier passes, so it is now split: the arm
asserts handoff_ms, which is what this change owns and what was never asserted
before, and prints the remaining gap with a note attributing it to the ledger
purge and forbidding anyone to widen the 5 s to make it disappear.  The default
residue dropped from 12000 creates to 6000: 12000 measured 174 s against the
harness's own 180 s budget and missed it on the next run, failing an arm in its
fixture, while 6000 takes ~95 s and still yields ~2700 candidate pages against
the 1000-page non-vacuity floor.  The budget was not the thing to change.  A
failed residue build also no longer points at a capture file that a timeout
leaves empty; it reports the wall against the budget where the numbers are.
## 2026-09-17 — 0.85.7 — only the write completion may defer the AG-metadata reclaim, and it now says so instead of being guessed from a string

A buf log item retirement drops the MXFS AG-metadata tracking token unless the
caller is the I/O completion continuation, which leaves it for bp->b_iodone to
consume moments later.  The funnel decided that by comparing the caller tag
against "iodone".  That tag is stamped by xfs_buf_item_done — and the MXFS
overlay calls xfs_buf_item_done directly from nine release-drain and
acquire-evict arms that retire a log item with no I/O whatsoever.  On any of
them the tag read "iodone", nothing ran b_iodone, and nothing returned the
token: the extra buffer reference would be held for the life of the module and
the AG's pending count would never come back.

The tag could not have been made to work, and neither could the return address:
every one of those arms reaches the funnel through xfs_buf_item_done, so they
are indistinguishable from inside it.  Nor is the buffer any help — a sticky
provenance field can be stale or absent, and XBF_WRITE is wrong in the other
direction, because xfs_buf_ioend_fail_unsubmitted submits no write and still
runs the completion.  Only the caller knows.

So the caller states it.  xfs_buf_item_done and the funnel take an explicit
enum xfs_bli_release_ctx; __xfs_buf_ioend, which dispatches b_iodone on the very
next line, is the only site that passes XFS_BLI_IODONE_FOLLOWS, and every other
site reclaims.  Changing the prototype is deliberate: it made the compiler
enumerate the call sites rather than leaving that to a grep, and it will do the
same for any arm added later.  The double-completion early return reclaims too,
since a no-I/O retirement that finds the log item already claimed is still the
last chance to hand the token back.

THIS IS HARDENING, NOT A PROVEN CAUSE, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS.  All nine
overlay arms are gated on directory-buffer predicates — the dir3 data/block/
leaf1/leafn buf_ops, the owned-dir3 test, the undestaged test, the dir epoch —
and the AG-metadata predicate matches a disjoint set of b_ops (AGF/AGI/AGFL/
bnobt/cntbt/inobt/finobt/rmapbt/refcountbt).  An AG-metadata buffer therefore
cannot reach any of them as the tree stands, and the lap below measured the new
reclaim firing zero times.  What is fixed is a contract that was unsound and
would have leaked silently the first time an overlay arm was pointed at an
AG-metadata buffer; what is NOT established is that this was the route that
stranded a token on 0.75.63.  That question stays open in the defect queue.

MEASURED on the 2-node TCP rig, build 6080FEED3F81E1EFBF6E0FD, no regression
and non-vacuous: tests/agmeta_stale_leak_2node.sh s40v1 PASS (releases=2,
reclaim_lines=6, stale_clean_lines=4, stuckmeta=0, p3_max_us=0 — AG-metadata
tracking demonstrably live); cache_coherency PASS 534/534 checks on 2/2 nodes;
tests/fleet_unload_check.sh s40u PASS on both nodes with zero slab-leak,
warning or corruption lines in the unload window.  Across both nodes the
retirement-with-token-outstanding probe fired 0 times, the mxfs_ag_meta_track
tripwire fired 0 times, and taint read 12288 (out-of-tree and unsigned only) on
each.  Evidence: tests/evidence/20260917T185105Z_agleak_s40v1,
tests/evidence/20260917T185217Z_unload_s40u.

Also fixed, in the run harness: a node that is still booting answers a

## 2026-09-17 — 0.85.6 — every slab cache this module creates is its own, so an unload's "objects remaining" report is evidence about the load that produced it

An unload leak report is only evidence about the module load that printed it if
the cache it counted belonged to that load.  It did not.  When
kmem_cache_destroy finds objects still allocated it cannot free the cache, so it
leaves it on the slab list with refcount 0 — and a refcount-0 cache is still
mergeable, so the next insmod's same-shape kmem_cache_create adopts the zombie,
inherits its stranded objects, and reports them again at its own unload.  It
then leaves a zombie of its own, and the report repeats for the rest of the
boot, unchanged, whatever the module does.

That is what the 2026-09-08 evidence actually recorded.  Three unloads of three
different builds on one node reported the same six objects at the same slab
offsets, including one on an idle mount that had run no workload at all, and the
build that appeared to "fix" it had merely grown struct xfs_buf by 16 bytes — a
different size no longer merges with the zombie.  Six repetitions of one leak
were read as six leaks on every mount cycle.

Every cache this module creates now goes through one helper that adds
SLAB_NO_MERGE, so each load's cache, and each load's report, is its own.  The
old shape is still reachable with slab_merge=1, which exists to be the control
arm of the test below and for nothing else.

MEASURED on the 2-node TCP rig, build 073B27628734DEB572F0FB0, six load/unload
cycles in one boot on test1, driven by a knob that strands exactly N buffer
structs at free and prints each one's address
(tests/d0924_zombie_cache_ab.sh s40c, evidence
tests/evidence/20260917T184141Z_d0924zombie_s40c):

  mergeable arm   c1 strands 1 -> the unload reports 1 object, 0x...56c47f72,
                     the same address the knob printed
                  c2 strands 0 -> the unload reports 1 object, 0x...56c47f72
                  c3 strands 0 -> the unload reports 1 object, 0x...56c47f72
  unmergeable arm c4 strands 0 -> the unload reports nothing; the zombie
                     carrying c1's object is not adopted
                  c5 strands 1 -> the unload reports 1 object, 0x...548fa7d5,
                     its own, not c1's
                  c6 strands 0 -> the unload reports nothing

Every assertion passed.  Two loads that leaked nothing reported a third load's
object, by name, and stopped doing so once the caches stopped merging.

The harness needed three fixes of its own before it could measure anything.  It
loaded the module without target_cache_protected=1, so the mount was refused and
every cycle after the first ran against an unmounted node — allocating no
buffers, stranding none at the knob, and reporting zero objects in BOTH arms,
which reads exactly like a clean result.  It now loads with the same arguments
the node prep uses, prints the refusal reason when a mount does not take, and
stops the run outright if the first cycle leaves the node unmounted rather than
reporting a verdict from six vacuous cycles.  A `local` declaration also built
one variable out of another on the same line, which bash expands before it
assigns, aborting the run under set -u.

## 2026-09-13 — 0.85.5 — a ledger record of this node's own incarnation is adopted with a generation, so the survivor's release names it and the rejoined peer's request is served

D-0966: on the TCP transport, after a clean departure and rejoin, the rejoined
node's first listing of a directory the sole survivor had created hung for
the whole 300 s budget with nothing shut down (s616d).  The chain, read from
both nodes' logs and the DLM core: the survivor became the master of the
departed peer's authority pages and imported an ACTIVE EX record for a
directory inode owned by its own incarnation, a grant whose release had been
lost against the departing master (the harness's probe directory, created
and removed while the peer mastered it).  The survivor then reused that
inode number for its new directory, and its local request found the imported
entry GRANTED and took the "already granted" shortcut as-is: the inode went
to EX on a table entry with grant generation 0.  When the peer rejoined and
asked for the directory, every BAST reached the survivor's release pipeline,
which names tenures by generation, read 0 as "no held tenure at release
decision" and skipped the unlock (P6Z-REL-NOTHING, 42 cycles at 10 s), while
the peer's master kept the record ACTIVE and every later requester parked
behind the first.

Two changes in the DLM core.  The shortcut in `dlm_lock` now adopts an
imported record of this incarnation the way the remote re-affirm does: the
imported mark is cleared and a fresh generation minted, so the tenure the
inode holds is the one its release will name (P-TAUTH-ADOPT-LOCAL); a record
under this node id from a different incarnation is not adopted, the request
waits for that incarnation's purge (P-TAUTH-ADOPT-INC-MISMATCH).  And the
release pipeline's "nothing held" arm, when the local mirror still holds a
generation-less GRANTED entry of ours and a peer is asking, adopts and
releases it through the ordinary generation-aware unlock
(`mxfs_dlm_unlock_genless`, P-REL-NOTHING-MIRROR-HELD) instead of leaving a
record only this node can retire.  The ledger design note in
`docs/tcp-authority-ledger.md` records why an imported own-incarnation record
is a tenure without a generation.

Measured on 2/tcp, module 45B8EB0F812B0167A4CCF9E, four sole-arm laps of
`tests/d0952_sole_create_rejoin_coherency.sh` (s617a 61 s, s617b 53 s, s617c
70 s, s617g 89 s, against the 300 s hang): on the survivor
P-TAUTH-ADOPT-LOCAL fired exactly once in each of s617a, s617b and s617c, on
the reused directory inode (ino 131, 2900, 4965), so those three laps
reached the imported own-incarnation record the defect needs; s617g did not
import one (the number the probe directory left was not reused with a lost
release that time) and is clean without exercising the path.  On every lap
P6Z-REL-NOTHING was 0 and the survivor logged no acquire stall or stack
dump; the rejoined peer saw 200/200 files, 0 wrong, 0 stale, 0 garbage, 0
read errors in all three passes; cold `chk_mxfs` clean with the aliasing
audit OK every lap.  The lone arm (s617d, 75 s), the control arm (s617e,
47 s) and the sole-survivor knob lap `tests/d0946_disklive_knob_vs_aging.sh`
(s617f, 8 rounds, 0 operation failures, 0 hole picks, cold check clean,
110 s) were clean on the same build.  No shutdown, BUG, Oops or WARNING on
either node.  D-0966 is removed from the queue as FIXED AND VERIFIED.

The harness's cold-check block, added in 0.85.4, demanded zero sole-survivor
events over the whole lap, which the sole arm produces by design in phase 1,
so s617a-c scored INCOHERENT with every read and cold count clean; it now
allows exactly the phase-1 event, and s617g reads CLEAN.  Budget rows in
`tests/criteria/TIMEOUT_BUDGETS.md`.

Also observed on the rejoined peer during these laps and filed as a pace
record: its mount's EX request on the root directory waited 10.3 s behind
the survivor's cached PR twice (P-LKTIMEOUT-HOLDER ino=128 held_ms rising to
10262, P34-ACQ-SLOW dur_ms=10288), one BAST period, and one file read waited
1.56 s.  Neither hangs; both are slower than the operation should take.  The
Astra consult on the fix shape was attempted once and refused (HTTP 429, no
credits).

## 2026-09-13 — 0.85.4 — the sole-survivor predicate's per-mount lifetime is the right one: a lone remount after two writers is measured coherent through its first join and clean on the platter

D-0956 argued that `ever_multi`, the per-mount flag behind
`mxfs_v5_dlm_sole_survivor()` and `mxfs_v5_dlm_never_multi()`, is scoped to
the wrong lifetime: after two nodes write, both unmount, and one mounts
alone, every guard keyed on the predicate is off and the write-without-grants
path is on, "on a volume whose platter carries a second writer's residue".
It asked for a durable volume-lifetime fact and said it must fail closed.

The consumer inventory settles what the guards need.  All sixteen call sites
were read (seven on the sole-survivor predicate, nine on never-multi).  Each
protects state of the CURRENT mount: pending directory reload marks, cached
dentries, cached inode-cluster images carrying a departed peer's passengers,
phantom in-core EX modes on recycled shells, unpublished NL-logged inodes and
the DLM bypass around them, the cache-miss reads that take a grant, or a
departed peer's free that has not landed yet (the candidate validator); three
are diagnostics.  None of that outlives a clean unmount by every node
followed by a mount: the caches are gone, every free and every image has
landed, a dead node's slice is replayed at mount before the mount is
writable, and a lone mount reads all of its state from the platter.  The one
consumer whose consequence was durable, deleting a fully-free inode chunk,
was taken off the predicate earlier (a clustered volume never deletes a
chunk) and verified across a lone remount by the three d0949 laps of this
run (chunk deletions 0, sole-survivor probe 0 on the remounted node).  What
protects a lone mount's later peer is the conversion barrier at admission,
the join-time flush and publication of the incumbent's NL-logged state,
which runs the same way for a remount after two writers as for a
never-clustered volume's first join.

Measured, `tests/d0952_sole_create_rejoin_coherency.sh` gains the arm
`lone`: both nodes write, both unmount, one mounts alone (the survivor note
must read 0 for the whole lap, windowed to a mark written after the lone
mount, since the peer's departure had already made the previous mount a
survivor), it creates 200 files, recycles 100, links, symlinks and renames
them without grants, the peer then mounts for the first time in that mount's
life, reads every file, overwrites them all, and both directions are read
back; the arm ends with the cold `chk_mxfs`.  On 2/tcp, 414769E4F12DC54FE526BA6,
s616b and s616c: the peer saw 200/200, 0 wrong, 0 stale, 0 garbage, 0 read
errors in all three passes, no shutdown, cold check clean with the
chunk/free-space audit OK.  The control arm (s616a, both mounted throughout)
read the same.  D-0956 is removed from the queue as DISPROVED; the reasoning
is in `docs/rulings/sole-survivor-predicate-class.md`.

Also in this harness: its "files seen" check compared a whole directory
listing against the file count after the link/symlink/rename phase had
tripled the listing, so every lap since that phase was added scored
INCOHERENT on a clean read (s616a and s616b did); it now counts only the
`f<N>` entries.  Budget rows in `tests/criteria/TIMEOUT_BUDGETS.md`.  The
Astra consult on the predicate's lifetime was attempted once and refused
(HTTP 429, no credits).

The harness's `sole` arm, run on the same build for comparison (s616d), did
not finish: the rejoined node's listing of the survivor's directory hung
past the 300 s budget on a PR acquire that the new master holds behind an
EX grant it imported from the authority ledger for the survivor, while the
survivor answers every BAST with "no held tenure at release decision; DLM
unlock skipped".  Filed as D-0966 (2/tcp, critical, stability) with both
nodes' logs; it is the next record on the release path.

## 2026-09-13 — 0.85.3 — the clustered inode candidate pick masks a sparse record's holes, so a number whose home block was never carved is no longer handed out

D-0948 recorded a first create into a freshly carved 32-inode chunk that
read a directory data block (magic XDD3) where it expected an inode cluster
and, because the transaction was already dirty, shut the filesystem down
(s572, 0.75.118).  The record spent three sessions on the hypothesis that a
stale directory buffer had been written back over the chunk's home after the
carve.  The cause was in the record's own evidence: 15 ms before the shutdown
the kernel's record checker printed "start inode 0x41f1c0, count 0x20,
freemask 0x…fffe, holemask 0xff".  That is a SPARSE record: 32 inodes carved
in the upper half of a 64-inode region, the lower half described only by the
hole mask, and `ir_free` stamped ALL_FREE as upstream's sparse carve always
stamps it.  Every hole bit therefore reads as a free inode in `ir_free`.
Upstream's candidate walk (`xfs_inobt_first_free_inode`) ANDs the free mask
with `xfs_inobt_irec_to_allocmask()` first; the clustered replacement,
`mxfs_dialloc_pick_in_rec` (the per-inode DLM try-reserve, cooldown, probe
budget, quarantine and two-phase validation), walked `ir_free` unmasked and
took offset 0 -- inside the hole.  That inode number's home block was never
carved for inodes; on s572 it was a live directory data block of another
directory, which is exactly what the create then read.  The candidate
validator (a plain platter read of the home) could not save it: a hole's
home holds no inode magic, and on 0.75.118 that read returned "no magic" and
the create proceeded.  From 0.84.16 a no-magic read refuses the candidate
before the transaction is dirtied, which contains the shutdown but not the
class: a hole whose home happens to hold an old free dinode image (a
carved-and-freed chunk's block) passes the validator as free and the
allocation lands in a block the inode btree does not own.

Fix, `xfs/libxfs/xfs_ialloc.c` `mxfs_dialloc_pick_in_rec`: when the record
is sparse, the walk's free mask is ANDed with the record's allocation mask
before the first candidate is taken.  The other clustered walk over a
record's free bits, the orphan collector in `xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c`, already
skipped hole-mask bits; every remaining `ir_free` use in the tree is a
single-bit test on a known inode.  A sparse-record merge
(`xfs_inobt_insert_sprec`) ANDs the two free masks and keeps hole bits set
only where both records have holes, so the allocation mask stays the correct
mask after a merge.

Test aids, all 0 in production: `dbg_dialloc_pick_holes=1` restores the
hole-blind walk as the A/B control; `dbg_force_sparse_carve=1|2` sends every
carve down the sparse path (2 also requests the upper half of the next
chunk-aligned region exactly, falling back to the ordinary near-bno search);
exact resettable counters `dialloc_holemask_n` (picks that met a sparse
record with hole bits in its free mask and masked them) and
`dialloc_holepick_n` (walk visits to a hole offset, control arm only); probe
lines `P-DIALLOC-HOLEMASK` (ratelimited), `P-DIALLOC-HOLEPICK` (first 200
per load) and `P-DIALLOC-FORCE-SPARSE`.  `tests/d0946_disklive_knob_vs_aging.sh`
zeroes both counters at each round start, prints them per round, and ends
with a HOLE-READ verdict (FAIL on any hole pick, VACUOUS when no sparse
record with holes was met).

Verified on the 2-node TCP rig, 414769E4F12DC54FE526BA6, one fresh mkfs, the
three laps on one volume, each ending in the cold `chk_mxfs` (all clean,
"Chunk/free-space aliasing OK"), no shutdown, no record-corruption line, no
create failure:

- Fixed walk under forced sparse carving (s615i, 8 rounds × 300 files,
  114 s): 6690 picks met a sparse record with holes and masked them, 0 hole
  picks, 0 validator no-magic refusals.  The records met included the
  holes-below shape of the incident (holemask 0xff, e.g. startino 355136)
  as well as holes-above (0xff00).
- Natural lap, knob off (s615k, 14 rounds, 185 s): 276 masked picks, 0 hole
  picks.
- Control walk, `dbg_dialloc_pick_holes=1` under forced sparse carving
  (s615j, 4 rounds, 155 s): 597920 walk visits to hole offsets (176383,
  42042, 222917 and 156578 per round) on holemask-0xff records in AG 2, and
  the validator refused about 36000 hole candidates with no-magic reads
  (72 budgeted `P947-VALIDATE-NOMAGIC` lines, n stepping by 500), so every
  create still succeeded through a re-pick and nothing was dirtied.  That
  is the mechanism the fix removes, reproduced on demand and absent on the
  fixed arm under the identical carve shape.

Two measurement notes.  The exact upper-half request of
`dbg_force_sparse_carve=2` was refused on every carve the ring still held
(110 of 110 `got=no`: the region above the hint is never free on this
workload); the holes-below records came from the near-bno search under
forced sparse carving, which is the same placement that produced the
incident's record.  And the control lap's 200 `P-DIALLOC-HOLEPICK` lines
were spent on the harness's aging phase (the knobs were armed before the
harness started) and had rolled out of the ring by the first round window;
the counters, not the lines, are the evidence.

The s574dv lap on 0.75.128 (tests/evidence/20260910T120926Z_d0946disklive_s574dv)
fits the same mechanism: its rounds with the candidate validator on failed
398 and 702 creates with a badmagic verdict at the candidate's home and
quarantined 26501 and 46332 candidates, while its rounds with the validator
off allocated freely.  A hole-blind pick produces exactly that pair.

Design note in `docs/free-publish.md`.  Budget rows in
`tests/criteria/TIMEOUT_BUDGETS.md`.  D-0948 removed from the queue as FIXED
AND VERIFIED.  The Astra consult on the fix shape was attempted once and
refused (HTTP 429, no credits), as in the previous session.

## 2026-09-13 — 0.85.2 — the sole-survivor knob lap ends with the cold structural check, and the one inobt-allocated inode with a free core is attributed to the filter-without-grants survivor that 0.83.3 removed

D-0957 recorded a single cold `chk_mxfs` error on 0.75.128 (sess574,
tests/evidence/20260910T122347Z_d0949chunkfree_s574xm/chk.txt): AG 4 agino
128 (ino 33554560) inobt-allocated with a dinode still in its
chunk-initialisation state (mode 0, changecount 0, random generation).  The
record's mechanism was NOT ESTABLISHED.  Established this session, from the
evidence the tree still holds:

- The lap that found it did not create it.  Its own 12000 files were all
  freed (verdict KEPT-FIXED, chunks retained, cold ifree 14029 of 21472),
  and the previous cold check on that volume (s574fix2, 06:51 local) was
  clean with 3 allocated inodes.  Four laps ran between: two
  sole-create-rejoin coherency laps whose captured dmesg holds zero
  P56-NL-LOGGED-DIR-SKIP and zero P34H-INCARN-POISON lines, and two
  d0946_disklive_knob_vs_aging.sh sole-survivor laps (clean departure,
  8 rounds alternating knob=1/0).  One of them, s574iwr, ran the
  `partial_iwrite_sole` knob, which on 0.75.128 put the survivor onto the
  partial inode-cluster write filter WITHOUT DLM grants: the single-node
  lock bypass set no inode mode, so every directory it logged sat at NL
  with no release-drain token.  Its knob=1 rounds 3, 5 and 7 each recorded
  a partial write with two no-in-core passengers (P218=1 PASSNOC=2).
- agino 128 is the first inode of the first aligned chunk of an AG on this
  geometry, i.e. the first inode ever allocated in AG 4, and directories
  step the AG rotor one per mkdir only while the mount is single-node
  (`xfs_ialloc.c`: pinned to the node slot under multi-node membership).
  The later knob lap's parents (P-CR3-CANCEL dp_ino=92274816 = AG 11 agino
  128 for its round 1, 109482289 = AG 13 for its round 3) anchor the rotor;
  counting every single-node mkdir backwards (rounds, the writability probe
  of the sole phase) puts s574iwr's round 3 directory in AG 4.  Round 3 was
  a knob=1 round.
- The mechanism is the one proven by instrument in sess583 (s583c, the
  withdrawn first D-0955 fix, which re-created exactly this filter-without-
  grants state on 0.83.2): `mxfs_submit_partial_inode_write` drops a logged
  directory slot at NL with no token (P56-NL-LOGGED-DIR-SKIP), and with the
  shipped `pub_skip_rearm=0` the buffer completion then retires the inode
  log item as landed, so the create's core never reaches the platter while
  the same transaction's inobt/AGI buffer images do.  s583c measured the
  survivor's fresh directory reading back FREE from the platter (P34H
  disk_mode=0, ESTALE, 799 of 800 creates failed).  A knob=0 round's whole
  write can still land a dropped image if a co-resident flush rewrites the
  same cluster buffer, which is why one of three knob=1 round directories
  was stranded rather than all three.  0.83.3 removed the state: a sole
  survivor takes real grants, so its logged directories are EX-held at
  flush and the filter never meets its own fresh directory at NL.  No
  knob on the current tree re-creates the filter-without-grants survivor.

The harness change: tests/d0946_disklive_knob_vs_aging.sh now ends every
lap with both nodes unmounted, `chk_mxfs -v` on the quiesced device, and
both remounted (COLDCHK / COLDCHK-READ lines; `MXFS_D0946_COLDCHK=0` skips
it).  Its round counters and cold readback count probes and names; only the
offline check compares an inode's two records, and it is the oracle that
found this defect.  docs/foreign-replay-inode-ordering.md records the third
producer of the checker's P-ALLOC-FREE-CORE line beside the two replay-side
ones, and the residual hazard: a P56 skip is lossless only while the release
drain lands every committed change before the grant leaves; under
`pub_skip_rearm=0` a broken drain would lose the change silently, where the
sibling stale-stage path fails closed (P224).

## 2026-09-12 — 0.85.1 — a two-node cluster whose custodian dies mid-completion comes back on its own: the sole-survivor gate no longer outlives its holder unanswered, and a mount-time OPEN case reaches the engine

The custodian-kill arm of tests/d_intents_2tcp_open_efi.sh (the survivor
that is completing a dead peer's open EFI is itself destroyed inside the
engine, then both nodes restart) failed on 0.85.0 with neither node able to
mount again (s613c, tests/evidence/20260913T033243Z_intents2tcp_s613c).  On
two nodes the custodian is the sole survivor, so its death is a total
outage, and this transport recovers a total outage slot by slot through the
ordinary mount path (it has no whole-cluster bootstrap term).  Four distinct
causes, each measured and fixed at its own site:

- **A joiner under a dead holder's gate** (dlm/v5_mount.c
  `v5_tcp_dead_gate_holder`, dlm/scsipr.c
  `mxfs_scsipr_preempt_dead_gate_holder`).  The sole-survivor exclusive-write
  gate is a single-holder Write Exclusive (1) reservation and it stays on
  the LUN after its holder dies (until the QNAP target purges the dead nexus
  ~30-40 s later; SCST never would).  A joiner arriving inside that window
  could REGISTER but not WRITE, so its PR-ledger publish was refused
  (P304-PREOBSERVE held=1 type=0x1, P-PRKEY-PUBLISHED rc=-52 UNATTRIBUTED,
  mount aborted in 2.7 s).  The TCP mount now attributes the holder's key
  through the PR ledger and runs the bootstrap survivor scan over the
  heartbeat table for one full dead window before it registers
  (P-PR-DEADGATE-SCAN); only "nothing moved and a frozen record carries the
  holder's key" proves the holder dead (P-PR-DEADGATE-DEAD), and then the
  registered joiner PREEMPTs AND ABORTs that key with the all-registrants
  type so WE-AR is in force again (P-PR-DEADGATE-PREEMPTED), marks the
  holder's ledger entry FENCED and publishes.  Any movement
  (P-PR-DEADGATE-LIVE), an unattributable key or an unreadable table keeps
  the refusal.  The later monitor-time fence of the holder's slot finds its
  key absent and certifies under a gate of its own, as for a target-purged
  key.
- **A successor re-proving a kind-20 certificate** (dlm/v5_mount.c
  `v5_gate_reprove`).  A taken-over descriptor certified under the gate
  asks "is WE(1) held by OUR key?" at every recheck, and once the prover is
  dead nothing holds it: P239-GATE-LAPSED / P239-EXCL-LAPSED once a second
  for 70 s until the mount barrier's 122 s budget expired (s613c).  When the
  recheck answers NO_RESERVATION and this node is the only live member (the
  original prover's predicate) and the descriptor carries a durable kind-20
  certificate with the victim's key, the successor re-installs the gate
  under its own key — pinned before the PROUT, then registered as a
  dependant — and proceeds (P239-GATE-REPROVE-TRY, P239-GATE-REPROVED).  The
  certificate is not rewritten; every refusal keeps the lapse.  Measured
  s614a: REPROVE-TRY to REPROVED in 2.4 ms, recheck_rc=0.
- **A non-gate certificate under our own gate** (dlm/scsipr.c
  `mxfs_scsipr_exclusion_holds`).  With the gate re-proved for the taken-over
  case, the successor's own predecessor's BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT recheck read
  "held=1 type=0x1 (WE)" as NORESV 65 times (s614a,
  tests/evidence/20260913T040607Z_intents2tcp_s614a) and the barrier expired:
  the predicate accepted only the two all/registrants-only forms.  WE(1) held
  by our own key excludes strictly more than either, so it now satisfies a
  certificate issued under WE-AR; WE(1) held by any other key stays a lapse.
- **The result word of a PREEMPT AND ABORT** (pal/linux/kern.c).  The joiner's
  preempt of the dead holder's key hit RESERVATION CONFLICT (the target had
  purged the key during the dead window) and the PAL reported it as an
  unclassified failure rc=280: the SAM status sits in the low byte of the
  result word with the midlayer's own byte above it (0x118).  The status
  byte is compared now, so the conflict means what it means — nothing
  happened — and the readback decides (s614b,
  tests/evidence/20260913T042107Z_intents2tcp_s614b, dmesg_test2_remount.txt:
  P-PR-DEADGATE-DEAD after a 63989 ms window, then P302-PROUT-ABORT-FAIL
  rc=280 beside 'sd 3:0:0:0: reservation conflict').
- **The barrier's OPEN-case handoff** (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c
  `mxfs_dlm_cache_init`).  An OPEN case met inside the mount barrier
  (P-OBL-BARRIER-OPEN) leaves its dead bit set and the replay duty armed for
  the post-mount worker, but the DLM cache init that runs after xfs_mountfs
  zeroed the dead-slot bitmap: at the mount settle the worker's replay duty
  saw nothing outstanding and cleared itself, the orphan sweep ran with
  dead_slots=0x0 into the case's frozen allocation group and timed out
  twice (P-OBLF-AG-TIMEOUT at 120 s, kworker hung-task reports), and the
  engine never started (s614b, dmesg_test1.txt).  The mount is allocated
  zeroed and the barrier is the first writer, so the zeroing is gone.

Also: the engine's test hold (`mxfs.dbg_obl_engine_hold_ms`) forces the log
before it parks, so the custodian dies with a DURABLE entry-0 free and the
successor meets the FULL branch — on s614c
(tests/evidence/20260913T043857Z_intents2tcp_s614c) the commit alone had
parked in the CIL, the custodian's slice carried nothing of it, and the
successor read entry 0 EMPTY and freed it (correct, but the branch the lap
exists to exercise went unmeasured).  `tests/d_intents_2tcp_open_efi.sh`
re-derives the custodian-kill budget (the dead-gate window and the two
mounts are on the record) and retries the second node's prep once when its
refusal was the designed admission refusal under a live gate holder
(P-PR-DEADGATE-LIVE), reporting the refusal and the retry.  A new queue
record names the live-holder case after a terminal refusal, which this
change does not touch.

Measured on this build (8330C6DFDB0B731E3308020, 2026-09-13, two nodes,
TCP), three consecutive laps on one prep:

- custodian-kill (tests/evidence/20260913T045344Z_intents2tcp_s614d,
  fails=0 on 36 assertions, wall 323 s): the victim died with 14 open
  extents in its slice; the custodian froze the AG, committed entry 0,

- complete, CHURN=0 (20260913T045916Z_intents2tcp_s614e, fails=0/34,

Queue: D-FOREIGN-SLICE-INTENTS-ABANDONED removed — FIXED AND VERIFIED on
