withdrew, retired its PR key and was fenced and replayed by the node it was
joining.  Every two-node re-form on this filesystem had a ~3.5 minute window
in which a joiner died.

Three defences, per the design consult ruling recorded in ccmemory as
`ruling-joiner-during-authority-takeover-priority-service-progress-aware-wait-staged-mount-abort`
(priority service alone must not close it):

- **Priority service.**  Every {node, incarnation} handed to the bulk takeover
  is recorded as settled (`dlm_authority_settle_record`, keyed by incarnation,
  never by node id) and `dlm_authority_dead` answers true for it, so the
  bootstrap's `dlm_ledger_prepare` takes a requested page over ahead of the
  pass (`P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-ONDEMAND via=takeover-ondemand`, or
  `via=takeover-request` for a FREEZE_REQ from a joiner that masters the page
  itself).  `takeover_pages_done` counts one completion per page on every
  path.
- **Progress-aware waiting.**  A page in a transition a live bootstrap is
  making is a distinct outcome, `MXFS_ERR_AUTH_TRANSITION`, never REMASTER:
  the master's deny carries the bootstrap's completion count in `grant_gen`
  (`P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-TX`), a FREEZE_REQ decline relays it in NOT_OWNER's
  `prepared_seq` (`P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-DECLINE`), and the requester's retry
  loop spends none of its budget while that count advances
  (`P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-WAIT`).  Thirty seconds without an advance is
  `P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-STALLED`, which fails ONLY a caller the fallible
  oracle names (-EREMCHG); every other caller keeps waiting and says so every
  30 s — an AG acquire inside a dirty transaction handed an error would
  cancel dirty and shut down, the escalation this exists to avoid.  A NOQUEUE
  request answers would-block at once (`P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-NOQUEUE`).  The
  wait is cancellable and holds nothing the takeover needs.
- **Staged mount abort.**  The mount's root lookup and lock are one fallible
  boundary (`mxfs_iget_root_fallible`; the untrusted iget's AG 0 acquire is
  `mxfs_ag_dlm_lock_fallible_for`, fallible for the task that registered the
  inode, plain for everyone else): a stalled transition fails the MOUNT
  ("Failed to read root inode ... a cluster acquire was refused; the mount is
  refused, not shut down"), which unwinds through the ordinary failure path,
  leaves membership and releases its slot cleanly.  The acquire hook
  classifies -EREMCHG ahead of the quarantine and pending-recovery arms
  (`P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-FAIL` for a fallible caller,
  `P960-AUTH-TRANSITION-PARK` for one that restarts) and never takes the
  force-shutdown arm for it.  The refused mount's unwind takes no cluster
  acquire either: `xfs_log_quiesce` writes no SB summary for a mount that
  never set `m_mxfs_mount_complete` (`P960-REFUSED-MOUNT-NOCOVER`) — measured
  s590j, the summary lock's own page was in the transition and the unwind
  parked on it for 70 s, until the takeover moved again.  Such a mount
  committed nothing; the counters are derived state the last node out
  recounts under the lock and the next clustered mount recounts anyway, and
  the unlocked lazy-counter cover is not taken either.

Test-only `mxfs.dl_no_ondemand_takeover=1` (disables priority service on the
node it is set on) and `mxfs.dl_takeover_pause_ms=N` (holds the bulk passes
between pages).  New harness `tests/join_during_takeover.sh`: B leaves first,
A holds a 32000-entry directory alone, A unmounts last and remounts, and B
mounts inside the pass; the lap names which node mastered the mount's first
requests (a per-incarnation hash, so it repeats up to six times until the
wanted shape arrives) and measures one defence per arm.  Measured shape
worth knowing: a joiner that masters the page itself asks the bootstrap by
FREEZE_REQ and is answered DEFER until the bootstrap installs the two-node
view (~7-10 s after the first ask, s590i, three of three), only then a
decline that carries the count.

## 2026-09-12 — 0.84.4 — readdir can fail its cluster acquire instead of waiting without bound

The next audited site under the D-0958 ruling (one caller class at a time,
behind an explicit error-returning acquire, never a timer on a caller that
holds dirty state).  A listing acquires the directory's cluster lock at up to
four places, and until now every one of them took the void `xfs_ilock` and
restarted the wait for ever when a live master never acknowledged the request.
Each is now a fallible acquire that names its stage in `P958-READDIR-REFUSED
ino= stage= rc=`: `refresh` (the consumer refresh at the top of
`xfs_file_readdir`, now `mxfs_dlm_dir_consumer_refresh_fallible`; a refusal
skips the eviction and leaves the refresh pending for the next call, since the
eviction gate compares `dir_gen` with `evicted_gen` and only a completed
eviction advances it), `sf` (the shortform outer lock), `map` (`xfs_readdir`'s
dispatcher through `xfs_ilock_data_map_shared_fallible`, which checks the
verdict after EACH `xfs_ilock` so the map recheck's relock to EXCL is a second
acquisition asked separately and a refused first lock never becomes a second
180 s wait; transactional callers keep the plain acquire), `leaf` (the per
data block re-acquire of `xfs_dir2_leaf_getdents`: entries from earlier blocks
were already emitted, `ctx->pos` still names the unread block, so getdents64
returns the bytes copied and the NEXT call resumes there and gets the error),
and `shard-pin` / `shard-sf` for a sharded directory, whose actor re-encodes
`ctx->pos` from the last emitted entry's cookie on any inner error.  A
refused listing fails with EIO to the caller and shuts nothing down.

Test-only `mxfs.readdir_leaf_pause_ms` (with `mxfs.watch_ino` naming the
directory) sleeps between the data blocks of a leaf listing with no lock
held, so a peer's create in the gap revokes the cached grant and the next
block's acquire is a real request a fault can meet — the only way the `leaf`
stage is reached.  `tests/tcp_lockreq_blackhole.sh` gains
`WORKLOAD=held_dir_readdir` (getdents64 driven directly on a held directory
fd by the new `tests/getdents64.py`, because opendir is an open() and
fdopendir fstat()s first, both already-audited sites that would take the
refusal before readdir was reached) and `WORKLOAD=leaf_midlist`.

Verified 2 nodes / TCP on sv BBB43E3B599DDD5CC1F895C.  s589b
(`WORKLOAD=held_dir_readdir EXPECT=bounded ARMED_S=300`,
tests/evidence/20260912T032630Z_lockreqbh_s589b): 22 of 22 checks, the
refusal at stage=refresh, LOCK_CANCEL sent and acknowledged ABSENT, no
shutdown.  s590a (`WORKLOAD=leaf_midlist EXPECT=bounded ARMED_S=400`,
tests/evidence/20260912T034634Z_lockreqbh_s590a, 584 s inside its 600 s
budget): 24 of 24 checks — the first getdents64 returned the 102 entries
emitted before the pause, the refusal was the leaf per-block re-acquire
(stage=leaf, one refresh refusal beside it), the following call returned
EIO, the drop instrument fired 360 times during the armed read, the master
stayed a healthy member serving its own read of the file in under 15 s, and
the listing recovered once the requests flowed.

## 2026-09-12 — 0.84.3 — An unmount no longer frees the DLM under a departure worker still taking over ledger pages

A node that had left a cluster as its last member keeps every ledger page it
served under its own authority (nobody to hand them to).  When it mounts again,
alone, it settles its previous incarnation's heartbeat record and its departure
worker begins the takeover-only pass over that incarnation's pages — one
durable prepare and one durable activate per page, ~15 ms each, 15,600 pages
behind 16,000 creates on this LUN — outside any recovery.  If the node was
unmounted inside that pass, the teardown joined the worker for 30 s, printed
that it was quarantining the context, and then destroyed the engine, closed
the ledger and freed the context anyway; the worker's next page-state byte
store faulted on the freed vmalloc array and the guest panicked
(`dlm_page_now_mine`, netconsole s574xm, page 9569).  A store that lands inside
a live allocation instead of an unmapped page is the same bug without the
panic.  The record (D-0953) had been filed on the observation that a node
"rebooted itself during mount" with no crash record anywhere; the netconsole
listener installed since then captured the stack, and the harness this entry
ships reproduces the shape deterministically.

The engine's `shutting_down` flag, set before the worker is stopped, is now
consulted BETWEEN pages by the named takeover (`P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-INTERRUPTED`,
naming the page reached and the candidates remaining) and by the orphan sweep
(`P-TAUTH-ORPHAN-SWEEP-INTERRUPTED`), never inside a page: a page's takeover is
prepare, activate, purge, import, and one left activated but not imported
would be a page this node claims and cannot serve.  The ledger-successor write
and the settle-wait loops answer -ESHUTDOWN once the flag is set.  The worker
refuses new work once asked to stop (`P-DEPART-WORK-REFUSED`), and a page
handed to a mount that is leaving is left PREPARED to it for the successor's
takeover instead of being activated (`P-TAUTH-HANDOFF-REFUSED-LEAVING`).  The
normal unmount now joins the worker WITHOUT bound — a slow join is reported
every 30 s (`P-DEPART-WORKER-SLOW`) and is never licence to proceed — while
the refused-mount unwind keeps its bounded stop and quarantine, and that
quarantine now gates the engine destroy, the ledger close, the peer shutdown
and the disklock destroy alike, which is the whole closure the worker reads.
Every departure this node processes ends by queueing the orphan sweep, so
pages an interrupted pass left are picked up by a survivor that stays mounted,
not only by the next bootstrap.  The design consult on this change ruled the
cancel-only-between-pages boundary, the unbounded join, and the whole-closure
quarantine; its ruling is recorded in ccmemory as
`ruling-departure-worker-teardown-cancel-between-pages-unbounded-join-no-quarantine-by-deadline`.

Verified 2 nodes / TCP on sv F8FE750AC5A5D2F8C207D2E with the new
`tests/depart_takeover_unmount.sh` (`DEATH=ghost EXPECT=clean NFILES=16000`):
s588b/c/d/e, four laps, each with the pass proven in flight when the unmount
was issued (activations still arriving), the unmount returning rc=0 in
0.4-0.8 s, the interruption line at page 1683-1834 with 14,486-14,556 pages
remaining, no `P-DEPART-WORKER-STUCK`, `DLM shutdown complete`, nothing on the
netconsole, and the next bootstrap's sweep then taking the leftover pages
(14,966-14,995) before both nodes read all 16,000 files; s588e is the 0-fail
lap (277 s), the earlier three failed only their re-form step (see D-0960
below).  `DEATH=destroy` (s588a, 16000 files) measured the other takeover
shape: a dead peer's pass runs inside the elected replayer's recovery and
put_super waits for that recovery before the DLM teardown starts, so an unmount
issued 139 s into a 7999-page pass returned after 105 s with the pass complete
and the interruption path never reached — that arm is kept as the regression
check of the ordering and cannot exercise the fix.

Two things the laps found and this entry does not fix.  A node that joins
while the bootstrap node's orphan sweep is in flight exhausts its root-inode
lock retries on remaster in 18 s, shuts its own filesystem down at mount,
withdraws and is fenced — recorded as D-0960 in the queue; until it is fixed
`scripts/module_swap_deploy.sh` accepts `MXFS_JOIN_WAIT_PATTERN` /
`MXFS_JOIN_WAIT_S` so a harness re-form joins after the sweep's summary line,
and the harness uses it.  And a node that rebooted came back without its
`/src` NAS export, so three consecutive re-forms failed with nothing but
"join failed" to show for it: the deploy script now mounts the export the
way the other rig scripts do and keeps a failed join's whole output.
`dlm/dlm_user_compat.h` gives the user-mode tests/tauth build the atomic and
module-parameter stubs the kernel-only knobs need.

## 2026-09-12 — 0.84.2 — stat, read and splice can fail their cluster acquire instead of waiting without bound, and a killed task leaves its wait

A remote inode acquire whose live master never acknowledges the request
(D-0958) could be refused, since 0.81.0, only by open(): the refusal is
opt-in per call site, through a per-task registration the acquire hook reads,
and open was the only site that had registered. A stat through an fd opened
before the fault was measured (s581c) blocked in vfs_fstat past 495 s, and a
read through such an fd had the same shape. Every other caller still restarted
the wait for ever. The design consult on this defect ruled that a caller that
cannot unwind has no safe bounded completion, so the defect closes by
widening the class of callers that can fail, one audited site at a time,
behind an explicit error-returning acquire — never by a timer on a caller that
holds dirty state.

`mxfs_ilock_fallible(ip, flags)` is that acquire: 0 with every requested
component held and the grant established, or -EIO (-EINTR for a killed task)
with exactly those components released again. Only the named inode may give
up — the registration now carries the inode number, because an audited call
takes other inodes' locks inside it (a parent, a routed conversion) and none
of those has been audited — and a registration's verdict is cleared on entry,
so a later registration on the same stack slot cannot inherit it. Three sites
use it, each sitting where nothing is dirty and no transaction is open: getattr
(`mxfs_getattr_dlm_lock`, which now returns the verdict and the caller fails
the stat), the read path (the sticky-PR coherency envelope at the top of
read_iter, and the IOLOCK ride for buffered, direct and DAX reads), and splice
read. Writes keep the unconditional acquire; a failed acquire there has not
been audited. Open is re-audited to the inode-scoped registry.

A task that has been sent a fatal signal no longer sits in a legitimate,
receipted wait for the length of the holder's drain. The engine asks a new
callback (`acq_fallible_cb`) whether the waiting task is at a fallible
boundary, and if so leaves the wait with -EINTR at the next one-second attempt
boundary; the classifier abandons the acquisition by name (LOCK_CANCEL, as in
0.84.1) and the operation returns -EINTR. An unregistered task is never
interrupted — the engine asks before it acts — so a bare -EINTR from an
unregistered path is treated as an error like any other. A new PAL query,
`mxfs_pal_fatal_signal_pending`, keeps the engine free of the kernel API.

Two test-only changes. The drop knobs (`dl_drop_lockreq_ino`,
`dl_drop_grant_ino`) now reset a readable counter (`dl_drop_lockreq_n`,
`dl_drop_grant_n`) on every write, arm or disarm: the harness chose its target
inode by counting the drop probe's printed lines, and that probe prints only
its first 8 drops and every 64th after them per module load, so two laps
(s585c2, s585e) found no remotely mastered candidate at all once the budget
was spent and a third (s585d) found one only because a hit landed on n=64.
The count is per arm now and the harness reads it. The user-mode build of the
engine (tests/tauth) gained the parameter and atomic stubs it needed to
compile the knobs at all.

`tests/tcp_lockreq_blackhole.sh` gained WORKLOAD=held_fd_read — one bare
read(2) on an fd opened before the fault, issued from python3, so the acquire
under the fault is the read path's and not getattr's (md5sum fstats first) —
and asserts which refusal fired by name. `tests/live_holder_wait.sh` gained
KILL_AFTER_S. The drop_grant control arm's checks were rewritten from what
the control measured (see 0.84.1).

Measured on two nodes over TCP, build sv 4AF63181C23A95B06E802B8, one inode's
LOCK_REQ discarded at the sender for 300 s (tests/evidence/lockreqbh_s586*.log
and the directories they name):

- held_fd_read (s586e): the bare read blocked in xfs_file_read_iter's acquire
  and gave up at the budget (P912-ACQ-UNRECEIPTED, laps=1, receipted=0),
  P958-READ-REFUSED rc=-5, python3 got EIO, the abandonment was cancelled by
  name and acked ABSENT, 180 requests dropped, no shutdown; a fresh read after
  the disarm returned H's bytes. 19 of 19 PASS.
- held_fd (s586d, s586h): md5sum's fstat blocked in mxfs_ilock_fallible under
  vfs_fstat and was refused (P958-GETATTR-REFUSED rc=-5) at its budget; md5sum
  ignores a failed fstat and went on to read, which is a second fallible
  acquire with its own 180 s budget — so at a 300 s window (s586d) the read was
  still waiting and two checks read FAIL for that reason alone. At the
  two-budget 420 s window (s586h) both waits gave up in turn (two
  P912-ACQ-UNRECEIPTED, two cancels acked ABSENT, 360 requests dropped),
  md5sum reported EIO, nothing shut down, and the fresh read after the disarm
  was correct: 19 of 19 PASS, wall 528 s.
- KILL (s586f, live holder pausing its release drain 240 s, reader SIGKILLed
  30 s into its wait): P958-ACQ-FATAL-SIGNAL at retries_left=29, the reader
  gone 2 s after the signal with rc=137, LOCK_CANCEL acked outcome 2 (waiter
  removed) at the master, the holder's pause ended on its own clock and W's
  fresh read afterwards matched H's digest. 20 of 20 PASS.
- the plain 240 s holder-wait control (s586g) and the three open-workload
  laps of 0.84.1 below all passed on this build.

What this does not do, by the ruling's own terms: a caller that cannot be
failed — a write, a namespace operation, writeback, inactivation, deferred
metadata work — still waits, reported DEGRADED. The record stays open for that
class.

## 2026-09-12 — 0.84.1 — An abandoned remote lock wait is cancelled at the master by name, so nothing it queued outlives it

When a fallible caller gave up a remote acquire (0.81.0), the master learned
nothing: the re-sends just stopped. A waiter it held for that request, or a
grant it had already decided and committed for it, stayed in its table under
the requester's name. Until now the only thing that retired such a grant was
the requester's phantom reconcile — two blocking notifications inside 15 s for
an inode it holds no mirror of queue a mirror-bypassing release — which needs
those notifications to reach the requester over the very transport that lost
the grant, and needs another node's request to provoke them.

The engine now sends LOCK_CANCEL {resource, owner incarnation, acquisition
sequence, mode} when a wait is abandoned. Under the master's table lock, in
one place: a cancellation tombstone is recorded for the acquisition so a late
re-send cannot recreate the waiter; a WAITING or BLOCKED entry for it is
removed and the queue promoted; a GRANTED or CONVERTING entry — delivered and
lost, or never delivered — is retired through a release transition and the
queue promoted; an entry still committing is marked so that finalize retires
it instead of delivering it. Identity must match on all of incarnation,
sequence and mode, so an entry re-affirmed for the sender's next acquisition
is left alone. Every cancel is acknowledged with what was found (absent,
waiter removed, grant retired, grant retiring, not master) and re-sent from
the release tick until acknowledged or the send budget is spent; the cleanup
is engine-owned, so the abandoning task may be gone before the ack arrives. A
grant the acquisition had adopted between attempts is handed back as before.

Two test-only knobs: `dl_drop_grant_ino` (the master records a grant for this
inode and never delivers it — the shape a lost delivery produces) and
`dl_no_cancel` (abandon without telling the master: the previous behaviour,
kept as the control arm). The harness gained FAULT=drop_grant and
CONTROL_NO_CANCEL=1.

Measured on two nodes over TCP, first on build 391ED25AEC850F60A3E9E34
(s585c, tests/evidence/lockreqbh_s585c.log; its single FAIL was the harness
comparing a read taken before H's write against a digest taken after it,
fixed) and again on 0.84.2's build 4AF63181C23A95B06E802B8 (s586a/b/c):

- drop_grant (s586a): W's open gave up at the budget, sent the cancel, and was
  acked GRANT RETIRED in 3.5 ms; the master logged 180 undelivered grants and
  retired W's on the cancel; H's write of the file, which needs EX against
  that grant, completed in 1 s; zero phantom-reconcile lines for the inode.
  17 of 17 PASS.
- drop_grant control (s586b, cancel suppressed): the master received no
  cancel, H's write blocked behind the orphan grant until W's phantom
  reconcile released it, 11 s (10 s on s585d), and completed. 17 of 17 PASS.
  That control was first asserted, from reasoning rather than measurement, as
  a 40 s block; the measured second defence is what the harness now asserts.
- drop_req (s586c): the master never saw the request; the cancel was acked
  ABSENT and a tombstone recorded; 180 requests dropped, W's open refused with
  EIO, no shutdown, the fresh read after the disarm correct. 15 of 15 PASS.

## 2026-09-12 — 0.84.0 — A grant that lands between two attempts of a remote lock wait is kept for that wait, not bounced

A remote inode acquire registers a pending entry only for the one second each
attempt waits. Between attempts there is none: 50 ms between the three
descents, and up to five seconds of classifier backoff between restarts once
the budget is spent behind a live master. A grant landing in one of those gaps
had nothing to complete, so the receiver read it as unsolicited — it unwound
the mirror it had just installed, sent a gen-stamped release, the master
retired the grant and promoted the next waiter, and the wait's own next
re-send queued again at the back. The wait had solicited that grant; only the
attempt's accounting was missing. A design consult on the open defect
(D-0958, the unbounded wait for callers that cannot be failed) named this as
the first thing to fix, because every later step — exact cancellation, a
status lookup, re-delivery — assumes that whether a grant was solicited is
decided by the logical acquisition and not by a one-second bookkeeping entry.

The acquisition record now carries the grant. A first grant that completes no
pending entry is offered to the live acquisition for that resource (same
resource, a mode the grant covers, from the node this view names master); if
one exists the mirror stays and the grant is recorded on it. The wait's next
attempt claims it before sending anything, after checking under the table
lock that the mirror is still this node's at that grant generation — a
blocking notification the XFS layer answered on a not-yet-installed grant, or
a membership purge, releases the mirror under the wait, and a claim on a grant
the master has already retired would mint a phantom holder; that case clears
the adoption and sends again. A wait that ends any other way — a grant or
denial that completed a pending entry, a send failure, a membership retry —
or is retired idle hands an unclaimed adopted grant back exactly as the bounce
did, and a record holding one is never the eviction victim. The nonce ring a
receipt is judged against grew from four to sixteen: at one attempt per
second, four held about four seconds of history against a fifteen-second
allowance, so a reply inside the allowance could be rejected because its
nonce was gone.

Two test-only knobs. `dl_acq_gap_ino` / `dl_acq_gap_ms` hold the requester
after a timed-out attempt of one inode with no pending entry, so a holder's
release lands in the gap predictably. `dbg_probe_ino` makes the master-side
and holder-side blocking-notification probes (P7S-BAST-FIRE, P7B-BASTNOTIFY)
print for a named inode whatever its number: both printed only for inodes up
to 256, and on this aged filesystem `tests/live_holder_wait.sh` — which reads
which node masters a candidate from which node logs the notification — read
all eight candidates (3713..3720) as undetermined and aborted. The harness
now names each candidate and the chosen target, and refuses a build without
the knob rather than guess.

Measured on two nodes over TCP, 0.84.0 sv 125D4834DEBB73147496CFB,
`tests/live_holder_wait.sh` GAP_MS=10000 PAUSE_MS=240000 MASTER=remote
(tests/evidence/20260912T000529Z_livewait_s585b, console
tests/evidence/livewait_s585b.log), 21 of 21 PASS. The holder's 240 s
release-drain pause ended at 18412.51 on its own clock; the requester logged
P958-ACQ-GRANT-ADOPTED for the target (gen 17) and P958-ACQ-GRANT-CLAIMED
3881 ms later at its next attempt, with no re-send and no re-queue; its read
returned 4.5 s after the pause end with the holder's digest; zero bounces for
that inode, zero adopted grants vanished or released unclaimed, the master
fired 23 notifications for the wait against a derived budget of 29, and the
wait was never reported DEGRADED. The two P74-GRANT lines for the inode on the
requester are the candidate probe's grant and the adopted one.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.83.4 — The first join freezes the incumbent, installs the view under the freeze, and admits the newcomer only on its beacon

D-0959 was filed by code reading during the 0.83.3 correction: a mount that
has never had a peer modifies everything at NL with no grant, so when its
first peer can take a grant nothing at any DLM master represents its dirty
images, no BAST can land them, and whichever side flushes last reverts the
other. The record said nothing drained the incumbent. The tree in fact had an
ordered join — `mxfs_dlm_peer_joined_flush`, run on the incumbent's first
sight of a peer (the discovery announce on the lease UDP thread or the inbound
TCP connect on the accept thread) before the two-node view was installed: up
to five rounds of log force, AIL push, device flush and cached-view
invalidation — and it was that join that lost the data. Measured with
`tests/d0959_first_join_peermod.sh` (lap s584c, 2 nodes/TCP): the incumbent
ran a create/append loop round-robin over 96 objects while the peer mounted,
the invalidation never completed against the live workload, the fifth round
called `xfs_force_shutdown`, the incumbent's create got EIO two milliseconds
before its membership line, the peer fenced it and replayed its slice, and
after both unmounted every appended line in 32 files and the entries of 34
directories were gone, plus the peer's own synced adds to three of them. Three
earlier laps had measured nothing because the incumbent's loop touched every
object again after the flip (a full `dmesg` per join check cost over a
second), and that re-acquire under a real grant relogged or merged the dirty
image; the harness now spreads the adds over many objects and detects the join
in milliseconds from a persistent `/dev/kmsg` reader.

Design consult (Astra) on the shapes: a freeze-ordered transition alone is
insufficient because the newcomer's PR grants were never gated (a shared read
served before the incumbent's drain is a stale base for the EX that follows,
and no BAST can correct it); a newcomer-side gate alone is insufficient
because the flush wrote no page-cache data and the incumbent kept dirtying at
NL after it; the transition must run on a worker, never on a protocol thread;
a join preparation taking too long is not a corruption and must not shut the
node down; and removing the never-multi bypass altogether (a lone node taking
grants from itself, as a sole survivor already does) is the better long-term
ownership model. Shipped now, the first three:

- `mxfs_dlm_join_prepare` / `mxfs_dlm_join_commit` replace the notify: on a
  mounted filesystem prepare takes `freeze_super(FREEZE_HOLDER_KERNEL)` — new
  writers and page faults block, every dirty page is written back, the log is
  quiesced — then walks the cached views (repeated briefly against readers
  holding buffer locks) and returns with the freeze HELD; the view is
  installed and the sticky `ever_multi` bit set under it; commit thaws. The
  first modification after the flip already takes a real grant. A prepare
  that does not succeed leaves nothing frozen and nothing installed; the
  destage rounds no longer force a shutdown (the foreign-replay callers
  already treated a non-zero return as refuse-and-retry). A mount still in
  progress (the newcomer's side) keeps the unfrozen destage rounds.
- The cached-view walk now also marks every clean, unlocked, unpinned
  non-AG-meta block (directory data/leaf/node, bmbt, symlink) for a re-read:
  those were read with no peer, nothing at a master represents them, and the
  inode reload the epoch advance forces keeps a loaded fork whose blocks it
  serves from this cache.
- The transition runs on a per-context join worker (`v5_join_queue`,
  `v5_join_worker_fn` in `dlm/v5_mount.c`): the discovery and TCP-accept
  callbacks queue the sighting and return; the worker runs prepare,
  registers the peer in the lease, adds/connects it, refreshes the view and
  commits. The peer is registered only after prepare succeeded, so no path
  can install or beacon a view that includes it earlier.
- The membership-settle gate in `mxfs_dlm_lock` covers every acquiring mode,
  not only EX, and is fail-closed: once the wall-clock window has elapsed it
  stays closed while a live member's beacons still carry a different view
  (for a first join, the incumbent still preparing), and an acquire whose
  bounded wait expires in that state is refused with EAGAIN rather than
  served on a view nobody confirmed. A silent member keeps the previous
  wall-clock behaviour.

Verified (build 93FDFE518C608ADB0117544, lap s584d, same harness and load):
the incumbent froze for 104 ms (24 AGs, 97 cached blocks marked for re-read),
installed the view, thawed, and its first post-flip acquire waited 400 ms for
the newcomer's confirming beacon; no shutdown, no refusal, every entry of both
sides survived a cold remount of each node, and the newcomer read every object
complete on its first cold read. A second lap (s584e) repeated it: freeze
327 ms, gate confirmed after 200 ms, nothing lost. The two-node formation
the deploy itself performs went through the same transition and converged
in 8 s. Unchanged acceptance criteria on the same build: cache_coherency
PASS 9 s of 60, posix_multi PASS 4 s of 30, dir_reuse_coherency PASS 104 s
of 120 (its history on this rig is 103 to 110 s). D-0959 is removed from
the queue as FIXED AND VERIFIED.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.83.3 — A sole survivor takes real grants, so its inode-cluster writes carry only slots it owns

D-0955 recorded that the survivor of a peer's departure keeps whole-writing
inode-cluster buffers while still holding the images it cached when the peer
owned slots in them, because `mxfs_submit_partial_inode_write` — the
cross-node protection that masks un-logged slots this node has no write
tenure for, and the always-on authority detector inside it — was gated off by
`mxfs_v5_dlm_is_single_node()`, which is dynamic membership. The six
"unauthorised passengers" the record was filed on were the mkfs realtime
inodes 129/130 riding the root cluster: reserved, never owned by the peer, not
stale. Five workload shapes with a platter-comparing probe on every cluster
write found no stale slot published by the whole-buffer path. The mechanism
stayed open by code reading, so the gate is closed on the predicate rather
than left to the allocator's cooling rule.

The first fix, from the previous session's design consult, merely let a
survivor take the partial path (`partial_iwrite_sole` default 1, `ever_multi`
latched by the membership callbacks). Measured, it lost data: on the second
lap the survivor's freshly created directory, on a number the peer had freed,
was dropped from its cluster write by the logged-directory-at-NL rule (no
release-drain token), the platter kept the peer's FREE image, and the next
reload poisoned the directory ESTALE — 799 of 800 creates in it failed, and
the rejoined peer saw the slot free behind a live dirent. The root directory's
shortform dinode was dropped the same way in both laps and only landed because
the A/B harness alternated with the pre-fix whole write. The cause is that the
partial path's authority rule assumes the multi-node ownership protocol: under
single-node membership `mxfs_dlm_ilock_begin` bypasses the DLM and sets no
mode, both new-inode grant paths and the create-time stale clear are gated
off, and the release-drain token is set only by the BAST machinery. A survivor
on the filter alone had every logged directory at NL with no token.

Second consult (Astra): "logged this round is authorised while single" is
unsound — A caches directory X, B publishes X+b and leaves, A modifies its
stale X and publishes X+a, same generation throughout — and a read-merge is
not a standalone fix. The sound shape is the ownership protocol itself: a
survivor must take grants from the master (itself) so every multi-node
invariant, including the release drain, applies unchanged. Implemented as a
third membership predicate, `mxfs_v5_dlm_never_multi()` — single-node now
and never had a peer, the only state allowed to modify and publish without a
grant — on the inode-lock entry bypass and its paired exit gate, both
new-inode grant paths (`grant_local_new`, `rearm_unpublished`), the iget
stale-shell reloads and both publish workers. The 0.72.2 inline survivor
reload in the bypass is gone with it; the slow path services pending
invalidations for a survivor as for any member. A new incarnation now clears
the previous incarnation's stale mark at create whatever the membership. Peer
signalling shortcuts (heartbeat-ring notes, the CAW barrier, the
leaf-before-dinode flush, the open-bits publish) stay on `is_single_node`.
`docs/sole-survivor-sweep.md` has the design record and the site table.

Measured on build B472103A0C16F7288085915, two nodes over TCP, every round on
the fixed path (`MXFS_D0946_ARM=1`), platter probe on every cluster write, the
harness now summing the workload's own create/delete failures, counting
directory skips and poisons over the whole survivor phase, and reading the
survivor's namespace back cold from the rejoined peer. Clean unmount, tight
(s583e): zero operation failures, zero skips, zero poisons, 8 of 8 round
directories complete from the peer's cold cache. Clean unmount, touch
(s583f): 58 no-tenure slots masked across two writes, 300 of 300 peer files
read back from both nodes. Clean unmount, stale-source (s583g, the consult's
counterexample: A caches S, B adds 300 names and leaves, A adds 3200): both
nodes read back 600 a, 300 b and 3200 r names. The A/B lap (s583h): both arms
clean, cold readback 8 of 8. Death (virsh destroy, then the survivor
unmounted and remounted so it reads its own namespace cold): tight (s583i,
s583n) 8 of 8 directories complete; touch (s583j, s583l) 300 of 300 peer
files; stale-source (s583k, s583m) 600 a, 300 b and 3200 r names. Every lap:
zero directory skips, zero poisons, zero survivor reloads, zero operation
failures, zero platter regressions in the I/O, no shutdown, no oops. Round
walls on the survivor fell from about 11 s to about 3 s once it stopped
re-reading the platter on every access. Under the withdrawn fix on the same
rig (s583c) the same laps produced the stranded directory.

Instrument corrections in the same version, each the difference between a
false regression and a measurement: the clobber probe's per-slot detail buffer
was 96 bytes and truncated the generation mid-number (a survivor's own free at
generation g+1 read as a different incarnation); a free bumps the generation
by exactly one, so "platter LIVE gen g, memory FREE gen g+1, changecount
ahead" is counted as the node's own free landing; and "platter LIVE, memory
FREE, unrelated generations" is a live revert only when this node does not
hold the slot — a slot held at EX or PR was reloaded at grant time and the
platter image is one it superseded (the survivor's own churn two incarnations
ahead of the platter). The harness gained `MXFS_D0946_ARM`, the
`stalesrc` mode, `COLD_READBACK`, `SOLE-DURABILITY-READ` and `MASK-READ`.

Still owed by the class, not by this record: the remaining `is_single_node`
guards in the overlay (the census in `tests/criteria/sole_survivor_sites.json`
lists them, all of the shape "skip coherency or publication work when alone")
need converting to the same predicate, and a never-multi mount that receives
its first peer has dirty NL images no join barrier drains.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.83.2 — The deferred-free evict check is re-verified on the current build, and its harness stops reading silenced probes

The shutdown on ordinary rm that D-0529 recorded (every deferred inactivation
certificate misclassified as another incarnation at evict, because xfs_ifree
bumps the generation by one and the check compared the install-time
generation with the current one) was fixed in 0.64.14 with the consulted
narrow window: class 0 also when the certificate is DEFERRED, the free has
committed, and the generation is the install-time one plus one. It had not
been verified since 0.64.2x. No module code changes here; this version is the
verification, the design record of why the window is sound, and the harness
fixes that verification required.

Design consult (Astra, sess582): the window is a proof rather than a
probability if two invariants hold, and both do. The old certificate and the
free-committed flag never survive into a reissued incarnation: the check
retires the certificate, a fresh inode's authority block is reset, and the
flag is in the reclaim reset set. The flag is set only after a successful
commit. And class 0 does not license a release after a log shutdown, because
every release from a poisoned session is refused by the gate closed in
0.83.1. docs/authority-certificate.md now says so.

Measured on 0.83.1 sv A6167379C89B55536EEA269, two nodes over TCP,
tests/inact_cert_arms.sh. The defer arm: four deferred frees, four installs,
zero misclassifications, no shutdown (s582d). The new reuse arm, which is the
reused-number proof the record still owed: two create, publish, rm cycles in
one directory reused all four inode numbers with new epochs, eight installs
printed, eight deferred frees, a census of exactly eight on a fresh module
load, zero misclassifications, no shutdown (s582g,
tests/evidence/20260911T200725Z_inactcert_reuse). The injection arm: a
deferred certificate made to look like another incarnation's still classes 2
and shuts down (s582f), so the window masks nothing. The record is removed
from the queue as FIXED AND VERIFIED.

Two harness readings on the way were instrument errors and are fixed. The
install probe prints the first 96 lines per module load; the defer arm's
1100-file filler spends that budget, so later arms on the same load asserted
against a silenced probe and failed. The harness now reports such an
assertion as UNREADABLE with the budget state, never as FAIL or PASS. The
census baseline was read from the whole dmesg ring, which survives a module
reload while the counter does not, giving a negative delta; per-load reads
are now anchored on the mount's first membership line.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.83.1 — No wire release of its own leaves a poisoned node, from any emitter

On the TCP transport the inode FREE path used to release the durable inode
grant while the session was POISONED (log shut down, heartbeat slot WITHDRAWN,
PR key retained, a survivor still to fence and replay the slice); the survivor
then sealed a fence-time manifest without that grant, answered notheld to a
VALID token, skipped the transaction and quarantined its allocation groups,
and with AG 0 in the set the victim could not mount again. The gate on that
arm landed in 0.75.114. What this version adds is the rest of the class and
the proof.

The cause was reproduced on demand, which the record had owed since it was
filed. The free is a reclaim, not a create: the previous incarnation of a
just-unlinked inode, ifree committed and destaging deferred, reclaimed after
the shutdown. The control (tests/d0945_chokepoint_positive_control.sh) primes
one, fires the one-shot dirty-cancel shutdown, and forces the reclaim at once.
Timing decided whether the defect was visible at all: the survivor seals the
fence about 2.4 s after an explicit withdrawal, and the master refuses any
release from a sealed owner, so a reclaim that landed at 2.65 s (s582a) was
caught by that second line and read clean. Inside the window (s582b, s582c),
with the victim-side gate disabled, the release was accepted and the manifest
sealed with 3 entries instead of 4. With the gate on, the same free is refused
at the victim, the manifest holds 4 entries, and the replay completes with
notheld=0, no ATOMIC-SKIP, no torn refusal, no quarantine.

The class was closed by primitive rather than by scenario. A LOCK_RELEASE is
built in exactly two functions, dlm_send_release_msg and
mxfs_dlm_send_unconditional_release. Every path into them from the front-end
wrappers was already refused while poisoned; two were not: the re-send tick for
a release the master has not acknowledged, and the rejection of an unsolicited
grant. Both now refuse through the same poison oracle
(dlm_refuse_release_while_poisoned, P945-RELEASE-REFUSED-POISONED). Nothing is
lost: an un-ACKed record already stays a ledger blocker until the recovery
purge, and the purge that follows the fence retires every record of the dead
incarnation. The choke-point probe at the two primitives was proven live with
the gate off (it named mxfs_v5_dlm_inode_unlock_free), so its zero census over
the death laps now means something; the two new refusals have not been
witnessed firing.

Measured on two nodes over TCP, 0.83.1 sv A6167379C89B55536EEA269
(tests/evidence/20260911T194702Z_d0945ctl_s582c, console
tests/evidence/d0945ctl_s582c.log): both arms decided on their first attempt,
gate=1 refused with a clean survivor, gate=0 choke point live with the release
inside the window, RESULT PASS. Death laps (tests/d0944_death_rejoin_ab.sh
s582c, tests/evidence/20260911T194829Z_d0944death_s582c): 2 valid laps, both
REJOIN mount_rc=0, notheld=0, 0 ATOMIC-SKIP, 0 choke-point lines, 0
sealed-owner refusals on the survivor. The defect record
D-TCP-INODE-FREE-RELEASES-GRANT-WHILE-POISONED-MANIFEST-LOSES-IT-0945 is
removed from the queue as FIXED AND VERIFIED with that evidence. Publish-side
parity between transports, which the design consult separated from this
record, is noted in the DLM subsystem notes as an audit item with no observed
asymmetry.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.83.0 — A remote lock wait its master has stopped confirming is reported DEGRADED inside a derived bound, and listed in debugfs

On the TCP transport an inode-lock wait whose remote master is a live member
but never answers is unbounded for every caller that cannot be failed — a stat
through a held fd, a read, a write, writeback — and until now the only trace
of it was a dmesg line once a budget. The design consult for this record ruled
that for such a caller the achievable bar is bounded detection and reporting
over a path that does not need the stalled lock, not bounded completion; that
the evidence must belong to the acquisition and not to the resource; that the
bound must derive from the status-delivery cadence and never from the acquire
budget; and that silence from a live master must not be turned into a fence
victim. This is that increment, and nothing in it ends a wait.

The master already answers every one-second re-send of a queued request with
a receipt echoing that attempt's id. Those receipts are now the wait's status,
judged before they count: the requester records each attempt's nonce and
issue time before the send, and accepts a receipt only from the node the
attempts went to, naming an attempt still kept, arriving inside the response
allowance from that attempt's issue time. Accepted, it moves the wait's anchor
to the ISSUE time, never the arrival time, so a delayed reply cannot buy an
arbitrary interval; rejected, it is counted and refreshes nothing. The bound
is N x P + D: thirty one-second status opportunities unanswered plus a
fifteen-second allowance, 45 s, overridable by mxfs.acq_degrade_ms. Past it, a
still-pending wait on a live master is DEGRADED_UNCONFIRMED: said once with
its acquisition, resource, mode, master, re-send count, unanswered and total
age; listed in /sys/kernel/debug/mxfs/<dev>/acquire_degraded, which reads only
the requester's own acquisition table under its spinlock; and said once on the
way out, whether a receipt reconfirms it or the wait ends. Re-sends, restarts,
socket state and heartbeats never reset the clock.

Measured on two nodes over TCP, 0.83.0 sv CC1FEA75AB3D73669B77DA7. Fault lap
(tests/tcp_lockreq_blackhole.sh WORKLOAD=held_fd EXPECT=degraded, requests for
one inode discarded at the sender, a stat through a held fd on the requester;
tests/evidence/20260911T192018Z_lockreqbh_s581c, console
tests/evidence/lockreqbh_s581c.log): DEGRADED reported at unanswered_ms=45045
against bound_ms=45000 with age equal to unanswered (the master never
confirmed), acquire_degraded listed ino 131 with its master and 242 re-sends
while the fault stood and was empty after it cleared, P958-ACQ-RECONFIRMED on
the first receipt after the disarm, the peer served its own read of the same
file in 3 ms throughout, the requester took no shutdown and read the correct
bytes afterwards; 21 of 21 PASS. Control lap (tests/live_holder_wait.sh
MASTER=remote, a confirmed 240 s release drain behind a live holder;
tests/evidence/20260911T192501Z_livewait_s581d): zero DEGRADED, zero rejected
receipts, 25 notifications against a budget of 29, 17 of 17 PASS.

What this does not do, stated because the record stays open: the wait for a
non-fallible caller is still unbounded. The stat in the fault lap was still
blocked at the end of the armed window, by design of this increment. The
consult's ordering puts a status probe (a master-side lookup that can answer
QUEUED, GRANTED-again or UNKNOWN by acquisition identity) and further fallible
boundaries after this, each audited for a grant arriving around abandonment.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.6 — The exclusive-write gate is lifted only when nothing on the platter still owes it

One gate per LUN, more than one recovery under it. 0.82.4 made the restore wait
for every recovery that had VALIDATED its exclusion; it did not wait for one
this node had certified and not yet claimed, because a set built from
validation holds nothing for an obligation that has not started. Measured on
0.82.5 (tests/evidence/20260911T180314Z_d0932own_s580k): slot 0 certified under
the gate at 18:09:03, slot 1 published at 18:09:13 and the set emptied, the
restore landed the same second, and slot 0 was claimed at 18:09:14 to find no
reservation, once a second for 147 s until the mount gave up. The design
consult on 0.82.4 had already said "account for all outstanding obligations,
not merely currently running threads"; that half was not built.

The platter is now the authority on what is owed. A new disklock sweep reads
every heartbeat sector and reports each validated descriptor whose certificate
kind is the exclusive-write gate, whose stage is below completion and which is
not terminally refused; a sector that cannot be read or validated is reported
separately and refuses the restore exactly as an owed slot does. Unowned,
claimed, taken over, certified by a dead peer: none of those exempt a
descriptor, and nothing releases on elapsed time. Two in-memory sets close the
windows the platter cannot see: a victim slot is pinned before the gate's PR
command is issued for it and unpinned only once its certificate is durable (a
gate in force with no certificate keeps the pin and says so), and the running
set from 0.82.4 stays. All three are read, and the two sets written, under one
lock that the restore holds across the sweep and the conversion, so a reliance
admitted after the restore has decided cannot exist; the lock is taken after
the scsipr departure mutex and never held while waiting for it. The PR worker
re-drives a refused restore every 2 s rather than every 250 ms tick, because
each attempt reads all 64 sectors. A terminal refusal now releases the
dependant as publication does.

Measured on two nodes over TCP, same harness and shape (DEPART=crash,
tests/evidence/20260911T184939Z_d0932own_s581a, console
tests/evidence/d0932own_s581a.console), 0.82.6 sv 956A8B8AD3C6255EBC43D2D
against 0.82.5: the pin at 18:55:29 before the gate was issued, unpinned at
18:55:32 with the certificate durable; slot 1 published at 18:55:39 and the
restore was refused with P-PR-GATE-RESTORE-OWED owed=0x1 naming the
not-yet-claimed slot; slot 0 claimed one second later under the held gate,
registered, replayed and published at 18:55:49; then one restore. Exclusion
lapses 67 to 0, gate lapses 67 to 0, replay failures 68 to 0, both recoveries
complete, MOUNT_RC=0 in 83 s against MOUNT_RC=32 at the 147 s bound, zero
shutdowns, BUG or Oops. The lap the record was filed on passes 8 of 8.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.5 — The mount barrier resumes a taken-over recovery at its recorded stage instead of replaying it again

A survivor may take over a recovery whose previous owner died part-way through.
The stage contract says it RESUMES FROM THE RECORDED STAGE and never re-runs an
earlier one, because peers may already have acted on the later one. The live
reap path honoured that: it reads the durable stage and, at IMAGES_REPLAYED or
beyond, skips the slice replay and completes the remaining ladder. The mount
admission barrier had the same shape — take the lease, then replay — with the
check simply absent, so it replayed every slot in a mask built from death state
rather than recovery stage.

For a descriptor already at GRANTS_RELEASED that replay cannot succeed, and the
reason is that passing the stage legitimately releases both of the things it
reads: the descriptor is no longer at FENCED, so token enforcement aborts it
("the victim's FENCED descriptor is unproven"), and the authority manifest is
gone (manifest_rc=-2). The slice failed EIO, the barrier retried it every round,
and the mount never completed.

It was not only wasted work. Replay is idempotent against the state it was gated
on, but re-running it over metadata legitimately written since could roll that
metadata back — so the enforcement refusing is what stopped something, and
issuing the replay at all was the defect. The enforcement was left exactly as it
is.

The accessor this needs already existed and its header already said what it was
for: mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_stage(), "lets the replayer skip a redundant slice
replay once IMAGES_REPLAYED is on the platter". It was called at one of the two
sites that need it. Now it is called at both.

Measured, same harness and shape, 0.82.5 against 0.82.4
(tests/evidence/20260911T180314Z_d0932own_s580k against
tests/evidence/20260911T162838Z_d0932own_s580j): "foreign replay of dead slot"
68 to 0, "P227-FR-ENFORCE-DESC-ABORT" 68 to 0, "replay FAILED (-5)" 68 to 0.
The skip is logged once, naming the stage it found, and the slot then publishes
cleanly.

THE MOUNT STILL DOES NOT COMPLETE, and the reason is worth stating because this
change is what moved it. With the replay skipped, that recovery now finishes
FASTER — and it is the last dependant on the exclusive-write gate, so the gate is
restored, and the OTHER slot's recovery is claimed one second later and finds no
reservation. The dependent set added in 0.82.4 accounts for recoveries that have
already validated their exclusion; one this node still owes but has not yet
claimed registers nothing, so the set empties while work remains. A design
consult named that gap before either fix was built — "account for all
outstanding obligations, not merely currently running threads" — and this is the
half that was not implemented. It is filed with its own timeline as the
successor record and is the last known blocker for this shape.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.4 — One recovery finishing no longer takes the exclusive-write gate away from another that is still running under it

A node that returns alone after a crash carries more than one recovery. It must
recover its own previous incarnation, and it must fence the peer that had been
recovering it — and fencing that previous executor is itself part of a safe
takeover, not an unrelated act. Both run under one per-LUN SCSI PR
exclusive-write gate, because there is only one reservation to have.

The restore was written for one recovery per gate. Its own comment said so —
"never called while the gate's recovery is still pending", singular — and the
completion path acted on it: when any recovery published, it converted the
single-holder Write Exclusive back to Write Exclusive - All Registrants. So the
first recovery to finish removed the exclusion the second was still executing
under. That second recovery then refused to replay anything at all, for ever,
which is the correct and fail-closed response to losing its exclusion, and the
mount driving it never completed. The only surviving node could not mount the
filesystem.

Measured on two nodes over TCP, with the causal chain landing in the same
second: the gate installed at 16:07:25 to fence the departed owner, that
recovery publishing at 16:07:43, P-PR-GATE-RESTORE at site=recovery-complete at
16:07:43, and the other recovery's exclusion check failing at 16:07:43 and once
a second thereafter until the mount gave up 72 seconds later
(tests/evidence/20260911T160134Z_d0932own_s580i).

A recovery that has proved its exclusion is the gate now registers that it
depends on the gate, from the same evidence it proceeds on, so the set cannot
name a dependant that never validated. Completion releases its own dependency
rather than restoring the reservation itself, and the restore lands only when
nothing is left. A worker parked mid-purge issues no I/O and consumes no CPU and
still depends on the gate, so the dependency is released by completion or a
recorded block and never by a timer: an unjustified release is the exclusion
itself, while retention costs availability — joiners are refused at admission —
and says so in the log instead of failing quietly.

After (tests/evidence/20260911T162838Z_d0932own_s580j, same shape, same
harness): the two recoveries register as deps=0x2 then deps=0x3, the first to
publish clears its own bit, and the restore is refused with
P-PR-GATE-RESTORE-HELD deps=0x2. Exclusion-lapse events went from 58 to ZERO,
and the gate was correctly never restored while a recovery still needed it.

What this does NOT fix, stated because the symptom is unchanged and it would be
easy to read that as the fix failing: the node still does not mount. That is a
different defect, now isolated and filed separately — a survivor taking over a
recovery whose descriptor already stands at GRANTS_RELEASED re-runs the REPLAY
stage instead of resuming at the recorded stage, and the replay cannot succeed
because its inputs were legitimately released when the recovery passed that
stage. It is visible on the previous build too, before this change existed, so
it is neither caused nor masked by it.

Three things were deliberately NOT done, recorded because each is the obvious
move and each is wrong. The exclusion check was not relaxed to accept WE-AR: a
gate certificate is issued exactly when the victim's key was ALREADY absent, so
"victim key absent" proves nothing about it and a re-registered victim could
write under WE-AR — the single-holder gate is the only thing keeping it out.
The check was not made to compare against the certificate's original prover key
either: if the old prover still held the reservation the new executor could not
write at all, so that would convert accidental progress into guaranteed
refusal. And the dependency is not a bare count, because a count cannot say
which recovery pins the gate or whether a cancelled worker left an obligation
behind.

Whether this was a liveness defect or an integrity one was settled before the
fix was chosen, by reading the stage contract rather than inferring from a
teardown message. The victim's slice is protected by the on-disk GUARD record,
not by the reservation — a slot carrying a descriptor cannot be claimed,
mounted on, or have a fresh journal laid over it until the sector is zeroed —
and at GRANTS_RELEASED every replay stage is already past, so the only
outstanding obligation is the purge. Restoring the reservation there opens no
writable window. Liveness, and no exclusion semantics needed changing.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.3 — A recovery-takeover harness stops answering from captures it never took, and immediately reproduces a critical defect

The owner-departure takeover harness could not measure the thing it exists to
measure, and it said so as a result about MXFS rather than as a failure of its
own. Two defects, both in the same family: something absent was being read as
something proved.

Its platter dump ran on a node that had just booted, where the NFS share
carrying the dump tool is not mounted until a build check much further down the
same script. The shared ssh helper sends the remote command's stderr to
/dev/null, so python3's "no such file" vanished and the capture came back as
ZERO BYTES. The descriptor count taken from that empty file was 0, and the lap
exited VACUOUS reporting "a descriptor is still standing for the judge got=0" —
about a platter it had never read. The console showed it plainly and nothing
checked: the stage that prints the platter printed nothing at all, where the
comparable lap printed a slot line. The dump now ensures the share is mounted
first, puts the stderr redirect INSIDE the remote command so a remote failure
returns as text, requires the output to contain slot lines, and exits ABORT
rather than VACUOUS when it does not — because a zero from a broken instrument
and a zero from a clean platter are the same number and only one of them is a
result.

Then the same lap discarded a state it HAD reached. The vacuous gate required a
RETIRE_PENDING flag in both departure modes, two lines after the script itself
prints that a crashed node cannot publish one and that its absence is expected.
The crash lap had produced exactly the state it was built for — a descriptor
standing at GRANTS_RELEASED naming the crashed node as owner with its own slot
recorded, which is the precise input the platter fallback exists to judge — and
threw it away on the absence of something it had just called unexpected. Only
the standing descriptor is common to both modes, and only that is required now.

With both fixed, the first lap that got past the harness's own gates reproduced
a critical defect in the product, deterministically, and it is filed with the
causal chain: one recovery completing lifts the SCSI PR exclusive-write gate
that a different, still-running recovery on the same node is executing under,
and that second recovery then refuses to replay anything for ever. The
surviving node could not mount at all (MOUNT_RC=32 at 155 s inside a 300 s
bound, so a refusal rather than a timeout), with no crash and no shutdown.
Evidence tests/evidence/20260911T160134Z_d0932own_s580i.

That lap also settled something about the defect it was originally aimed at.
Its assertion that the platter fallback must answer REVOKED is aimed at the
wrong mechanism for this shape: all 57 UNKNOWN verdicts happened while the
crashed owner's slot still read ACTIVE, i.e. before it had been fenced at all,
and once its fence was certified the ordinary route noted the incarnation dead
and the judge answered from that correctly, claimed the recovery and ran the
ladder. The platter fallback was never the thing that needed to answer. That
assertion has to be re-aimed or made conditional before this harness is used to
adjudicate anything about the fallback.

The class behind all of this is now filed as its own defect, because it is not
confined to one harness: the shared ssh helper appears in 134 definitions across
122 files, and 538 lines across 103 files take a grep -c or a wc -l from a
capture path. Most remote commands do not fail, so most of those are not live —
but every one of them turns a failed capture into a clean zero if it does, and
the ones whose counts reach an assertion can retire or fabricate a defect. The
fix there is shared, not 538 edits: keep the remote stderr, refuse to count from
a capture that lacks the shape the tool always emits, and exit ABORT rather than
FAIL when it does. This harness is the worked example of all three.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.2 — The acquisition table says when it loses a wait, and the lap that reads it stops deciding locality from silence

0.82.1 recorded four limits in the logical-acquisition table that a design
consult had named, and ranked the shared record key as the worst of them. All
four were arguments. This makes them measurements, and the first answer is not
the one that was predicted.

Three counters and three probes, one per way the table can lose a live wait's
history: a second task joining a record that already exists
(P958-ACQ-KEY-COLLIDE), a full table taking a live record to make room
(P958-ACQ-EVICT-LIVE), and a record retired as abandoned by its own next attempt
(P958-ACQ-IDLE-LOST). Each line carries its own running total, because all three
are rate-limited and a reader who counts lines counts the wrong thing. The
record also now remembers which task opened it — recorded, not keyed on, purely
so the collision can be seen at all. Nothing on the product path behaves
differently; every branch that existed still runs in the same order.

MEASURED, two laps on one build, one target, differing only in how many tasks
waited on it. One reader: 25 notifications for a 240 s drain, and zero
collisions (tests/evidence/20260911T152202Z_livewait_s580c). Two readers of the
same inode in the same mode: 25 notifications, and 114 collisions
(tests/evidence/20260911T152635Z_livewait_s580d). Both 13/13 and 14/14 PASS,
both with the other node proven to have fired nothing for that inode across the
whole lap.

The remote path shares this table, so it was re-measured on the same build
rather than assumed unaffected: 25 notifications for a 240 s drain, the master
absorbing 11 re-sends of one acquisition, and a waiter age reaching 197345 ms,
all three loss counters zero, 15/15 PASS
(tests/evidence/20260911T153348Z_livewait_s580e). That is also the first time
the 0.82.0 remote fix has been confirmed against a target whose locality was
established by first-hand evidence instead of by a probe's silence.

So the shared record is reached constantly and costs nothing here — because
sharing it is exactly what makes two waiters cost the holder ONE stream of
notifications instead of two. What sharing does cost is narrower than the
argument for changing it: two waiters take identical queue times from one
record, and the promotion sort is the kernel's heapsort, which is not stable, so
their order relative to each other becomes arbitrary where it used to follow
their stamps; and the first of the two to finish retires the record while the
other still waits, which restarts the survivor's age and its notification clock.
Both are fairness between two waits on one node. Neither hangs, corrupts, or
shuts anything down. Eviction and idle retirement were not observed at all in
either lap.

The naming stays as it is, and the reason belongs in the record rather than in a
future session's head: the master's lookup is the resource and the SENDING NODE,
so it models one wait per node per resource and always has. A name made unique
per task would fail the master's identity test on a second task's re-send and
drop it onto the replace-and-requeue path — which is one notification per
re-send for that shape, the very thing 0.82.0 removed.

The harness that produced all of this had a defect that had already scored a
wrong result, and it is the same defect in a new place. Locality was decided by
arming the request-drop knob and calling the target LOCAL when the knob did not
fire. The drop site sits on the remote-master send path, so its firing proves
remote and its silence proves nothing — an absence was being read as an answer.
A lap picked an inode that way, declared it local, and measured the remote path:
the holder's own master fired 26 notifications for it while the node the lap was
counting fired none. It survived only because the previous change had added an
assertion that the fire count came from a node that actually fired.

Locality is now established from which node LOGS the blocking notification, with
the holder taking a conflicting grant and the waiter reading, so both answers
are first-hand and a candidate that produces neither is skipped as undetermined
instead of guessed. The lap then asserts after the fact that the other node
fired nothing for that inode, so a target remastered mid-lap is loud rather than
silent — which matters, because master assignment is re-decided whenever the
cluster re-forms, and a module swap does exactly that. The holder-side
notification count is also scoped to the target inode; unscoped it counted every
resource's notifications and made a count taken on the wrong node look
corroborated.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.1 — The node that masters its own contended inode stops notifying the holder once a second

0.82.0 taught a remote master that a re-sent lock request is the same wait. The
same pathology had a second site, and which of the two a given inode reaches is
a hash of its resource id — so on a two-node cluster roughly half the contended
inodes were never touched by that change. When the waiting node is itself the
master there is no wire message at all: it allocates a waiting entry, waits one
second, times out, FREES the entry, and the next attempt allocates a fresh one.
Two things followed from that, and both are the same two things the remote path
lost.

The entry's queue time was re-stamped on every allocation. Waiters are promoted
oldest-queued-first, so a wait that re-queued once a second was permanently one
second old however long it had really been waiting — it returned to the back of
its own queue on every attempt, and any waiter whose age does not reset
outranked it indefinitely. And the blocking notification was fired from the same
block that allocates the entry, so a holder that was already draining was
notified once a second for the whole length of its drain.

Measured on the two-node TCP rig, one 240 s release drain behind one live
holder, on a target proven to be locally mastered rather than assumed to be.
Before: 237 notifications fired and 238 received for ONE 243 s wait
(tests/evidence/20260911T141243Z_livewait_s579b). After: 26 fired and 26
received across 244 s, against a budget of 29 derived from the drain length and
the re-fire interval (tests/evidence/20260911T145737Z_livewait_s580a, 11/11
PASS). The requester's re-send count did not fall — 234 against 233 — so the
notifications collapsed because the rule changed, not because the requester
slowed down. The read still returned the holder's bytes, still ordered after the
holder's release on the holder's own clock, with no self-shutdown on either
node.

A per-node table of logical acquisitions carries what the entry cannot: when the
wait began, and when its holder was last notified. The re-created entry takes
its queue time from there, so it carries the age of the WAIT rather than the age
of this attempt; and the deferred notification fires on its own ten-second
interval rather than on the re-attempt cadence. A wait with no record in the
table fires anyway, because failing to notify a holder is the one outcome that
must never happen.

Of those two halves only the notification collapse is directly measured. The
queue-time correction is established by reading the code: a single-waiter shape
has no second waiter for the backdated entry to be ordered against, so
promotion order is not observable in the lap that measured the notifications. It
is not claimed as measured.

The entry is deliberately NOT kept alive across attempts. Keeping it alive is
the obvious shape and it is the wrong one here twice over: a queued entry whose
waiter has gone — signal, real error, budget exhaustion — would block peers
indefinitely with nobody to grant it to, and the existing-entry branch on this
path returns a code the acquire classifier reads as unrecoverable, which would
force-shut the mount instead of waiting. The residual is that the entry is
briefly absent between attempts, so a newly arriving compatible request can
still be granted in that window. That is unchanged from before this change and
is a different question from the ordering of waiters that ARE queued.

A design consult on the built fix found four limits in the table itself, none of
which the measured shape exercises, and all four are recorded rather than
glossed because they are the next change:

- The record is keyed on the resource and mode, which identifies CONTENTION,
  not one acquisition. Two tasks on one node waiting for the same inode in the
  same mode share one record, so the second inherits the first's age, and
  whichever finishes first retires the record from under the other. The same
  key cannot tell the ending operation's record from a newer one that has
  since taken that key.
- The sixty-four slots evict the least-recently-touched entry when full. Sixty
  five contended resources on one node therefore miss on every lookup and
  return to the pre-change behaviour.
- A record untouched for fifteen seconds is retired as abandoned. An attempt
  whose turnaround exceeds that — a long drain, storage latency, preemption —
  loses its age and its notification clock mid-wait.
- The notification interval is keyed on the REQUESTER's wait, not on which
  blocking grant has been told. If the holder releases and a different
  conflicting holder appears inside the interval, that new holder's first
  notification is suppressed for up to the remainder of it.

The first three fail OPEN: on a miss or a retirement the code mints a fresh
record, does not backdate, and fires — which is exactly the behaviour this
change replaced, so under that pressure the fix stops helping rather than
causing harm. The fourth is a real regression in notification latency, bounded
at the ten-second interval because the blocker list is re-collected unqualified
on every attempt and only the fire is gated. Collection was audited for this: it
copies holder and mode into a local array and mutates no lock state, takes no
references and clears no flags, so a suppressed fire loses that one message and
nothing else.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.82.0 — A re-sent lock request is the same wait, and the master now knows it

A remote inode acquire re-sends its request about once a second for as long as
it waits — three descents of sixty attempts, then however many times the
acquire classifier restarts behind a live master. Nothing on the wire said
those re-sends belonged to one wait. Each carried a fresh per-attempt id, so
the master could only read each one as a NEW request: it freed the requester's
queue entry, inserted another, and fired another blocking notification at a
holder that was already draining.

Two things were lost every second by that. The entry's position in the chain,
and its first-enqueue time — and waiters are promoted oldest-first, by exactly
that time. A remote waiter therefore returned to the back of the queue once a
second for its whole wait, and its recorded age could never exceed the re-send
interval however long it had really been waiting, so a waiter whose age does
not reset outranked it indefinitely. An arrival barrier added earlier stops a
newly ARRIVING request from being granted past a queued waiter; it does nothing
for a waiter whose own age is erased by its own retries.

The request now carries the logical acquisition it belongs to, stable across
every re-send and every classifier restart, and qualified by the requester's
node and mount incarnation so it cannot collide across a restart. A re-send
whose acquisition, incarnation and mode all match a waiting entry is that same
wait: the master keeps the entry, so it keeps its queue position and its
first-enqueue time, answers with a fresh queue receipt, and re-fires the
blocking notification only on its own interval. A lost notification is still
recovered, within that interval, rather than by turning the re-send cadence
into the notification cadence. Anything that does not match — a different mode,
a different incarnation, or a sender that mints no acquisition at all — takes
the original replace-and-requeue path untouched.

Measured on the two-node TCP rig, one 240 s release drain behind one live
holder, both laps on a target proven to be remotely mastered rather than
assumed to be. Before (0.81.0): 234 re-sends by the requester, 238 blocking
notifications at the holder. After: 249 re-sends — more, not fewer — and 26
notifications. The master absorbed 192 re-sends of one acquisition and
re-queued none of them, and that waiter's reported age rose from 1019 ms
through 197306 ms on a single acquisition id, where before it could not have
exceeded one re-send interval. The read still returned the holder's bytes,
still ordered after the holder's release on the holder's own clock, with no
self-shutdown on either node. Evidence
tests/evidence/20260911T142948Z_livewait_s579d against
tests/evidence/20260911T123631Z_livewait_s578f.

The same wait-destroying pattern exists on the local-master path, where a
one-second timeout frees the node's own waiting entry and the next attempt
re-queues it and re-fires. That site is untouched here and is measured: one
243 s local-mastered wait cost its holder 237 notifications
(tests/evidence/20260911T141243Z_livewait_s579b). It is the next change, on its
own evidence.

Two harness defects fixed alongside, both of which had already produced a false
result. tests/live_holder_wait.sh took whatever inode it happened to create,
and which node masters a resource is a hash of its id — so a lap could silently
measure the local path while its predecessor measured the remote one, and the
two BAST counts would read as a before/after when they were two different
mechanisms. That is not hypothetical: it scored a full set of passes doing it.
The target is now chosen by probing which node masters it, the choice is
asserted against what the lap says it is measuring, and the run aborts rather
than measure the other path. It also now reports what one wait cost its holder,
against a budget derived from the drain length and the re-fire interval instead
of from what the numbers happened to be.

tests/tcp_lockreq_blackhole.sh gained a second workload. Its existing one
drives everything through a fresh open(), which is the single call site that
was already made fallible — so it was refused at open before a read was ever
issued, and could say nothing about any other caller. The new workload opens
the fd first, lets the holder revoke the grant, arms the fault, and only then
reads through the fd it already holds, so the acquire under the fault carries
no fallible registration. It asserts that the blocked task is in an inode
acquire and that the open path is absent from its stack, so a run that drifts
back onto the fixed site fails instead of passing.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.81.2 — The scripts that CAPTURE a per-rig yardstick stop naming the file after a rig they assumed

Making the fio comparison resolve the rig it reads a yardstick for left the
other half untouched: the scripts that WRITE those yardsticks were naming the
files after a rig nobody had established, and that direction is the destructive
one. An audit of every consumer of .xfs_fio_baseline.* and .raw_fio_ceiling.*
found that only the comparison inferred a rig at all — the rest take the
filename suffix as a caller-supplied string and are correct only insofar as the
caller passes the right one. Two of them did not.

The two-node TCP chain hardcoded the literal tag into both the ceiling capture
and the baseline capture. That is correct exactly as long as nobody runs the
chain anywhere else; run it on another rig and it silently OVERWRITES this
rig's baseline and ceiling with that rig's numbers, corrupting the very files
the tag exists to keep apart, after which every later comparison here is scored
against foreign hardware and looks authoritative doing it. It now derives the
tag, and if the rig cannot be established it captures nothing rather than write
somebody else's file.

The ladder rung refreshed a baseline named for the TRANSPORT only. The same
transport exists on more than one physical rig, so a rung run on one of them
replaced the other's numbers. It now appends the resolved rig when there is
one, keeps the historical name when there is not so nothing that worked before
stops working, and logs which of the two happened.

Neither change alters what is measured. They change only which file the
measurement is written to, which is what decides whether a later comparison is
about this machine.

Verified on the two-node TCP rig: a module swap now carries the recorded rig
through instead of dropping it — "SWAP_OK sv=744E282C1A42942A0FEAA15 nodes=2
dev=/dev/sda rig=qnap marker updated" — and a full prep records it
independently, so the identity survives both paths that rewrite the cluster
marker. The acquire regression that runs against these yardsticks passed
unchanged on that build: a 240-second release drain waited out, 9/9, with the
read returning after the holder's release and matching bytes.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.81.1 — The rig is identified by what the hardware says it is, not by how its device was spelled

Several measurements are only meaningful against a yardstick captured on the
same hardware: the native-XFS fio baseline and the raw N-sharer ceiling are
per-rig files, and scoring one rig's numbers against another's produces a
confident verdict about the wrong machine. That identity was being inferred
from the device path — a by-path name containing "qnap" resolved to the qnap
rig, /dev/sda resolved to nothing, and the two are the same LUN. So which
physical machine the board believed it was on depended on which spelling
whoever last prepped the cluster happened to type, and the module-swap
redeploy had been carrying the short spelling forward through every swap.

Unresolved, the fio comparison declined to score rather than compare across
rigs — correctly, and the alternative is on record: this rig's 109 MiB/s once
scored against the other rig's 820 MiB/s baseline and was recorded as a 62%
failure with no filesystem change behind it. But declining is not a result, and
the two-node TCP configuration — the one being shipped — had gone unscored
across four consecutive runs while a yardstick captured on that very rig sat
beside the untagged one.

The identity now comes from the array. tools/mxfs_rig_tag.sh is the single
resolver and answers in order: an explicit override, the tag recorded in the
cluster marker at prep time, a device path that carries the vendor, and finally
the LUN's own SCSI vendor string read out of sysfs. The last is the one a
rename cannot defeat. run.sh records the answer into .cluster_marker.json when
it preps, which is the moment the identity is actually established, so later
invocations that reuse the cluster read it rather than re-derive it.

Reading it from sysfs has to work where the question is asked, and that is not
where it first appeared to be. The suite's detectors run ON THE NODES, and a
node holds no ssh credentials for its peers — the lab secrets live on the dev
host alone. A resolver that reached the hardware only over ssh answered
"unknown" in the one place the answer was needed, while sitting on the very
device it was asking about. It now reads local sysfs first and falls back to
asking a node only when the device is not present, which is the dev host's
case and not the detector's.

Two further holes closed while the mechanism was open:

A resolved rig with no yardstick of its own used to fall through to the
untagged file. That is the same cross-rig comparison the tag exists to prevent,
