only with a tag in hand, which makes it look deliberate. It now names the
capture command that is missing, so the answer is a command rather than a
mystery.

The module-swap redeploy rebuilt the cluster marker from a hardcoded list of
fields. That list is exactly what failed once before — omitting the device
there tore the rig down on the second consecutive swap — and it would have
silently dropped the new rig field on the first swap after this change. It now
merges what the swap actually altered into what is already recorded, so fields
nobody thought about survive by default, and it resolves and records the rig
itself when the marker predates the field.

Measured on the two-node TCP rig: the resolver answers "qnap" from the dev host
(via a node) and from a node (from local sysfs), for a cluster whose recorded
device is /dev/sda and whose SCSI vendor is QNAP. The comparison that had
skipped four runs running now scores seqW=100% seqR=100% randW=135% randR=101%,
worst write 100% against a 70% floor. The full two-node TCP board on the same
build ran all 28 criteria with zero failures.

## 2026-09-11 — 0.81.0 — A master now says it has your lock request, and an open stops waiting on one that never answers

An inode lock acquire that runs out of its retry budget asks whether the party
it is waiting on is alive, and keeps waiting if it is. On the TCP transport a
requester cannot read a remote master's holder table at all, so for every inode
it does not master itself that question was answered by cluster membership
alone — it never established that a holder exists, that a request is queued, or
that anything is moving. Any acquire failure whose cause was not a draining
holder therefore produced an unbounded wait.

That was measured, not inferred. With one inode's lock requests discarded at
the sender — so the master creates no queue entry, sends no reply, and is
otherwise completely healthy — a two-node TCP rig blocked an open() for 495
seconds, 2.7 acquire budgets, still blocked when the window ended. Its kernel
stack never moved off the acquire inside xfs_ilock. It logged the wait three
times and nothing else: no error, no shutdown, no escalation. The peer read the
same file in 5 ms and wrote it in 44 ms throughout. Clearing the fault let the
blocked open finish in under 5 seconds with correct data, which is what proves
it was waiting on a message rather than wedged on its own state.

The cause is that a queued request and a lost request looked identical from the
requesting end. A master that cannot grant a remote request queues it and, until
now, said nothing; the requester then saw a one-second wait expire, about sixty
times per attempt, three attempts, exactly as it would have if the request had
never arrived. Two fixes, and they only work together:

The master now answers a queued request with an acceptance receipt naming the
blocking holder's mode and the request it answers. It is sent after the waiting
entry is in the table, so the receipt never runs ahead of what it attests to,
and outside the table lock like every other send on that path. The requester
records the arrival time per resource. A receipt is an acceptance, not a promise
of progress — a master can queue a request behind a holder that never releases —
but it rules out the case where nothing at the far end has the request at all.

The acquire's post-budget decision now needs both answers: the party is live,
AND it has said it has this request, within a window derived from the request
cadence — ten missed one-second re-sends plus a five-second allowance for
scheduling and response jitter. The window is deliberately not derived from how
long a release drain takes: a drain of any length keeps refreshing receipts, so
tying the two together would blind the check for exactly as long as the longest
drain. A locally mastered resource and the CAW transport need no receipt, since
there the holder table is read first-hand by the waiter itself.

Silence alone still does not stop a wait. Most callers of the inode lock cannot
be failed safely — inactivation, writeback, rolling transactions and deferred
metadata work have no error boundary — and for them the acquire keeps waiting and
now says in the log that it is waiting without evidence. What changed is that a
caller sitting at a boundary where nothing is dirty and no transaction is open
can register as fallible, and opening a file is the first to do so. Its acquire
refuses instead of waiting, and the open returns EIO to userspace. Nothing about
the acquire changes for a path that has not been audited for a failed acquire,
which is what stops this from quietly widening into the paths that cannot take
one.

A design consult reviewing the patch was explicit that the other candidate
disposition — treating an unanswered request as a liveness failure of the peer
and driving the existing death, fence and recovery machinery — must not be taken
on a requester's own timeout. A requester cannot distinguish its own broken
transmit path from a broken peer, and in this very measurement the fault was on
the requester's side while the peer was healthy; a node that cannot get an answer
must not be able to fence the node that is answering everyone else. That path is
left to authorised membership arbitration and is not entered from here.

Verified at two nodes over TCP on one build, both directions of the same
decision:

- With requests for one inode discarded at the sender, the open ends inside the
  budget with "Input/output error" to userspace, having refused an unreceipted
  acquire. No unrecoverable-timeout line, no filesystem shutdown, the peer still
  mounted and serving its own reads in 3 ms. The give-up fired 190 seconds after
  the last receipt for that inode, so the decision rested on a receipt that had
  gone stale rather than on one that was merely missing. Clearing the fault, the
  same node read the file correctly again with no poisoned inode state left
  behind, and the refused process was gone.
- With a genuine release drain held open for 240 seconds on the holder, the same
  open waits it out, and the classifier records that it is waiting on evidence
  rather than on membership. The receipts arrive at the re-send cadence — nine
  consecutive ones for that inode at 1.024 s apart — and then the probe's print
  budget stops the logging at sixteen lines, 176 seconds before the read
  returns. What establishes that receipts kept arriving through that unlogged
  stretch is the classifier line itself: it is stamped 176 s after the last
  printed receipt and reads receipted=1 against a 15-second staleness window,
  which cannot hold unless a receipt landed inside the last 15 of those
  seconds. The read returned after the holder's release with matching bytes and
  zero refusals. (The line count is NOT the receipt count, and was briefly
  written up here as though it were; every printed line now carries the mount's
  true running total so the truncation is visible in the evidence itself.)

The instrument that produced the first case is a test-only parameter that
discards one inode's outbound lock requests, filtered to a single inode number
so heartbeats, lease renewals, membership traffic and every other resource are
untouched — the peer has to stay a healthy live member for the measurement to
mean anything. The harness that drives it finds an inode that is actually
remotely mastered by asking rather than assuming, since which node masters a
resource is a hash over the resource id and changes with every cluster
formation. An earlier version of that harness counted probe lines from the whole
kernel ring instead of its own run, selected a target from the previous run's
lines, armed the fault for an inode that was locally mastered that time, and
scored a full set of passes on a read that never went near the code under test;
every count it takes is now scoped to its own run and compared against a
baseline taken immediately before the measurement.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.80.0 — The clustered structural audit reports three outcomes and stops erasing its own evidence

The whole-volume structural audit now runs clustered, and this is the first
time in the project's history that a filesystem checker has examined a volume
more than one node wrote. Verified at two nodes over TCP: after a concurrent
shared-directory workload the cold audit reported no errors, no inode-chunk
block also on the free list, and a cold superblock inode count that moved with
the workload (64 on a freshly formatted volume, 192 after the clustered run),
in 10 to 13 seconds of a 180 second budget.

Two defects in the gate itself are fixed, both of which would have mattered
only on the one outcome anybody cares about.

It remounted unconditionally. A remount replays the log and rewrites metadata,
so the audit that had just condemned a volume was followed immediately by the
operation most likely to destroy the state proving it. Coming back up is an
obligation of the success path, not an obligation to erase a failure, so on a
corruption verdict the auditing node now stays out. What that preserves is
bounded and the script says so rather than implying more: the other nodes
decide for themselves and will remount, so on a shared LUN this preserves the
audit output and the auditor's abstention, not the image. A corruption verdict
is a reason to stop the run.

It had no way to say "I did not establish anything". The verdict was computed
from an exit status and a grep for error words, so a checker that printed
nothing, died before reporting, or never ran the cross-tree comparison produced
exactly the same green row as a genuinely clean volume. Absence of the word
corrupt is not evidence of coverage. The row now reports CLEAN, CORRUPT or
INDETERMINATE as an explicit field, decided before anything remounts, and
requires positive evidence that the audit happened — non-empty output, the
cross-tree aliasing result, and the cold inode count — before it will say
CLEAN. A clean audit followed by a failed remount is still a failure, because
the fleet is degraded either way.

The audit output moved out of /tmp into the tree, and the row now carries its
path. These nodes are reset constantly and /tmp does not survive that; on a
corruption verdict that file is the only forensic record there is.

The cold inode count is reported, never treated as ground truth. It is kept
lazily and the last unmount is what writes it, so a stale or node-local value
can survive into a cold read. It is a cross-check against the counts derived
from the btrees, not an oracle.

This closes the record that no clustered condition had ever run the filesystem
checker. Its cause -- an applicability default that capped the whole tooling
category at one node -- was already gone from the tree; what was missing was
that the row had never actually run clustered, and now it has, three times,
passing each time including once directly after concurrent two-node work. What
that record does NOT close is carried by a new one: the row still does not
prove the workload exercised the allocation paths it claims to cover, and the
checker has never been calibrated against deliberately corrupted images, so its
clean verdict is so far an untested instrument.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.79.0 — Directory index/data divergence is detected at tenure start instead of silently repaired

A shared directory's LEAF hash index and its DATA blocks can end up at
different points in history, so readdir lists a name whose hashed lookup
returns ENOENT, or the index reflects an unlink whose dirent is still in the
data block. Three separate paths in this tree repaired that condition without
ever recording it, and the third is the reason the producer has never been
named.

The leaf rebuild runs at the top of every cross-node tenure, armed once per
handoff and fired from createname BEFORE that tenure's first mutation. The
leaf it finds there is therefore the one this node ACQUIRED, and comparing it
against the set derived from the data blocks is the only direct measurement of
whether a handoff delivered a directory whose two halves agree. The rebuild
overwrote that image and reported only the rebuilt entry count, so a directory
that arrived torn was made whole in place and never reached a board row. Every
instrument aimed at this defect so far has looked after recovery, which is too
late to see a tear that was handed over rather than produced locally.

The rebuild now snapshots the acquired (hashval, address) set before
overwriting it and diffs it against the derived set. Both are sorted and
deduped, so one merge pass separates the directions exactly: missing entries
are in the data but absent from the acquired index, extra entries are in the
index with no dirent behind them. Both outcomes are reported, including the
clean one, because an instrument that speaks only on failure cannot be told
apart from an instrument that never ran. Detection is now separable from
repair; the repair itself is unchanged, and so is every code path around it.

Cost is one array and a merge over entries already in hand — no extra I/O. If
the allocation fails the census is skipped and the repair proceeds as before.

First measurement, two nodes over TCP on the shared-directory reuse workload:
36 censuses, matching the 36 rebuilds exactly, zero divergence — the volume
acquired coherently every time it was observed. That is bounded in two ways
the same evidence shows: 81 further rebuilds declined on directory format, so
the window covers single-leaf directories only, and the comparison ran against
this node's in-core data rather than the platter image. It is also the wrong
shape to reach the defect, which needs a node death and a foreign replay.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.78.1 — A fence can no longer preempt a key a live member is holding

The SCSI PR key is derived per BOOT, from {host_uuid, boot_uuid, fs_uuid}, and a
host reaches the LUN over a single I_T nexus. Two consequences follow that the
fencing protocol did not account for together: a successor incarnation mounting
in the same kernel re-registers the IDENTICAL key its dead predecessor left
behind as the fence target, and the target has no way to tell the two
incarnations apart. A PREEMPT AND ABORT naming that key therefore cannot reach
only the dead one — it strips the live successor's registration and aborts its
outstanding task set, and a healthy mounted node loses its write access without
ever having been at fault.

Half of this was already handled. A node was protected from preempting its own
previous incarnation: the slot fence compares the victim key against the
fencer's own and issues nothing when they match. That guard covers only the self
direction. When a PEER fences a dead incarnation whose host has already
remounted, the victim key differs from the fencer's own and the guard never
fires. The symmetric direction was open.

It is now closed at the primitive rather than at the call sites.
`mxfs_scsipr_fence_node` consults a new "is this key carried by a LIVE member
other than the incarnation being fenced?" guard in its pre-command section,
before anything is submitted, so all four fence paths are covered by one check —
an invariant enforced at four callers has four chances to be forgotten. The
answer comes from the disklock slot table, which is the only authority on
membership: `mxfs_disklock_key_live_elsewhere` scans this node's own identity
and every live monitored record, excluding the victim BY NODE. Excluding by node
is what makes the guard both safe and sufficient: a mount's node id is derived
from a per-mount uuid, so a successor on the victim's host carries a different
node id with the same per-boot key and is still detected, while a legitimate
fence of the victim keeps working even if its record has not yet been marked
not-live. The refusal fails closed — "cannot tell" refuses too — and reports a
new fence kind, KEY_HELD_BY_LIVE_MEMBER, which proves no exclusion, so no replay
gate can mistake it for one.

Verified on the two-node TCP rig, both directions, because a guard that refused
every fence would pass a positive test while making recovery impossible.
Pointed at the peer's real registered key the fence refuses, logs the reason,
issues nothing, and the peer's registration is still on its own nexus afterwards
and still writes; pointed at a key nobody holds it does not fire at all and the
attempt classifies as key-absent exactly as before. Whose key is whose was read
from READ FULL STATUS throughout: READ KEYS reports only that a key is
registered somewhere and never says on which nexus, which is why it cannot
answer any question about ownership. Two death/replay laps pass unchanged on the
same build, fencing still certifying exclusion and every acknowledged file
readable with its acknowledged md5.

A default-off module parameter, `dbg_fence_probe_key`, drives one real fence
attempt against a named key so the guard can be exercised against live
membership; production paths read zero and behave as before.

This does NOT dispose of the unmountable-volume defect that prompted the work.
That volume was never reproduced and its cause was never proven — the kernel log
window its record quotes had already rolled out of the capture that was kept, so
the archive can neither establish nor refute it. What was fixed is a real and
separately demonstrated gap found while investigating it. Two further findings
from that investigation are recorded in the defect ledger and remain open: the
reservation-health check decides "our key is gone" from READ KEYS, which cannot
attribute a registration to a nexus, while the fenced-self inspection it hands
off to uses READ FULL STATUS, so the two readers can disagree; and the
inspection's launch latch is never reset on any exit path, so a mount gets one
fenced-self inspection for its lifetime and every later observation is swallowed.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.78.0 — The memory store holds lessons again; its records became documents

`.ccmemory` had grown to 2,801 files and 44MB, of which 2,254 were named for the
session or ccloop run that wrote them — handoffs, end-of-session state, next-step
plans, "what is in flight right now". A memory named for when it happened is a
record, and a record is worth nothing to a session working on something else: it
crowds out the lessons, and the listing every session pays for degrades until the
corrections it exists to surface no longer fit inside it.

What the store holds now is what a future session on a different task would be
wrong without: 157 files — 104 corrections and traps, 23 environment and
reference facts, 27 techniques and collected articles, 3 standing user
directives. The store went from 44MB to 9MB, most of that a SQLite index that
had to be vacuumed before it gave the space back.

Everything else moved rather than vanished:

| what | where it went | n |
|---|---|---|
| design-consult rulings | `docs/rulings/` | 216 |
| compiled campaign articles and the records still cited by name | `docs/history/` | 357 |
| pre-v5 bug history, prior-version narrative, the mkfs and roadmap plans | `docs/project-history.md` | 8 |
| cost, quota, delegation and ledger audits | `docs/cost-audit.md` §§2.1–16.5 | 16 |
| the native XFS format plan, the btree-engine replacement, the NET2 plan of record | their own `docs/` files | 5 |
| the v0.2.2–v0.3.22 development log | this file, at the end | 1 |

Those 32 were **merged into their host documents, not appended to them**: each
one sits at its own depth in the host's heading structure, in the host's order,
with the pointers that used to say "the full write-up is in this document" cut
out. `cost-audit.md` keeps every figure from all sixteen audit memos — verified
figure by figure, since that document is read weekly — and they now live as
numbered subsections of the era they belong to (§2.1, §3.2.6, §3.2.7, §3.3.1,
§5.5, §10.1, §11.7, §11.8, §12.7, §12.8, §12.9, §14.1, §15.7, §16.5) plus a new
§13 for the two ledger-health audits that had no home. `project-history.md` was
restructured chronologically from nine pasted documents into one narrative.
`sole-survivor-sweep.md` became one document instead of three overlapping notes.
`net2-plan-of-record.md` leads with the plan and follows with the verification.
The GFS2 coherency contract joined the prior-art section it belongs in, and the
CAW-vs-TCP transport rationale now opens `dlm-protocol.md` where a specification
should state which transport is normative.

**Nothing was deleted while a pointer to it survived.** The defect queue cites 69
memories by name and the awareness docs cite 116 — those are the evidence behind
open defects, so every one of them was preserved as a document and all 428 citing
files were rewritten to the new path. A name that was folded into a compiled
article and had no document of its own redirects to that article, so a citation
always lands on the material. The check that decided this ran to zero: no
citation in the tree dangles.

The rest — 2,618 files — were records with nothing left to teach, and the
material worth keeping from them had already been folded into the compiled
articles that are now in `docs/history/`.

`tools/ccmemory_triage.py` is the tool that did it, and it stays: it classifies
every memory, exports what must survive, rewrites citations, and renames a
lesson that is still named for a session. Run `plan` before `apply` — `plan`
changes nothing and reports how many citations would break.

Two things worth knowing for next time:

- The store's filename and its `name:` field can disagree. 27 files were named
  one thing on disk and another in their frontmatter, so a sweep keyed on either
  one alone silently misses them. They were routed by hand.
- A path scan that strips a leading `./` with `lstrip("./")` also eats the dot of
  `.claude`, so every awareness doc resolved to a path that does not exist and
  the rewrite pass skipped all of them without reporting a single error. The
  hole was invisible in the run's own output: it reported success. Fixed, and
  the 116 citations in those files were rewritten.
- A record that already cited its memory with a `.md` suffix produced `.md.md`
  when the name was replaced by a path, and collapsing pairs is not idempotent —
  `.md.md.md` becomes `.md.md` again. Collapse the whole run at once.

Moving the memories into `docs/` re-imported 798 rule-number citations that the
2026-09-10 sweep had just cleared out of the tree. They were swept again with
the same vocabulary — instrumented evidence, design-consult ruling, the
zero-defect bar, the derived-budget rule — across 222 files. `RULE0_CALIBRATE`
and the defect id `D-TMPFILE-CHURN-RULE0-PERF-400` are names, not citations, and
were left alone.

The listing budget was raised to 20,000 tokens in `.claude/settings.json`: 104
corrections do not fit the default 6,000, and the listing was reporting them as
withheld and unsearchable — which is the failure the store was cleaned up to
end.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.77.2 — Rule numbers removed from every comment and document in the tree

User directive: never write a rule number in a comment, document, commit message
or record — say the rule itself. **2,149 substitutions across 604 files.**

A number is a pointer at a file the reader may not have, and it is the first
thing to go stale. The argument arrived unprompted earlier the same day:
reorganising the project rules made 830 comments in this tree instantly cite a
retired stub. What a comment actually meant survives that; the number does not.

What the labels became:

| was | now |
|---|---|
| the instrumented-evidence label (783 uses) | `PROVEN BY INSTRUMENT`, `PROVEN by`, `instrumented`, `instrument step N` |
| the design-consult label (680) | `design-consult ruling` / `review` / `design` |
| the budget label (546) | `derived time budget`, `budget:`, `the 2x-native-XFS ceiling`, `a timeout IS a test failure` |
| the defect-bar label (46) | `the zero-defect bar` |
| the source-tree label (47) | `the source-tree rule` |

Two things the sweep was built not to break, and did not:

- **`dlm/disklock.{c,h,md}` use lowercase "rule 3" and "rule 6" for the disklock
  protocol's own internal rules** — recovery-descriptor invariants,
  broadcast-predicate splitting, owner-tuple constancy across takeover. Every
  pattern requires an uppercase `RULE`, which excludes them by construction.
  Missing a citation is acceptable; destroying protocol documentation is not.
- **`RULE0_CALIBRATE`**, the harness environment variable, is untouched — the
  trailing underscore defeats the word boundary. Verified by direct test rather
  than by reasoning about the regex, and nothing in the tree pattern-matches on
  the literal string, so no test logic depended on any of this.

Verified structurally rather than by eye: across all 2,124 changed line pairs,
**not one altered its count of `/*`, `*/`, quotes or braces.** No replacement
string contains a comment delimiter, so the sweep could only ever edit prose
inside a comment or string — never the structure around it. Every shell and
python file in the tree still parses, and the board and queue still render.

Nothing real was left behind: the 25 lines the sweep still flags are all
`RULE0_CALIBRATE`, matched because the detector sees `RULE0` inside the variable
name. There is no residual citation to fix by hand.

`data/derule-journal.txt` records every changed line with its before and after,
so a bad replacement is findable and hand-reversible. The sweep script itself is
archived to `/src/archive/mxfs/scripts/derule.py` — a migration that has run is
dead weight in the tree.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.77.1 — CLAUDE.md audited against the global rules: 770 lines to 558

The project rules file was audited line by line against the global rules file
ccenv installs at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Roughly a sixth of it restated rules the
global file already carries, another sixth was design and topology filed in a
rules file, and the rest carried its arguments at essay length.

Retired as duplicates, each leaving a stub that says where the rule now lives and
why the number is not being reused:

- **The scripts-in-the-source-tree rule** existed to override a global guideline
  that said the opposite. That guideline is gone and the global rule now says what
  this rule said, so it was 33 lines arguing a case already won — plus a stale
  note to relocate two files relocated in sess31.
- **The troubleshooting loop** and **read source with the Read tool** are carried
  in full by the global file.
- **Never run a command that can trigger a permission prompt** moved to the global
  file this session, where every project gets it.
- The Development Notes never-poll block restated the global delegation rule. What
  survives is the one part no global rule says: rig work fired at the nodes counts
  zero toward the ccloop Stop gate, so ending a turn on it gets the session kicked.

**The queue-integrity rule folded into the zero-accepted-defects rule.** Three of
its four imperatives were already stated there, and keeping them apart meant
reading two rules to learn one thing about one object. The unique one — commit
`data/defects.json` with the change that caused it, because a queue with no date
fields takes its dates from its own history — now sits alongside the closed:found
argument it protects.

**The design-consult rule moved into the prohibitions block.** It had been sitting
500 lines below the header that calls itself "READ FIRST, NO EXCEPTIONS", and the
rule above it carried a parenthetical apologising for the ordering rather than
fixing it.

Design and topology moved to where they are already written down: the four design
tensions to `docs/` and the subsystem docs, the rig topology and harness notes to
`.claude/awareness/subsystems/tests.md`, and the wrapper-timeout derivation to
`tests/criteria/TIMEOUT_BUDGETS.md`. The architectural invariants stay, stated
flat with a pointer each, because each constrains a decision made before the
relevant file is open — a fifth "invariant" was a third copy of the scripts rule
and is gone.

No rule number was reused and none was renumbered, and a new section — "Rule
labels used in the tree" — records why that constraint exists. A census found
**2,133 rule citations across 605 files**, and they are mostly not pointers to
the rules file: one label (783 uses) means established by instrumentation rather
than by reading code, another (680) means the shape came from a design consult
recorded under a named ccmemory note, a third (523) means a budget assertion.
Retiring two of those rules left 830 comments citing a stub, so each stub now
states what the label meant and where the rule went.

Sweeping those 2,133 sites was considered and rejected. Beyond the size, it
would corrupt real content: `dlm/disklock.{c,h}` and `dlm/disklock.md` use
lowercase "rule 3" and "rule 6" for the disklock protocol's own internal rules,
which have nothing to do with the rules file. New code should write the reason
rather than the number — "proven by instrument" survives a reorganisation, and
this file has now been reorganised twice.

**One conflict found and deliberately NOT resolved here.** The global rule on
`pgrep`/`pkill` offers `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` as a safe way to identify a process.
On this host that read is itself the wedge: it takes each process's `mmap_lock`,
and one task stuck holding its own hangs the reader forever in uninterruptible
sleep. The project rule has it right — `comm`, `stat` and `stack` are safe,
`cmdline` and `maps` are not — and it is kept intact for that reason. Right now the project file
corrects the global one, which only works if someone reads 100 lines into it.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.77.0 — The harness stops writing the board; criteria.py owns every cell

`run.sh` no longer touches a board file. Every read and every write now goes
through `tools/criteria.py`, which is the only thing that knows the board's
shape, and `criteria.json` — the file the harness used to hand-edit with jq —
is archived to `/src/archive/mxfs/` along with `scripts/gen_criteria.py` and
`scripts/matrix_check.py`. The board is `data/criteria.json`.

This is what 0.76.0 left unfinished. Two programs writing the same JSON with
independent notions of its schema is exactly the divergence the ledger cutover
was meant to end.

`tools/criteria.py` grew the operations the harness needs, so nothing had to be
reimplemented in shell:

- `update --reason` — WHICH check failed. The flake rule reads this to tell a
  real fault from the rig failing to form, and the import had dropped it from
  the live cell, so rig noise in a current failure would have counted as a
  genuine flake.
- `update --calibrate` — a measurement run establishing a budget that does not
  exist yet records its elapsed time without being scored against a number
  nobody has set.
- `pending` / `executing` / `finalize` — the PENDING lifecycle. A run marks what
  it intends to run, stamps the one test in flight, and converts whatever
  markers survive its exit: a test that was executing when the run died reads
  ABORTED, a test the run never reached reads NOT RUN. Conflating those two
  painted whole boards red with tests that never executed.
- `rows` — the matrix as TSV for the dispatch loop.

Two bugs fixed by moving these into one place. The harness's own
`finalize_pending` replaced the cell wholesale and **dropped its flake
history**, so a run that died erased the evidence that a criterion was
intermittent; and `tests/suite/run_one.sh` did the same on every single-test
invocation. `criteria.py` pushes the outgoing verdict onto the bounded history
before any write, so neither can happen again.

The scaled-budget comparison stays in `run.sh`, which is the only place that
knows the per-node-count scaling. `criteria.py` independently enforces the
criterion's own `budget_s`; with every `budget_scale` currently `flat` the two
numbers are identical, and the tool can only ever be the stricter of the two.

`MXFS_CRIT` still selects an alternate board file for a second rig —
`criteria.py` honours it now instead of `run.sh`.

Not migrated, and they will read empty rather than wrong: a handful of one-off
session diagnostic scripts under `tests/` still parse the archived schema
(`tests/d3_dirring.sh`, `tests/degraded_member_cascade.sh`,
`tests/net2/gate3_cawsanity.sh`). They are historical single-session harnesses,
not part of the board path.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.76.0 — The defect ledger is retired; the queue holds only what is still broken

`tests/criteria/OPEN_DEFECTS.json` and everything that read it are archived to
`/src/archive/mxfs/`, with a `README.md` there explaining what they were. The
queue is now `tools/defects.py` over `data/defects.json` and the board is
`tools/criteria.py` over `data/criteria.json`.

The ledger had become an archive wearing a work queue's clothes. 182 of its 277
records were closed dispositions; the file was 3.2 MB, the median record 8,157
characters and the largest 61,757, so no session could read it and every
question about it was answered by a script that sampled it. Worse, a record
recorded no configuration, so nothing could tell a 32-node CAW defect from one
that blocks a 2-node TCP release. `tests/suite/open_defects.sh` therefore failed
the board while any record anywhere was open, whatever configuration that record
described. A board that can never read green reports nothing about whether the
work is converging — and under the 2026-09-10 classification, 64 of the 95 open
records named configurations a 2-node TCP cluster cannot physically run.

The verbosity was not cosmetic either. Three independent sweeps at "how many of
these block 2-node TCP", over the same data, returned 39, 40 and 49: the `next`
fields (median 3,473 characters) are design essays, and every record mentions
fencing and replay and membership and pace, so no text classifier can separate
them.

Removed from this tree and moved to `/src/archive/mxfs/`: `defects.sh`,
`showstat.sh`, `tests/suite/open_defects.sh`, `tests/criteria/OPEN_DEFECTS.json`
(with its `.prev` and `.backup`), `tools/ledger_validate.py`,
`tools/ledger_backfill_dates.py`, `tools/ledger_set.py`,
`tools/ledger_owed_work.py`, `tools/ledger_session_dates.py`,
`tools/hook_ledger_guard.sh`, `scripts/ledger_repair_backtick_damage.py` and
`scripts/ledger_update.py`.

The two migration scripts went with them — `tools/defects_import.py` and
`tools/criteria_import.py`. They had already run, they refuse to run twice, and
their input files are now in the archive, so keeping them meant shipping
scripts whose only source path does not exist in a clone. What remains in
`tools/` for this job is `defects.py` and `criteria.py`.

Unwired with them, so nothing in the tree calls a file that is no longer here:

- `.claude/settings.json` — the `PostToolUse` hook that ran `hook_ledger_guard.sh`
  is gone, and the file now has no `hooks` block; the `./showstat.sh` allowlist
  entry is replaced by `tools/defects.py` and `tools/criteria.py`.
- The `open_defects` criterion is out of `tests/suite/manifest` (replaced by a
  comment recording why), out of `criteria.json`, and out of `data/criteria.json`.
  The 2/tcp board is 29 rows where it was 30, and the 32/caw board likewise.
- `run.sh`, `scripts/caw_ladder_fua.sh`, `tests/suite/run_suite.sh` and
  `README.md` point at `tools/criteria.py` instead of `./showstat.sh`.

The release question is now asked per configuration and answered by the queue:
`tools/defects.py 2 tcp --release` reports 27 of 95 open records blocking a
2-node TCP release. `nodes` and `dlm` both default fail-closed, so a record
nobody has classified blocks every configuration rather than sliding out of one
silently.

The project rules were rewritten to match. The zero-accepted-defects rule now
names the queue, its fail-closed `nodes`/`dlm` fields, and the release bar —
100% data integrity and stability, nothing else gates a 2-node TCP release. The
rule that had enforced a date schema and its three tools, all now gone, became
the rule that keeps the closed:found ratio computable without date fields: every
queue change goes through the tool, a removal states what was measured, and
`data/defects.json` is committed with the change that caused it, because the
commit date is now the date.

This change does not close, disprove or relabel a single defect — all 95 open
records came across intact, and narrowing a record's configuration disposes of
nothing. It also left the harness still writing the old `criteria.json`, so a
fresh board run was invisible to the new renderer; 0.77.0 closes that.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.128 — A clustered volume keeps its fully-free inode chunks, unconditionally

The guard that stops a fully-free inode chunk's blocks from re-entering the AG
free pool — where a directory reallocates them and writes its data over an
inode cluster some node still believes in — has now been asked three different
questions, and the third is to stop asking.

It began as "am I alone right now". That is dynamic membership, so the sole
survivor of a peer's departure answered yes and resumed deleting chunks exactly
when a departed peer's view of them was least trustworthy: 187 chunks freed in
one measured lap, essentially every chunk a 12000-file workload had carved.

0.75.125 moved it to "has this mount had a peer", which closed that case and was
verified on the rig. It is still the wrong question, and a design review found
the reason before a test did: that predicate rests on `ever_multi`, a per-mount
in-core bool with no durable backing. The moment every node unmounts and one
mounts again alone, `ever_multi` is false and the guard is back to upstream
behaviour on a volume whose platter carries a second writer's residue. Nothing
was repaired in the interval; only the in-core flag that remembered the peer was
discarded.

The durable fact the guard needs — has any other node ever written this volume —
is recorded nowhere that survives a clean shutdown. Both candidate sources are
cleared on the way out: a departing node's disklock slot is zeroed, and the
committed membership-epoch record whose member mask names its peers lives in
that same per-node heartbeat sector. After a full clean shutdown the volume
looks, to every structure on it, exactly like one that has never been clustered.

So the question is unanswerable, and the guard fails closed. This is a
shared-LUN filesystem: another node may mount at any moment, and the proof of
exclusivity that would justify the optimization cannot be obtained. A clustered
volume keeps fully-free inode chunks, always — no membership test remains.

The cost is stated precisely because it is the whole trade. The chunk's blocks
stay committed to inode space instead of returning to the AG free pool; its
inodes stay free and reusable, so nothing is leaked and later creates reuse
them. That is the same trade every multi-node mount already made, now made
unconditionally. What it prevents is a directory data block landing on a live
inode cluster, the verifier failing on the next read, and the filesystem
shutting down — measured, not hypothetical: a create was killed reading
`58 44 44 33` (XDD3, a dir3 data block carrying its own address) at the home of
an inode the allocator had just handed out.

The cost is bounded by the filesystem's own geometry, which is what makes
"never delete" safe rather than merely conservative. Inode space cannot grow
without limit: the allocator refuses to carve a new chunk once
`icount + ialloc_inos > maxicount`, and `maxicount` is `sb_imax_pct` of
`sb_dblocks` — 25% by default, which on the rig's 50 G volume is 25,991,808
inodes across 3,248,976 of its 12,995,925 blocks, exactly 25.00%. That ceiling
is upstream XFS's own, and every multi-node mount already lives with it. The
behaviour also converges rather than diverging: a kept chunk's inodes stay free,
so churn re-fills the chunks it emptied instead of carving new ones. What it
does not do is return those blocks to the data pool, and that is the whole
trade.

`tests/d0949_sole_survivor_chunkfree.sh` gains the arm that would have caught
the scoping error: after the cold audit it takes the surviving node out again,
mounts it alone so it comes up with no in-core memory of the peer, refills and
empties the chunks that were kept, and asserts the deletion probe stays silent.
It also asserts the sole-survivor probe reads zero in that arm, because a mount
that did observe a peer would have tested the easy case over again.

The class is now frozen against silent regrowth. `tools/sole_survivor_audit.py`
gained `--baseline` and `--check`, and `tests/criteria/sole_survivor_sites.json`
is the reviewed inventory of every single-node fast path that skips work — 77
of them, keyed by file and function rather than by line so unrelated edits do
not move them. A new board row, `guard_census`, fails when a guard appears that
the inventory does not account for. Passing is a much weaker claim than "these
guards are safe" and must not be read as the stronger one: a guard in the
inventory is not thereby correct, it is thereby known. What the row prevents is
a new one arriving without anyone deciding whether the work it skips has
consequences that outlive the membership change — which is how this class
survived being closed twice.

The check fails closed: a missing inventory, a missing tool or a missing
python3 is a failure, not a pass. All three arms were exercised rather than
assumed — a dropped site, a shrunk count, and an absent inventory each produce
a red, and the real tree produces a green.

Fixing the census found a bug in the census. Instrumenting a guard puts a probe
line between the test and its `return`, and the next-line-only scan stopped
recognising it: the count fell from 77 to 70 the moment seven guards were
instrumented. A safety census that shrinks when you look at something is worse
than none, so the scan now steps over probe and comment lines and stops at a
closing brace or at any real work.

Also in this build: the census probe at `iclus_publish_open_bits` no longer
fires when open tracking is simply switched off. Folding that into the
membership test reported every skip as a membership fast path, and on this rig
open tracking is usually off — the site would have looked like the busiest
sole-survivor skip in the tree while measuring a knob.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.127 — The structural audit now runs on clustered conditions

No clustered condition had ever run the filesystem checker. `chk_clean` is the
only test that runs `chk_mxfs` and asserts it reports no errors, and it was
applicable only at a single node — so the 2-node board printed "every criterion
passed" over 28 rows in which nothing had read a btree and compared it to
another. Every structural defect this project has chased — inobt against
finobt, AGI freecount against both, a block that is inside an allocated inode
chunk and also on the free list, a dinode home holding a directory image — was
invisible to that board by construction.

The cause was one default. `gen_criteria.py` capped `max_nodes` at 1 for the
**entire** tooling category, on the grounds that "all tooling is single-node
device ops". A whole-volume structural audit is not that: the divergences it
looks for are produced by concurrent multi-node allocation and by nothing else,
so being clustered is the case it exists for, not an exclusion from it. The cap
appeared in no manifest — the visible `MINNODES` column was 1 and satisfied —
which is why it survived this long. An explicit declaration now also outranks
whatever an existing board file recorded, because the point is to correct a cap
the old default had already written into every one of them.

`chk_clean` itself now works across a fleet, and the shape is forced by what
the tool does. `chk_mxfs` compares btrees against each other, so reading a live
mount makes in-flight allocation look like a disagreement between two trees
sampled microseconds apart — it would announce corruption on a healthy
filesystem, which is the one outcome that would make the row worthless. So
every node unmounts, one node audits the device cold, and every node mounts
again. The rendezvous is the MQTT barrier, never an on-filesystem one: this
test unmounts the filesystem it would otherwise coordinate through. A node that
cannot come back is a failure of this test and says so, because leaving the
fleet unmounted after an audit would silently poison every row that follows.

The audit now also carries the cold `Superblock icount` and the chunk/free-space
aliasing verdict onto the board. MXFS keeps `sb_icount` lazily and writes it at
unmount, so that moment — every node out — is the only point in a run where
reading it means anything.

Budget 180 s, derived: unmount ~5 s, `chk_mxfs` measured ~45 s cold on this
50 G LUN, and a remount measured at up to 80 s when it meets a frozen slot and
has to fence it.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.126 — Two instruments for the guards a departing peer silently switches off

Nothing in this release changes behaviour. It adds the two measurements that a
whole class of guards has never had, and both are inert until a knob is set.

`mxfs_v5_dlm_is_single_node()` answers "is this mount single-node right now".
Several guards ask it when the question they actually need answered is "has
this volume ever had another node", because that is what decides whether
anybody else can still hold a view of the metadata in hand. The sole survivor
of a peer's death or clean departure answers yes to the first and no to the
second, so those guards switch themselves off at the moment a departed peer's
residue is on the platter and nobody is left to publish it. The inode-chunk
keep guard was found to be one of these and was fixed in 0.75.125; this release
instruments the next two rather than assuming they are the same.

`mxfs_submit_partial_inode_write()` is the cross-node false-sharing protection:
it omits the sectors of in-core inodes this node released to a peer, because a
cached image of a slot we no longer own is stale prior-tenure and whole-writing
the cluster reverts the peer's durable inode. It also carries
`P218-CLUSTER-AUTHORITY`, the always-on detector for writes that carry slots
this node neither logged nor holds. Both sit behind a single single-node test
at the top of the function, so for a sole survivor the protection is off and
the detector that would have noticed is unreachable in the same breath — the
same shape that kept the inode-chunk deletions of every previous run silent.
`partial_iwrite_sole=1` lets a sole survivor enter the function so the detector
runs and states what the shipped path is publishing.

`mxfs_dialloc_two_phase()` is the containment that reads a picked inode
number's platter home before anything is dirtied and refuses a number whose
home still carries a live dinode. It is gated the same way, and at the same
instant `mxfs_ag_inode_owned()` opens the departed peer's allocation groups to
this node — so the survivor starts picking numbers out of the groups it has
just stopped checking. `P951-VALIDATE-OFF-SOLE` counts that path, which has
never been counted; `dialloc_validate_sole=1` keeps the validator running for a
sole survivor so a run can say whether it refuses anything.

`tools/netconsole_listen.sh` closes a hole in the rig's evidence, not in the
filesystem. Every test node has always been configured to send its kernel log
to the dev host — `netpoll: netconsole: remote IPv4 address 192.168.120.1,
remote port 6666` is in each node's boot log — and nothing has ever listened on
that port, so every datagram a guest sent while dying was discarded. A node
that panics reboots, its journald has no record of the boot that crashed, and
these guests carry no pstore backend, so until now a guest panic and a guest
that "just rebooted" were the same observation. The listener is deliberately
dumb: it appends what arrives with a timestamp and parses nothing. Guest
console loglevel is 1, so ordinary probe output never reaches it and it cannot
flood — but a panic prints at emergency level and does.

The sole-survivor A/B for both lives in `tests/d0946_disklive_knob_vs_aging.sh`
under `MXFS_D0946_SOLE=umount|death`: it ages both nodes, removes the peer,
waits for the membership transition to actually be observed rather than assumed,
and then alternates the knob in place across rounds on the survivor.

`tests/d0949_sole_survivor_chunkfree.sh` no longer gates on a mid-flight inode
count. MXFS keeps `sb_icount` lazily and writes it at unmount, so `chk_mxfs`
sampling a live mount reports the value from the previous unmount: the first
verification lap read 64 three times while the run it was measuring carved 187
chunks, and reported itself VACUOUS. The carve gate is now the count of files
the workload actually created, and the post-state is the cold read taken with
both nodes unmounted. The create budget is 180 s, twice the 85.5 s measured for
12000 files on this rig.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.125 — The keep-the-chunk guard now covers the survivor of a peer's departure

MXFS keeps a fully-free inode chunk instead of deleting it, so its blocks can
never re-enter the AG free pool where a directory would reallocate them and
write its data over an inode cluster some node still believes in. The guard
asked `mxfs_v5_dlm_is_single_node()`, which is dynamic membership, not
configuration — so the sole survivor of a peer's death or departure answered
"yes, I am standalone" and resumed the upstream behaviour the guard exists to
prevent, precisely when a departed peer's view of those chunks was least
trustworthy.

That path had never been measured, because the only probe on it could not fire:
`P103-CHUNKFREE` sat inside a branch requiring not-multi-node while itself
requiring multi-node. The two conditions are complements. Every inode-chunk
deletion this filesystem had ever performed was silent.

Made reachable, it measured, in a single lap on two nodes over TCP: a node
created 12000 files, its peer unmounted cleanly, and the node then removed the
directory — **187 chunks deleted and their blocks handed back to the AG free
pool**, essentially every chunk the workload had carved. The unbudgeted alert
counted 187; the rate-limited companion counted 10, so a `pr_warn_ratelimited`
would have under-reported it eighteenfold.

The fix is the predicate. The question is not "am I alone now" but "has this
volume had another node during this mount", because that is what decides
whether anyone else can still hold a view of these chunks —
`mxfs_v5_dlm_sole_survivor()`, which already existed for this class of mistake
and which this path did not consult. Both sibling call sites are covered:
`xfs_difree_inobt` and `xfs_difree_finobt` shared the guard verbatim, and
fixing one alone would have left the two btrees disagreeing.

A mount that has never been multi-node keeps upstream behaviour and gives up
nothing. What a survivor gives up is blocks staying committed to inode space
for the life of the mount; the inodes in them remain free and reusable, so this
is not an inode leak — it is the same trade a multi-node mount already makes.

`P103-CHUNKFREE-SOLE` is now unreachable by construction and is left in place
as the regression assertion: if it ever prints again, the predicate has
regressed.

Also here:

- `tests/d0949_sole_survivor_chunkfree.sh`, the reproducer. It reaches the
  condition with a clean peer unmount rather than a death — the same membership
  state for a fraction of the cost, and with no fencing or replay to
  disentangle, so the result cannot be blamed on either. It refuses to start
  against a mounted-but-unwritable filesystem, and it scores itself VACUOUS
  unless both halves of its gate fired, because a harness must be able to tell
  "I could not run" from "I ran and saw nothing".
- The carve counter reads `chk_mxfs`'s `Superblock icount`, not
  `df --output=itotal`. The latter reports XFS's dynamic *maximum* inode count
  and was measured unchanged at 25991808 across 12000 creates and their
  removal — it cannot see carving at all.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.124 — Instrumenting a guard that switches itself off when the peer dies

A create was shut down reading `58 44 44 33` — XDD3, a directory data block
carrying its own address `0x41f1c0` in its header — at the home of an inode the
allocator had just handed out. Two things previously believed about that
incident are wrong, and both were settled by reading the tree rather than by
running anything.

The bytes are not a stale cache read. `mxfs_buf_coherent_reread_verify()`
re-reads through `mxfs_pal_scsi_read_fua_bdev` — a SCSI READ(16) with FUA —
whenever `mxfs_fua_disable` is off, which is the default. The eight retries in
the captured incident all returned the same bytes and ended `P-DIRCRC-RETRY-FAIL
... durable, not transient`. The medium itself holds directory metadata at that
block.

And `chk_mxfs` calling the filesystem clean never supported the conclusion drawn
from it. It has no block-ownership map and no cross-tree duplicate detection at
all: its free-space check validates those btrees against themselves, its inode
check validates those against themselves, and the two are never compared. A
block claimed at once by an inobt chunk record and by the free-space trees
passes every test it has. The verdict was silent on this class, not evidence
against it.

What the source does show is a guard that turns itself off at the worst moment.
MXFS keeps a fully-free inode chunk rather than deleting it, so its blocks can
never re-enter the AG free pool and directory data can never alias an inode
cluster — the comment on that guard names the resulting shutdown in the exact
words of the observed failure. But the guard asks `mxfs_v5_dlm_is_single_node()`,
which is dynamic membership, not configuration. From the moment a two-node
cluster's peer dies until it rejoins, the survivor deletes chunks and frees
their blocks exactly as upstream does. The predicate that would have been right
already exists — `mxfs_v5_dlm_sole_survivor()`, written precisely because the
single-node fast paths must keep honouring what a departed peer left behind —
and this path does not consult it.

That went unmeasured because its probe could not fire: `P103-CHUNKFREE` sat
inside a branch requiring not-multi-node and itself required multi-node. The two
conditions are complements, so it never printed once, and every inode-chunk
deletion the filesystem has ever done was silent.

This release adds measurement, and changes no behaviour:

- `P103-CHUNKFREE` is reachable, carries `sole=0/1`, and is joined by an
  unbudgeted `P103-CHUNKFREE-SOLE` alert for the sole-survivor case.
- `P949` in `mxfs_dbg_disk_di_read_coherent()`: when a candidate inode home
  reads with no inode magic, the same LBA is re-read with FUA and classified —
  `P949-PLAIN-STALE` when the two reads disagree, `P949-HOME-FOREIGN` when both
  agree there is no dinode but the block is not empty (somebody else's metadata
  at a block the allocator calls a free inode home; unbudgeted, with the bytes),
  `P949-HOME-EMPTY` when it is all zeroes. Module parameter
  `p949_plain_vs_fua`, default on.
- `chk_mxfs` gains the cross-tree audit it never had: a bitmap of inobt chunk
  blocks, honouring the sparse holemask, and a bitmap of BNO free extents, ANDed
  at the end. A block inside an allocated inode chunk is allocated by
  definition and must never also be free. Reports `Chunk/free-space aliasing`.

The deciding measurement is now cheap: if `P103-CHUNKFREE-SOLE` never fires on a
death lap, the guard hypothesis is dead and the shutdown needs another root.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.123 — Reverting a change that sounded right and measured worse

0.75.122 made the inode allocator hand an AG back early when a run of candidates
was refused for having unpublished frees, instead of re-picking up to the
generic 64-restart bound. The reasoning was that nothing an AG can offer changes
inside a tight re-pick loop — only the passage of a few milliseconds does, once
the kicked writes land — so spinning was waste and yielding to the sweep
back-off was free.

Measured on directory churn, twelve rounds, same harness:

| | unnecessary chunk carves / fix round | fix-arm wall | control-arm wall |
|---|---|---|---|
| re-pick (0.75.121) | 0–4 | 4779–5417 ms | 4838–5545 ms |
| yield early (0.75.122) | 8–13 | 4636–7452 ms | 4180–6124 ms |

Both numbers it was meant to improve got worse, and the fix arm went from level
with the control arm to clearly behind it. Handing the AG back sends the
allocation to another AG or to a grow, and that costs more than finishing the
re-pick. The storm-exit count did drop to zero, which is what made the change
look successful if you only read that one counter.

Reverted. The module is byte-identical to 0.75.121. The reasoning and the
numbers are recorded at the constant it would have introduced, so the next
person to have the same idea has the measurement instead of the intuition.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.121 — A number we owe a write to is not a busy AG

The allocator's cooldown ring is its peer-contention signal: an inode whose DLM
slot a peer held at a recent try-reserve is parked there for 500-1000 ms, and
when a sweep finds every candidate parked it concludes the AG is spent and grows
a fresh inode chunk.

0.75.117's transient refusal put its own candidates in that same ring, so the
allocator read "this node still owes that home a write" as "a peer has it". The
kernel log said so plainly, and it is what failed a soak row:

    P-DIALLOC-RESV-SWEPT agno=0 probes=0 contended=0 cool=56 demand=1
        — every free inode in this AG is peer-held or cooling; AG returned
    P-DIALLOC-RESV-GROW agno=0 — all free inodes peer-held; grew a fresh chunk

Fifty-six cooling candidates and *zero* contended. None of them were peer-held;
they were ours, and they would have been reusable in a few milliseconds.

Growing chunks that were not needed is not cosmetic. Every fresh carve is an
opportunity for the defect where an inode chunk laid over a recycled directory
block keeps the directory image on its platter — which shut a filesystem down
earlier the same day.

The ring entries now record *why* they are cooling. A publication-pending
candidate is tallied against the publication counter instead of the contention
counter, so it steers the pick without ever voting that the AG is exhausted, and
it cools for 40-80 ms rather than 500-1000 — the owed write is local and was
already kicked at the moment of refusal, and a measured one landed in 8 ms.
Peer-held candidates are untouched.

## 2026-09-10 — 0.75.120 — Kicking the owed writes instead of waiting for them under the grant

The D-0946 ruling gave a progress rule for the allocator's transient refusal and
listed its hazards in the same breath. One of them:

> do not hold the cluster AG grant across a synchronous flush — that is
> cluster-wide head-of-line blocking. Worst-affected workload is exactly rapid
> unlink/create churn in a small inode population.

0.75.117 and 0.75.119 did precisely that. `mxfs_pubob_drive_publication()` forced
the log synchronously and then polled for up to 200 ms, and `mxfs_pubob_flush_owed()`
forced it synchronously with no cap at all — both called from
`mxfs_dialloc_two_phase` with the AG EX held. The justification written into the
comment was that the AG EX is what sanctions a publication write, so holding it
is required. That is true, and it is not the objection: every peer and every
local task queues behind that grant for the duration.

Both now start the owed writes and return. `xfs_log_force(mp, 0)` instead of
`XFS_LOG_SYNC`, no polling, no sleeping. The candidate goes on the ordinary
500-1000 ms reservation cooldown and the *next* visit reads a home that has had
time to land — if it was this mount's own un-destaged inode cluster it now has
its magic and allocates through the normal path; if it never belonged to us it
still has none and is refused again. Same decision, one cooldown later, with
nothing waited on under the grant.

    P946-PUBDRIVE-KICKED ino=N kind=N gen=N epoch=N chain=N waited_ms=N

`P947-VALIDATE-DESTAGED` is gone with the synchronous re-read that produced it;
the un-destaged case is now indistinguishable from an ordinary free home by the
time it is allocated, which is the correct outcome and one probe fewer.

Progress is still guaranteed: the write has been started, the cooldown bounds the
retry, and a storm still reports `P946-DIALLOC-PUBPEND-STORM` and returns
`-EAGAIN` into the sweep back-off — never `-EUCLEAN`, never ENOSPC.

## 0.75.119 — 2026-09-10 — Telling "not written yet" from "not ours" by acting, not inferring

0.75.118 taught the inode allocator's candidate validator that a home which
reads cleanly with no inode magic has never had anything written to it, and
allocated on that basis. The rig disagreed within one run. A candidate whose
home read cleanly with no magic held `58 44 44 33` — XDD3, a directory data
block, carrying that same block address in its own header. Allocating it let
`xfs_imap_to_bp` read the platter, fail the inode verifier eight times and shut
the filesystem down on a dirty transaction.

The premise was too strong. "No inode magic" rules out a *dinode* ever having
been written there; it does not rule out anything else having been. Both causes
produce the same bytes, so no amount of reading separates them:

- an inode cluster this mount initialised and has not destaged — ours, and the
  candidate is good;
- a home that belongs to something else — not ours to hand out.

What separates them is a write. `mxfs_pubob_flush_owed()` forces the log and
pushes the AIL once; the validator then reads the home again. An un-destaged
cluster of ours now has its magic and the allocation proceeds:

    P947-VALIDATE-DESTAGED ino=N agno=N agino=N dmode=0N dgen=N n=N

A home with still no magic after everything owed is on the platter is refused —
transiently, on the ordinary reservation cooldown, so the pick moves on, no
create fails and no transaction is dirtied:

    P947-VALIDATE-NOMAGIC ino=N agno=N agino=N n=N

This keeps what 0.75.118 got right — creates no longer die wholesale on a
filesystem 7% full, because the un-destaged case is real and common — without
the inference that broke. Neither blanket answer was correct: the old build
failed every create, and 0.75.118 shut the filesystem down.

`mxfs_dbg_disk_di_read_coherent()`'s three-way result stands unchanged; only
what the validator does with the no-magic case is different.

## 0.75.118 — 2026-09-10 — A home with no inode magic is not an unreadable home

Creates stopped. Not slowly, and not with ENOSPC: on a two-node TCP filesystem
7% full with 1% of its inodes used, mounted and otherwise healthy, six hundred
consecutive `fallocate` calls returned EIO, and a single one issued by hand
minutes later still did. The allocator was refusing to hand out any inode at
all.

`mxfs_dialloc_validate_candidate()` reads the candidate's home dinode straight
off the platter before the transaction is dirtied, and treats "I could not read
that" as a reason to fail the create — which is right. But the reader it used,
`mxfs_dbg_disk_di_mode_coherent()`, returns the same `0xFFFF` for two completely
different outcomes: the read failed, and the read succeeded and there is no
inode magic there. For a detector that only printed the number those were
interchangeable. For a gate that decides whether a create lives they are
opposites.

A home with no magic is the ordinary state of every inode in a chunk this mount
has allocated and not yet destaged. `xfs_ialloc_inode_init` logs the new inode
cluster; it does not write it. So the moment the allocator's search reached a
fresh chunk, every candidate in it read as unreadable, every create failed, and
the condition was self-sustaining because the next create searched the same
chunk again.

No magic is in fact the safest verdict the validator can get. A dinode keeps its
magic once written, even after the inode is freed, so its absence proves nothing
was ever durably written at that home — and a peer cannot have one in flight,
because we hold the AG EX and a peer must publish every owed image before
releasing it. `mxfs_dbg_disk_di_read_coherent()` now separates the three
outcomes and the validator allocates on the third:

    P947-VALIDATE-NOMAGIC ino=N agno=N agino=N n=N

`mxfs_dbg_disk_di_mode_coherent()` keeps its old two-in-one contract for the
diagnostic callers that only ever printed the value.

Also fixed, because it made the above much harder to read: when `xfs_dialloc`
fails, `xfs_create` never assigns an inode number, and the P-CR62 post-mortem
went on to read "the dinode of inode 0", found no magic there and printed
`verdict=disk-read-err/badmagic` for every one of those six hundred creates —
a confident disk fact about a number nobody had allocated. It now says
`verdict=DIALLOC-FAILED-BEFORE-PICK` and leaves the errno to speak for itself.

## 0.75.117 — 2026-09-10 — An owed write is a reason to refuse a number, not to allow it

Two gates in the create path disagreed about a state that is entirely legal,
and the disagreement cost a healthy filesystem three times on the two-node TCP
rig with nothing killed.

When this node frees an inode, the free commits in core — the generation is
bumped, the inobt record says free — before the freed dinode image is written
back to its home on the platter. Between those two moments the number's home
still carries the previous life, live, at one generation lower. That window is
by design; a publication obligation records it.

The inode allocator's candidate validator knew about the obligation and treated
it as permission: it allowed the number *without reading the platter*, reasoning
that a live image at home could only be this node's own unpublished free. The
recycle gate in `xfs_iget_recycle` knows nothing about obligations — it reads
the platter, finds a live dinode where a free one was promised, and correctly
refuses. By then `xfs_dialloc` has logged the AGI, the inobt, the finobt and the
counters, so the refusal cancels a **dirty** transaction, which shuts the
filesystem down and takes the node out of the cluster.

The allocator's inference was the weak link. Consistency with the state is not
proof of ownership of it, and pushing the same inference downstream into the
recycle gate would only make a false accept overwrite a live inode instead of
shutting down — strictly worse. So the validator now refuses:

    P946-VALIDATE-PUBPEND ino=N agno=N agino=N okind=N ogen=N oepoch=N ochain=N n=N

The refusal is transient and deliberately *not* the mount-lifetime DISK-LIVE
quarantine. An inode whose only problem is that we still owe it a write is not
corrupt; quarantining it would leak inode space, force needless chunk allocation
and manufacture false ENOSPC. It goes on the existing reservation cooldown, the
pick moves on, and the allocator's contention back-off — which never returns
ENOSPC — already covers an AG where every candidate is in that state.

Refusal alone starves, though: the inobt says free, every candidate is refused,
and nothing makes the owed write happen. `mxfs_pubob_drive_publication()` is the
progress path. After four refusals in one allocation it forces the log (so the
ifree is stable and the inode item unpinned — a pinned inode is never flushed)
and pushes the AIL, then waits up to 200 ms for the obligation to clear:

    P946-PUBDRIVE-OK ino=N waited_ms=N
    P946-PUBDRIVE-TIMEOUT ino=N kind=N gen=N epoch=N chain=N waited_ms=N

It runs at the one point where it is safe: the AGI and the btree cursors are
dropped, the transaction is clean, and the AG EX is held — which is not a hazard
here but the very thing that sanctions a publication write, while holding the
AGI the publisher needs would deadlock.

A storm of these refusals is now reported as its own condition rather than
borrowing the corruption verdict:

    P946-DIALLOC-PUBPEND-STORM agno=N restarts=N pubpend=N drives=N

Both arms live in one build. `dialloc_pubpend_refuse=0` restores the old
inference as an A/B control so the shutdown can be reproduced against the fix
without changing anything else, and the obligation kinds moved from the DLM
overlay into `xfs_mxfs_dlm.h` because the allocator now has to name them.

## 0.75.116 — 2026-09-10 — Naming which way the allocator's guard said yes

`mxfs_dialloc_validate_candidate()` is the guard that reads the platter dinode
while the transaction is still clean and refuses a candidate whose image is
live. It works — and three times it said yes to an inode whose dinode the
recycle gate found live a millisecond later, then shut the filesystem down.
`P-DIALLOC-DISKLIVE` was absent every time, so the guard ran and allowed.

It has two ways of allowing, and they are not variations of one defect. The
`mxfs_pubob_lookup` arm allows *without reading the platter at all*, on the
grounds that this node holds an open obligation on the number and so the live
image at home must be its own. The other arm reads the platter, through
`mxfs_dbg_disk_di_mode_coherent`, and is told the inode is free — while the raw
reader used by the post-mortem probe reports it live moments later. The first
would be a wrong belief about ownership; the second would mean two platter
readers disagree about one inode, and the guard depends on the one that is
wrong. Those have opposite fixes, so the branch is now named rather than
inferred:

    P946-VALIDATE-ALLOW via=pubob ino=N agno=N agino=N okind=N ogen=N ...
    P946-VALIDATE-ALLOW via=coherent-free ino=N agno=N agino=N dgen=N

This is the inode allocator's hot path and every create reaches it, so the
`pubob` arm is capped at 32 per boot and the ordinary free-candidate arm prints
nothing at all: an allocation that proceeds and then succeeds needs no
explanation, and only a number this mount has already quarantined as live is
worth a line when it comes back reading free.

## 0.75.115 — 2026-09-10 — Asking the release question where the callers are not known

The poison gate — an incarnation may not surrender an on-disk grant once its log
has shut down, because the grant is what a survivor's fence-time manifest is
sealed from — lives at each of the mount layer's release wrappers. That is one
gate per caller, and therefore one gate to forget. The inode free path was
forgotten for exactly that long, and it was found only after the damage it did
had been traced back through a survivor's refused replay. Reading the callers is
what had been missing it all along: a caller nobody thinks of has no missing
gate to notice.

So the question is now also asked at the two primitives in `dlm/dlm.c` that
every release funnels through, where the caller set does not have to be known in
advance to be covered. A new `local_poisoned_cb` lets that layer ask the mount
layer whether this node's own session is poisoned, and a release that happens
anyway is named with its call site:

    P945-RELEASE-WHILE-POISONED fn=unlock_gen type=1 ino=132 ag=0
                                comm=kworker/2:1 n=1 caller=<symbol>

It logs and does not refuse. Whether a release while poisoned is a defect
depends on which path it is — a survivor purging a dead peer's slots is the
opposite operation and must never be gated — so the disposition is made per site
with the evidence in hand, and this says which sites still owe one. It is
reachable only after a shutdown has poisoned the session, and capped so a
teardown releasing thousands cannot flood the log.

## 0.75.114 — 2026-09-10 — The symlink half of the fix now answers to the same knob

The remote-symlink grant added in 0.75.113 was taken unconditionally, while the
ilock-time diversion it completes answers to `unpub_publish_owned_meta`. The two
are one fix for one defect, so an A/B that turns the knob off has to restore the
pre-fix behaviour on *every* form. Left ungated, the symlink call would keep
publishing in the control arm — the control would quietly become a second
treatment arm, and the difference the experiment reports would be smaller than
the fix it is measuring. The call is now behind the same knob.

The inode free path also gained a probe. That path was the one release primitive
that let a TCP grant go while the session was poisoned, and the gate that now
stops it only logs when it *refuses* — so with the gate disabled the log says
nothing, and "the gate did not refuse" reads exactly like "no inode was ever
freed there". A run that proves nothing and a run that proves the defect were
indistinguishable, which is why the behaviour had been reasoned about but never
reproduced on demand. `P945-INO-FREE-RELEASE ino=N poisoned=1 gated=0|1` is now
emitted by that path in both arms, so the failing arm states its own failure and
a lap that never took the route is reported as untested rather than as clean.
The line is reachable only after a log shutdown has withdrawn the session.

## 0.75.113 — 2026-09-10 — The one inode form that has no later transaction

Every inode that owns metadata outside its core now takes a real grant before it
can log any of it — but that diversion happens at the inode's first exclusive
modify, which is a *later* transaction than the create. A remote symlink has no
later transaction. Its target block is inode-owned metadata and it is written
inside the very transaction that allocates the inode, so there is nowhere to
split: the inode number does not exist before that transaction begins.

Measured on the two-node TCP rig, 40 symlinks with a 900-byte target:

    P239-OWNAUTH-NONDUR blkno=104 len=8 blft=9 outcome=6 ino=133
                        mode=5 unpub=1 gen=2 try=0 comm=ln

Forty symlinks, forty images, every one stamped AUTH_NOT_HELD — unreplayable by
any peer, and enough on its own to cost the cluster its mount if the node dies
holding one. So the symlink create path takes the real grant itself, for the
remote form only. An inline symlink keeps its target in the inode core, logs no
such block, and never reaches the call.

The first version of the probe that looked for this reported the symlink case
CLEAN. It built its targets 3000 bytes long; XFS_SYMLINK_MAXLEN is 1024, so
every `ln -s` failed and the stage asserted that zero unauthorized images were
logged by zero symlinks. A stage now reports what it actually produced —
`made=40 links=40 tgtlen=903 blocks=8` — and the assertion reads that, because
"the condition is absent" and "the condition was never created" are not the same
result and had been indistinguishable.

## 0.75.111 — 2026-09-10 — One release path in eight forgot to ask, and only on TCP

A grant is the proof that lets a survivor replay a dead node's journal. So an
incarnation may release an on-disk grant only while no replay-eligible image of
that incarnation can still require it; once the log has shut down, the slot is
WITHDRAWN and the key retained, that can no longer be proven for any grant, and
every release is refused until a survivor has fenced and replayed the slice. Two
gates in dlm/v5_mount.c enforce that, one per transport, and every release entry
point in the file asks them — the plain inode unlock, the unconditional release,
the inode-cluster release, the allocation-group release.

The inode FREE path asked only on CAW:

    if (ctx->dlm)
        mxfs_dlm_unlock_gen(ctx->dlm, &res, 0);          /* nobody asked */
    else if (ctx->dlm_caw) {
        if (v5_caw_release_gate(ctx, "ino-free", ino))
            return;

On TCP, freeing an inode after the filesystem had shut down therefore dropped
the very evidence the survivor needed. Measured: after an injected log error a
kworker reclaimed inode 132 on the create-failure path and released its grant
with no refusal, while the allocation-group release in the same teardown was
refused as it should be — the two lines sit next to each other in one log:

    P88-PUBOB-RECLAIM ino=132 clean=1 flushed=0 nlink=0 shutdown=1
    P52-GRANT-FREE    ino=132 ret=mxfs_dlm_unlock_gen
    P-TCP-RELEASE-POISONED ag=0 — wire release REFUSED: session poisoned
    P220-EPOCH-LEDGER-OPEN ino=132 pend=2761 — tenure ended with a committed
                                               change not yet at home

The survivor then sealed a manifest that did not hold inode 132 and refused the
image the dead node had logged under it — a token that was VALID, answering
notheld. The whole transaction was atomically skipped, AG 0 was quarantined, the
root inode became unreadable and the victim could not mount again.

The TCP arm now asks the same question the CAW arm always did. Freeing an inode
does not make the images already committed under its grant unnecessary.

All eight release primitives in that file are now behind a gate. The one call
that stays ungated purges a dead peer's slots from a survivor, which is the
opposite operation.

## 0.75.110 — 2026-09-09 — An unpublished inode may not log a block nobody can replay

On a completely healthy two-node lap — nothing killed, no injected error, every
assertion green — 6662 of 27413 logged buffer images captured no durable
authority. All 6662 were bmap-btree blocks of a single fallocate'd file, and the
peer doing ordinary work in the same lap captured 26112 durable and zero
without.

    P228-TOKCLASS n=27413 ag=20751 mislabel=6662  mis_blft: t4=6662
    P239-OWNAUTH  n=6662  unpub=6662  durable=0
    P239-OWNAUTH-NONDUR blft=4 outcome=6 ino=135 mode=5 unpub=1 comm=fallocate

The cause is the deferred-publish optimization meeting recovery. A newly created
inode gets a local-only EX grant and no on-disk slot; it is published later, on
the first BAST that could expose it to a peer. That is sound for live coherency
— every path by which a peer could name the inode transits a lock this node
holds, and each of those publishes before releasing — but the recovery half of
the argument was never made. A metadata block outside the inode core (a bmap
btree, a non-shortform attr fork, a remote symlink target) is authorized by the
owning inode's EX grant and by nothing else; while that grant is local-only
there is no durable epoch to name, so every image of such a block ships
AUTH_NOT_HELD. A peer replaying this node's slice after a death must refuse the
transaction that carried it, the refusal atomically skips the transaction, and
every allocation group it touched is quarantined. When that set includes AG 0
the root inode is unreadable and the filesystem cannot be mounted again.

The condition is present on every lap. A death only decides whether anyone ever
asks a peer to replay one of these images.

An unpublished inode now takes a real grant before it can log such a block.
Directories already diverted to a real acquire at their first exclusive modify;
the same question is now asked for every other inode, and answered one step
early — an operation adds at most one extent to a fork and the conversion to
btree format happens on the add that no longer fits inline, so a two-extent
margin cannot be stepped over. The trigger is ownership of metadata outside the
core, not ownership of data: a file whose extents fit in the inode logs nothing
a peer could have to replay, and making every created file take a synchronous
on-disk grant is the cost that had publish-on-create removed in the first place.

`unpub_publish_owned_meta=0` restores the previous behaviour so the two arms can
be measured against each other. `P-UNPUB-OWNED-META` counts and names each
diversion; the residual is the same `P239-OWNAUTH unpub` counter that found it.

## 0.75.109 — 2026-09-09 — A kernel panic behind a VACUOUS verdict

A new probe arm brought back a lone survivor to meet a standing fencing attempt.
The harness reported VACUOUS: the mount produced no evidence. The mount produced
no evidence because the node had panicked and rebooted.

    BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000000
