    #PF: supervisor instruction fetch in kernel mode
    RIP: 0010:0x0
     v5_dispatch_slice_recovery+0x1fc/0x270 [mxfs]
     v5_fence_retry_worker_fn+0x295/0x780 [mxfs]
    Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

A supervisor instruction fetch at address zero is a call through a NULL function
pointer. `v5_dispatch_slice_recovery` holds exactly two indirect calls, both to
`ctx->dead_node_notify_fn`, and every other call in it is direct.

That function states its own contract: the caller must have verified
`ctx->dead_node_notify_fn`. Three of its four call sites do. The fourth — the
fence retry path — did not, and it is the one reached from a kthread.

The hook is NULL for the entire mount window by design; it is registered by
`mxfs_dlm_cache_init`, which runs after `xfs_mountfs` returns. The fence retry
worker is started at mount and runs inside precisely that window, so a retried
fence that certifies there dispatches into nothing. The measured mount sat in
`slice slot=1 NOT replayed (-1)` while the retry backed off 204 ms to 6389 ms,
and the node died at 228.9 seconds. The cost is the whole node, not the mount.

The fix takes the direction this file already takes everywhere else the hook is
absent: do not dispatch, leave the slice frozen and durably recovery-pending.
Skipping the dispatch alone would trade a panic for an abandoned recovery, so
the slot is also handed to the late-death mask, which the mount settle's phase 3a
consumes to elect a replayer once the mount is live and the hook exists.

A defensive NULL check inside the dispatch function was deliberately not added.
It would absorb the precondition violation for every caller instead of fixing
the one that breaks it, and two changes at once make neither attributable.

Worth noting for the next probe that returns VACUOUS: the node journal here is
volatile and kept no prior boot, so a node that reboots mid-run leaves a journal
that begins at a fresh boot banner with no filesystem lines in it at all. The
dying boot survives only in the libvirt serial log. VACUOUS meant a kernel panic.

## 0.75.108 — 2026-09-09 — A two-valued knob cannot exercise two fixes

Two independent fixes now live on the poisoned-shell retirement path: wait for
the revocation the poisoning queued, and retire the shell when the wait watches
its reference drop. `poison_retire_wait` gated both together, and that made the
second one unmeasurable.

Measured across eight injected node-laps with the knob on, P566-POISON-DRAINWAIT
fired zero times. The escalating sleep retired every shell inside the try
budget, so the budget never expired and the drain path was never entered at all.
The arm was clean, and its cleanliness was entirely the first fix. Gating the
second fix behind the same knob had left exactly one setting that reaches it —
the setting in which it is disabled.

The knob is now three-valued: 0 is the pre-fix control with neither fix, 1 is the
shipping default with both, and 2 turns the escalating sleep off while leaving
the drain-assisted retirement on. Mode 2 lets the short budget expire the way it
does in the control, which is what puts the drain path under test.

Nothing about shipping behaviour changes; the default is unchanged. What changes
is that a clean arm can now be attributed to a specific fix instead of to the
pair.

## 0.75.107 — 2026-09-09 — The fix escaped the knob that exists to measure it

0.75.106 put the drain-assisted retirement outside the `poison_retire_wait`
guard. The knob exists for one reason: to run the defect and the fix against
each other in one build and one boot, because a re-prep between arms resets
every other piece of accumulated state and makes the two incomparable.

A change that alters the outcome but sits outside the knob does not just weaken
that; it inverts it. The retire_wait=0 arm on 0.75.106 reported unretired=0 and
lkerr116=0, where the same arm on 0.75.105 had tracked poison_n one for one. The
control had become a second treatment arm, and an A/B whose control silently
contains the treatment reports success no matter what the treatment does.

The drain-assisted retirement is now behind the same knob as the wait. This
changes no shipping behaviour — the knob defaults to on — but it restores the
measurement.

It is worth recording what the accident measured before it was corrected, since
it is a real result: with the escalating wait disabled and only the drain-assisted
retirement active, the injected arm still came back clean. The drain observation
alone is sufficient; the wait is what makes the observation likely to happen
early.

## 0.75.106 — 2026-09-09 — A retirement that gave up on a shell it had just watched become free

The escalating wait added in 0.75.103 removed the poisoned-shell ESTALE in seven
of eight injected node-laps. The eighth is a second, unrelated cause, and its
own diagnostic named it:

    P566-POISON-DRAINWAIT ino=8388742 i_count_first=3 i_count_after=1
                          drained_at_ms=10
    P34H-POISON-UNRETIRED ino=8388742 i_count=1 tries=9

An i_count of 1 is this lookup's own reference and nothing else. The shell was
retireable at the instant the code declared it unretireable and failed the
lookup with -ESTALE, for a file that exists and whose dirent resolves.

The holder was not the poison's own revocation, which is what the first cause
was about. The per-inode reference ring names mxfs_dlm_bast_work_fn and
mxfs_dlm_bast_dwork_fn — the DLM BAST pipeline — taking a transient reference
that pushed i_count from 2 back to 3 at try 8 and dropped it ten milliseconds
later. The budget was not too short for the holder it was written for; it was
spent by a different holder arriving late.

That is the general shape of the bug: a fixed try count cannot be the exit
condition for a wait whose references arrive from paths the loop does not
control. The correct exit condition is the one the wait already measures — the
reference is gone. When it observes that, retirement now proceeds on the
observation rather than discarding it and failing the lookup.

The fail-closed behaviour is unchanged and deliberately so. A shell whose
reference never drains — an open fd on a dead incarnation — still returns
-ESTALE, because that is a genuinely different situation and a longer wait must
not paper over it. The new path is bounded to two drain-assisted retirements, so
a pinned corpse fails closed after a bounded observation instead of looping.

## 0.75.105 — 2026-09-09 — The verification harness was manufacturing its own failure

The poison injector added for the shell-retirement fix poisons a live inode to
exercise retirement on demand. The revocation that a poisoning queues truncates
the inode's pages, and every real poison site can afford that because it only
fires when the generation DIFFERS: the number was freed and reused, so the pages
belong to a dead incarnation and discarding them is correct.

An injector poisoning arbitrary live inodes has no such licence. It threw away
dirty pages of files the test had just written, and the row failed on
`rv content node2_after_4(exp=content_2_4 got=)` — a file that exists reading
empty. That has nothing to do with the defect under test and everything to do
with the harness, and a verification that manufactures a distinct failure of its
own cannot verify anything.

The injector now holds to the same precondition the code it exercises relies on:
no pin count, no dirty log-item fields, not in the AIL, no delayed allocation,
and no dirty or writeback pages.

The measurement that prompted it is worth recording, because both arms ran on one
build in one boot with the knob flipped live between them and read back on both
nodes. Without the wait, unretired shells tracked poisonings essentially one for
one — 13/12, 43/43, 19/19 on one node — with nine to twenty ESTALE returns per
node per lap and the row failing on `uv gone`. With the wait, poisonings
continued at the same rate and unretired shells and ESTALE returns were zero on
every node in every lap; the `uv gone` symptom did not appear at all. With
injection off entirely the row passed three for three at its usual wall, so the
wait costs nothing on the ordinary path.

## 0.75.104 — 2026-09-09 — The defect queue was hiding a third of its own guidance

The RULE 6 ledger accumulated three spellings of the same field over time —
`next`, `next_step`, `next_steps` — and the queue reader returned the FIRST of
them that was populated. Eighteen open records populate two, so whichever one
lost the race was written by one session and then shown to no later one.

That is about 130,000 characters of guidance, and it is not filler. On several
records the hidden field holds MORE text than the part being displayed; on the
newest ones it holds the only current plan, because `tools/ledger_set.py` writes
whichever field it is told to and recent sessions have been writing
`next_step`. So a session could prepend a full analysis to a record that already
carried `next`, see the tool report success, and have deposited it somewhere
nothing reads. The session-start state hook reads the same function, so the
effect compounds: every session opened on a partial view of its own queue.

The list view now shows every populated variant, labelled and newest-spelling
first. Nothing is merged and nothing is moved — consolidating the fields is a
data migration and belongs in a deliberate pass, not in a display function. The
single-record view was never affected; it prints each field separately, which is
why the gap survived this long.

Writing that up produced a second lesson worth a guard. `tools/ledger_set.py`
takes its value as a shell argument, so backticks in the prose are
command-substituted before the tool sees them: a note about the ledger's own
`next` field ran `next` as a command and stored the word as nothing. The writer
reported success and the schema validator passed, because a date validator
cannot see a missing noun. `scripts/ledger_repair_backtick_damage.py` scans the
whole ledger for the structural signatures of an eaten word and can repair one
by exact substring. It reports zero across all 264 records now; the one wound it
found was the one that prompted it.

## 0.75.102 — 2026-09-09 — A lookup that could not retire a dead shell, and a way to prove it

When a peer reuses an inode number, a node can still hold an in-core inode for
the previous incarnation. The reload detects that and poisons the shell; the
lookup path then retires it so a fresh iget reads the live inode, and if that
fails it returns -ESTALE rather than serve a corpse.

Retirement was failing for files that plainly existed. Measured on two nodes,
24 of a peer's 64 just-created names came back -ESTALE while their dirents
resolved correctly and the on-disk inodes verified; `ls` drops the failed names,
so the directory silently under-reported the peer's content by exactly those 24.

The reference blocking retirement was the poisoning itself. Setting the flag also
takes a reference and hands it to a revocation work item, which drops it only
once it runs. So a poisoned shell always has two references, and retirement
cannot succeed until that work completes. The retry loop gave it four
back-to-back attempts with no delay of any kind — 23 microseconds end to end,
against a revocation that took 2.9 ms at best and 68 ms at worst. It was not a
race that was sometimes lost; it could not be won, and all ten poisoned shells in
that capture failed. The failing names were a contiguous prefix of the directory,
which is what a queue catching up looks like and what nothing else would produce.

The retry now waits: its own counter, separate from the one a neighbouring arm
also increments, and eight attempts escalating 2/4/8/16/32/64/128 ms — about
3.7x the worst latency measured. The fail-closed -ESTALE is unchanged, because a
reference that genuinely never drops, such as an open descriptor on the dead
incarnation, is a different situation and must not be papered over by waiting
longer. Flushing the workqueue was rejected: it also carries BAST work, and
flushing it from inside a lookup invites a deadlock the sleep cannot cause.

Reaching this state naturally needs a cross-incarnation reload with the cluster
buffer protected — it happened in one lap out of eighteen and resisted three
purpose-built reproducers. Verifying a fix against a one-in-eighteen event is not
verification, so `dbg_poison_nth` (default off) poisons every Nth cross-node
lookup. Poisoning a healthy inode is a faithful exercise of the same machinery:
retirement evicts the shell and re-igets the same live incarnation, so a correct
implementation succeeds and a broken one returns -ESTALE for a file that exists.
The trigger is synthetic; the response is entirely real.

Poison counting also moved off the per-site log lines, which are ratelimited and
saturate at the burst — one lap printed exactly ten, which is the ceiling, not a
count, and reading it as a count would have been wrong.

## 0.75.101 — 2026-09-09 — A throughput gate that could not tell which rig it was scoring

The RULE 0 throughput row compares this rig's measurement against a yardstick
captured on this rig, because the rigs differ enough that a cross-rig comparison
is meaningless — its own header has said so since the rig tag was introduced.
The tag, however, was derived only from `MXFS_RIG_TAG` or a substring of
`MXFS_DEV`, and nothing requires either to be present: a run that reuses an
already-prepped cluster never touches the device, so the caller has no reason to
export it. With the tag empty the row silently fell back to the untagged legacy
files, which describe different hardware.

That produced a red board cell attributable to nothing in the filesystem. Four
consecutive runs on the QNAP LUN measured 108, 110, 111 and 111 MiB/s sequential
write; the first three recorded `rig=qnap` and scored 100-101%, and the fourth —
the fastest of them — lost the tag, was scored against the SCST/mpath rig's
179 MiB/s two-sharer ceiling, and came back 62% FAIL. 111 MiB/s over a 1 GbE hop
is approximately line rate. The gate was equally capable of the opposite error:
a genuinely slow rig handed a PASS by a foreign ceiling that happens to be lower.

The rig identity belongs to the prepped cluster, not to whoever invokes a test
afterwards, so `run.sh` now records the device it prepped against in the cluster
marker and the row reads the tag from there. And if the tag still cannot be
established while any rig-tagged yardstick exists for the transport, the row now
reports SKIP naming the files it declined to use, instead of publishing a
confident percentage computed from unknown-provenance hardware.

## 0.75.100 — 2026-09-09 — The reference that blocks retirement now names itself

When a lookup cannot retire a poisoned inode shell it reports `i_count` and gives
up.  That number says a reference exists; it never said whose.  With the dentry
alias list empty — which is what the alias probe measured — there was nothing
left to read, and the holder had to be guessed from whatever else happened to be
in the log nearby.

Nothing needed to be built to answer this.  Every reference this filesystem takes
already goes through a tracked `igrab`/`iput` that records its call site into a
per-inode event ring and an outstanding-grab stack, and that stack is reset at
the `i_count`-to-zero transition, so it holds only the current tenure's grabs.
It was written for the unmount-busy-inode work and no other site consulted it.

The retirement failure now dumps both, plus the running grab and put totals and
the last grab site.  Call sites are tagged by file id: 1 is the DLM overlay,
2 the inode cache, 3 the VFS iops glue, 4 the filestream allocator; an untracked
reference — upstream XFS or the VFS itself — prints as a symbolised return
address instead, which is itself the answer to a different question.

Measurement only; the lookup still fails ESTALE exactly as before.

## 0.75.99 — 2026-09-09 — Name what pins a poisoned inode shell, and find out whether it ever lets go

When a peer reuses an inode number, this node can still hold an in-core shell
for the previous incarnation.  The reload detects that, poisons the shell, and
the lookup path then tries to retire it so a fresh iget can read the live inode.
If retirement fails the lookup returns -ESTALE rather than serving a corpse.

That fail-closed choice is right, but it is being reached for files that plainly
exist: measured at two nodes, 24 of a peer's 64 just-created names came back
-ESTALE while their dirents resolved correctly and the on-disk inodes verified.
`ls` drops the failed names, so the directory silently under-reports the peer's
content.

The retire attempt could not say why.  It printed `i_count` and nothing else,
the alias probe printed nothing at all — no dentry holds the shell — and all
four attempts run back to back with no delay whatsoever, 23 microseconds end to
end, so a reference that would be released a millisecond later loses every time
and is indistinguishable from one that is held forever.

Two additions, both measurement only.  The retire attempt now prints everything
on the inode that can account for a reference: reclaim and inactivation state,
log-item fields and AIL residency, pin count, and the DLM grant mode.  And at
the point of giving up, it samples `i_count` over a bounded wait and reports
whether the reference drains and how long that took.  The lookup still fails
-ESTALE exactly as before; the wait runs only on a path that has already
failed, so a healthy lookup pays nothing.

## 0.75.98 — 2026-09-09 — The stale-buffer crosscheck could not see a directory change

`P-RELOAD-IDENTICAL` decides that an on-disk dinode image equals our in-core
state and keeps the loaded fork without rebuilding it.  Immediately after that
verdict a crosscheck reads the same inode straight off the coherent medium and
compares it against the buffer image the verdict was issued on, so that a
verdict served by a stale cached cluster buffer is named at the moment it is
made.

That crosscheck compared exactly two fields: mode and generation.  Neither of
them moves when a peer adds or removes names in a directory it already owns.
For the entire class of faults this branch can produce — the identical verdict
keeping a fork that still carries a peer's deleted dirents — the crosscheck was
vacuous: it read the medium, compared two fields that cannot differ, and
reported nothing.  A probe that cannot fire for the case it exists to catch is
worse than no probe, because its silence reads as evidence.

It now compares the fields a dirent change actually moves — changecount, size,
extent count and link count — alongside mode and generation, and prints both
images side by side with the buffer's flags and the calling task.  Behaviour is
unchanged; only what the probe can see is.

## 0.75.97 — 2026-09-10 — Check whether the completion actually consumed the token

The AG-meta track token is armed when a buffer is logged and must be consumed by
exactly one of the write completion or an explicit reclaim.  Everything written
about this leak so far has instrumented the *reclaim* side — the retirement
routes, which of them cover the token, which do not.  The completion side was
assumed correct because `mxfs_ag_meta_track` installs its callback in `b_iodone`
and `__xfs_buf_ioend` calls it.

That assumption is worth exactly one `atomic_read`.  `b_iodone` is a single slot
with three writers (the AG-meta callback, the inode-buffer one and the dquot
one); `mxfs_ag_meta_track` guards only the direction where it finds the slot
already occupied, and nothing guards a later writer replacing ours.  A token can
also be stranded for reasons that have nothing to do with that slot — a buffer
reused for another purpose, a completion routed past the callback block at all.

So the check goes where the answer is unambiguous rather than on any one writer:
immediately after the completion callback returns, a buffer that was tracked
must read a token of zero.  If it still reads one, the write landed and nothing
gave the hold back, and `P-AGMETA-IODONE-MISSED` names the buffer, its ops and
the callback that was actually installed — which identifies the cause from a
single line instead of a per-writer probe that would still miss the other
reasons.

It is a pure diagnostic and deliberately does not consume the token it finds, so
a leak stays visible to the existing tripwire on the buffer's next dirty epoch
instead of being quietly healed at the point of detection.

Measured context for why this is the next question: a two-node crash-restart with
the log killed mid-churn (7963 operations, 7839 of them failing after the
shutdown) produced zero reclaims of any tag, because the CIL abort path routes
through unpin-remove into a normal completion rather than the abort branch.  The
one confirmed instance of this leak fired its tripwire on a healthy mount with no
shutdown at all, so the completion path is where it has to be looked for.

## 0.75.96 — 2026-09-09 — The one retirement route that never returns the AG-meta hold

`xfs_buf_item_free` has exactly one caller, `xfs_buf_item_relse`, so that
function is provably the only place a buf log item is freed and its call sites
are the complete enumeration of the routes a tracked AG-metadata buffer can
retire through.  Three of the four cannot leave the one-shot track token
outstanding.  The write-completion route consumes it in the very next call.
The stale route reclaims it in `xfs_buf_item_finish_stale` before the item is
freed.  The clean route is only reached for a log item that was never dirtied,
and tracking is installed from `xfs_trans_log_buf`, so there is nothing to
return.

`xfs_buf_item_put` is the exception, and it is the route the evidence has
always pointed at.  It frees a dirty log item that is not in the AIL — which
upstream permits once the log has shut down and a checkpoint aborted the item
instead of inserting it, typically when a btree cursor still held a clean
reference and released it through `xfs_trans_brelse` — and nothing anywhere on
that path returns the track hold.  The extra buffer reference taken when the
buffer was first logged then pins it for the life of the module.  A pinned
buffer leaves the buftarg LRU when it is staled but stays hashed in its AG
cache, and the unmount drain walks only the LRU, so it is invisible until the
slab shutdown counts it — which is exactly the shape of the objects left in the
`mxfs_buf` cache at unload, and of the tripwire that fired one boot earlier
when the next dirty epoch of such a buffer found its token already set.

The reclaim is now done at the funnel for every caller except the completion
one, where a reclaim would race the completion that owns the token.  It is a
no-op everywhere else: the token is one-shot, so the exchange simply fails once
another path has consumed it.  The diagnostic that found this runs before the
reclaim rather than after, so a route that needed the repair still says so
instead of being silently mended.

## 0.75.95 — 2026-09-09 — The retirement probe has to know who is retiring the item

The first cut of the AG-meta retirement probe (0.75.94) fired 145 times across
three reproducer laps and proved nothing, because it could not tell a leak from
the ordinary shape of a healthy write completion.  `__xfs_buf_ioend` calls
`xfs_buf_item_done` — which funnels into `xfs_buf_item_relse` — and only then
calls the buffer's `b_iodone`, so on EVERY successful write-back of a tracked
AG-metadata buffer the track-hold token is still outstanding at the moment the
log item is retired, and is consumed microseconds later.  A probe that looks
only at the token sees all of those and calls each one a leak.

The caller is therefore part of the condition, and it is passed in rather than
guessed at: `xfs_buf_item_relse` now takes a `why` tag, and its four call sites
name themselves — `iodone`, `stale`, `put` and `release-clean`.  The probe fires
only when the token is outstanding and the caller is not `iodone`, which is the
one route where a completion is guaranteed to follow.  Firing from any of the
other three means nothing will consume the token, the AG's pending count never
returns, and the buffer survives to module unload.

Passing the tag rather than deriving it from a return address also keeps the
condition honest under inlining, which is what made the first cut's
`caller=%pS` field agree with itself 145 times and still say nothing.

## 0.75.94 — 2026-09-09 — Name the buffer and the caller when a tracked log item retires

`xfs_buf_item_relse` is the funnel every buf-log-item retirement path reaches,
and it does not consult the AG-meta one-shot token.  Only two callers reclaim
that token: the stale-completion path and the shutdown/abort branch of
`xfs_buf_item_release`.  `xfs_buf_item_put` reaches the funnel without either,
and its own comment names the route — a dirty log item that is not in the AIL,
released through `xfs_trans_brelse` while a btree cursor holds a clean
reference.

That is the only route the evidence has ever pointed at.  The one confirmed
firing of the `mxfs_ag_meta_track` tripwire came out of a btree split logging
its records, in the boot that then leaked six buffers to module unload.  A
tracked item freed at the funnel leaves the token at 1, so the buffer's next
dirty epoch trips the tripwire and neither the hold nor the AG's pending count
is ever returned.

`P-AGMETA-RELSE-OUTSTANDING` names the buffer, its ops, the item's flags and
the caller whenever a log item is retired with the token still outstanding.  It
changes no behaviour.  If it fires under a workload that exercises the
tripwire's own stack the path is proven and the repair belongs at the funnel,
where reclaiming is a no-op on any buffer that holds nothing; if it never fires
there, the path is ruled out and the leak is elsewhere.

## 0.75.93 — 2026-09-09 — The power cut where one node does not come back

Every whole-cluster restart harness on this rig brought both nodes back
together, and that turns out to be the easy case.  Two nodes that crash and
return together make each victim a previous boot of a host that is live again,
so boot-succession proves exclusion immediately and no harder question is ever
asked.  The shape a real outage produces just as often — the cluster loses
power and one machine does not come back — had no harness at all, which meant
the survivor's route to proving its absent peer excluded, and the fate of the
data that peer had already acknowledged, were both untested.

`tests/sole_survivor_restart.sh` runs it with nothing injected: both nodes
write and fsync a numbered file set, both are destroyed with their mounts in
flight, and only one is started again.  Every heartbeat record, PR key, ledger
page and journal slice the survivor then meets was written by a real mount.

The data check is the point, not the mount.  A mount that completes over a
slice it silently discarded is worse than one that refuses, so the survivor
must read back every file *both* nodes acknowledged, with the content each name
implies.  The peer's files are scored separately from the survivor's own,
because those are the ones that can only arrive through foreign replay of a
dead slice.

First lap: the survivor mounted with no operator action in 92.5 s, and read
back 60 of 60 of its own files and 60 of 60 of the absent peer's, with nothing
missing and nothing wrong.  It reached that by taking the sole-survivor
exclusive-write gate and certifying the absent peer by boot succession, then
replaying its slice.  The peer, brought back afterwards, mounted in 3.0 s and
saw all 120 files.

The lap also answers a question that had been standing against the bootstrap
orphan sweep: whether any two-node shape elects a bootstrap owner and lets that
sweep run.  A sole survivor is the strongest candidate — one node returning
alone is a total outage from its own point of view — and it still elected none,
because it could prove exclusion without the total-outage adoption path.  With
the both-return shape measured the same way earlier, the sweep is unreachable
on a two-node configuration by two different routes to a proof of exclusion.
An unreachable recovery path is not a safety net, and that is now a decision to
make rather than an assumption to keep.

## 0.75.92 — 2026-09-09 — Measure the recovery drain's peak pin instead of assuming it

The untrusted-replay drain deferral holds every buffer a recovery pass dirties
in one list until the pass ends, and nothing bounds that list except the number
of distinct buffers the slice's records name.  A recovering node has to hold all
of it while still allocating for the rest of the pass, and one small logged
region retains a whole buffer, so "the deferral count is small" was never an
argument that the pin is small — `drain_deferred` counts submits it skipped, not
buffers it kept.

`xlog_do_recovery_pass` now walks the list at the single submit point, where it
IS the pass's peak pinned metadata, and reports the count and the byte total as
`P-DRAIN-PEAK`.  Measured on a two-node whole-cluster crash restart, both nodes:
`deferred=4 queued_buffers=0 queued_bytes=0` — the deferral retained nothing at
all on that shape.  The instrument stays because the interesting case is a
heavily dirtied slice, and that one has not been measured yet.

## 0.75.91 — 2026-09-09 — An unattributable shared holder is re-asked when a waiter times out

A shared holder bit imported from the durable ledger while its heartbeat slot
was unresolvable was recorded with an owner of `MXFS_DLM_NODE_UNKNOWN`.  The
sentinel means "unresolvable at this instant" — the peer had not yet claimed its
slot — but it was stored as though it meant "unresolvable for good", and nothing
re-evaluated it.  Both the collect-holders and the fire-BAST paths skip an
unknown owner by design, so such a bit could never be BASTed and never released,
and an EX request queued behind it never completed.

On a concurrent no-mkfs remount that deadlocked both nodes: one mount waited for
the root inode behind the phantom holder, the other waited for AG 0 behind the
first, and neither returned — past the mount's own bound, past the harness's,
with no shutdown, no error, and both nodes left loaded and unmountable.  The
existing repair ran only on a re-import of the page, and a page imported once at
mount is never re-imported.

An acquire timing out behind such a holder is exactly the moment to re-ask, so
that is where the slot is now looked up again.  If it names a node the bit is
attributed to it and can be BASTed and released; if it still names nobody, the
log says so plainly instead of leaving a bare `4294967295` to be decoded by
hand.  Nothing is retired and nothing is dropped, so a live successor in the
slot cannot lose its own records.

The race is one lap in four, which no number of passing laps can verify, so
`dl_inject_import_unresolvable` (TEST ONLY, consumable) answers the next few
slot lookups during a page import as unresolvable — the same answer the
heartbeat table gives before the peer claims its slot.  The holder bit, its slot
and its page are all real and were written by real mounts; only the timing of
the table's view is forced, and that timing is the race.

`tests/d0940_unknown_blocker_probe.sh` drives it, and it took two corrections to
stop reporting a vacuous pass.  It destroys the nodes rather than unmounting
them, because a clean departure purges the very bits the defect needs; and it
arms both nodes, because whichever wins the page-takeover race is the one that
imports, and which one that is cannot be predicted.  The probe asserts the fix's
own line, not merely that the mount completed.

## 0.75.90 — 2026-09-09 — A prover can now be killed with its fencing attempt still standing

The attempt-takeover path — a peer proving that the incarnation holding a
fencing attempt is revoked, and taking the attempt over to issue its own
PREEMPT AND ABORT — had no way to be reached on a two-node rig.  Measured
across a two-lap whole-cluster-restart chain, both nodes, all four journals:
`P238-FENCE-HOLDER-SLOT`, `verdict=REVOKED` and `P238-FENCE-TAKEOVER` are all
zero.  The reason is structural rather than luck: two nodes that crash together
and return together make every victim a previous boot of a host that is live
again, so boot-succession proves exclusion immediately and no attempt is ever
left standing for anyone to inherit.

That matters because several defect records share one list of verification legs
with their siblings, and those legs pass.  Passing them proves nothing about
code they never enter.

`dl_fence_postintent_pause_ms` (TEST ONLY) holds a prover in the one window
that produces the shape: after its fencing intent is durable on the platter —
"the PREEMPT AND ABORT may now be issued" — and before it is issued.  Killing a
prover parked there leaves exactly the on-disk state a prover that died
mid-attempt leaves, written by a real prover in the ordinary way.  Nothing is
forged onto the platter and no view is injected into any decision, which is the
difference between exercising the takeover and exercising a mock of it.

The knob is writable at 0644 so a harness arms it on one node at runtime
through `/sys/module/mxfs/parameters/`, rather than giving the two nodes
different insmod arguments.  The hold is interruptible, so it cannot park a
kernel task in D state for its duration.

`tests/d0932_fence_takeover_probe.sh` drives it, and asserts the attempt's
holder was actually evaluated before it asserts anything about the outcome.

## 0.75.89 — 2026-09-09 — A reservation assertion that was really a missing variable

`tests/tcp_death_replay.sh` documented a default for `MXFS_DEV` in its own Env
header and never had one.  Every use of it sits inside a conditional arm, so
under `set -u` a direct invocation did not fail at the top — it died partway
through the sole-survivor gate arm, at the single line that reads the target's
persistent-reservation state.  That left the reading empty, and the two
assertions built on it compared against the empty string:

    FAIL exactly one registration (the survivor's) after the restore got= want=1
    FAIL WE-AR reservation in force after the restore got=0 want=1

Two red lines about the reservation everything in this filesystem's fencing
rests on, produced by an unset shell variable, on a run whose gate had in fact
certified, restored, and published recovery-complete cleanly, with 327 of 327
acknowledged files verifying and zero bad or missing.  A reader of that output
would have gone looking for a fencing regression that the run never observed.

Both halves are fixed: the default now exists alongside the one every sibling
harness carries, and an unreadable PR state is reported as a failed
MEASUREMENT — naming itself a harness fault and saying not to diagnose the
reservation from it — rather than as a failed reservation.  An assertion that
cannot distinguish "the thing is broken" from "I could not look at the thing"
is worse than no assertion, because it is believed.

## 0.75.88 — 2026-09-09 — The post-register hold reaches the TCP mount too

0.75.87's `mount_postregister_pause_ms` was placed in the CAW mount path only.
The two transports do not share their slot-claim sequence: each branch has its
own `mxfs_disklock_set_slot_limit` / `mxfs_disklock_claim_slot` pair, so on TCP
— the only transport this campaign qualifies — the hold was dead code and the
knob silently did nothing.

It was caught by the probe rather than by reading, and only because the probe
refuses to proceed on an assumption.  It waits for `P238-POSTREG-PAUSE` to
actually appear before mounting the other node, and reports VACUOUS when it does
not.  Had it simply slept and carried on, the run would have produced a clean,
plausible, entirely meaningless pass: the second node would have mounted
normally, no registrant would have been held anywhere, and the gate would have
been credited with a refusal it never made.

The hold is now one helper called from both branches at the same point, so a
transport cannot silently lack it.

## 0.75.87 — 2026-09-09 — A barrier that fails now says why, and a node can be held where it is a registrant but not a member

Two changes, both instruments, both made before touching the behaviour they are
meant to explain.

**A failed coordination barrier kept its own diagnosis and threw it away.**
`coord_barrier` knows exactly which of two unrelated things went wrong: either
the test's reporting budget was already spent, in which case it returns without
waiting at all, or it waited its whole window and the peer never arrived.  It
said so on stderr, with the counts.  The wrapper every coordinated test calls ran
it as `coord_barrier "$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1 &` — both streams discarded — so the
recorded failure named only the barrier tag.  Every barrier timeout this project
has filed is therefore an undifferentiated symptom, and a two-node failure from
2026-09-05 cannot be diagnosed from its own capture for that reason alone.

The wrapper now captures that stderr and hands it back on the failure path only,
so a successful barrier still prints nothing and callers that read stdout are
unaffected.  Both messages carry the numbers that settle it: the window actually
used, how long it waited, the elapsed time and the budget it was clamped to, and
the distinct-rank count it saw.  `dir_reuse_coherency` puts the string in its
terminal record, so the next occurrence arrives already diagnosed.
`tests/coord_barrier_diag_selftest.sh` exercises both failure branches and the
success path against the broker alone, with no cluster and no filesystem.

**`mount_postregister_pause_ms` (TEST ONLY) holds a mount between registering
its PR key and claiming a heartbeat slot.**  A node in that window is a genuine
persistent-reservation registrant that no peer can see as live.  That is the
premise of the sole-survivor exclusive-write gate defect — a node believing
itself alone issued PREEMPT AND ABORT, which removes every other registration,
and evicted a live joiner mid-log-recovery.

The window was reachable only as a race, and the arm that looked obvious cannot
reach it at all: bringing both nodes up together with the boot-succession proof
injected off makes them members of each other before the fence runs, so the
gate's own guard declines and the gate is never attempted.  Measured, twelve
times on each node: `P238-FENCE-GATE-NOTSOLE ... nlive=2 other_live=2`.  A lap
like that has measured nothing, and must not be read as a pass.

Holding the second node in the window supplies the other registrant
deterministically while keeping it real — a genuine registration by a genuine
node, not a fabricated view fed to the gate.  The hold is interruptible on
purpose: an uninterruptible one would park the mount as an unkillable task for
its whole duration, which is a shape no test knob should be able to create.
`tests/sole_survivor_gate_probe.sh` drives it and asserts the gate was reached
before asserting anything about the outcome.

## 0.75.86 — 2026-09-09 — The last-install-attempt record is reset with the rest of the authority block

An inode carries five fields describing the last time something tried to install
an authority tenure on it: what was attempted, at what mode and epoch, from which
line, and at which authority generation.  Every other member of that block is
reset when an inode is initialised, with a comment saying why — the inode cache
does not zero, so a recycled inode would otherwise read the previous tenant's
state.  These five were the only ones left out.

So on a reused inode the record described a different file.  The documented
readings — "no install was ever attempted here", and "a revoke happened after the
last attempt and nothing retried" — were unsound for precisely the recycled
incarnations that need them most, because the authority generation restarts while
the generation stamped on the attempt did not, and the comparison between them
could then fall either way on evidence belonging to someone else.

Nothing gates on these fields; they exist to be read by a person deciding where a
missing authority came from.  That is the reason to fix them rather than to leave
them: an instrument reporting a refusal that never happened sends the next
investigation at the wrong code, and this one nearly did.

## 0.75.85 — 2026-09-09 — A publish that takes a real lock installs the authority it just earned

Three paths publish an inode by claiming a real, exclusive on-disk grant for it
and delisting it from the unpublished list.  None of them installed an authority
tenure from that claim: two asked the lock layer for no grant result at all, and
the third passed the sentinel generation snapshot reserved for probe and nudge
callers, which makes the installer a no-op.

So a published inode came out of its publish holding exclusive access with its
authority state still reading `local-only, no on-disk slot` and its last install
attempt reading `never attempted`.  The two records disagreed, and nothing
retried: the inode is cached exclusive from that moment, every later operation is
served from the fast path, and the fast path never descends into the lock layer.
The tenure stayed unprovable for its whole life, and every metadata image it
authorised shipped with a token that proves nothing — which is enough for a
foreign replayer to refuse the entire journal slice and quarantine the dead
node's allocation groups cluster-wide.

Measured on the two-node rig, reproducible in about ten seconds of workload: on
one lap all forty-eight refused directory images belonged to one directory whose
last install attempt read `never attempted`, and on the next lap all forty-eight
belonged to a reused directory whose attempt had been refused because the inode
was still flagged unpublished at the moment it was made.  Both publish sites that
touch such a directory were named by the same instrument on the same inode.

Each of the three now takes its provenance snapshot before the claim, asks for a
grant result, and installs under the inode's lock once the inode is off the
unpublished list — the discipline the inode-cluster arm of the publish drain has
followed since it was written, and which a directory missed only because it is
not routed there.  A claim that yields no provable epoch still installs nothing,
but now says so through the ordinary refusal counters instead of silently never
asking.

## 0.75.84 — 2026-09-09 — Name every publish that claims a real lock and proves nothing with it

A directory whose buffers ship unattributable — class NONE, refused on foreign
replay, one allocation group quarantined cluster-wide — reads
`i_mxfs_auth_state == UNPUBLISHED_EX` at the instant of first protected dirty
while the node holds a writing DLM mode on it and `i_dlm_unpublished` is already
clear.  The two disagree, and the install-attempt field settles which is stale:
it reads `never attempted`.  Nothing refused the install; nothing asked for one.

Three publish paths take a real on-disk EX slot for an unpublished inode and ask
the lock layer for no grant result at all — two pass a NULL result, the third a
sentinel generation snapshot that makes the installer a no-op.  All three delist
the inode, so the flag says published while the authority state still says
local-only, and because the inode is now cached EX every later operation is
served from the fast path and never descends into the lock layer again.  The
tenure therefore never becomes provable, and every image it authorises is
classless for as long as it lasts.

This build only names the site.  P242-PUBCLAIM is printed at each of the three,
capped, carrying the inode number so a classless image can be attributed to the
claim that produced it — or to something else.  No behaviour changes.

## 0.75.83 — 2026-09-09 — The sole-survivor write gate asks whether anyone else is registered before evicting everyone else

The sole-survivor exclusive-write gate issues PREEMPT AND ABORT with a zero
service-action key against the all-registrants reservation, which removes every
other registration on the LUN and aborts those nexuses' task sets.  Its whole
authority is that the node issuing it is the only live member of the cluster.

It never checked the one set that would have told it: the registrations it was
about to remove.  Every refusal in that path asks about our own key or about the
victim's; sole survivorship was established one layer up, from lease membership
and the heartbeat table, and a node joining the cluster registers its key — and
can therefore write — before it appears in either of those.

Measured on the two-node rig.  One node came up on an unreserved LUN, registered
as the only key at persistent-reservation generation 1817, and began fencing an
incarnation left behind by an earlier lap.  The other node registered at
generation 1818, claimed its heartbeat slot, was admitted, and started its own
log recovery.  The gate's command landed at generation 1819 and took that
registration with it: the joiner's next log-recovery write returned a
reservation conflict, and its mount died a second and a half in, reporting a
failure to locate the log tail — indistinguishable, from the outside, from a
media fault.  The same hole evicts a healthy peer on any cluster wider than two,
where a membership count can be stale for entirely ordinary reasons.

The gate now refuses while any other registration exists, and says so.  The
attempt stays unproven and retryable, which is what it already does for every
other unmet precondition, and a victim that is a previous boot of a host that is
live again is provable without touching anyone's registration at all — the route
the two-node whole-cluster restart actually takes.  Refusing costs a retry; not
refusing costs a live node its I/O.

## 0.75.82 — 2026-09-09 — An unattributable metadata image says on the wire why it could not be attributed

A foreign slice replay refuses any transaction carrying an image whose authority
cannot be proved, and refusing one transaction refuses the whole slice and
quarantines the dead node's allocation groups cluster-wide.  So when a slice was
refused over two directory buffers whose tokens read `class=0 st=4`, the only
thing the cluster could say about the cause was "mislabelled" — and the node
that produced them had been destroyed, taking with it the one log line that
would have named the reason.

The classifier had a specific status for each way the owning inode's authority
can be unprovable: the owner could not be derived, the owner is not in the
inode cache, the authority exists but is not held, the tenure is durable but
has no published epoch.  The arm that runs when this node holds an allocation
group grant that is not the buffer's authority overwrote all four with the
coarsest of them, which states only what that arm already implies.  It now keeps
whichever reason the inode arm gave, and MISLABELLED is left to mean what it
says: the inode arm had nothing more specific to add.

Admission is unchanged in every direction.  Only a VALID token proves anything,
the replay gate refuses on anything else, and each of these statuses was already
part of the fixed wire contract and already emitted by the same helper one
branch further down.

## 0.75.81 — 2026-09-09 — A shared grant on a heartbeat slot a published recovery has emptied is retired, not imported as a blocker no node can release

With the admission cut of 0.75.80 holding, both nodes of the two-node TCP rig
finally replayed and published each other's dead slices after being destroyed
mid-mount — and both mounts still failed, on the root inode.

A shared holder bit in the authority ledger names a heartbeat SLOT, not an
incarnation.  test1 replayed and published dead slot 0, which zeroes that
slot's heartbeat record, and its recovery purge for that owner walked nothing
because at that instant it mastered no pages.  Three seconds later it took the
root inode's page over on demand and imported the dead incarnation's PR bit for
slot 0.  By then nothing could name a node for slot 0, and the purge is keyed
on node id — it must be, or a later occupant of the same slot loses its own
live records — so the bit was installed as a grant owned by the "no live
tenant" sentinel.

Nothing can retire one.  Blast collection and BAST delivery both skip an
unknown owner by design, and the rule that resolves such a bit later needs a
node to appear in a slot that a published recovery has emptied for good.  So
test1 queued the root inode's EX behind a holder that does not exist, waited
its entire acquire budget, and shut the filesystem down at 120 s; test2, whose
own AG 0 EX was queued behind test1, failed its root-inode read at 62 s.  Every
whole-cluster restart, both nodes.

At import, a shared bit whose slot has no occupant at all is now attributed
back to the owner recorded for that slot by the recovery purge, and retired
through that purge instead of installed.  An empty slot is what makes it safe:
the hazard the node-id-only rule exists to prevent is a live successor in the
slot losing its records, and there is no successor; the purge re-checks
occupancy before honouring a slot anyway.  A slot nobody has been purged from
is untouched, so a bit that is merely unattributed during cluster formation
still blocks, as it must.

An owner reaches the purged set from two directions — the recovery purge, which
knows its slot, and the takeover of one of its pages, which does not.  Whichever
arrives second no longer leaves the slot unnamed.

The rig harness gated its unmount on `mountpoint -q`, which stats the path.  A
mount whose root inode answers ESTALE — exactly what a quarantined allocation
group leaves behind — therefore reported "not a mountpoint" and every unmount
was skipped, the module stayed loaded, and the node was declared unusable after
a power cycle.  Two consecutive preps failed that way on a node whose mount a
plain `umount` took immediately.  Teardown now reads `/proc/mounts`, which is
the kernel's own list and does not touch the filesystem.

`tests/dir_retype_authcap_probe.sh` measures the producer side of an
unattributable metadata image on a live cluster, with nobody killed: it grows a
shared directory past shortform and past one block and reports every
`P239-OWNAUTH-NONDUR` capture by buffer type and outcome.  A slice that carries
one such image is refused wholesale on foreign replay, so this is the cheap way
to find them without a death lap.

## 0.75.80 — 2026-09-09 — An empty admission cut is not a clean one while a frozen foreign heartbeat record is still being watched

Both nodes of the two-node TCP rig were destroyed with their mounts in
flight and came back onto the LUN.  Neither mounted, every restart alike:
`Failed to read root inode 0x80, error 5`, ~74 s in, on both nodes
(tests/evidence/20260909T011714Z_ghost_s567).

The two leftover heartbeat records were plain ACTIVE — no WITHDRAWN stamp,
no recovery descriptor — so the mount barrier's platter sweep for
requires-recovery evidence found nothing, the membership gate discounted
them as crash leftovers, and this node's monitor cannot call a frozen
record dead until it has watched it stay frozen for the whole dead window
(31 heartbeat intervals, ~62 s).  Eight seconds into the mount the barrier
therefore read an empty cut, called it clean and admitted.

It was not clean.  The root inode's AG-0 ledger page named one of those
dead incarnations as its authority, so the AG lock could never be granted;
the untrusted-iget budget burned its five escalations in ~58 s and failed
the root-inode read with EIO.  The monitor's death declaration, its fence
(certified BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT) and the sealed descriptor all landed
five to seven seconds *after* the mount had already given up, leaving both
slices fenced, grant-frozen and never dispatched for replay.

The barrier now holds admission while any frozen foreign record is still
unresolved, counted by the same helper that already extended the wait for
undeclared provers: monitored, not our own slot, seen at least once, not
yet live, not yet recovery-pending.  A genuinely live peer leaves that set
within a couple of heartbeats and costs the mount nothing; a crash leftover
leaves it when the monitor declares it dead, at which point the slot
arrives in the pending cut and the ordinary replay rounds own it.  A record
that resolves as neither within the bound now aborts the mount with a named
reason instead of admitting it over a slice whose owner may still hold
grants.

The per-round "still requires recovery" notice is suppressed when the cut
is empty, so a wait for the dead window does not emit one line per second.

## 0.75.79 — 2026-09-08 — The quota probe ends a week at the exhaustion that actually ended it, counts requests, and the delegation audit survives a model rename

The weekly-credit probe read a week as ending at the FIRST "out of usage
credits" message inside it. Two ways that is wrong, both observed on the
08-28 week: a refusal 35 seconds after the Thursday reset is the previous
week's refusal still being retried, and taking it as the boundary reported 7
turns for a week that ran 5.66 days; and an isolated mid-week refusal at
3,679 requests was followed by 2,129 more, so it was a shorter-horizon limit
rather than the weekly cap, and reading it as the cap understated the week by
37% and produced a projected exhaustion three times too early.
ccloop_quota_probe.py now takes --boundary-grace-min (default 45) and
--terminal-quiet-min (default 30): an exhaustion counts as the week's cap
only if no Fable request follows it. The probe also reports distinct
requestIds per model family, which is what the pool is actually metered in —
it had been reporting only token totals, the currency nobody is charged.

ccloop_delegation_audit.py matched its --model argument by equality against
a default of claude-fable-5. When the pool model was renamed to
claude-fable-5-1 it reported "no sessions with requests" — a silent zero that
reads as "delegation is unmeasurable" rather than "the filter missed". It now
matches on a prefix, default claude-fable.

docs/cost-audit.md §15 records both closed weeks (08-28 and 09-04) with the
corrected boundaries, §15.5 records that transcripts age out at about 29 days
so weeks older than a month cannot be re-derived and this document is their
only record, and §16 measures why a 2-node TCP board whose 27 functional
criteria all pass still reports FAIL: 52 of the 91 open ledger records name a
configuration 2-node TCP cannot run, and the release gate was never narrowed
when the work was.

## 0.75.78 — 2026-09-08 — A test-only injection makes the untrusted-iget AG acquire answer EAGAIN, so the D-0930 bound has a deterministic exerciser

The root-iget bound of 0.75.72 (untrusted_aglock_budgets, then EIO) had no
way to be exercised on demand: the shape that produced D-0930 — AG 0's
ledger page with no reachable authority at mount — came from a crash-restart
pile-up that the recovery fixes since 0.75.70 now resolve, and a negative
fence arm fails the mount in the admission barrier before the root iget runs.
mxfs.untrusted_aglock_inject_eagain (0 = off) answers the next N
untrusted-iget AG acquires with EAGAIN without asking the DLM
(P-IMAP-UNTRUSTED-AGLOCK-INJECT), exactly what a request that outlived its
retry budget returns. tests/d0930_root_iget_bound.sh: the peer mounts
normally, then the node under test insmods with untrusted_aglock_budgets=2
and the injection armed; its mount must return non-zero to userspace inside
60 s with P-IMAP-UNTRUSTED-AGLOCK-GIVEUP budgets=2 and 'Failed to read root
inode' in the journal, no mount process in D state, the module unloadable,
and a following normal mount must succeed; then both leave cleanly.

## 0.75.77 — 2026-09-08 — A guard record's identity block validates under the flags its victim bound it to, and a descriptor holder whose slot the descriptor no longer names is located by its tuple

Measured on 0.75.76 (tests/evidence/20260909T010224Z_ghost_s565): the
admission sweep read every guard record but froze nothing — 'P-ADMIT-
VICTIM-UNFROZEN ... identity block invalid' for all six on both nodes. The
identity crc covers the record's flags, the guard writers move the flags
from ACTIVE to RECOVERY_GUARD without re-binding the crc (only the
retirement paths re-bind), so the victim's own intact identity block failed
the validator on every guard. mxfs_hb_guard_identity_valid now checks a
guard's block under the states its victim writer could have bound it to
(ACTIVE, WITHDRAWN, RETIRE_PENDING) with every other binding — slot, mkfs
generation, node, epoch, the block itself — unchanged; non-guard records are
judged exactly as before.

The same lap also showed the holder-slot proof of 0.75.75 refusing all six
attempts with 'descriptor owner is not the holder being judged'
(P238-FENCE-HOLDER-STATE x280 per node): after the s564 takeovers the
attempt holder is the prover field while the execution owner was cleared
when that prover unmounted (owner 0, owner_slot 0), so the descriptor no
longer says which slot the holder occupied. The proof now uses the
descriptor's owner slot only when the owner IS the holder, and otherwise
reads the whole table fresh from the platter for the one record carrying
the holder's exact tuple. A record found EMPTY or RETIRE_PENDING under that
tuple is the holder's own final image (release_slot re-binds it), and no
record carrying the tuple in any slot means every slot it held was purged
behind a certified fence or re-tenanted; both end the tenancy and the
verdict is REVOKED. A record still standing under any other flag, or any
slot that cannot be read, keeps the verdict UNKNOWN.

## 0.75.76 — 2026-09-08 — A victim found already dead at admission gets its PR key frozen from its own record, and a fencing-attempt takeover carries the victim key, not the victim's node id

Measured on 0.75.75 (tests/evidence/20260909T005301Z_ghost_s564): the slot
proof above judged all six dead holders REVOKED (their slots had been
re-claimed by the joiners themselves), one node won all six attempt
takeovers (P238-FENCE-TAKEOVER, the other's refused rc=-16 as already
taken), and then nothing was fenced: 'P-PRKEY-FENCE-REFUSED slot=N ... no PR
key frozen for this incarnation on this node; laying no fencing intent
(NO_VICTIM_KEY)' six times per slot, on every re-drive, and both mounts
failed at the bound. On the platter every taken-over descriptor now read
fence_key = the victim's node id (0x176608a9 is 392562857).

Two causes. First, a victim that is ALREADY a RECOVERY_GUARD or WITHDRAWN
record when a node mounts was marked pending with no frozen key: the only
freezers were the monitor's death snapshot, for a death this node watched,
and the whole-cluster bootstrap's sealed manifest. The mount's pending sweep
now reads the victim's own record and, when it names the exact incarnation
and carries a valid identity block with a key, freezes that key, key
generation, host and boot (P-ADMIT-VICTIM-FROZEN) — the same identity block
the monitor observes and the manifest is built from; anything short of that
falls back to the plain mark and says so (P-ADMIT-VICTIM-UNFROZEN), and the
fence stays refused. Second, the fencing-attempt takeover in
mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire passed the victim's node id where
mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_takeover expects the key the new attempt
intends to remove; it now passes the frozen victim key and refuses the
takeover (P238-FENCE-TAKEOVER-NOKEY) when there is none, rather than write
an intent no target could honour.

## 0.75.75 — 2026-09-08 — A recovery descriptor's holder is judged from its own heartbeat slot on the platter when the in-memory view cannot say

Measured on 0.75.74 (tests/evidence/20260909T004439Z_ghost_s563, the LUN as
s562 left it): the four dead-incarnation notes above never fired, because
the two provers had been certified and published on an earlier boot and
their heartbeat records were all-zero; every joiner judged the six FENCING
holders UNKNOWN — P238-FENCE-HOLDER-STATE state=UNKNOWN why='node not in
the heartbeat table', 51-54 lines per slot per node for the whole 155 s
bound — took nothing over, and both mounts failed again. A fresh mount after
both completers are gone is the same shape: nothing durable outside the
descriptors themselves named those incarnations any more, so a cached dead
set can never be the whole answer.

The takeover arms of mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire (fencing attempt or
unsealed snapshot at -EPERM, execution owner at -EBUSY) now ask the holder's
own slot on the platter when v5_incarnation_state returns UNKNOWN
(v5_holder_slot_state, P238-FENCE-HOLDER-SLOT). Every holder wrote its own
slot into the descriptor, and a slot's record changes tenant only through a
terminal event for the tenancy it carried: an all-zero record is written
only by the purge that ends a published recovery, which runs only behind a
certified fence of the tuple that occupied the slot; a record carrying
another incarnation proves the slot was re-claimed, which needs an EMPTY or
zero record first; an EMPTY record under the holder's own tuple is the
holder's own release. Each of those is REVOKED and the standing attempt is
taken over with a new term (P238-FENCE-TAKEOVER, then a new fence of the
victim). The holder's record still standing under any flag, an unreadable
sector, an unrecognised magic, a bootstrap holder (which has no slot) or a
descriptor whose owner is not the holder stay UNKNOWN and keep waiting:
heartbeat silence alone still authorises nothing; this is the holder's own
slot showing the end of its tenancy.

## 0.75.74 — 2026-09-08 — A certified-fenced or completed incarnation is noted dead on the ordinary path, so the fencing attempts it left behind can be taken over

Measured on 0.75.73 (tests/evidence/20260909T003455Z_ghost_s562, the LUN
as s561 left it): the per-slice publish above worked — test1 published slot
7 and test2 slot 6 (P-BARRIER-SLICE-PUBLISHED), each peer saw the other's
sector zeroed (P163-RECOVERED) and retired the slot from its cut, and the
still-requires-recovery mask shrank from 0x7f/0xbf to 0x3f on both nodes.
The six remaining slices then failed every claim to the 30 s bound
(P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED stage=1 kind=0 x126 per slot per node) and both
mounts failed. tools/disklock_hb_dump.py read their descriptors: all six at
stage FENCING, provers = exactly the two incarnations the joiners had just
certified fenced (kind 21) and, on s562, completed.

The fence-attempt takeover (mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire, the -EPERM arm)
takes a dead prover's standing attempt over only when v5_incarnation_state
judges that prover REVOKED, and for a prover that is not a later incarnation
of a live node and not our own earlier epoch the only route to REVOKED is
the exact-incarnation dead set (v5_note_dead_inc). That set was populated
only by the whole-cluster bootstrap paths; the ordinary path never noted an
incarnation dead, however many certificates it wrote or read. A prover that
died mid-attempt therefore kept every attempt it held for good, on every
node, even after its own fence was certified and its recovery completed.
The incarnation is now noted dead at the four places the ordinary path
proves it: when this node certifies a fence (v5_pr_fence_prove, after
mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_certify), when a claim passes the certificate
check whoever proved it (a stage return or -EBUSY from
mxfs_disklock_recovery_claim), in the completion ladder next to the
identity retirement, and in the monitor's recovered callback when a peer
watches the slot zero (the tracker's last epoch for the slot, as the
departure queue already uses). Each fires P-DEAD-INC once per tuple.

Also new: when a FENCING or SNAPSHOTTING attempt is NOT taken over, the
holder's incarnation verdict is printed (P238-FENCE-HOLDER-STATE ... state=
LIVE|UNKNOWN why='...', rate limited). Until now the only line a stuck
attempt produced named the stage, not why the holder counted as unrevoked.
On the s562 LUN the two provers' own records are all-zero (their recoveries
were published), so neither the certificate nor the completion route fires
on the next restart; that line is what will say whether the remaining gap is
'node not in the heartbeat table', measured in the entry above this one.

## 0.75.73 — 2026-09-08 — The mount barrier publishes each foreign slice as soon as it is durably replayed, instead of after the whole cut is clean

Measured on 0.75.72 with both nodes of the two-node TCP rig restarting onto a
LUN whose eight pending slices carried the previous laps' dead incarnations
(tests/evidence/20260909T001304Z_ghost_s561): the fix above let each joiner
declare the dead provers, certify the boot-succession fence of one slice
each (kind 21), take that slice's execution lease and replay it. Then each
node polled the OTHER node's slice — 'slice slot=N is being recovered by
another survivor — waiting for completion', 66 polls per node,
P238-RECOV-OWNED why='heartbeating' — until the extended bound, and both
mounts failed -EBUSY. The barrier completed and published its replayed
slices only once its own cut was clean, and neither cut could be clean
before the other node published: two concurrent joiners, each owning one
slice, waited on each other by construction. The replays themselves were
lost with the failed mounts (both descriptors stayed at FENCED and
unowned).

The end-of-cut ordering dated from a rule that clearing one victim's
authority before another victim's slice was replayed would strip evidence
the second replay gate still needed. That has not been true since the gate
moved to the victim's own fence-time manifest: every image is judged against
the sealed manifest of the slice being replayed and that victim's own live
bits (P-RMAN-EVAL, the current-safety check), never against another
victim's grants, and the live reap path has completed each slot right behind
its durable flush all along. The barrier now runs the same completion ladder
over each slot the moment that slot's replay is durable and its cached views
are dropped (P-BARRIER-SLICE-PUBLISHED), so a peer waiting on the slice sees
its heartbeat sector zeroed (P163-RECOVERED) and retires it from its cut. A
per-slice publication that fails is retried by the end-of-cut completion,
which fails the mount exactly as before if it still cannot publish. Under a
whole-cluster bootstrap term the sealed set still completes only after every
manifest slice is replayed, so the per-slice publish is skipped there.
tools/disklock_hb_dump.py now decodes the recovery descriptor of every
RECOVERY_GUARD record (stage, victim, owner, prover, fence kind), which is
how the six older descriptors on that LUN were read: all at stage FENCING,
provers = the two incarnations the joiners had just certified fenced.

## 0.75.72 — 2026-09-08 — The mount barrier waits out the dead window when its blockers are provers not yet declared dead, and a mount whose first metadata acquire keeps failing gives up with an error instead of looping in D state

Two changes on the crash-restart path. First, the admission barrier. On
0.75.71 both nodes came back onto a LUN whose six pending slices carried
FENCING-stage descriptors owned by the provers of the previous lap, which
had died with their boot (tests/evidence/20260909T000123Z_ghost_s560): the
barrier refused every claim (P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED x204 per node, 'slice
slot=N NOT replayed (-1)' x204), and after 34 rounds and its 30 s bound
aborted the mount on both nodes with a clean teardown. Nothing can take a
dead prover's standing attempt over until this node's monitor has declared
that prover dead, which takes the dead window of 31 samples at 2 s, and the
bound expired first, on every restart alike. While the monitor still holds
frozen records it has not declared dead (mxfs_disklock_deaths_undeclared),
the barrier's bound is now the ordinary wait plus that window plus a fence
and replay budget (30 + 62 + 30 s), logged once as P-BARRIER-GHOST-EXTEND;
once every death is declared the ordinary bound applies.

Second, the root iget. The DLM answers an acquire that outlived its retry budget with EAGAIN
('lock request failed after 60 retries'), the untrusted-iget bracket that
brackets xfs_imap_lookup with the AG DLM passed that value through, and
xfs_iget's out_error_or_again arm retries any EAGAIN forever with an
uninterruptible one-jiffy delay. The mount's root iget (inode 128 in
allocation group 0) therefore sat in D state for good whenever AG 0's ledger
page had no reachable authority: 'lock request failed after' every ~6 s and
P-IMAP-UNTRUSTED-AGLOCK-FAIL comm=mount rc=-11 between them, 173 of each per
node 21 minutes after boot, the mount unkillable by SIGKILL or timeout, a
second mount of the device queued behind it in super_lock, and only a reset
of the machine ending it (tests/cluster_restart_nomkfs.sh s556-s558,
tests/ghost_slot_restart_probe.sh s559c). The bracket now retries the AG
acquire for a bounded number of DLM budgets (mxfs.untrusted_aglock_budgets,
default 5, about 30 s: a departed authority's page is taken over in 2-6 s
and the bootstrap node's orphan sweep of the whole ledger takes 4-8 s), then
fails the lookup with EIO (P-IMAP-UNTRUSTED-AGLOCK-GIVEUP), which the mount
reports as 'Failed to read root inode' and returns to userspace. A pending
fatal signal ends the retry at once. Also new, test only:
mxfs.fence_bootsucc_inject_refuse refuses the 0.75.71 boot-succession proof
even when every condition holds, so the absent-key shape can be made
non-proving on demand — the negative arm for that fence kind and the way to
exercise this bound. Measured in the entry above this one.

## 0.75.71 — 2026-09-08 — A dead incarnation of a host that is live again under a later boot is fenced by the boot boundary and the reservation

0.75.70 declared the crash leftovers dead, and the fences then showed the
next wall (tests/evidence/20260908T234712Z_ghost_s559c, six dead
incarnations from three earlier boots of the two hosts): the target had
purged every dead registration with its iSCSI session, so each attempt
classified KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN, no self-succession record existed to consume
(the plain REGISTER at mount had succeeded, there was nothing to replace),
the sole-survivor exclusive-write gate does not apply with two live members,
and every series ended FENCE_BLOCKED after 120 s (83-86 attempts per node,
three P238-FENCE-BLOCKED each) with no slice recovered, no bootstrap node and
both mounts still parked. On this target class a whole-cluster restart could
therefore never complete without an operator.

A new fence kind, BOOT_SUCCESSION_ABSENT (21), is certified when all of the
following hold, each checked by the prover in this order: the victim's
identity block was frozen for the exact dead incarnation; the host that ran
it is live again under a different boot (the prover's own identity, or a
monitored slot whose heartbeat is advancing, carries that host_uuid with
another boot_uuid); no record on the table carrying the victim's boot_uuid
advanced across a heartbeat interval (no clone or snapshot-resumed copy is
heartbeating); and the registration table still excludes (a Write Exclusive
form that excludes non-registrants held, our key present, the view complete,
the victim key absent — the same check every replay gate re-runs). The OS
instance that issued the victim's I/O is gone from its host, a new session
from that host is unregistered and refused by the reservation, and this code
never re-registers a lost or fenced registration, so the exclusion holds by
the boot boundary plus the reservation; the certificate records the observed
reservation type and the read on a certificate requires that type. With two
hosts every dead incarnation is either the peer while this node is alone
(the sole-survivor gate) or a previous boot of one of the two hosts (this
kind). Measured in the entry above this one.

## 0.75.70 — 2026-09-08 — A heartbeat record that was already frozen when this mount first saw it is declared dead like any other

The heartbeat monitor's dead-detection arm fired only for a slot it had once
seen live. A record that was ALREADY frozen when the mount began monitoring
it (a crash leftover: an incarnation that died in an earlier boot, its
ACTIVE record and stale stamp still on the platter) accumulated silent
samples forever and was never declared dead, so nothing fenced it, nothing
replayed its slice, its heartbeat slot never resolved, and no node could
become the bootstrap node behind it. Measured on the two-node TCP rig after
both VMs were reset with their mounts in flight and both came back onto the
LUN without a mkfs (tests/evidence/20260908T232151Z_restart_s558, boot
journals; the slot table read with the new tools/disklock_hb_dump.py): four
dead ACTIVE records in slots 0-3 from two earlier boots, each auto-monitored
at mount and reported stale after 5 s, and 21 minutes later zero deaths,
zero fence attempts, no recovery, the orphan sweep refused for want of a
bootstrap node (P-DEPART-WORK-ORPHAN-SWEEP rc=-1) on both nodes, and every
ledger-page request parked (P-TAUTH-PAGE-PARKED x186, 'lock request failed
after' x173 per node) with both mount processes in D state. The
whole-cluster bootstrap path did not engage either, by design: each joiner
saw the other's fresh claim heartbeating, took that as a survivor, and left
the dead slices to it.

A monitored ACTIVE record that has stayed frozen for the whole dead window
(31 samples, 62 s) is now declared dead whether or not it was ever seen
live, on the same path and with the same FUA confirm read; the baseline
must exist (a first sight of the record), and a slot whose recovery is
already pending never re-fires. P-HB-GHOST-DEAD names the case once per
declaration. tools/disklock_hb_dump.py reads the 64 heartbeat records with
plain reads, because tools/recov_forge's FUA READ is refused by the QNAP
target; tests/ghost_slot_restart_probe.sh is the deterministic arm for this
shape. Measured in the entry above this one.

## 0.75.69 — 2026-09-08 — Whether a ledger page's authority is alive is answered by the heartbeat slot map, and every orphaned page is swept up at mount

0.75.68 was not enough. The LUN the s556 restart hung on was mounted again
on that build (tests/evidence/20260908T231212Z_restart_s557) and both
mounts hung the same way: the page carrying allocation group 0 was PREPARED
by a third-era incarnation to another third-era incarnation, the fourth
era's mount had settled that authority and then hung on this very fault
before finishing its takeover, and no fifth-era mount ever named either
incarnation again, so no takeover pass could reach the page; the bootstrap
node declined the on-demand takeover for the same reason (its purge list
knows only what it saw), and the other node parked every request
(P-TAUTH-PAGE-PARKED page=21394 ... in_view=0 purged=0 bootstrap=0, 371
times) until its mount's retry budgets ran out ('lock request failed after'
17 times) with both mount processes in D state. Whether an incarnation is
alive cannot be per-mount memory; it is a property of the shared disk.

The DLM now asks the disklock table whether {node, incarnation} is the
current occupant of any heartbeat slot. An incarnation this mount purged is
dead; one still occupying a slot (heartbeating, or dead and not yet
recovered) is alive and its pages wait for recovery exactly as before; one
in this mount's view is alive; anything else belongs to an era whose slot
has moved on. That test decides whether a PREPARED page's target consumes
it and whether the bootstrap node may take a page over on demand. And once
its membership has settled after mount, the bootstrap node runs an orphan
sweep: one bulk read of every page's authority, every distinct incarnation
judged once, every page of a dead one taken over to its owner under the
view (P-TAUTH-ORPHAN-AUTH per incarnation, P-TAUTH-ORPHAN-SWEEP for the
pass). Measured in the entry above this one once the stranded LUN mounts.

## 0.75.68 — 2026-09-08 — A page prepared to a target that left with the previous era is taken over, not left to it

A whole-cluster restart without a mkfs could hang every node's mount for
good. When both nodes unmount together, each one's departure hand-off
prepares its ledger pages to the peer and the peer, already past its own
teardown gate, drops the frozen notice, so the platter is left with pages
PREPARED to targets that left with the era. The next era's mount takes over
the pages of the predecessor it settled, and the takeover found every one of
them (cand=29, cand=36 on the two nodes) and prepared none: a PREPARED page
was consumed by its target whenever this mount had not itself marked that
target purged, and a previous era's incarnation never is, because no mount
of the new era ever had it in view. The page carrying allocation group 0
stayed under a dead authority, every request for it parked
(P-TAUTH-REMASTER-PARKED page_state=0), the retry budgets expired ('lock
request failed after' ten times per node), and both mount processes sat in
D state until the machines were reset (fourth era of
tests/cluster_restart_nomkfs.sh, tests/evidence/20260908T230313Z_restart_s556;
the third era had mounted only because that page had been taken over on
demand in the second while its target was still known). A target consumes a
prepared page only while it is a live member: in this mount's view and not
purged. A target outside the view is retargeted to the page's owner under
the view, as a purged one always was. Measured in the entry above this one
once the stranded LUN mounts on this build.

## 0.75.67 — 2026-09-08 — A peer closing its socket no longer kills the process that was sending to it

The kernel TCP send in the platform layer sent with no message flags, so
when the peer had closed its side the stack returned EPIPE and also
delivered SIGPIPE to the calling task (net/core/stream.c sk_stream_error).
The DLM sends on whatever task is inside it: the unmount process
broadcasting its goodbye after the peer's socket closed first was killed on
its way back to user space, exit 141 after the unmount had completed
(tests/evidence/20260908T224242Z_unload_s552base2/unload_test1.txt on
0.75.65, tests/evidence/20260908T224533Z_unload_s5531/unload_test1.txt on
0.75.66, each with 'communication with node N lost (err -32)' in the same
instant as P-GOODBYE-SENT), and any user process whose file operation sends
a lock message as a peer resets its connection would die the same way. The
send now carries MSG_NOSIGNAL, as the user-mode platform layer always has;
the EPIPE return is unchanged and the peer manager still treats it as a hard
break and reconnects. Measured: the same ordering on 0.75.67
(tests/evidence/20260908T225316Z_unload_s5542/unload_test1.txt, the EPIPE
line still logged before the goodbye) returns umount 0; seven further
unmount laps on the build returned 0.

## 0.75.66 — 2026-09-08 — A node tearing down still serves the releases of a peer that is tearing down with it

When both nodes of the two-node TCP cluster unmount at the same time, each
one's clean departure sends the grants it still holds to their master, and
for half of them the master is the peer. The peer had already cleared its
mounted flag, and the message gate that keeps lock traffic out of a session
in teardown dropped every one of those releases (P-TEARDOWN-MSG-DROP type=1)
along with the resends, so each node sat out the whole 3 s ack bound before
finishing (P-TAUTH-RELEASE-WAIT unacked=N after 3000ms), and the records
the peer never retired stayed ACTIVE on the platter for the next mount to
import as residue. Measured on the unfixed build with a workload that leaves
