about 300 live grants per node, half of them mastered by the peer
(tests/cross_grant_workload.sh, laps tests/evidence/unload_laps_s552base.log):
each node released 237 to 303 grants over the wire, the peer dropped 680 to
916 messages at its gate, 102 to 160 releases were still unacked after 3 s,
and the concurrent unmounts took 5.1 to 7.7 s each.

A release now passes the gate for the same reasons the ack already did. The
ledger stays open until the engine is destroyed, so the retirement commits on
a page this node still masters exactly as it would have a moment earlier; a
page the departure hand-off has already prepared refuses the commit and the
ack says REMASTER, which re-routes the releaser as before; and no local lock
state is minted, since the one path that could re-enter the filesystem, a
post-promotion BAST addressed to this node, is dropped once the mount is
past its lock-holding life (release_all retires those holdings itself,
which is what the waiter is waiting for). The goodbye line now carries how
many of the peer's releases were served in the teardown and how many local
BASTs were dropped, and tests/fleet_unload_check.sh reports both together
with the departure's own wire-release outcome. Measured on the same
workload (tests/evidence/unload_laps_s553.log, unload_laps_s554.log, eight
concurrent laps and one serial): every release acked, no release wait on
any node, 129 to 168 of the peer's releases served per node after its own
teardown began, and the concurrent unmounts fell to 2.3 to 2.6 s for the
first node out and 4.9 to 5.2 s for the last. What remains of those walls is
named in the ledger: the departure's per-page hand-off of about 300 pages to
a peer that is leaving too (1.2 s, one ledger write each), the last node's
takeover scan of the peer's pages run inline from the goodbye (2.6 s), and
the half-second join of the fence-retry worker.

The same laps surfaced a second, unrelated fault: when the peer's socket
closed first, the departing node's goodbye broadcast took EPIPE and the
kernel delivered SIGPIPE to the unmount process, which exited 141 after the
unmount had completed. That is the TCP send path sending without
MSG_NOSIGNAL, and it is fixed separately.

## 0.75.65 — 2026-09-08 — A departed peer's ledger purge reads no platter, and the takeover scan reads it in the largest runs the LUN accepts

Every unmount on the two-node TCP rig cost the surviving node four to nine
seconds of departure work for the peer that left first, and the departing
node the same for its own peer when both left together. The departure
worker's line attributed it: the purge that retires the departed holder's
records read both copies of the whole ledger region (26426 pages, 206 MiB
at about 50 MiB/s in 64 KiB runs) to find a handful of candidate pages,
and the page takeover that follows read the same region again to find the
departed authority's pages. The purge no longer reads the platter at all:
the only pages it may write are the ones this node masters, and every
transition that makes a page this node's (activate, prepare, and every
commit since) installs the written image in the page cache, so the
candidates are found by walking the cached images. A page whose image was
dropped by an unreadable reload, or whose last write is uncertain, stays a
candidate so the per-page path re-reads and fails closed on it exactly as
the platter pass did. The takeover scan keeps reading the platter, in
512 KiB runs (the LUN's transfer limit; a larger read is refused) stepping
down to 128 KiB and 64 KiB when contiguous memory is short. Measured on
the two-node TCP rig: the purge pass went from 3969 to 4568 ms to 1 ms, the
last node's unmount after its peer left from 4525 to 4776 ms to 817 ms,
a concurrent unmount of both nodes from 4445 to 11107 ms to 569 and 849 ms
(tests/evidence/unload_laps_s549.log, unload_laps_s549p.log), and on a
death lap the survivor still retired every record of the dead peer from
its cache (165 cleared over 164 candidate pages, 2 ms to find them) while
the takeover scan fell from about 4 s to 2.4 s
(tests/evidence/tcp2dc_s549d.log). The three-second release-ack wait of
a concurrent unmount after a workload is a separate mechanism and is not
changed here.

## 0.75.64 — 2026-09-08 — A buffer that survives to module unload is named at the two places that should have ended it

Unloading the module after the AG-meta leak reproducer on the two-node
TCP rig reported the buffer slab still holding six objects (a kernel
WARNING from kmem_cache_destroy at rmmod, test1, tests/evidence/
20260908T212931Z_unload_s544g), the same count as the stale reclaims that
lap fires for the collapsed free-space btree blocks. Nothing in the log
said which buffers or who still held them: the buftarg drain walks the LRU
only, a staled buffer has left the LRU, and the module unload sees just a
count. Two probes now name the leak. The stale completion of an
AG-metadata buffer reports the hold count it leaves behind when it is not
the single reference its caller is about to drop, and the per-AG buffer
cache teardown at unmount describes every buffer still hashed there. The
unload harness tests/fleet_unload_check.sh captures the unmount and
unload kernel window per node before the next lap can wrap it. Both probes
stayed silent on the first run while the six objects leaked again, so the
leaked buffers are not held in any cache at teardown: a live registry of
every allocated buffer (joined at allocation, left at free) is now reported
at module unload after the RCU barrier, naming each survivor with its hold
history. Measured in the entry above this one once the leak is attributed.

## 0.75.63 — 2026-09-08 — The directory hole detector no longer reports a legitimate shrink as a torn map

The flush-time detector that reports a hole between a directory's data
blocks was written for one cause, a divergent cross-node grow, and its
message asserted that cause. On the two-node TCP rig it fired on a 2000-entry
private directory while its owner was removing the files: the node-format
removename path frees every emptied middle data block, which leaves exactly
such a hole, and the directory was intact on both nodes (350 surviving
entries, contiguous names, identical views). The report cost a session an
investigation into a tear that did not exist. The directory inode now
remembers when its hole has a known legitimate origin, set where a non-last
data block is punched and where a holey canonical disk image is adopted at
acquire, and the detector stays silent for such a map. A hole with no known
origin is still reported, now worded as the possibility it is.

## 0.75.62 — 2026-09-08 — A freed allocation-group btree block no longer makes every later release of that group wait two seconds

Every allocation-group metadata buffer this node logs takes a buffer hold
and a per-group pending count that the release pipeline waits on, for up
to two seconds, before the group's grant is handed to a peer, so that a
peer never reads a free-space or inode btree image that has not landed.
The count was returned only by the write completion, or by the
shutdown-abort detach added for the unmount wedge. A btree block that is
freed after being logged in the same dirty epoch, which is what a leaf
merge or a root collapse does when a free-space tree shrinks, is a third
case: it never writes back, and its log item is freed through the stale
completion with no I/O completion at all, so the hold and the count
leaked for the life of the mount. From that point every release of that
group on that node spun to the two-second bound and then forced the
release, while the peer's one-second request deadline expired and it
retried. On the two-node TCP rig a truncate lap failed with a
2045-millisecond truncate behind a 2.003-second release whose every other
stage took microseconds, and the stuck-metadata probe showed the same
four never-written buffers at the next release 47 seconds later. The
reproducer (tests/agmeta_stale_leak_2node.sh: punch every other block of
an 8 MiB file so both free-space trees split, remove the file so they
collapse, then have the peer unlink two files in that group) showed both
peer unlinks at 2.05 and 2.07 seconds with two expired deadlines. The
stale completion now returns the hold through the same one-shot reclaim
the abort path uses, which names its caller in its probe line, and the
stuck-metadata probe now also counts stale and still-tracked buffers.
Measured: the reproducer on the unfixed 0.75.61 had the peer's two unlinks
take 2067 and 2051 milliseconds with two expired deadlines and a stuck
count of six; on this build (three laps, one after a fresh prep) every AG
release's stage-3 wait was zero, the peer's unlinks took 51 to 85
milliseconds, the stale reclaim fired six times per lap for the collapsed
blocks, and no deadline expired. Four truncate laps on the same mount
truncated in 20 to 39 milliseconds. The unmount that had reported a
non-zero group reference count on the unfixed build reported none on this
one, but the module unload after it reported six buffers still allocated
in the buffer slab; that leak is named and instrumented in 0.75.64.

## 0.75.61 — 2026-09-08 — The directory leaf-range coherence scan runs once per exclusive tenure, not on every create

On the two-node TCP rig a private-directory small-file workload (2000
creates, 2000 overwrites, 1000 unlinks per node) did not finish inside its
30 second budget on either node; a single node needs 27 seconds for the
2000 creates alone, 6 to 7 milliseconds each while the directory is small
and 13 to 22 once it passes a few hundred entries. Function-graph tracing
of the create in a 1000-entry directory found 0.66 to 1.17 milliseconds of
every create in the leaf-range coherence scan: it re-read one to three
leaf blocks from the platter and compared them on every modify, because
its gate deliberately ignored the directory generation (which does not
advance on slow-path acquires) and so had no notion of a tenure at all.
The scan exists to catch a stale clean leaf at the start of a tenure that
follows a peer's writes. While this node holds the directory's exclusive
grant continuously, which the DLM epoch (advanced on every grant loss or
stale mark) and the inode incarnation together witness, no peer can have
written a leaf block, so the scan now runs once per such tenure and is
skipped after that; a new module parameter restores the per-modify scan.
The larger per-create cost, one durable authority-ledger commit for the
new inode's grant, is measured in the same trace and stays open under the
small-file pace record. Measured on one warmed mount with the knob toggled
1, 0, 1, 0 across four 2000-create runs (tests/leaf_scan_ab.sh): the first
run after a fresh prep is dominated by first-touch ledger-page activation
(14 milliseconds per create throughout, 33 seconds), the second still
carries it in its early batches; the two runs that follow are the honest
pair, 14.3 seconds with the scan once per tenure against 16.9 seconds with
the per-modify scan, and their first batches show what a create costs once
the pages are owned and the directory is small: 2.8 to 4.0 milliseconds,
rising to 6.5 to 6.7 by the two-thousandth entry.

## 0.75.60 — 2026-09-08 — The allocation-group release no longer sleeps between two flushes that issue nothing

The release worker's final stage issued a device flush, slept 2
milliseconds and flushed again, a sequence written for a target whose
write cache could still be draining to the platter after the first flush
returned. With FUA reads disabled, which is the default and the only
configuration the two-node TCP rig runs, the flush helper issues no
SYNCHRONIZE CACHE at all: peers read the shared target cache, so a
completed write is already visible to them and there is no platter lag to
cover. The stage line put that sleep at 3.0 to 5.0 milliseconds on every
one of 22 releases, the largest remaining piece of a 5.4 to 8.9
millisecond release. The sleep and second flush now run only when the
helper actually flushes. Measured on the two-node TCP rig
(tests/evidence/sess541_trunc_s541{a..d}): the stage read 0 on all 16
allocation-group releases, the whole release fell to 1.7 to 5.6
milliseconds typical (mean 3.6, one 10.8 with a slow remote unlock) from
5.4 to 8.9, what remains is the publish gate at 1.3 to 1.9 and the wire
unlock at 0.4 to 0.7 local or 3 to 9 to a remote master; the four
peer-truncate laps read 24/36/38, 26/47/26, 84/19/35 and 82/19/34
milliseconds, all inside the bound with integrity and both kernels clean,
and the alternating append stayed at 0.1 milliseconds per append.

## 0.75.59 — 2026-09-08 — A write open asks for the exclusive grant it will need, and the file window defaults to 15 ms

Two changes to the same peer-truncate hand-off. First, the file tenure
window's default drops from 30 to 15 milliseconds. The A/B on 0.75.58
(six laps at 30, three at 15, tests/evidence/sess538_* and sess539_*) kept
the two-node line append at 0.1 milliseconds per append and seven hand-offs
per 2000 appends at both settings, while the truncates went from 70 to 98
milliseconds typical with one at 248 to 39 to 73 milliseconds. Second, the
grant ride that protects every open used to take the shared mode even when
the open was for writing, so the first write or truncate had to convert
shared to exclusive. With two nodes doing that on one file, both hold
shared and both ask to convert; the master denies the later request, which
then drops its shared grant and re-requests exclusive from nothing, behind
the winner's whole tenure. The 67 millisecond truncate in lap s539c spent
31 of them on exactly that: shared granted, conversion denied, shared
dropped, then the appender's window and release drain before the exclusive
grant arrived. A write open's ride now acquires exclusive outright, under a
new module parameter that restores the old ride when set to 0; read opens
are unchanged. Measured on the two-node TCP rig (tests/evidence/sess540_*):
eight peer-truncate laps with the ride on put all 24 truncates inside the
100 millisecond bound, 22 of them between 13 and 50 milliseconds and the
other two at 61 and 89; the three laps with the ride switched off on the
same build and window read 55 to 80. The conversion denial never fired on
the truncated file with the ride on (it fired once per lap, on the file,
with it off), and no deferred-release retry, lock timeout, hold underflow
or open-protect restart was logged. The alternating 2000-line append
stayed at 0.1 milliseconds per append (5 and 4 hand-offs) and the 100 by
64 KiB append at 7.2 milliseconds; every integrity and coherency assertion
passed on all thirteen laps and both kernels stayed clean.

## 0.75.58 — 2026-09-08 — A regular file's exclusive tenure under a peer request is a bounded window, not one operation

On the two-node TCP rig every syscall of a peer truncating a hot-appended
file was its own cross-node hand-off: open, ftruncate, close and stat each
round-tripped, because the appender's next operation took the grant back in
the sub-millisecond gap between them, and the alternating two-node line
append handed the file off once every 1.2 appends (3096 hand-offs for 4000
appends at about 13 milliseconds each). The minimum-hold defer already
covered files, but the tenure keep-delay consulted at every operation
completion returned zero for anything that is not a directory, so the first
completion after a peer's request released the grant, and the batch arm for
a request that arrives during the acquire was directory-only as well. A
regular file now carries its own tenure window, 30 milliseconds by default
under a new module parameter, through the same four sites a directory uses:
the defer at notification, the keep-delay at operation completion, the
quiet-age gate in the deferred work and the acquire-time batch arm. A peer
waits at most the window plus one release drain; an idle holder still lets
go at the first idle sample past the grace, and the one-operation adaptive
floor is unchanged. Setting the parameter to 0 restores the previous
behavior. Measured on the two-node TCP rig at the 30 millisecond default
(tests/evidence/sess538_*): the alternating 2000-line append went from
19.2 milliseconds per append and 2839 hand-offs with the window off to 0.1
milliseconds and 7 hand-offs, the 100 by 64 KiB append from 29.8 to 6.9
milliseconds per append, every integrity and coherency assertion passed,
and no deferred-release retry, lock timeout or hold underflow was logged.
The truncates paid for it: 16 of 18 inside the 100 millisecond bound but
70 to 98 milliseconds typical and one at 248, because a truncate now
waited out the appender's window at its open and again after its
allocation-group wait. The window is retuned in the entry above.

## 0.75.57 — 2026-09-08 — The allocation-group release settles on the pin count instead of a sleep

After the prepass change, the stage line put the allocation-group release
at 10 to 15 milliseconds, 4 to 6 of them in the 3 millisecond sleep and
second log force that follow the first post-commit force. That pair was
written for a checkpoint completion the worker could not observe, and the
pinned-buffer count read right after the first force observes it directly:
a buffer whose commit has not been checkpointed and inserted into the AIL
is still pinned, and the count was zero on every one of the 56 releases
measured across ten peer-truncate laps. The sleep and second force now run
only when that count is nonzero, and say so when they do. Measured: that
stage went from 4 to 6 milliseconds to under 10 microseconds on all 22
releases in six laps, the count was never nonzero, the whole release is now
5.4 to 8.9 milliseconds, and the six peer-truncate laps put 17 of 18
truncates inside the bound with one at 107 milliseconds; integrity and
kernel health were clean.

## 0.75.56 — 2026-09-08 — The allocation-group release prepass no longer sleeps when the group has nothing in the AIL

The 0.75.55 stage line put 11 to 13 milliseconds of every allocation-group
release in the prepass, on 16 of 16 releases across four peer-truncate laps,
and the pinned and in-AIL counts after the first post-commit log force were
zero in every one, so the group had nothing waiting when the prepass ran.
The bounded AIL push the prepass calls was written when that push was the
drain, and it forces one push, log force and 10 millisecond sleep before it
will believe an empty first sample, because items flagged as flushing or
queued for delayed write were invisible to its filter and needed the AIL
worker to run. Since the release worker's prepass became advisory, the
post-commit drains write those buffers synchronously, so the forced sleep
guarded nothing for that caller. An A/B with the prepass push turned off by
its module parameter took the peer truncate from three of four laps failing
the 100 millisecond bound to twelve of twelve truncates inside it, 59 to 89
milliseconds. For a hard-capped caller, which is only the release worker,
an empty first sample now wakes the AIL worker, starts a checkpoint and
returns at once; a capped caller that does find items polls as before, and
the uncapped callers are unchanged. Measured on the two-node TCP rig: the
prepass stage went from 11 to 13 milliseconds to under 20 microseconds on
all 25 releases in six laps, the whole release to 10 to 15 milliseconds,
and the five steady-state peer-truncate laps passed with every truncate
between 52 and 85 milliseconds; the first lap after the mount still carried
one 140 millisecond truncate, which is a separate cold-path cost.

## 0.75.55 — 2026-09-08 — The allocation-group release prints its stage split

With the inode hand-off shortened, eight laps of the peer truncate put 21 of
24 truncates under the 100 millisecond bound and three at 103 to 113, and the
merged two-node timeline of a slow one puts about 28 milliseconds in the
allocation-group hand-off the extent free waits on: 11 from the worker's
entry to its commit and 11 more from the commit to the on-disk unlock. That
pipeline carries a forced push-and-sleep cycle before the commit and two
hardcoded sleeps after it, from the era before the inode path had a
deterministic wait, and no probe said which of its stages held the time.
The worker now stamps its entry, the end of the prepass, the commit, each of
the two post-commit log forces, the drains, the second metadata drain, the
in-flight wait, the final flushes, the publish gate and the unlock, counts
the group's pinned and in-AIL buffers after each of the two forces, and
prints them on one line after the unlock. No behavior change.

## 0.75.54 — 2026-09-08 — The release drain writes the data pages before it flushes the inode

Every terminal-gate defer in the 0.75.53 laps was a live one: 455 of 455
across three peer-truncate laps and one alternating-append lap, and in the
truncate laps 32 of 33 sat within a millisecond of a setfilesize commit on
the same inode, with the page-writeback wait the only stage carrying time.
The drain flushed the inode first and wrote the data pages second, and the
page writeback's completion then committed the new size, under the inode
lock, after the inode had already been written. The terminal obligation gate
found that one commit unlanded, deferred, and the re-fire coalesced onto the
pending minimum-hold slice, so the drain re-entered eleven to twelve
milliseconds later to spend another five landing it. Each hand-off from a
node with dirty pages was therefore two drains and an idle gap, about 24
milliseconds, with the local writer parked and the peer waiting. The data
pages are now written and invalidated before the settle and the targeted
inode drain, which is the order the filesystem's own writeback keeps: the
size and unwritten-extent updates exist only once the pages are on disk, so
the settle waits for those commits, the inode written by the drain carries
them, and the coalesced device flush covers the pages too. The writeback and
invalidate error captures are unchanged. The stage fields on the completed-
release and deferred-release lines are each stage's own duration in the new
order. Measured on the two-node TCP rig against 0.75.53 on the same laps:
the peer truncate of a hot-appended file went from 112 to 133 milliseconds
to 73 to 97 across three laps, every one inside the 100 millisecond bound,
with zero terminal-gate defers on either node where the previous build had
ten to twelve per lap; the alternating 2000-line append went from 28.2 and
22.1 milliseconds per append to 15.5 and 13.4, and the 100 by 64 KiB append
from 56.6 to 30.8, with integrity clean throughout.

## 0.75.53 — 2026-09-08 — A lock request parked on a ledger-page handoff retries within the handoff's own duration

The 0.75.52 watchdog caught the appender's release drain, on every one of
its 117 to 121 millisecond page flushes, asleep inside the DLM retry wrapper
under the allocator's non-blocking allocation-group probe. The delayed
allocation being converted for writeback could not use the inode's home
group, which the truncating peer held, and the next free group's ledger page
was being handed to its view master for the first time since the last
membership change. The master answered that the request must be re-routed,
and the wrapper then slept a flat 100 milliseconds before asking again,
while the handoff itself finished well inside that. The wait was two of the
three per-truncate hand-offs in every lap, with the appender parked and the
truncator waiting the whole time. The wrapper now backs off from 4
milliseconds and doubles per retry, settling at the previous 100 millisecond
cadence, so a short park is re-tried at about its own length and a long one
still does not become a message loop on the master. Measured on the same
laps in the entry below.

## 0.75.52 — 2026-09-08 — A stack watchdog names the wait inside the release drain's page flush

The 0.75.51 stage split attributed the residual peer-truncate cost to the
page flush stage of the appender's release drain: three drains across two
laps spent 117 to 121 milliseconds inside the page writeback wait and then
ended in a terminal defer, with the appender parked and the truncator waiting
the whole time. Reading both nodes' logs across one of them shows the drain
task hunting for an allocation group for the delayed-allocation conversion,
refused on the two groups the truncator held, granted a third by remaster,
and then silent for about 110 milliseconds before its first read of that
group's free-space tree. No probe covers that silence. The drain now arms a
timer around both of its page flushes; if the flush is still running when
the timer fires it prints the drain task's kernel stack, up to three times
per flush, so the wait site is read off the stack. The timer is a module
parameter, defaults to 50 milliseconds, which is above every healthy flush
measured and below every outlier, and 0 disarms it.

## 0.75.51 — 2026-09-08 — The live-commit re-fire coalesces onto a pending arm again; the release stage split names the page flush

The 0.75.50 immediate re-fire of a live-commit defer was measured against the
build before it and reverted. It changed nothing for the peer truncate of a
hot-appended file (240, 138 and 227 ms against 220 and 119) and made the
two-node alternating line append four and a half times slower (18.4 against
4.1 ms per append), because with the appender parked and the release re-fired
at once every append became its own cross-node hand-off, where the pending
arm's ten milliseconds had let each node batch a run of appends per tenure.
The re-fire goes back through the ordinary delayed arm with a zero delay,
which is immediate when nothing is pending and coalesces otherwise. The
0.75.50 reset of the release-abort backoff streak on a live defer stays. The
stage split on the defer line and the completed-release line now separates
the page writeback wait from the page invalidation and carries the settle and
directory-flush sub-stages, because the split showed the residual truncate
cost sitting in the page flush stage, about 120 milliseconds once per lap,
and in the settle-and-drain stage, about 63 milliseconds, without saying
which call.

## 0.75.50 — 2026-09-08 — A live-commit release defer re-fires at once, and the defer line names its stages

The 0.75.49 re-fire after a live-commit defer asked for a zero delay through
the ordinary delayed-work arm, which refuses when a delayed work is already
pending. Measured on the two-node TCP rig: every live defer was followed by
its re-entry 10 to 12 milliseconds later, never at once, because an earlier
arm had left that much on the timer. The live re-fire now modifies a pending
arm to run immediately, and a live defer resets the release-abort backoff
streak, since it is progress rather than the stuck case the streak exists for.
The defer line also prints the same stage split the completed-release line
does, because two drains in the same lap spent about 120 milliseconds before
deferring and nothing named the stage.

## 0.75.49 — 2026-09-08 — A release deferred by the local writer's own last commit no longer re-admits that writer

When a peer asks for a regular file this node is appending to, the release
drain lands the file's committed changes and then refuses to unlock while any
committed change is still unlanded. Measured on the two-node TCP rig, that
refusal repeated twenty-one times in a row about four milliseconds apart for
one peer truncate, each time with exactly one commit unlanded: the drain had
entered with the appender already admitted, landed everything but that
holder's commit, deferred with the inode's state reset to cached, and the
appender's own lock release re-fired the drain a hundred microseconds later,
by which time the appender was inside its next write again, because the cached
state had reopened the fast path to it. A peer truncate cost 167 to 236 ms
against the 100 ms hand-off budget, and with both nodes appending the same
loop drove the re-arm backoff to its one-second cap, so when the holder's
writer paused the peer sat behind a one-second retry and its acquire deadline
expired. The terminal gate now records the publication sequence at drain entry.
A regular-file defer whose sequence advanced during the drain is a live local
commit that one more flush lands: the state stays at the pending-request state,
which parks new user admissions of that file in the demote wait, and the drain
re-fires at once. A defer whose obligation did not move during the drain keeps
the cached state and the exponential backoff, which exists for a fenced victim
whose writes cannot land. Directories never reach this gate.

Instrumentation: the inode-cluster clobber detector is now evaluated against
the sectors actually submitted. It ran before the partial-write authority mask
decided which slots leave the node, so a stale slot the mask then dropped was
reported exactly like a landed clobber. The two-node create-race lap s528o
printed one such event for a free image of a peer-allocated inode, the very
class the mask drops as free-and-unlogged, and the platter was never touched.
A regression confined to masked slots is now counted separately as masked, and
the clobber line is reserved for a regressed slot that is in the I/O.

## 0.75.48 — 2026-09-08 — Losing a cross-node create race no longer fails a plain O_CREAT open

When two nodes open the same new name with O_CREAT at once, the node whose
lookup found the name absent but whose create then finds the peer's entry
under the directory lock orphans its own allocation and reports EEXIST.
The VFS hands a create error straight to open(2), so the losing node's open
failed even though the file existed, which POSIX forbids for O_CREAT without
O_EXCL. On the two-node TCP rig the losing appender's first 64 KiB record
was never written: the shell saw EEXIST, the harness discarded it, and the
file came up one record short. The create entry point now turns that EEXIST
into ESTALE for a non-exclusive create on a multi-node mount. The VFS
retries the open once with a revalidating lookup, the dropped dentry is
re-resolved under the directory the loser already reloaded, and the open
proceeds on the winner's inode with the VFS's own truncation and permission
handling. O_EXCL still gets EEXIST, and so do mkdir and mknod.

## 0.75.47 — 2026-09-08 — Lab knob to make the cross-node create race lose on purpose

Instrumentation only. The create-race loser branch, where a node finds the
peer's entry under the directory lock after its own lookup said the name
was absent, is reached only when the peer's create lands in the microseconds
between those two steps of one open call; scheduled races hit it once in a
thousand attempts. The new knob create_race_delay_ms (default 0) sleeps
that long at the top of every regular-file create on a multi-node mount,
between the lookup and the directory lock, so a peer creating the same name
inside the window wins every time. The concurrent-create harness arms it on
one node for the loop through CREATE_DELAY_MS and clears it afterwards.

## 0.75.46 — 2026-09-08 — A core-only flush no longer publishes a stale extent list under an adopted inode core

On a multi-node mount the inode cluster buffer is not always this node's
last image of every inode in it. A reload that keeps the cached buffer
protected, because it carries this node's uncheckpointed changes to other
inodes of the cluster, adopts the peer's dinode from a private platter read
and leaves the buffer slot as it was. The flush copies a fork into the
staged dinode only when that fork was logged, on the upstream premise that
the slot already holds the fork's last flushed image. For an adopted inode
that premise is false: an append inside the peer's block dirties only the
core, and the flush wrote the adopted extent count and size over the slot's
old fork bytes. Measured on the two-node TCP rig with the concurrent-create
race: the slot held the create-time image with no extents, the peer wrote
one extent, this node adopted it and appended, xfsaild flushed the core with
sixteen zero bytes staged under nextents=1, and the peer's next platter read
of that inode failed extent validation, so 89 of 200 files read empty on one
node while the other still served them from cache. The flush now re-encodes
each in-core fork the way the logged copy does and writes it into the staged
image whenever the staged bytes differ, which is a no-op wherever the
upstream premise holds. Each repair prints a ratelimited P-IFLUSH-FORK-STALE
line with a running total. The iflush_fork_heal knob from 0.75.45 is gone:
a switch that turns a data-integrity repair off has no place in a release.

## 0.75.45 — 2026-09-08 — A local racer taking the AG's last free inode no longer turns a create into a corruption report

The two-phase inode allocator releases the AGI buffer between picking a
candidate and reading its platter image, so that no platter I/O runs under
the AGI and btree nesting. The AG's exclusive grant keeps peers out of the
AG during that window, but not this node's own tasks: a second create on
the same node, in another directory of the same AG, could take the AG's
last free inode while the first create was validating its candidate. The
first create then re-read an AGI with a free count of zero and searched an
empty free-inode btree, and the near-search treats a tree with no record
on either side of the parent as corruption. The create failed with
"Structure needs cleaning", the free-inode btree was marked sick, and the
log said to unmount and run xfs_repair, on a filesystem with nothing wrong.
Measured on the two-node TCP rig: four concurrent create loops on one node
produced 131 such failures in 3200 creates, and none in 3200 with the
two-phase disabled. Phase 2 now checks the re-read AGI's free count and,
when it is zero, hands the AG back as swept, which is the path the caller
already takes for an AG whose free inodes are all peer-held: grow a chunk,
or move to the next AG. A ratelimited line records each occurrence.

Also in this version, instrumentation only: a staged-fork audit at inode
flush on multi-node mounts. The fork copy into the cluster buffer runs only
for a fork that was logged, on the premise that the buffer already holds
that fork's last flushed image. A reload that keeps the cluster buffer
protected adopts the peer's dinode from a private platter read without
touching the buffer slot, so that premise can fail and a core-only flush
would publish the adopted extent count over stale fork bytes. The audit
re-encodes each in-core fork the way the logged copy would and reports a
mismatch on an unlogged fork as P-IFLUSH-FORK-STALE; the new knob
iflush_fork_heal (default 0) additionally writes the in-core fork into the
staged image. The default stays 0 until the detector has been measured
against the concurrent-create-race reproducer that showed 137 of 200 files
reading empty on 2026-09-05.

## 0.75.44 — 2026-09-05 — The dentry-revalidation trace never drops its re-verification lines

The affine lap on 0.75.43 reported one affine blessing of a flagged binding
with no re-lookup between the flag and the blessing. The re-lookup had
happened: eight lookups of the traced directory in 150 milliseconds hit
the ratelimit's burst on the lookup line, so the blessing that followed
read as unverified while the blessing line itself, which is not
ratelimited, kept printing. Under the per-directory trace knob the lookup
line and the stale-flag line now print uncapped like the blessing line;
under the wide instrumentation knobs they stay ratelimited. Instrumentation
only, no behaviour change.

## 0.75.43 — 2026-09-05 — A shared writeback admit during a release drain no longer leaks an exclusive hold

The release-drain deadlock breaker admits the writeback submitter's SHARED
request on a file whose grant is being drained away (the FIX-27 widening),
but it booked every admit as an exclusive hold while the matching unlock
decrements the shared count. Each such admit therefore underflowed the
shared count and left one exclusive hold on the in-core inode for good,
and a phantom holder defers every later BAST on that file forever. On the
two-node TCP rig the writer never released its hot file to the peer's
unlink, the peer held the parent directory inside its relock while waiting
for the file, the writer's next open waited for the directory, and the
live-holder wait kept both parked: 476 and 479 request deadlines over
eight minutes, neither node able to unmount. The admit now increments the
counter the requested mode's unlock will decrement, and the admit probe
prints both counts.

## 0.75.42 — 2026-09-05 — DEMAND means the same thing on the TCP engine as on CAW

The 0.75.41 pre-acquire poll relied on a demanding non-blocking acquire
reaching the node that caches the AG. Only the CAW engine honoured the
demand flag (its sticky revoke bit); the TCP master denied a NOQUEUE
request against a held resource and told the holder nothing. Measured on
the two-node TCP rig: 84 of 84 polls expired at their full 100 ms, and
holding both inode locks through those expiries turned the convoy the
poll was meant to end into a 41 s unlink with 51 request deadlines and one
lap that overran its bound. On TCP a NOQUEUE request carrying DEMAND now
BASTs the conflicting granted holders exactly as a queued request would,
at both the local-master and remote-master denial sites, without queueing
the requester; when the holders release, nothing is promoted and the
requester's next probe is granted. Probe `P-DEMAND-BAST`.

## 0.75.41 — 2026-09-05 — The remove/rename pre-acquire asks for a peer-held AG before handing its inode locks off

On the two-node TCP rig a peer's unlink of a file another node writes in a
tight loop could take many hand-off cycles even with the 0.75.39 file yield
in place: one lap needed 16 cycles and 1533 ms, another 6 and 415 ms, four
others one cycle and about 85 ms. The cycle is the remove path's AG
pre-acquire. It trylocks the file's AG silently, and a miss releases both
inode locks, blocks for the AG holding nothing, pre-grants it to cached,
relocks the inodes and restarts. During the relock the writer's own round
blocks for that AG with the file's ILOCK held, the cached pre-grant is
handed to it at zero holders, its round completes and hands the file over,
and the restart's trylock misses again because the AG is now cached on the
writer. The two sides use opposite lock orders, and the cached pre-grant
that keeps the inversion deadlock-free turned it into a convoy whose length
was timing luck.

The sweep now first asks in the writer's own inode-then-AG order, bounded:
one demanding non-blocking acquire that registers the waiter and BASTs the
cacher, then silent retries every few milliseconds for at most
`preacq_poll_ms` (default 100 ms, about four measured hand-offs). With the
inode locks held the writer is parked on the file, so the AG has no holder
on the peer and arrives in one hand-off. A hit registers the grant like a
trylock hit; an expiry falls back to the unchanged hand-off. The poll runs
only when no other AG grant is registered on the transaction, so it adds no
AG-then-AG hold-and-wait. Probe `P271-PREACQ-POLL`, counters
`preacq_poll_hit_n` and `preacq_poll_miss_n`.

## 0.75.40 — 2026-09-05 — The file yield applies only when this node counts no local holder

The 0.75.39 yield parked any user task asking for a file whose grant a peer
had requested, including one arriving while this node still counted a local
holder. The release drain cannot begin while a holder is counted, so parking
behind one serves no peer, and when the holder is the same task taking its
nested inode lock under a counted I/O lock the park is a self-deadlock that
only the demote wait's three-second rescue polls break. The first full board
on 0.75.39 showed it: the directory-reuse coherency row timed out at its
barrier after 116 seconds while one node printed the yield line for the same
inode with an exclusive holder counted every three seconds. The gate now
requires zero counted holders, which restores the pre-0.75.39 admission for
that case; the hand-off the yield exists for still happens the moment the
holders drop, which in a write loop is between every two rounds.

## 0.75.39 — 2026-09-05 — A file's cached grant yields to a peer's pending request instead of starving it

On the two-node TCP rig a node writing one file in a tight loop (open with
truncate, write, close, under a millisecond per round) kept a peer's unlink
of that file waiting until the loop ended of its own accord: 2.5 to 4.5
seconds in every lap, with the peer's request deadline expiring once or
twice each time. The trace on the writer showed why. The peer's request
arrived, the release worker entered with no local holders and began its
drain, and the drain then waited for the inode to come clean while the
cached-mode fast path went on admitting the writer's next rounds, thousands
of them, each re-dirtying the inode. Directories have had a state gate on
that fast path since 0.3.13; regular files kept a mode-only check so that
the writeback completion workers the release itself dispatches could re-enter
under the still-held grant. That exemption was never meant to cover a user
task starting new work. A regular file's fast path now falls through to the
demote wait when a peer's request is pending or its release drain is in
flight and the caller is a user task with nothing pinned; kernel threads,
the demoter itself and pinned chains keep the fast path, so the writeback
re-entry the exemption exists for is unchanged, and the nested-hold breaker
still admits a task that already holds the inode. The narrower release-flush
admission that covered the same re-entry is now likewise kernel-thread only.
The behaviour is a module parameter, on by default, so the two shapes can be
measured against each other. A fresh VFS lookup under the traced parent is
now also named in the kernel log, which is the name-level re-verification
the affine harness needs to separate a blessing of a re-established binding
from a blessing of a destroyed one, and the peer-unlink measurement has its
own harness.

## 0.75.38 — 2026-09-05 — The stale-flag rejection trace names its source

The stale-flag rejection line printed under the dentry revalidation trace
now carries the source code that set the flag, so a lap can tell a child
flagged by the peer's lock request from one flagged by a lookup or a recycle.
The two-node affine harness gains the shape that matters in the default
configuration: a name the node has read and closed carries no grant on the
child, so the peer's unlink requests nothing from this node and nothing
flags the child; the harness asserts the name is gone afterwards and then
writes through it after recycling its inode number, checking that the new
occupant keeps its content. It also measures a peer's unlink wall under an
unpaced local truncate loop, since the first lap saw that unlink wait until
the loop ended, with a remote lock-request deadline expiring on the child.

## 0.75.37 — 2026-09-05 — The affine dentry exit is traceable and its audit counters readable

The dentry revalidation trace knob, which named every zero-I/O epoch
blessing under one parent, now also names every arrival at the affine
regular-file exit under that parent, whether blessed or diverted into the
audit, and every stale-flag rejection there. Without it a two-node lap could
not tell a name served stale from that exit apart from a name whose dentry
had already been evicted before the lookup, and a first lap read both as the
same zero. The affine audit's six counters, previously visible only in the
summary printed every ten thousand audits, are exposed read-only as one
module parameter line, because a harness that audits a few hundred lookups
had no denominator at all. The two-node affine harness now records the
inode number together with the birth time for every write in its create
loop, since a recycled inode number made a fresh incarnation look like the
freed one, and reports per-name exit counts from the trace.

## 0.75.36 — 2026-09-05 — The phantom-bail injection now loses the grant on the wire instead of lying to the check

The 0.75.35 injection forced the phantom bail's backing-record check to
answer "not held" while the transport still recorded the node as the
directory's exclusive holder. That is the opposite divergence from a phantom.
On the two-node TCP rig the bail duly dropped the cached grant without any
wire release, the peer's request then BASTed a node that had nothing it could
prove to release, the bounded release episode wedged after fifty-nine tries,
the mount shut down and, once its persistent reservation was gone, withdrew
itself. A phantom is the wire having lost a grant the cache still believes in,
so a shot now releases the inode's grant on the wire behind the cache and lets
the unchanged check read the wire for real; only a genuine sample may demote,
as before. The consumption line carries the release result and the re-sampled
answer. The harness's positive name is now a subdirectory, because a regular
file in the creating node's own affine allocation group exits revalidation
through the affine fast path before the epoch stamp and never enters the epoch
fast path at all; it makes that name durable before arming so the peer can
remove it; and it saves both nodes' full kernel window to its evidence
directory and judges health on that, case-insensitively, including wedge,
withdraw and lock-timeout lines, since the previous verdict pattern read zero
across the shutdown it had caused.

## 0.75.35 — 2026-09-05 — Verification instrumentation for the phantom-grant bail

The phantom-grant bail, which demotes a cached exclusive directory grant to
null when its backing record turns out not to exist, gained its epoch bump
in 0.66.1 but the branch had never been observed to run, so the fix was a
landed patch and not a verified one. Three debug module parameters and one
counter make the path forceable and its effect observable without touching
the lock state directly. The injection, gated on one directory inode and an
atomic one-shot budget, makes the backing-record check answer "not held"
exactly once, so the existing code reaches the bail on its own. A one-shot
pause after the bail holds the node in the authority gap so a peer can
change the namespace inside it. A read-only counter records how often a
directory serve reached the check at all, which is the denominator that a
probe count alone never gave. A per-directory trace names every zero-I/O
dentry blessing under that directory with the stamp and the epoch it
matched, which is what lets a harness prove a dentry was fast-path valid
before the grant was lost and is not afterwards. The bail line now also
prints the epoch and the source line that advanced it. A new two-node
harness drives the whole sequence and asserts the epoch advanced, the
cached positive and negative dentries stopped taking the fast path, and the
node's lookups reflect the peer's changes.

## 0.75.34 — 2026-09-05 — The periodic log cover runs inside the superblock summary critical section

Since 0.64.30 the clustered summary counters in the on-disk superblock are
written only inside a cluster-wide critical section: the dedicated summary
lock, a recount from uncached allocation-group headers, the cover, the
device flush and a durable re-read. That section had a hole. Every node's
periodic log cover, which stamps the log tail by logging the superblock
once its log is idle, folded that node's private lazy counters into the
image and let the AIL write the whole sector whenever it got to it, with no
lock at all. Measured on 32 nodes and again on the two-node TCP rig: an
idle peer's one-second cover landed unlocked inside another node's
critical section every time, so the lock was not exclusive against all
writers of the sector.

The clustered cover now runs inside the same section. It takes a node-local
mutex without waiting, since a busy section belongs to this node's final
sync or freeze cover and a skipped period costs nothing, then the cluster
summary lock, reads the durable counters at the coherence point and logs
those instead of the private view, commits synchronously, writes the sector
itself so the AIL item is retired before the unlock, flushes the device and
unlocks. Any failure skips the cover; there is never an unlocked write. The
final sync in put_super and the freeze cover take the same mutex, which is
what keeps the two entrants on one node from both holding a lock that is
granted per node. The rare superblock loggers that run inside their own
transactions and cannot take the cluster lock, such as quota changes, grow
and on-line feature upgrades, now log the durable counters read coherently
instead of the private ones, and each such write is named in the kernel
log. A two-node harness parks one node inside its section while the peer
covers at one-second intervals and requires the peer to submit no unlocked
superblock write. The log worker's period, which upstream exposes only as
the sysctl under fs/xfs and this fork's fs/mxfs table does not surface on
the rig, is now also the module parameter syncd_centisecs, so the harness
can make the peer cover every second.

## 0.75.33 — 2026-09-05 — A namespace operation denied by a refused victim's grant fails instead of committing without one

Since 0.75.25 the lock manager has denied an acquire whose grant is held by
a dead node whose slice replay was terminally refused, the same way it
denies one held by a node in blocked recovery. The filesystem's entry
gates, which turn such a denial into an EIO before any transaction, did not
know that: they short-circuit on a count of blocked recoveries that
excluded refused victims, and the lock hook that receives the denial
returns nothing. Measured on the two-node TCP rig (lap s518i): after the
victim's replay was refused, a mkdir at the root, whose exclusive grant the
dead victim still held, was denied three times, the hook returned, and the
directory entry was committed with no cluster grant and reported success.
Since 0.75.30 the refused victim leaves the membership at the verdict, and
on a two-node cluster that makes the survivor a sole survivor: measured on
0.75.32 (lap s520d), four directories the dead victim held exclusively were
denied at the verdict for the lookups already in flight, and every create
under them in the four seconds before the departure purge retired those
grants then succeeded through the single-node bypass, with the directory at
mode NL and both authority sensors silent because they are guarded by the
same single-node predicate.

Two changes close it. The entry gates' short-circuit now also counts
refused victims, so both the pre-lock gate and the post-lock backstop see
the dead holder and answer EIO until the purge retires the grant. And the
lock hook's denial now latches on the inode; the backstop that runs right
after the lock, still before any transaction dirt, refuses the operation on
that latch when the inode has no authority at all, which covers a holder
table that lives on a remote master this node cannot read. The latch is
cleared by every grant install and by the backstop itself whenever an
admission has happened since the denial, including the single-node bypass,
so no directory can be left refusing for the rest of the mount.

The two-node death harness's early arm no longer depends on which node
happens to master the root: the survivor pre-creates seven directories and
opens a directory fd on each and on the root before the writer starts, the
victim takes a sticky exclusive grant on each and checkpoints, and at the
kill one thread per target creates relative to its fd, so no path walk
touches the root and every acquire is in flight across the verdict. The arm
requires at least one denial, at least one EIO inside the window, and zero
creates committed under a frozen grant. The harness also treats a directory
committed without exclusive authority, or an inode logged without it, as a
failure on every lap.

## 0.75.32 — 2026-09-05 — The block allocator skips a quarantined allocation group

The same shape as 0.75.31, one layer down. When an extent allocation walks
the allocation groups looking for space, each group's cluster lock is taken
before the group is examined, and the quarantine gate on that lock answers
EIO for a quarantined group, which ended the walk. Measured on the two-node
TCP rig with AG 1 quarantined and the survivor's own AG 0 filled by one
large preallocation: the walk left AG 0, met the gate on AG 1, and the
preallocation failed EIO with twenty-two healthy groups behind it. The
group-iterating walk now skips a quarantined group the way it skips a full
one. Allocations that name a specific group, which is only ever a group an
existing in-domain object already lives in, do not go through that walk and
still meet the gate. The two-node death harness gained an arm that fills
the survivor's group past its end and maps the resulting extents to their
groups, so the wrap is observed rather than assumed; a probe line names
each group the walk leaves out.

Also in this version, the board's readiness gate no longer convicts a node
on one snapshot of an mxfs worker in uninterruptible sleep. Every msleep
and every synchronous platter read is such a sleep for the milliseconds it
lasts, and the gate failed two healthy two-node boards on exactly that (a
worker in msleep on 2026-09-04, a worker in a pipelined block read on
2026-09-05). The deadlock it exists to catch does not move, so the gate now
samples twice, two seconds apart, and reports only a task found in
uninterruptible sleep at both samples on the same wait channel; a transient
sighting is logged to the kernel ring instead.

## 0.75.31 — 2026-09-05 — The inode allocator skips a quarantined allocation group

Under an AG-scoped quarantine the rest of the filesystem is meant to stay
in service, but a directory create in an untouched parent could still fail.
The inode allocator walks the allocation groups from a start it picks per
node, or from a spreading rotor once a node is alone, and it takes each
group's cluster lock before looking inside. The quarantine gate on that
lock answers EIO for a quarantined group, and the walk ends on any error
other than the "peer holds it" retry code, so the whole create failed
instead of moving on. Measured on the two-node TCP rig right after the
0.75.30 fix: with AG 1 quarantined and AG 0 spared, the survivor's first
root mkdir failed EIO in one millisecond because the rotor pointed at AG 1;
the next seven landed in AGs 2 to 8 and succeeded. The walk now skips a
quarantined group the way it skips a full one, and a filesystem-wide
quarantine answers EIO before the walk starts rather than sweeping every
group into the gate and reporting no space. The gate itself is unchanged
and still refuses an explicit in-domain object. The two-node death harness
now attributes a failed mkdir to the group named by the gate's own line, so
this shape counts as an in-domain refusal instead of an out-of-domain loss.

## 0.75.30 — 2026-09-05 — A terminally refused victim leaves the membership view

On the TCP transport a victim whose journal-slice replay was terminally
refused stayed a lease member for the life of every survivor's mount, and
therefore stayed master of its hash share of every lock resource. The
refusal path imported the verdict, purged the victim's out-of-domain grants
on the CAW slot table only, and released the recovery lease; it never
unregistered the victim, never remastered its pages and never ran the
ledger takeover, because the terminal-quarantine design had settled what
happens to the victim's held grants (frozen until repair and remount) and
said nothing about mastership. Measured on the two-node TCP rig with an
AG-scoped refusal that spared AG 0: the survivor could not create anything
at the root. Eight of eight mkdirs timed out at about fifteen seconds each,
with sixty-eight dead-master denials for the freshly allocated inodes,
every one of whose lock pages the refused dead node still mastered.

The refusal now takes the victim out of the view the way a completed
recovery does: identity retired, lease unregistered, active view refreshed
so its pages move to the survivors, and the certified page takeover on the
departure worker. What differs is the purge. The victim's ledger records
inside the quarantined domain must stay frozen, so the recovery purge and
the table purge gained selective forms driven by a new DLM oracle that
names a refused owner and classifies each of its records against the
verdict's AG mask through the same closure classifier the CAW purge uses.
Only records provably outside the mask are retired, by node id and by the
victim's heartbeat slot so its shared bits go too; everything else imports
as a frozen blocker wherever a page is activated, and the page-takeover
path no longer marks a refused authority as purged. A filesystem-wide
verdict retires nothing and only moves the pages. A survivor on a higher
heartbeat slot may act as the bootstrap node for the takeover once a lower
slot's recovery is terminally refused, since nothing will ever complete it.
The ledger's purge line reports whether a walk was selective and how many
records it kept.

## 0.75.29 — 2026-09-05 — A DLM wait no longer spins unkillably when a signal is pending

The kernel platform layer's condition waits slept interruptibly and
returned "signalled" whenever the sleep ended early. A task with a signal
pending never sleeps in that state, and every DLM caller loops on its own
predicate, so a signal arriving during a lock wait turned the wait into a
100 percent CPU spin in the kernel that the signal itself could never end,
because the task never returned to user space to take it. Measured on the
two-node TCP rig: the AG-mask probe's own ten second alarm landed inside a
one second lock wait on the root directory, whose exclusive grant the dead
victim still held; the probe spun for over thirty minutes with SIGALRM
pending, and every other root operation parked behind its acquire. The two
wait primitives now sleep uninterruptibly when a signal is already pending,
so the wait honors its interval and returns through the normal path where
the signal is delivered. A signal arriving mid-sleep costs one early
return and the next lap sleeps properly. tests/dlm_wait_signal.sh sends a
termination signal to a reader blocked behind a peer's paused release and
asserts the reader neither spins nor survives the release.

## 0.75.28 — 2026-09-05 — A requester waits behind a live holder instead of shutting itself down

When an inode acquire had spent its retry budget (three attempts of sixty
one-second retries on the TCP transport), the acquire path treated the
timeout as a local coordination failure and shut the requester's filesystem
down, unless the domain was quarantined or a peer's recovery was pending.
On the two-node TCP rig the first death-and-rejoin lap of the membership
purge harness measured that arm on an innocent reader: the survivor held
the file with its release drain paused for 323 seconds, the rejoined peer's
md5sum waited 184 seconds, shut its mount down with an in-memory corruption
report, withdrew, was fenced for the withdraw, and the holder released
normally 140 seconds later. A live holder's release ends when its drain
ends or when it dies; destroying the requester's mount hastens neither.
The DLM now answers whether the party a timed-out request waits on is
live: on TCP the resource's remote master must be a lease member whose
identity is not retired and whose recovery is neither blocked nor refused,
or a locally mastered resource must have granted holders that all pass the
same test; on CAW every on-disk holder must be heartbeating, the oracle the
wait extension already used. When it is, the acquire path parks with
backoff, logs one P-LKWAIT-LIVE line per exhausted budget so a slow release
stays visible, and re-asks. Nothing live to wait for keeps the fail-fast
shutdown. The bounded second-inode acquire of a lock-two pair and the
recovery-context requeue return before this classifier, unchanged.

The death-and-rejoin harness also measured wrongly in two places, fixed
here: an md5sum error line was reduced to the two hex characters it
contained and counted as a returned digest, and the pause-end check raced
the pause, reading the holder's log seconds before the end line landed.
The order is now decided on the holder's own clock, and only a 32-character
digest counts as a read. A dedicated harness, tests/live_holder_wait.sh,
exercises the slow-release wait without a node death.

The AG-mask arm of the death oracle pre-created the victim's directory
wherever the first mkdir landed, which was allocation group 0, so the
victim's transactions put AG 0 into the mask and every probe was refused at
the root lookup before it could reach a directory of its own. The arm now
creates candidate directories until one lands outside AG 0 and confines
the victim to that one, reading the superblock geometry before the kill.

## 0.75.27 — 2026-09-05 — Measuring what an AG-scoped refusal leaves out of service on TCP

Harness and tool changes only; the module is unchanged in behaviour. The
death oracle gains an AG-scoped refusal arm: the survivor is told to refuse
every multi-item transaction of the victim's slice, the victim's writes are
confined to a directory the survivor created, and after the verdict the
survivor performs mkdir and create pairs at the root with every operation
under a ten second alarm. Each directory is mapped to its allocation group
from the superblock geometry and the outcomes are split into inside the
quarantined mask, where EIO is the design, and outside it, where every
operation must succeed. That split is the measurement the mastership record
needs: on the TCP transport a terminally refused victim keeps its share of
resource mastership for the life of the mount, so out-of-mask resources it
masters cannot be granted. To make the mapping possible without XFS tooling,
which cannot read the enveloped superblock, chk_mxfs now prints agblocks and
the two log2 fields in its verbose superblock line. The admission matrix
prints the device it mounts: run by hand without the device exported it
mounted the multipath default and every row failed in zero seconds.

## 0.75.26 — 2026-09-05 — The elected replayer retires a recovered slot's tracking with the victim

When a survivor completed a dead peer's recovery it kept that peer's
incarnation as the heartbeat slot's tracked tenancy: the monitor's
recovered-slot path retires the tracking, but only on a node that learns of
the completion by seeing the zeroed sector, and the elected replayer clears
its own pending marker first, so on a two-node cluster the survivor never
took that path (22 laps, zero times). The next node to claim the slot in
the same filesystem generation, typically the recovered node rebooting and
remounting, was then read as "the dead node restarted": a second death of
an identity recovered minutes earlier, a refused recovery pending on a slot
a live member occupied, that member's goodbye ignored, forty seconds of
membership-view skew and a REMASTER storm, and once a rejoining mount that
exhausted its root-inode retries and shut down. The completion path now
retires the recovered incarnation's tracking itself, adopting a successor
that already holds the slot. The death harness gains a same-generation
rejoin arm, which the chain had never exercised because every death lap
was followed by a re-mkfs, and the admission matrix now saves both nodes'
kernel windows around its rejoin.

## 0.75.25 — 2026-09-05 — A request to a terminally refused dead master fails fast

After a refused foreign replay the victim keeps its lease membership, and
so its mastership of half the lock space on a two-node cluster, until
remount; that is the terminal-quarantine design. The acquire path only
knew to fail fast for a master in blocked recovery, so the survivor's
unmount sent its final SB-summary lock request to the sealed dead node 60
times over 42 seconds (measured with the unmount task's stack sampled
every two seconds: the whole wait was in the lock retry loop under
mxfs_sb_summary_lock), got a transport error, and then took the dirty
departure it was always going to take. The quarantine import now records
the refused victim in the v5 context, the recovery-blocked predicate the
DLM consults before every send answers for that node too, and the
unmount reaches the same dirty departure without the retries. The
departure stays dirty by design: the summary counters cannot be sealed
under a lock nobody can grant, so the slot is retained and the next mount
recovers this node's slice.

## 0.75.24 — 2026-09-05 — The blocked-holder refusal names itself

The entry gate that refuses an operation because a grant on its resource is
held by a dead node in blocked recovery logged nothing, while the
dead-master arm added in 0.75.21 did; which node masters the root inode
changes from lap to lap, so the same probe was sometimes refused with no
line at all. The holder arm now logs P-RBLK-COVERS-DEAD-HOLDER. No behavior
change.

## 0.75.23 — 2026-09-05 — A release to a sealed dead master is not sent either

After a refused foreign replay the victim stays sealed for the life of the
survivor's mount, since the quarantine is terminal, and the survivor's
unmount sent the release of every grant that node mastered to it: 34
releases, four sends each, 19 never acknowledged, the unmount parked five
to ten seconds in the acknowledgement wait, long enough for the harness's
teardown to treat the node as not releasing the module. The release path
now skips a sealed master the same way it skips a blocked one, and the
skip line names which of the two applied.

## 0.75.22 — 2026-09-05 — A release to a blocked dead master is not sent

The survivor's unmount while a dead peer's recovery is blocked spent eight
seconds in the departure's wire release: each remaining grant mastered by
the dead node was sent three times, and the un-acknowledged releases then
held the acknowledgement wait for its whole budget. The release path now
asks the same recovery-blocked predicate about the master that the acquire
path asks, drops the local mirror without sending when the master is a
blocked dead node, and leaves the frozen grant to the recovery purge that
retires it when that recovery completes.

## 0.75.21 — 2026-09-05 — The entry gate covers a resource mastered by a blocked dead node

0.75.19 made the acquire fail fast for a resource whose master is a dead
node in blocked recovery, but the synchronous entry gate that turns such a
verdict into an EIO for the operation only answered for resources mastered
locally. A stat of the victim's directory on the survivor therefore ran
its acquire, had it refused, and then served the cached attributes with a
success return, while the kernel had logged the refusal for that very
call. The gate now answers the same verdict for a resource mastered by the
blocked node as for a grant held by one, so the operation fails at the
gate instead of proceeding without a grant.

## 0.75.20 — 2026-09-05 — A departing node's hand-off announces the departure

The 0.75.18 and 0.75.19 re-checks narrowed the window in which a survivor
prepared a page back to the node that had just handed it over, but the
window was never a race in the ledger write. A clean departure hands its
pages out before its goodbye, mapped over the membership without itself;
until that goodbye arrives the survivor's membership still names the
departing node as the owner of those pages, so the survivor treated each
hand-off as a relay and its eager pass handed the page straight back on
the next half-second tick. The one recurrence in twelve departures on
0.75.19 is that cadence: the tick landed between the hand-off and the
goodbye.

The hand-off message now carries a departing flag, set on every FROZEN a
departing node sends. From the first flagged hand-off the receiver records
the sender as departing and maps hand-off routing over the membership
without departing members, which is the mapping the departing node itself
used: the page is served on arrival, the eager pass never selects a
departing node as a target, and the hand-off re-check refuses one that
was selected before the announcement arrived. The entry is dropped when
the goodbye removes the node from the membership. The flag lives in a
padding byte, so the message size and the protocol generation are
unchanged; a receiver that ignores it behaves as before.

## 0.75.19 — 2026-09-05 — A resource mastered by a node in blocked recovery fails fast too

Reproduced with the umount-while-recovery-blocked arm: the survivor's
umount(8) was not in umount(2) at all but in the statx it issues on the
mountpoint, parked in the root inode's DLM acquire, and the harness's own
stat of the victim's directory parked the same way instead of failing fast.
A dead member leaves the membership view only when its recovery completes,
so while that recovery is blocked it still masters its share of the ledger
pages; a request for one of those resources was sent to it, retried to
-ENOTCONN, and the central gate parked it as "recovery pending" because
only a live master's explicit deny carried the blocked verdict. The remote
path now asks the recovery-blocked predicate about the master before it
sends and answers the same fail-fast verdict (-EHOSTDOWN, then EIO to the
operation) that a blocked holder already produced, logged as
P-RBLK-DENY-DEAD-MASTER.

Also corrects the 0.75.18 hand-off re-check, which used the wrong mapping
for a departing node: that node hands its pages out over the view without
itself, while the general owner lookup still names it, so the re-check
refused every depart hand-off (measured on three laps: a stale-target
refusal on every clean leave, one page left behind each time, the root
inode's page stranded under the departed authority until the successor's
takeover, and every rejoin during a held purge taking fourteen seconds).
A departing node now requires only that its target is still a live member;
the owner equality applies to the view-change pass alone.

## 0.75.18 — 2026-09-05 — A page hand-off re-reads its target after the freeze drain

Measured once in eight rejoin cycles on the two-node TCP rig: the survivor
activated the pages its departing peer handed it, processed the peer's
goodbye, dropped it from the membership, and in the same second its
view-change pass prepared one of those pages back to the departed
incarnation, stamped with the new view's configuration. The pass had
computed the page's owner before the goodbye arrived, and the freeze drain
between that computation and the ledger write can wait seconds. Nothing
consumes a page prepared to a retired identity; it sat there until the
departure purge marked the identity and the pass retargeted it thirteen
seconds later under the purge-delay knob, while the successor's mount
parked its allocation-group request on it for sixty retries twice and
mounted in fourteen seconds. The hand-off now re-reads the owner under the
current view immediately before writing the prepared record and refuses a
stale target (P-TAUTH-HANDOFF-STALE-TARGET, leaving the page frozen for
the next pass), and the pass retargets a prepared page whose target has
left the view without waiting for the purge to mark it.

## 0.75.17 — 2026-09-05 — A release acknowledgement passes the teardown quiesce

The 0.75.16 lap released both leftover grants on every clean leave and no
successor met a residue any more, but each leave then sat the whole three
second acknowledgement bound: the receive callback's teardown quiesce, which
drops every message but the goodbye once the mount flag clears, was
discarding the master's RELEASE_ACK for the departing node's own release.
Processing that acknowledgement only retires a pending-release record — no
lock state changes, nothing re-enters the filesystem, no master work — so
it now passes the quiesce. The ack wait's timeout line names the releases
still outstanding (resource, release id, sends, master) so a genuinely lost
acknowledgement can be told from a dropped one.

## 0.75.16 — 2026-09-05 — A clean departure releases its remaining grants through the DLM before it says goodbye

The 0.75.15 census measured, on every clean leave of the rejoin harness,
exactly two shared grants freed without a wire release — the root
directory's and one more directory's — one of them mastered by the peer.
The peer's departure purge then cleared nothing at all: by the time it ran
(held fifteen seconds by the harness, about four seconds naturally) a
successor had claimed the departed heartbeat slot, and a live slot's bits
are the successor's, so the slot half of the purge is dropped. The bit
stayed on the platter until the successor imported it on its own slot as
residue, or until a master attributed it to the successor and refused the
successor's first exclusive request as a blocked upgrade. The clean
departure now releases every grant still in its table through the DLM
before the goodbye — the same collect-then-unlock walk the withdrawal path
uses: a LOCK_RELEASE to a remote master, a ledger transition on a local one
— and waits for the acknowledgements as it already did; P-RELALL-WIRED
reports the count and what remained. Nothing is left for the purge, so no
rejoin timing can meet a predecessor's bit; the purge stays as the backstop
for a death and for an unacknowledged release. The debug parameter
depart_wire_release=0 restores the old shape so the planted phantom lap
that verifies the blocked-upgrade heal can still be run.

## 0.75.15 — 2026-09-05 — A clean departure names the grants it leaves to the peers' purge

Measurement only. On the TCP transport a clean unmount frees the grants
still in its lock table (the root inode's shared grant at least: the DLM is
torn down before xfs_unmountfs reclaims the inode cache) without a wire
release, by design leaving them to the survivors' departure purge. That
purge is asynchronous, so a successor claiming the same heartbeat slot
within a few seconds meets those shared bits on the platter and the master
attributes them to the new occupant (the phantom of the 0908 record). The
unmount path now logs a census of what it frees — P-RELALL-LEFT with held /
shared / exclusive counts and up to twelve P-RELALL-LEFT-ENTRY lines naming
resource, mode, state and master — so the survivor's purge count and a
successor's imported residue can be matched against it before the release
path is changed.

## 0.75.14 — 2026-09-05 — A page taken over for this node has the departed authority's records retired at activation

The purge that runs before a takeover walks only the pages this node
already masters, so a page that becomes this node's BY the takeover keeps
the departed incarnation's records until something imports it, and the
import is lazy (the first decision on that page). Measured with the peer's
join held twelve seconds after the sole node's remount (the new delayed arm
of sameboot_remount): the remounting node took five of its predecessor's
pages over for itself, the next view change handed two of them to the
joining peer with this node as both writer and authority, so no takeover
marker travelled with them, and the peer imported the predecessor's
exclusive grant on allocation group 0 as a live blocker; its mount queued
behind a holder that no longer existed for the whole bound. The platter
census (tools/tauth_page_auth.py --entries) showed the record still on the
page after the takeover.

A page activated for this node by a takeover now has that authority's
records retired on that one page at once (a per-page variant of the
recovery purge, node id only) and is imported immediately, so this node's
own slot residue is released as well, before any decision or hand-on.
P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-RETIRE reports the page, the authority, the records
cleared and the import result. The delayed arm is step 12 of the chain
driver; tests/rejoin_residue.sh's held arm now rejoins with a fresh node id
(a departed id is a retired identity to the peer, and a rejoin under it is
ignored until fenced). Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.13 — 2026-09-04 — The parked-page line names a stall, not the first pass of an ask

On 0.75.12 every join printed exactly one parked-page line: the first pass
through the branch, with the request already in flight and answered within
a hundred milliseconds. The line now prints only when an ask has gone a
whole half-second cadence unanswered, which is the condition the line
describes. tests/rejoin_residue.sh: the random node id can exceed the old
upper pinned id, which made the parity arms unrunnable one lap in fifteen;
the upper pinned id is now one below the unknown-node sentinel. When the
blocked-upgrade arm fires on a plain rejoin, the harness now also asserts
that it healed in one lap with the unconditional release delivered.

## 0.75.12 — 2026-09-04 — The blocked-upgrade arm releases a phantom that lives only on the remote master

On the TCP transport a node that rejoins into the same heartbeat slot within
seconds can be denied its first exclusive request on the root inode as a
blocked upgrade, because the master of that inode's ledger page imported the
predecessor incarnation's shared holder bit and, the slot map by then naming
the successor, attributed it to the successor. Measured on 0.75.9
(rejoin_residue arm 2): sixty-five denials in a row, the arm's release
returning nothing to the master because the local table held no entry, then
the livelock guard shut the filesystem down. The same arm on the previous
build happened to import before the slot map changed and resolved through a
dead-holder BAST in nineteen seconds; the race decides which shape appears.

The arm now also sends the mirror-bypassing unconditional release to the
master when the local table holds no entry of any state, through the inode
flavour of the orphan-grant NAK the allocation-group path already had. The
master retires the imported record with a ledger transition, so the bit
leaves the platter and the next import cannot bring it back. The release
probe records both return codes. Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.11 — 2026-09-04 — The bootstrap node takes a page over for a requester whose incarnation its slot map cannot name yet

Measured on 0.75.10 (sameboot_remount arm 2, the peer joining three seconds
after the sole node's own remount): the bootstrap node declined the peer's
page requests for two seconds because the incarnation lookup for the peer
returned unknown, its heartbeat monitor not having read the peer's slot yet.
The request message already names the sender's incarnation; the per-page
takeover now uses it for the view owner when the slot map cannot. Patch
bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.10 — 2026-09-04 — A joiner whose own bootstrap election is unsettled asks the whole view for a departed authority's page

Measured on 0.75.9 (sameboot_remount arm 1, three laps): the joiner still
parked for about two seconds on a page of the last leaver's predecessor
before the bootstrap node took it over on demand. The parked-page line now
records the joiner's bootstrap lookup, and in seventeen of eighteen parks it
named the joiner itself: the lowest-live-slot election counts a slot live
only after the local heartbeat monitor has read its beat, one heartbeat
interval after the claim, so for that window the joiner believed no other
node could be the bootstrap node and sent no request. The earlier guess,
that the bootstrap node could not yet name the joiner's incarnation, was
