wrong: the bootstrap node declined nothing and served the first request it
received at once.

While the election names the requester itself yet the requester is not the
bootstrap node, the request goes to every node in the view on the same
half-second cadence. The real bootstrap node takes the page over for the
requester; the others answer NOT_OWNER naming the departed authority, which
keeps the cadence. Two probes stay: P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-REQUEST-DECLINED names
why a bootstrap node answered NOT_OWNER (authority not yet purged, or the
per-page takeover's return code), and P109-EDEADLK-NL-RELEASE records what
the blocked-upgrade arm's release returned. Patch bump: no format or
protocol change.

## 0.75.9 — 2026-09-04 — A settled predecessor's ledger page is taken over on demand for the request that needs it

On the TCP transport the pages a departed authority owned were transferred
only by the departure worker's bulk takeover: a purge scan and a takeover
scan over every ledger page, about eight seconds at 26426 pages over iSCSI.
Until that pass reached a page, every request routed to it parked and spent
its retry budget waiting. Measured on the 2-node TCP rig (sameboot_remount
arm 2 on 0.75.8): the node that remounted in the same boot as the last
leaver settled its own predecessor and became the bootstrap node, its
unmount two seconds later needed the superblock summary lock on a page
still under that predecessor, the request parked sixty times over six
seconds, and the bulk pass prepared the page one second after the budget
ran out. The clean unmount was recorded dirty, the heartbeat slot and the
persistent-reservation key were retained, and the next mount in the same
boot was refused. A joiner mastering such a page parked the same way and
asked nobody, because the parked branch only ever asked the departed
authority itself.

The per-page transition the bulk pass makes is now a helper the bulk pass
and two on-demand paths share: the bootstrap node's parked request takes
the page over itself the moment the authority is in its purged set, and a
peer's parked request asks the bootstrap node, whose FREEZE_REQ handler
takes the page over for the requester once the authority is purged there
and answers NOT_OWNER naming that authority until then. A NOT_OWNER that
names an authority out of view no longer resets the ask cadence, so the
wait is one request per half second rather than one per retry. The bulk
pass counts a page another path took over meanwhile as done, not skipped.
P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-ONDEMAND names each page, its departed authority, the
owner it went to and the path. Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.8 — 2026-09-04 — A page taken over from a departed authority no longer imports that authority's grants as live blockers

With 0.75.7 the remounting node takes over the last leaver's ledger pages,
and hands the pages the new view assigns to the joiner straight to it.
Those pages still hold the departed incarnation's ACTIVE records, and the
knowledge that the incarnation departed lived only on the node that settled
it. Measured on the 2-node TCP rig (sameboot_remount arm 1 on 0.75.7): the
joiner imported the last leaver's exclusive grant on allocation group 0 as
a ledger-backed blocker, queued its own mount's exclusive request behind a
holder that no longer exists, timed out against it a dozen times and sat in
the DLM wait five minutes on; the last leaver's node id was in the
remounting node's purged set and in nobody else's.

A page prepared to a node by anyone other than its authority is a takeover:
only the certified successor writes one, and only after the departed
record is settled and purged. The receiver now records that authority as
purged before activating the page, both when the FROZEN message arrives
(sender differs from the named authority) and when the parked request reads
the PREPARED image off the platter first (writer differs from authority),
so the import retires the departed records instead of installing them
(P-TAUTH-DEPARTED-AUTH names the page, the authority and the path).

The purge that follows is by node id only when the departed node's
heartbeat slot is already held by a different live incarnation
(P-TAUTH-PURGE-SLOT-LIVE): the slot half of a purge clears that slot's
shared holder bits on every page this node masters, and those bits are now
the successor's live grants. tests/sameboot_remount.sh arm 1 asserts zero
imported blockers naming the remounting node's predecessor and zero holder
timeouts on the joiner. Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.7 — 2026-09-04 — A mount that settles a departed incarnation's record takes over its ledger pages

After a whole-cluster clean stop the last node to leave still owns, on the
platter, every authority-ledger page the era touched: its own pages, and
the pages every earlier leaver handed to it. Nobody survives to take them
over, and the next era's first mount never named that incarnation, so the
pages stayed ACTIVE under a dead authority. Measured on the 2-node TCP rig
(sameboot_remount arm 1, 0.75.5 and the 0.75.6 probe): 12 of 26426 pages,
the root inode's and allocation group 0's among them. The lone remount did
not notice because a single node bypasses the DLM; the first join then
parked the joiner's mount on those pages for 80 s, denied the survivor's
first lookup the same pages sixty times over four attempts, and the
survivor shut its filesystem down and was fenced.

The place that knows the departed identity is the settle of its heartbeat
record. A TCP mount now runs the departure trio (ledger purge, table purge,
page takeover) for every incarnation whose record it settles: this boot's
own predecessor at P305, a peer's RETIRE_PENDING record proven retired by
the retire worker, and the records the admission barrier settles. A settle
that happens before the ledger is attached is deferred and flushed once the
departure worker starts. A departed incarnation that carries this mount's
own node id (a pinned id) runs the takeover only, since the two purges key
on the node id and would purge this mount's own records. A settled record's
takeover that finds this mount is not the bootstrap node is reported
(P-TAUTH-TAKEOVER-NOTBOOT) rather than skipped in silence, and a departure
already run for the same incarnation is not run again
(P-DEPART-DONE-ALREADY). Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.6 — 2026-09-04 — A parked ledger page names its unreachable authority

When a request lands on an authority-ledger page whose durable authority is
a node that is not in the membership view, the page acquire parks the
request and the requester's only trace is 'prepare=60' (local master) or
sixty REMASTER denials (remote). Measured on the 2-node TCP rig after a
whole-cluster clean stop and same-boot remount (sameboot_remount arm 1 on
0.75.5): the joiner's mount looped 80 s on allocation group 0 and the root
inode, the survivor's first lookup was denied the same pages sixty times
four attempts running and shut its filesystem down, and the joiner then
fenced it. Reading the platter by hand showed 12 of 26426 pages ACTIVE
under the survivor's previous incarnation, the last node to leave the
previous era; nothing had taken them over. The parking branch now logs
P-TAUTH-PAGE-PARKED with the page, its authority tuple, the node it would
ask, whether that node is in view or purged, and whether this node is the
bootstrap node, capped per boot. tools/tauth_page_auth.py reads the region
from the device and prints the page-authority census that this diagnosis
needed. tests/sameboot_remount.sh gains an ARMS selector and asserts, on
arm 1, zero parked pages and zero shutdown on either node plus the
predecessor takeover on the remounting node.

Also in this build: an inode acquire answered with a blocked-upgrade
refusal while the inode layer holds nothing (mode NL, no release in flight,
no cluster route) no longer enters the self-demote wait, which had no waker
when the inode was not yet in the perag radix tree (the s509d mount in D
state, 63 re-drives over 180 s). The table entry is a phantom of this
node's own making; the arm logs P109-EDEADLK-NL, releases it through the
DLM and restarts the acquire from NL, shutting the filesystem down after 64
laps rather than looping. Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.5 — 2026-09-04 — A slot's successor no longer inherits its predecessor's shared grants at page import

A shared holder bit in the authority ledger names a heartbeat slot, not an
incarnation. When a node leaves cleanly and rejoins into the same slot
within a few seconds, the view change hands ledger pages to the rejoined
node before the old master's departure worker purges the departed
incarnation's records; the purge then skips those pages as no longer its
own, and the successor, which never received the goodbye, purges nothing.
At import the predecessor's bit resolves to the successor itself and is
installed as a grant it holds. Its first EX request on that resource (the
root inode, in xfs_iget on the mount path) is then a blocked upgrade
against the peer's PR, the self-demote that follows has nothing to demote
and fires on an inode not yet in the radix tree, and the mount never
returns. Measured on the 2-node TCP rig on 0.75.4; the lap before it won
the race by two seconds.

The importer now recognises the residue by what this node knows about
itself: every grant of this incarnation has a local table entry or a
request in flight. A shared bit on the local slot with neither is released
through the ordinary local-master unlock, so the ledger transition retires
it and promotes anything waiting. An exclusive record on the local slot
under a different node id is purged by that node id, since no live node
shares a slot. A debug parameter, depart_purge_delay_ms, holds the
departure worker's purge so the race can be reproduced on demand. Patch
bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.4 — 2026-09-04 — The bootstrap outage scan no longer waits the dead window on a peer's clean release

With 0.75.3 the last node to leave remounts and settles its own record at
once, but its mount then sat the full dead window (64 s) in the bootstrap
survivor scan on the OTHER node's RETIRE_PENDING record, because the scan
counted every non-empty record as occupied and waited for one of them to
change. A clean release never heartbeats, so nothing about it changes on
its own: the wait ended either in a total-outage verdict (refusing the
mount when the record carried no fenceable identity) or, on the same-boot
harness, only because the peer happened to remount meanwhile. The scan now
counts only member-shaped records (ACTIVE, WITHDRAWN, RECOVERY_GUARD) as
occupied, matching the victim set it builds afterwards. The admission
barrier still holds on the pending record until its key is proven retired.
Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.3 — 2026-09-04 — A TCP mount settles this boot's own clean release the way a CAW mount has since sess451

The last node to leave a TCP cluster cleanly could not remount in the same
boot. A clean unmount leaves the node's heartbeat slot as a RETIRE_PENDING
record, consumable once its PR key is proven retired. With no peer left to
prove that, the same host remounted, reused its per-boot PR key, and the
claim path skipped the record (a RETIRE_PENDING slot is never claimed
fresh) and took another slot. Its own monitor then saw the old record with
a key that was PRESENT, its own, and could never retire it; the admission
barrier held, mount recovery looped 'slice slot=0 NOT replayed (-61)' for
27 rounds, and mount(8) was killed at 46 s. Every later mount by any node
then looped on that slot too. Measured on the 2-node QNAP rig, 0.75.1,
transport-conformance arms B and C.

The CAW mount branch has handled exactly this since sess451/452: it takes
the host-wide departure lock from REGISTER through P305, refuses beside a
quarantined worker, takes self-succession on a predecessor key, scans this
boot's own records, and settles a RETIRE_PENDING one of its own key with a
fresh registration proof before the slot claim. The TCP branch had none of
it and wired the retire machinery only after the claim. That sequence is
now ported to the TCP branch in the same order, and the retire machinery
(key-state lookups, probe thread, settle function, retire worker) is wired
before the claim on TCP as it is on CAW.

Also: the mount thread's immediate settle path asserted the departure mutex
but the admission-barrier rounds that call it run after the locked window
closed, so on TCP every such round was refused (P-PR-SETTLE-UNHELD, 27
times in the same log). It now takes the host-wide mutex itself when the
caller does not hold it, as every other local PROUT path already does.

Also: the departure worker now coalesces a request for the departed
incarnation it is running, not only one still queued. Measured on 0.75.2:
the clean-release observation arrived 4 s into the GOODBYE run of the same
departure and cost a second 8 s ledger pass for nothing.
Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.2 — 2026-09-04 — A peer's departure no longer runs the authority-ledger passes on the heartbeat or peer threads

Measured on the 2-node TCP rig (QNAP LUN, 26426-page ledger) with 0.75.1's
bulk takeover scan in place: one clean unmount and rejoin of the peer still
stalled the survivor's heartbeat monitor 18.6 s. The takeover scan was down
to 4 s, but it ran three times for two departures (the GOODBYE message and
the clean-release observation each asked for the same departed incarnation),
and the departed owner's ledger purge that precedes it loaded every page one
4 KiB read at a time on the heartbeat thread (the stall dump sat in that
read loop for 14 s). While the survivor was stalled the departing peer's own
final superblock-summary lock request exhausted its 60-retry budget parked
on a page still PREPARED for the peer's earlier incarnation, so a clean
unmount was recorded as a DIRTY departure with its heartbeat slot kept
active and its PR key retained: the next census then saw an unrecovered TCP
vote where the harness expected an empty table.

Two changes. The departed owner's purge now builds its candidate set from
one bulk pass over the ledger (the store's 16-page runs, both copies): a
page is visited only when its platter image is this authority's and an
active entry names the departed owner; an unreadable page stays a
candidate so the per-page path fails closed on it as before, and a failed
bulk pass falls back to the full walk. And the departure trio — ledger
purge, table purge, page takeover, in that order — moves off the heartbeat
thread (clean release, recovered) and the peer receive thread (GOODBYE)
onto a departure worker that runs one departure at a time and coalesces a
second request for the same departed incarnation. The callbacks keep only
the membership work that must be immediate: lease unregister, remaster,
beacon, notify. The elected replayer's recovery-complete path keeps its
synchronous trio because its held-failure gate must see the purge result
before the slot is republished. The worker stops, bounded, before the DLM
engine is destroyed and quarantines the context on a timeout exactly as a
stuck retire worker does. Each run reports its phases (P-DEPART-WORK) and
the purge reports its scan (pages, candidates, unreadable, scan and total
wall).

Also: the mount-time "DLM init" line printed the module-default transport
before the platter census could adopt the cluster's; it now names the
requested transport, and a second line after the census names the one the
mount runs. Patch bump: no format or protocol change.

## 0.75.1 — 2026-09-04 — A departed peer's ledger takeover no longer walks the whole ledger a page at a time on the heartbeat thread

When a peer leaves, the certified successor takes over the authority-ledger
pages the departed tenure still owned. That takeover ran on the disklock
heartbeat thread and decided every page by a fresh two-copy platter read,
one 4 KiB SCSI read per copy per page, across the entire ledger, to find the
handful of pages (usually none) that named the departed node. Measured on
the 2-node TCP rig on the QNAP LUN, first clean departure after the 0.75.0
transport-conformance harness started: the ledger there holds 26426 pages,
the walk ran twice (the GOODBYE and the clean-release observation), and the
heartbeat thread sat 48.8 s in its monitor stage inside that read loop, two
stall dumps deep in the page read. That is most of the way to the 62 s at
which the other node would have declared this one dead and fenced a live
survivor; and for the whole window every grant request from the node that
was rejoining failed its retry budget, so its mount could not take its root
directory's allocation group. Nothing in the takeover needed the per-page
walk: the store already reads the ledger in 16-page runs for the fence-time
manifest.

The takeover now builds its candidate set from one bulk pass over the ledger
(the store's run reads, both copies) into a bitmap, and keeps the per-page
fresh read only for the candidates, so each transition it makes is exactly
the one it made before. The takeover line reports the pages scanned, the
candidates, the unreadable pages and the scan wall so the cost stays
visible. Patch bump: one scan helper and a bitmap; no format or protocol
change.

## 0.75.0 — 2026-09-04 — A mount conforms to the DLM transport already on the platter

The kernel mount path selected its DLM transport from a module argument
alone: CAW unless force_transport=1. Nothing compared that choice with the
cluster being joined, although every discovery announce carries the sender's
transport and the userspace mount helper has adopted a peer's transport for
years. Observed on the QNAP LUN: a node loaded with default arguments joined
a live TCP cluster as a CAW node. Two lock managers then shared one
filesystem with no exclusion between them, the TCP survivor never recognised
the CAW node's clean departure, and the next TCP mount on that host stamped
the departed slot withdrawn and drove a recovery of a node that had left
cleanly, failing its own mount at the recovery barrier.

The transport is now a durable property of every heartbeat record: a new
bit in the crc-bound feature word says whether the tenure that wrote the
record ran TCP, stamped before the claim and never flipped. Before a mount
selects its transport it reads the slot table: with no votes it forms as
before; with votes for one side a default-argument mount adopts that
transport and a forced mount that disagrees is refused, because the
override applies only when forming; with votes for both sides the mount is
refused until an operator resolves the split. Unrecovered records vote too,
since a dead tenure's slice can only be recovered by the transport that
wrote it. The join gate treats a live incumbent on the other transport like
a protocol-incompatible one (the joiner withdraws), the monitor fences a
live intruder on the other transport, and a discovery announce on the other
transport is never registered as a peer. The protocol generation is bumped
to 19: an older build's records carry the bit clear, which would now read
as a CAW vote beside a live TCP node. Minor bump: a new on-disk feature bit
and a protocol-generation change.

## 0.74.2 — 2026-09-04 — A foreign-replay image refused by its write verifier fails the replay, not the survivor

A foreign-replay buffer write can fail three ways: the log-shutdown arm, an
I/O error at completion, and the write verifier refusing the image at
submission. The first two were routed by the buffer's foreign provenance to
the replay (refused slice, quarantined domain, survivor untouched). The
verifier arm shut the buffer's mount down unconditionally, and for a
foreign-replay buffer that mount is the survivor's. Measured on the 2-node
TCP death lap that found the drain defect above: the survivor logged
"Corruption of in-memory data ... Shutting down filesystem" 0.6 ms before the
provenance arm printed "failing the replay, NOT this mount", and withdrew.
The verifier arm now keeps the verifier's error and completes through the
same foreign routing, with no shutdown; a live-mount image keeps upstream
policy. A one-shot test knob corrupts the next outgoing foreign-replay image
so the arm can be exercised on demand. Patch bump: one branch and a knob.

## 0.74.1 — 2026-09-04 — A foreign replay keeps its recovered buffers in core until the whole slice has been applied

Upstream log recovery submits its recovered-buffer queue every time the
commit-record LSN changes, and that is safe upstream only because the
on-disk-LSN veto never lets an image older than the platter into the queue.
The untrusted (foreign-slice) replay overrides that veto for token-admitted
AG and inode-class images, since the stamp on the platter may be another
node's slice number. The override was argued idempotent because the slice's
later images follow; they do, but the per-LSN drain wrote the older image
first. A buffer log item carries only the dirty 128-byte chunks of its
transaction, so on a two-transaction slice the tail transaction's leaf/tail
chunk of a block-format directory (count N) was written next to the platter's
newer data chunks (entries N+1..N+k): the dir3 write verifier refused it, the
survivor's own mount was shut down by the verifier arm, and the dead node's
whole domain was quarantined with every acknowledged file unreadable. Measured
on the QNAP LUN, 2 nodes on the TCP transport, first dirty-death lap after
nine passing laps that had applied the identical override on a luckier chunk
alignment.

An untrusted replay now leaves its queue alone at LSN changes and submits it
once at the end of the pass, so every image of the slice overlays in core in
LSN order before anything is written. No image is vetoed that upstream would
not veto: the stamp compared against is the one the platter copy already
carried, because no mid-pass write restamps it. The count of deferred drains
is reported on the replay completion line and the 2-node death oracle
requires it to be at least one whenever an override was applied. Patch bump:
one branch in the recovery ophdr path and one counter.

## 0.74.0 — 2026-09-04 — A fence that cannot be proved reaches a bounded, durable RECOVERY_BLOCKED state

When a dead node's fence attempt returned before submitting any command and
proved nothing, the prover re-drove the identical attempt forever on a 0.25
to 6 s backoff: no attempt cap, no wall-clock bound, no state an operator or
a peer could read, and every path operation on the survivor that needed the
dead node's grants waited out the whole acquire budget. Measured on the QNAP
LUN at 2 nodes on the TCP transport: 120 retries in 15 minutes and a mount
operation held for 892 s behind the dead node's root-directory grant.

The retry series is now bounded. Only attempts that ran to completion and
proved nothing advance it; after fence_blocked_after_ms (default 120 s, four
times the healthy certify time on this target class) with the backoff table
exhausted, the slot becomes RECOVERY_BLOCKED: a flag on the standing FENCING
descriptor written under the same attempt lease and cleared by the certify or
takeover CAS, reason FENCE_BLOCKED in the recovery_blocked debugfs file with
an operator action, and one log line. The attempt is still re-driven every
30 s, so a change in PR state completes the recovery on its own, and the
fence gate now reads the single_node_exclusive assertion live so an operator
can supply it to a running survivor. While a slot is blocked, an inode
operation whose grant is held by that dead node fails with EIO at once: the
DLM entry gate refuses the acquire, a locally mastered request that times out
behind such a holder returns EHOSTDOWN instead of re-queueing, a remote
master denies with a new wire code, and the central incarnation gate answers
EIO. The check is synchronous with the prover's state, so nothing is latched
per inode and the fail-fast lifts the moment the recovery purge lands. Grants
held by live nodes, or by dead nodes whose recovery is still in progress, are
untouched. The 2-node death harness gains an injected arm that refuses the
sole-survivor gate, asserts the bounded transition, the durable flag, the
debugfs reason, the fail-fast, and then the full recovery after the injection
is lifted. Minor bump: a new descriptor flag and a new wire deny code, both
additive.

## 0.73.3 — 2026-09-04 — The TCP death-checker thread idles interruptibly

The TCP grace-checker thread, which exists for the life of every TCP mount
and wakes every 500 ms, idled in the plain uninterruptible sleep. That parks
it in D state for almost all of its life: every TCP node carried a load
average of one at idle, and the readiness precondition row, whose D-state
probe exists to catch tasks wedged in I/O, failed on every 2-node TCP board
with the thread named in msleep. Measured on 0.73.2 on test1: five of five
samples a second apart showed the same thread in D state inside its sleep
from the death-checker function, load average 1.00 on an idle mount. The
always-on fence-retry worker and the disklock claim scanner already used the
interruptible sleep for exactly this reason; the death checker is the one
always-on worker that did not, and it runs only on TCP, so the CAW boards
never saw it. Patch bump: one idle wait in one thread.

## 0.73.2 — 2026-09-04 — A refused TCP mount joins its death-checker thread before freeing the context

Every mount-refusal arm on the TCP transport that ran after the deferred
death-checker thread had been created (peer start failure, PR key selection,
PR register or ledger publish, PR reserve, authority ledger open, slot claim,
version gate) shut down the peer, destroyed the DLM and freed the mount
context without stopping the thread. The thread wakes every 500 ms and reads
the context, so the first tick after the refusal ran on freed memory. Proven
on test32 from its serial console: a mount refused at the slot claim on a
loop device was followed exactly one tick later by a page fault with the
instruction pointer in the death-checker, then a fatal panic; an earlier
boot on the same node shows the same thread faulting in unmapped module text
after a module unload. All seven arms now go through one unwind helper that
joins the thread, shuts down the peer and destroys the DLM, and then take the
shared PR unwind (unregister a live registration, close the ledger, unwrap
the device) instead of the bare context free, which had also leaked the
registration on the register and reserve arms. The version-gate arm, which
runs after the retire settle worker has started, takes the unwind that joins
or quarantines that worker. Patch bump: mount refusal paths only.

## 0.73.1 — 2026-09-04 — The TCP mount branch runs the fence-capability admission gate

A shared LUN whose target implements no SCSI persistent reservations at all
was admitted read-write on the TCP transport with no fencing of any kind.
The PR REGISTER answered -EOPNOTSUPP, the register helper mapped that to
success without registering, and the TCP mount branch took success and went
on to claim a slot and mount. Since 0.15.0 the CAW branch has refused that
device through the fence-capability gate (REPORT CAPABILITIES, verified own
registration, reservation type and persistence, abort capability), and since
0.60.0 the operator override admits only together with single_node_exclusive;
the TCP branch never ran the gate. The gate is now one helper called from
both transport branches, its refusal lines name the transport, and a refused
TCP mount joins its death-checker thread and shuts down its peer and DLM
before the shared PR unwind (unregister, ledger close, device unwrap) rather
than freeing the context under a running thread. The negative harness
tests/fence_capability_admission.sh runs its three arms on both transports.
Patch bump: an admission gate that already existed now covers the second
transport. The setup document states the PR requirement as enforced and
names the reservation type the protocol actually uses (type 7, all
registrants), which it had described as type 5 since before protocol
generation 5.

## 0.73.0 — 2026-09-04 — The TCP transport is admitted at mount in the production build

Since 0.55.0 a clustered read-write mount whose selected DLM transport was
TCP was refused at mount ("transport is not CAW"), because the TCP transport
minted no durable authority epochs and every dead peer's journal slice would
have been refused under token enforcement; only a lab build with a compile
flag could mount TCP. That reason no longer holds. The TCP authority ledger
(0.30.0 through 0.71.0) mints per-grant authority epochs, and the sealed
fence-time manifest gives foreign replay an authority source on TCP. On the
two-node TCP cluster on the QNAP iSCSI target a dirty node death is now
fenced (the sole-survivor exclusive-write gate when the target has purged
the victim's registration), its slice replayed with every buffer image
carrying an enforceable verdict, recovery published, and every
fsync-acknowledged file readable from the survivor with its acknowledged
content, in six consecutive laps of tests/tcp_death_replay.sh in both role
orders (sess502-504). The refusal and its lab flag are removed; both
transports are admitted, and a mount that reaches the transport check with
no transport selected at all is still refused. The admission matrix row for
force_transport=1 now expects ADMITTED. Minor bump: production behaviour
changes. What this does not claim: the same oracle at 32 nodes, where the
original refusal was found, is still an open verification leg of the
D-0288 ledger record.

## 0.72.2 — 2026-09-04 — Sole survivor: the single-node fast paths honour a dead peer's pending invalidations

On the 2-node TCP cluster the first dirty death to get its fence, ledger
manifest, foreign replay and recovery publish all the way through still
left the survivor answering ENOENT for the directory the dead node had
mkdir'd and filled with fsync-acknowledged files. The content was on the
platter; the survivor's view was stale. When the peer died the survivor's
membership dropped to one node and every consumer of a pending peer
invalidation returned on its single-node bypass before looking at the
signal: the lookup-path directory refresh, the per-inode DLM acquire hook
and the dentry revalidation hook all assume that a single-node mount has
no peer that could have changed anything. That is true for a mount that
never had a peer and false for the survivor, whose cached root inode had
been demoted and flagged for reload by the victim's mkdir and was never
reloaded because no BAST would ever arrive again. A readdir of the root
healed it (that path has an ungated reload arm), a lookup never did.

A new predicate, sole survivor (single-node now after multi-node
membership earlier in this mount), gates three changes: the acquire hook's
single-node bypass reloads an inode carrying a stale mark, the evict-ring
directory reload flag or a directory generation past its loaded generation
before returning; the lookup-path directory refresh runs for a sole
survivor instead of no-op'ing; and dentry revalidation keeps taking its
coordinated path for a sole survivor. A never-multi mount keeps its
behaviour unchanged. The per-call "single-node regression" warning that
fired on every hot-path call in this state is replaced by one note per
episode, since the state is legitimate. tests/tcp_death_replay.sh now
samples the survivor's view after a short verdict-time verify (name lookup,
root readdir, lookup again) and re-verifies the content, so a stale view is
told apart from lost content; it also pre-caches state on the survivor that
the victim then changes (a file rewritten at a different size, a negative
dentry the victim creates, a 40-entry block-format directory the victim
extends, five files the victim rewrites, checkpoints, then relogs beside a
sixth in the same inode cluster), re-verifies behind drop_caches, and arms
the inode-cluster clobber detector on the survivor. Patch bump: a
coherency fix, no format change.

## 0.72.1 — 2026-09-04 — Ledger-sourced manifest refused for indexes past the CAW table size

The first dirty death on the QNAP 2-node TCP cluster to reach the 0.71.0
ledger-manifest replay (the exclusive-write gate having certified the
fence) was refused at manifest load: the validator bounded every entry's
slot index by the fixed 65536-slot CAW lock table, but a ledger-sourced
manifest indexes the TCP authority ledger as page times entries-per-page
plus entry, over the pages the collector actually scanned, and that region
is sized per volume (26426 pages on this LUN, indexes to about 819k). A
90-entry manifest with any entry past page 2114 failed "out of range",
the replay was refused with a terminal filesystem-wide quarantine, and the
85 acknowledged files answered EIO. The bound is now the manifest source's
own index space: scanned pages times entries-per-page for a ledger
manifest, the CAW table size for a CAW manifest. The refusal now names the
offending entry, and a validated manifest logs its highest index against
the bound so the geometry is visible in the evidence. Patch bump: a fix in
the manifest consumer, no format change.

## 0.72.0 — 2026-09-04 — Sole-survivor exclusive-write gate: fencing a victim whose registration the target already purged

On a target that removes a node's persistent-reservation registration when
that node's iSCSI session dies (the QNAP TS-453 Pro does, about 34 s after
a power cut, PR generation unchanged; SCST and LIO keep the registration
until a PROUT removes it) the survivor's fence always found the victim's
key already absent. The only proving fence kinds were a PREEMPT AND ABORT
of a PRESENT key, the operator's single-node assertion, and a same-host
self-succession, so the attempt classified KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN and was
re-driven forever: the victim's journal slice was never replayed, the data
it had fsync-acknowledged stayed invisible, its DLM grants stayed frozen,
and on a 2-node cluster the survivor hung on every path operation behind
the dead node's root-inode lock. One peer death was a total outage.

When the victim's key is absent and the prover is provably the only live
member (lease membership minus the victim is one and no other heartbeat
slot is live), the prover now installs the exclusive-write gate: PREEMPT
AND ABORT with reservation key = own, service-action key = 0, type = WRITE
EXCLUSIVE (1), against the all-registrants reservation. Per SPC-4
5.9.10.4.4 that releases the all-registrants reservation, removes every
other registration and aborts their task sets, and installs a single-holder
Write Exclusive reservation for the prover's nexus, so no other initiator
can write at all until it is lifted, whether it re-registers or not. The
post-state is verified (READ KEYS = own key only, READ RESERVATION = type 1
held by own key) and certified as fence kind 20, EXCLUSIVE_WRITE_GATE,
which the replay gate, the certificate validator and the replay-time
recheck (which now asks whether the type-1 reservation is still held by
our key) all accept. The gate is refused, issuing nothing, when our key is
registered on more than one nexus (multipath: a zero service-action key
would remove our own sibling registrations), when the victim key is
present after all, when no all-registrants reservation is in force, and on
a wider membership. Once the recovery publishes, the prover converts the
reservation back to WRITE EXCLUSIVE - ALL REGISTRANTS with a PREEMPT of its
own key (no unreserved gap; measured on the QNAP), retried by the PR
worker if it fails. While the gate is held the reservation-health check and
the key-state bracket treat the type-1 reservation held by our key as the
fencing reservation rather than reporting it as the wrong type. Both PALs
accept the single-holder type only in the abort form with a zero
service-action key. Minor bump: a new fence kind and a new on-disk
certificate value.

## 0.71.0 — 2026-09-04 — TCP transport: a dead peer's journal slice gets a replay authority

On the TCP transport a crashed node's journal slice could never be replayed:
the survivor's fence-time prover wrote a structurally empty NO_CAW_TABLE
manifest (the CAW slot table does not exist on TCP), the foreign-replay gate
therefore certified no buffer image, every transaction was atomically
skipped, the slice ended TORN-UNPUBLISHED and the victim's recovery domain
was quarantined. Data the victim had fsync-acknowledged stayed invisible
until manual repair, on every crash. The durable authority ledger already
carries exactly the information the gate needs — one record per resource
with the exclusive holder's node, heartbeat slot, incarnation, lineage and
grant sequence, the same values the victim stamped into its images — so the
prover now collects the manifest from it: every page of the ledger region
is read fresh from the platter (both shadow copies, bulk runs; a page with
no committed image fails the snapshot closed) and each ACTIVE record whose
exclusive holder is the victim's incarnation becomes a manifest entry in
the CAW collector's format, flagged as ledger-sourced. Before the scan the
victim is SEALED in the DLM: a release of its that arrives after the fence
is refused (the releaser is dead; the record stays a blocker until the
recovery purge) and a release of it still committing is drained, so the
image the collector reads is the image the replay gate later re-checks.
That re-check, the gate's current-safety read, now reads the resource's
ledger record fresh from the platter on TCP instead of answering ENODEV
(which aborted the attempt); the pre-purge manifest verification runs on
TCP for the same reason. The manifest consumer refuses a ledger manifest
whose page count is not this region's. Minor bump: the TCP transport gains
a recovery capability it did not have.

## 0.70.19 — 2026-09-04 — FUA on passthrough CDBs follows the durability declaration

Every SCSI passthrough CDB the kernel PAL builds (READ(16), WRITE(16), and
COMPARE AND WRITE on both submission paths) carried a hard-coded FUA bit. A
QNAP TS-453 Pro iSCSI target, the home/small-office NAS class the first
production release is aimed at, rejects any CDB with that bit set (ILLEGAL
REQUEST, invalid field in CDB) while executing the same COMPARE AND WRITE
correctly without it, measured with raw CDBs (new `tests/scsi_caw_probe.sh`).
The read path already fell back to plain reads on that rejection; the
compare-and-write path did not, so the first PR-key ledger publish failed
with EIO and the mount refused ("registration UNATTRIBUTED on the LUN").
The bit now follows the operator's existing `fua_disable` declaration: with
`fua_disable=1` (no real FUA, power loss out of scope, how every rig and
this NAS run) no passthrough CDB sets FUA; with `fua_disable=0` the bit
stays set and a rejection still fails the mount closed, now with a message
naming the declaration to make instead of a bare EIO. The June conclusion
that this QNAP "has no CAW" was the FUA pre-read of `tools/caw_verify`
failing before the CAW was ever issued.

## 0.70.18 (sess498) — 2026-09-04 — the leaf-hash-hole heal can be switched off

Since sess22 a negative lookup in a multi-node directory has been answered
by scanning every data block of the directory for the name, and a remove
whose name has no index entry has expunged the dirent data-side, so that a
hash index left short of its data blocks never surfaced as ENOENT. The heal
is now behind `mxfs.dir_datascan_heal` (default 1, unchanged behaviour); at
0 the leaf and node index is authoritative exactly as in single-node XFS.
The lever exists because every hole the heal repaired on 2026-09-04 traced
to the new-tenure retire of an undestaged log item that 0.70.11 removed,
and the scan is the largest single term of the 32-node shared-directory
create: a control board with the heal off is the measurement that decides
whether the producer is gone and the scan can be retired. Patch bump: a
new runtime lever with the default preserving current behaviour.

## 0.70.17 (sess496) — 2026-09-04 — the directory durable-barrier warnings say why the barrier gave up

The shortform-parent and grown-directory durable-barrier warnings
(P13-SFPARENT-DURABLE-FAIL, P68-DIRINODE-DURABLE-FAIL) claimed the inode
cluster was "not destaged". A day of rig logs showed every one of the 393
occurrences was the destage-time tenure check refusing at its first try
because the on-disk slot already belonged to nobody, on an orphan release
whose in-core grant was already gone and whose dinode was clean; nothing
was un-destaged, and the release-time publication ledger never deferred or
unlocked open. The lines now carry the refusal flag, the in-core mode, the
in-AIL and pin state and whether the inode is clean, so a future
occurrence classifies itself as tenure-refused, budget-exhausted or
clean-but-skipped without a log correlation. Patch bump: diagnostic text
only, no behaviour change.

## 0.70.16 (sess495) — 2026-09-04 — the adopt-check skip no longer keys on the directory generation

On 0.70.14 the skip engaged on only 4 of 32 nodes and the per-create inode
read cost was unchanged. The recorded tuple included the directory's
generation counter, and peers' modify notifications keep bumping that
counter during this node's tenure for changes made before it; every bump
re-armed the read. Those changes reached the platter before the peer
released the grant, so they were already in the image the clean read saw,
and a later notification of them says nothing new while the grant is still
held. The tuple is now the hold-epoch and the inode incarnation under a
held, non-stale EX. A capped P495-ADOPT-READ line names the term that
re-armed a read, so the next run shows why any remaining read happens.
Patch bump: correction to the 0.70.14 fix; the verification chain re-runs.

## 0.70.15 (sess495) — 2026-09-04 — the lookup-window read trace

The lookup attribution run on 0.70.13 refuted the cold-FUA-read hypothesis
for the shared-directory lookup term: in-tenure lookups average 4.85 ms, of
which FUA passthrough reads account for 0.36 ms, while the node-wide plain
read-bio counter advances by about 23 per lookup (0.3 in a private
directory). Nothing in the log says which blocks those are or whose task
issues them. With mxfs.lkp_trace=1 and the create-cost probe armed,
xfs_create now opens a node-wide window around its existence lookup
(P495-LKP-WIN open/close) and every buffer read bio and FUA read submitted on
the node while it is open is printed as P495-LKP-RD with its task, block,
verifier and freshness flags. Diagnostic, capped per node, default off.
Patch bump: instrumentation.

## 0.70.14 (sess495) — 2026-09-04 — a directory modify under a continuously held EX grant no longer re-reads the directory inode from the platter

Every create, remove and rename into a directory that a peer has ever
touched began with a synchronous FUA read of the directory's inode cluster,
to catch a peer having converted or grown the directory (or added names
inside an existing block) since this node last looked. On the shared-directory
create row that read is about 1 ms of the 15 ms in-tenure create (rfr_ms 1.0
against 0.2 in a private directory, where the call site's dir-gen gate skips
it). A peer can only change the directory inode while holding its EX grant,
and this node only loses its EX through paths that bump the inode's
hold-epoch, so while the grant is still held and not stale, the epoch,
incarnation and dir generation are unchanged from a previous read that found
the platter not ahead, the read cannot find anything new. The adopt check now
records that tuple after a clean read taken under EX and skips the read while
it still matches; a demote, release, stale mark, reload, inode reuse or a late
peer-modify notification invalidates it by construction. dir_adopt_skip_held_ex=0
restores the unconditional read; two counters (reads taken, reads skipped, both
on the held-EX path) and a capped P495-ADOPT-SKIP line are the census.
Patch bump: a fix on the create path, behaviour unchanged for correctness,
verified by rfr_ms in-tenure and the directory coherency rows.

## 0.70.13 (sess494) — 2026-09-04 — the create-cost probe says what the shared-directory lookup term is

On the shared-directory create row the existence lookup costs 4.4 ms per
create with the per-modify flush on and 7.9 ms with it off, against 0.3 ms in
a private directory, and nothing in the log said why. The node now keeps two
always-on counters, one for synchronous FUA passthrough reads (count and
wall) and one for plain buffer read bios, and the create-cost probe samples
both around the lookup and prints them as lkp_fua, lkp_fua_ms and lkp_rd.
Two atomic adds per read, no lock, no output unless the probe is armed.
Patch bump: instrumentation.

## 0.70.12 (sess494) — 2026-09-04 — a fenced-and-quarantined victim no longer refuses the whole-cluster restart

The whole-cluster-restart survivor scan counted every recovery-guard record
that carries a recovery descriptor as a member-shaped victim, and then
required a valid identity block on it to obtain a fence key. A guard whose
descriptor is quarantined with a terminal refusal verdict names a victim that
a survivor had already fenced (the certificate is in the descriptor) and whose
journal slice the cluster had durably refused; a live cluster runs beside
that record until operator repair, so its presence is not evidence of an
outage, and its identity block is the guard writer's by design, here absent.
Measured on 0.70.11: after one refused fail-stop and a clean mass unmount, the
LUN held that one guard, twelve retiring records and no registered PR key at
all, and the first remount was refused as a victim without a key, leaving
the cluster unmountable. The scan now classifies such a record with the same
identity binding the closure gate uses (descriptor crc bound to the sector's
own generation, node and epoch, victim tuple equal to the record's own and to
its slot, quarantined, outcome crc-valid and canonical, or the exact legacy
all-zero outcome region) and excludes it from outage detection: nothing
fences, replays, adopts or zeroes it, the slot stays non-consumable, and the
admission barrier's terminal classifier imports the quarantine before the
filesystem is available, exactly as a joiner to a live cluster would. A
quarantined descriptor whose outcome bytes do not validate is a torn verdict
and now fails closed as an unreadable sector rather than being fenced under
a guard writer's identity. The classifier is exported context-free so the
offline checker can apply the same rule. Patch bump: a fix.

## 0.70.11 (sess493) — 2026-09-04 — a directory block's log item is retired at a stale-base evict only when the block is on disk

At the acquire-side evict of a directory's cached data blocks, the arms that
recognize a stale base from an earlier tenure (the master epoch advanced since
this inode's last evict, the block's epoch stamp behind the current epoch, or
its grant stamp behind the current grant) also retired the block's in-AIL log
item without writing it, on the argument that anything cached from a prior
tenure had been drained at our own release. The measurement on 0.70.9 showed
the argument did not hold for what the arms actually matched: the first evict
call of a tenure sees blocks this tenure has already logged, and the grant
stamp is taken at cold read and never refreshed by a modify, so all 2204
retires were of blocks logged in the current tenure and every comparable one
was missing at least one live entry on the platter. With the log item gone the
log tail could move past the transaction, leaving fsync-acknowledged entries
only in that node's cache until its release drain, and a crash would lose them
from journal and platter alike. The retire now requires the block to be
destaged, written sequence equal to logged sequence, which is the only state
in which dropping the item loses nothing; an undestaged block keeps its log
item for the ordinary AIL push or the release drain and keeps its in-core
image valid, since that image is the only copy of committed content. The
retained cases print P492-KEEP-UNDEST with the block's epoch relation so a
genuinely prior-tenure undestaged block, which would be an invariant breach,
is counted separately. The 0.70.8/0.70.9 platter comparison is removed with
the arm it measured. Patch bump: a fix.

## 0.70.10 (sess493) — 2026-09-04 — a dead holder's SB summary lock is released after an AG-scoped refusal instead of convoying every unmounting peer

When a withdrawing node dies holding the cluster-wide SB summary lock and the
replay of its journal slice is refused for one allocation group, its grants
stay frozen by design and only the out-of-closure purge (publisher) or the
survivors' demand scrub can free what is provably outside the refused domain.
The closure classifier maps an inode-class resource to the allocation group
its number decodes to and freezes anything decoding past the AG count, and
the SB summary key is built to decode past it. So the one lock every
unmounting peer must take stayed frozen, and seven peers waited out the full
lock timeout and departed dirty. The classifier now recognizes that exact key
and classifies it out of closure for AG-mask verdicts only: the lock guards a
recount from uncached AG headers, not logged state, and a refused AG's
transactions are never applied, so the recount stays correct. Every other
out-of-range key stays frozen, and a filesystem-wide refusal still freezes
this one. The exemption prints P487-SBSUM-OUT-OF-CLOSURE when it fires. Patch
bump: a fix.

## 0.70.9 (sess492) — 2026-09-04 — the retire discriminator asks whether our entries are on the platter, not whether the bytes match

The 0.70.8 comparison came back unequal on every one of 2074 retirements and
the run lost nothing, because at a tenure boundary the device legitimately
holds a peer's newer image of the same block. The question that decides
whether the retire drops an obligation is containment: every live directory
entry in the in-core image must be present by name in the platter image.
The probe line now carries that answer and the count of entries that are
absent, for data and block-format directory blocks, alongside the byte
comparison and the buffer's verifier name. Diagnostic only.

## 0.70.8 (sess492) — 2026-09-04 — each new-tenure retire of a committed-unwritten directory block says whether its content is on the platter

The acquire-side new-tenure retire drops the in-AIL log item of a cached
directory block without writing it, on the argument that the block was made
durable at this node's previous release. The 0.70.4 census counted 2313 such
retirements of blocks whose logged sequence was ahead of their written
sequence, which is either stale per-buffer bookkeeping (nothing is lost) or a
real committed image the device has never seen (a crash-durability hole and
the enabler of the lost-entry defect). The probe line for each such retire
now carries a byte-for-byte comparison of the in-core block against a plain
read of the device, so the two are told apart per block instead of argued.
One bounded read per printed line, diagnostic only.

## 0.70.7 (sess492) — 2026-09-04 — the reclaim-exit drain reports its result whenever it had something to drain

In the first verification run of the 0.70.5 drain, one of the two exercised
cases printed no post-drain line because every post-drain field was zero,
which is the success case and the one worth seeing. The post-drain census
line now prints whenever the pre-drain census found anything, as well as
whenever anything remains. Instrument only.

## 0.70.6 (sess492) — 2026-09-04 — the pinned-AIL fail-stop can be exercised while the SB summary lock is held

The convoy measurement showed that a node whose AIL is pinned before it
unmounts never reaches the cluster-wide SB summary lock: it waits in the
per-inode BAST workqueue flush at the top of put_super until the fail-stop
shuts it down, on both the fail-stop-only build and the build that pushes the
AIL before the lock. That leaves the case the record is about unmeasured: a
pin that arises after the lock is taken, where the quiesce under the lock is
what stalls. This build adds a one-shot debug arm (module parameter
dbg_sb_inject_unheld_agno, off by default) that the final SB summary sync
consumes after it has taken the lock and before its quiesce, committing an
unchanged header image for the first unheld allocation group at or above the
armed number, exactly as the existing debugfs injector does before unmount.
The injector's body is now a helper shared by both entry points. The
fleet-unmount harness gained a leg that arms it instead of injecting early,
and samples the victim's kernel-thread stacks during the grace period so the
work item the workqueue flush waits on is named. Instrument only, no
behaviour change.

## 0.70.5 (sess492) — 2026-09-04 — a btree-format directory reclaimed while held EX drains its committed blocks before the grant leaves

The 0.70.4 census proved the mechanism of the lost directory entry in three
laps of three: on the one node per lap whose entries were later missing, the
directory inode was reclaimed by the verify phase's cache drop while the node
held it EX, with two to five committed-unwritten data blocks cached and the
reclaim hook's drain arm skipped, because that arm only ran for extent-format
directories and the shared directory had grown to btree format. Four seconds
later the same node released the directory from a read grant, the release
drain re-landed the never-written block, the directory write fence refused
the sub-EX write, and the block was freed with its obligation open, so the
next peer to cold-read the block rewrote it without the entry.

The reclaim hook now drains extent-format and btree-format directories alike
before the on-disk grant is released: log force, the data-block flush (owner
scan, bmbt scan, extent walk), then the map-independent landing pass for
undestaged owned blocks that the owner scan cannot see because their log item
was already retired without a write, then the device flush. The drain is then
checked rather than trusted: a post-drain census prints what was landed and
what remains, and if committed-unwritten blocks remain while the node holds
EX the hook reports it and fails closed under the existing
evict_obligation_shutdown policy instead of releasing a grant whose content
exists only in this node's memory. The landing scan gained a check mode
(count without holds or writes) for that census. The release pipeline's own
post-drain census was clean on every one of the 1336 releases in the same
run, so this is the one exit that lacked the drain.

## 0.70.4 (sess491) — 2026-09-04 — every way a directory grant can leave a node now counts the committed-unwritten blocks it leaves behind

A committed directory entry was durably lost on a 32-node shared-directory
create run with the per-modify flush off: the block holding the entry was
logged under EX, never written, and when the node next released the directory
it held only a read grant, so the write fence refused the release drain's
re-land and the block was freed with its obligation open. The node had not
released EX through the release pipeline at all. Its verify phase drops the
page and inode caches, the directory inode was reclaimed while EX was held,
and the reclaim hook's data-block drain is written for extent-format
directories only; this directory had grown to btree format. Nothing measured
that path, because a clean EX-held reclaim prints no line.

This build measures it. The inode-reclaim hook counts the directory's cached
data blocks that still carry committed content the device has not seen
(undestaged, or still attached to a log item in the AIL), together with any
open committed-never-submitted obligations, and names the first such block
with its fork format, in-core and on-disk lock modes and whether the drain arm
ran. The release pipeline takes the same census after its drain and before the
handoff, with the entry mode. The acquire-side new-tenure retire, which drops
a block's log item without a write on the argument that the block was drained
at the node's prior release, now names every block it retires that is still
undestaged, with the epoch and grant values that justified it. Every overlay
caller that retires a log item without a write stamps its source line on the
buffer, and the census line printed when such an item is freed with an open
obligation carries that line and the block's sequence pair, so the free names
its caller instead of the shared retire routine. No behaviour changes.

## 0.70.3 (sess490) — 2026-09-04 — a synchronous buffer write that completes without a bio runs its terminal completion once, not twice

Every unmount that followed a directory-release drain or a create's durable
bmbt flush departed DIRTY: the departure gate found terminal buffer
completions it could not attribute to any admitted submission, refused to
prove the node quiescent, left its heartbeat slot ACTIVE and kept its
persistent-reservation key as a fence target, and the peers then fenced and
recovered a node that had unmounted cleanly. One 32-node run showed 8012 such
completions and all 32 nodes departing dirty.

They were not unattributed submissions. When a synchronous write completes
without issuing a bio — the FUA passthrough and skip arms inside the submit
path — the generic completion entry runs the terminal completion, which
retires the submission's departure token, and then wakes the waiter; the
waiter's wait loop, inherited from upstream, then runs the terminal completion
a second time and finds nothing to retire. Upstream has the same two passes
and tolerates them because its second pass changes nothing; the MXFS terminal
accounting (departure token, inode-cluster write token, committed-obligation
disposition, flush-epoch stamps) is not idempotent, and every stack trace of
an unattributed retire sat in the wait loop under xfs_bwrite with the write
flag already cleared by the first pass.

The completion routers that run the terminal pass now record that fact on the
buffer after claiming the waiter's wake credit and before completing it, and
the waiter skips its own pass when it finds the record. A real bio's end_io
never runs the pass and never sets the record, so that path is unchanged: the
waiter still owns its single pass. The record is cleared at every fresh
submission; a resubmit after a transient error keeps the credit and never had
the record set. A once-per-boot line names the first two buffers whose waiter
took the skip, so a run can show the path was exercised. Buffers completed
synchronously without ever being submitted (the foreign-replay batch failure)
still count as unattributed at their single pass; classifying that path is a
separate change.

## 0.70.2 (sess489) — 2026-09-04 — every refused log item reports how long it took to clear

The fail-stop of 0.70.0 shuts a mount down when xfsaild has refused one of
its committed AG-metadata images for ten seconds because the node no longer
holds the grant. Whether ten seconds is safe depends on a number nobody had
measured: how long a refusal lasts on a healthy handoff, where the next
transaction's commit lands in the gap between the release commit and the
drain that writes the image home. That gap is why the plain crash-consistency
row on 0.69.5 logged hundreds of refusals fleet-wide. This build measures the
answer instead of assuming it. When a buffer log item that was refused at
least once is finally freed, its age from the first coherent refusal goes
into a per-mount census (items refused, items cleared, cleared by a shutdown
rather than a home write, slow ones, sum, mean and maximum), readable at
debugfs ailpin_stats, and any item that took at least a second (module
parameter ailpin_clear_report_ms) is named in the log with its LSNs, count,
and whether a shutdown or an I/O error retired it. The maximum against the
grace is the margin the fail-stop has; the per-item line is what says which
image sat unwritten and why. No behaviour of the push changes.

## 0.70.1 (sess488) — 2026-09-04 — the unmount drains its own log before it takes the cluster-wide summary lock

The final superblock summary sync at unmount takes a cluster-wide lock and
runs a log quiesce under it — a log force, a wait for the whole AIL to drain
and a wait for the buffer target. A peer's request for that lock is refused
while it is held. On 2026-09-04 one node whose AIL could not drain sat in
that quiesce holding the lock for the entire budget, and twenty-six peers
that had reached their own final sync waited behind it. The unmount already
ran an explicit force, push and wait of its own, but after the sync. It now
runs it before: every wait that can depend on a grant this node no longer
holds happens before the lock is taken, so a node whose AIL is pinned stalls
alone — and, with the refused-item fail-stop of 0.70.0, shuts down before it
ever takes the lock, which the sync then skips. The quiesce under the lock
finds an AIL that only the sync's own counter transaction can have
repopulated. The cases in which the sync declines to run are covered by the
same push, exactly as before. The under-lock quiesce itself is still
unbounded; bounding it is a separate change.

## 0.70.0 (sess488) — 2026-09-04 — a log item the node may not write is retained and, in the end, fails the mount rather than pinning it

The push of a committed AG-metadata image (or a released directory's bmbt
leaf) for a grant this node no longer holds used to stale the buffer and
report success. The stale changed nothing about the item — it stayed in the
AIL at its LSN and was re-refused every cycle, so the log tail never moved
and any wait for the AIL to drain waited forever — and it armed a second
hazard: a later cache lookup reused the staled buffer with its verifier
cleared while the item was still attached, so the next push no longer
recognised it as AG metadata and wrote whatever the buffer then held.

The push now refuses honestly: the item stays as it is, the buffer is
unlocked untouched, and the push reports the item as locked, which is what
xfsaild already does with an item it cannot make progress on. If the item is
still refused after the grace period the mount is shut down with a message
naming the item, its LSN, its captured authority and the AG's current hold
state. The item is this node's own committed change to metadata it was not
entitled to change; writing it would revert the holder's newer image,
dropping it would lose a committed change, and nothing at push time can
prove the image already durable, so a named shutdown is the only honest
terminal state — the same policy the acquire-time preflight already applies
to the same condition. Once the log is shut down the refused push falls
through, the submit fails without I/O and retires the item, so the AIL
drains and an unmount completes as a shutdown unmount. The shutdown runs
from a work item because the push runs under the AIL lock.

The grace period is a diagnostic allowance, not a correctness mechanism: the
only legitimate reason the not-held predicate is briefly true is a lock-free
read taken across an acquire's publication, and the accounting starts only
from a coherent not-held snapshot. A held AG whose image was captured under
an earlier tenure's epoch is reported (P126-EPOCH-MISMATCH) but still
written, so that case is measured before anything is done about it.

## 0.69.6 (sess488) — 2026-09-04 — a refused log item is named, timed, and reproducible on demand

xfsaild refuses to write a committed AG-metadata image (or a released
directory's bmbt leaf) for a grant this node no longer holds, because writing
it would revert the holder's newer image. The refusal line said which block
and nothing else, and the refusal itself left the item in the AIL forever: on
the 2026-09-04 unmount campaign one node's three refused items (the AGI,
inobt and finobt of one allocation group, at one LSN) sat at the head of its
AIL for the whole 240 s budget while every peer waited behind the cluster
lock that node held. Each buffer log item now records when it was first
refused under a coherent not-held snapshot (the grant epoch read unchanged
around the hold state), how many times, and at what LSN, so a re-log of a
refused item is visible instead of restarting the clock; the refusal line
carries the item's LSN and its captured authority next to the AG's current
epoch and hold state; and an item refused past a grace period (module
parameter ailpin_grace_ms, default ten seconds) prints one PINNED alert with
that identity and queues a mount-level report. This version reports only;
the push still stales and skips exactly as before, so the pin is measured on
the unchanged behaviour before the behaviour is changed.

A per-mount debugfs injector, inject_unheld_agmeta_dirty, produces the item on
demand: for an allocation group the node does not hold it reads the AGI
through the ordinary transactional read, logs it unchanged, commits and
forces the log, bypassing only the DLM authorization. It exists so the
terminal behaviour can be verified without racing an unmount, and it poisons
the node's log slice by design — scratch filesystems only.

## 0.69.5 (sess487) — 2026-09-04 — the create-cost line separates the name lookup from the inode creation

Chain 137 measured that an in-tenure create on the shared directory spends 4.6 ms
between the directory refresh and the end of inode creation, against 0.3 ms in
a private directory. That span held two different things: the existence lookup
of the new name in a directory that has grown to thousands of entries, and
xfs_icreate, whose cost on a shared allocation group is the inode-cluster
buffer read and the cluster-grant claim. They are now stamped separately as
lkp_ms and icr_ms, so the next armed run says which of the two the 4.3 ms
excess belongs to before any allocation policy is touched.

## 0.69.4 (sess487) — 2026-09-04 — the directory-tenure probe measures its own tenures

The per-tenure create probe added in 0.69.2 reports how many creates a node
completed in one tenure of a directory's grant and how long that tenure took.
It was written to be always on, so that the run of interest is never the one
where it was off. Its wall field, however, was derived from the create-cost
probe's clock, which is only started when that separate probe is armed. On the
32-node crash_consistency run of 2026-09-04 04:37Z every one of the 662 tenure
lines therefore reported a wall of zero, which read as "tenures cost nothing"
until the derivation was traced. The clock is now stamped on every clustered
create; the create-cost line itself remains gated exactly as before, so the log
volume is unchanged and the cost is one clock read per create.

The create-cost line itself gains four fields that split the span between
inode allocation and the transaction commit, which on the 32-node shared
directory workload carried 9.6 of the 18 ms an in-tenure create costs and was
reported as one unattributed number: rfr_ms (the modify refresh and the
adopt-disk-format read of the directory inode), icr_ms (the existence lookup
and inode creation), mrg_ms (peer merge, stale-block reconcile and pending
replay) and cc_ms (adding the entry to the directory). Each is stamped at a
call boundary, so the four are mutually exclusive and sum, with the existing
fields, to pre_ms.

## 0.69.3 (sess485) — 2026-09-04 — the unmount finishes its metadata work before it gives the allocation groups away

An unmounting node used to publish every allocation-group grant it still held
as the first act of its DLM teardown, and only then do the metadata work an
unmount consists of: the deferred inactivation of every inode the VFS had just
evicted (AGI, inode btrees, free-inode btree), the final superblock summary
sync's log quiesce, and the AIL push and inode flush inside xfs_unmountfs.
The first part of that work ran with a DLM that re-acquired the grants it
needed and then let them be swept away undrained; the rest ran after the DLM
pointer was cleared, at which point the AG lock routine answers "granted" to
a mount that has no lock manager at all. A peer that had legitimately taken
one of the published groups was modifying the same AGI while this node was
still writing its own image of it. Mount does the opposite — the lock manager
is alive before any filesystem work starts — and unmount now mirrors it.

The release could not simply be moved later, because the heartbeat thread is
joined before xfs_unmountfs and a grant held past that point is held by a node
no longer proving it is alive. So the work moved earlier instead. put_super now
stops every producer first (the foreign-slice replay, the deferred reap, the
destage kick, block garbage collection), flushes inactivation, runs the summary
sync, then forces the log, pushes the whole AIL and waits for the buffer target
— all under live grants and a beating heartbeat — purges the inode cluster
locks after the last thing that uses them, and only then publishes the grants.
What xfs_unmountfs has left to do afterwards is the log covering and the
unmount record, neither of which touches allocation-group metadata.

The release itself was also missing eight of the nine drain steps the
cooperative release runs before an on-disk unlock. It now runs the alloc
buffer list, inode cluster and AG-metadata drains before every unlock, and
pays the second metadata pass and the device flush only for an AG where those
drains actually wrote something; the summary line reports how many groups that
was, which after the quiesce above is expected to be none.

The instrument that found the defect verifies the fix. The departure
accounting now also counts AG-metadata and inode-cluster writes made between
put_super entry and the publication of the grants, printed as pre_wr and
pre_iclus_wr on the P483-AGFREE-WINDOW line: on a workload that leaves work
for unmount those must be nonzero while every after-publication counter is
zero. A nonzero after-publication count while the DLM still existed is now
reported at alert level rather than notice, because it is the defect and not a
curiosity.

## 0.69.2 (sess483) — 2026-09-04 — a short tenure and a directory that never left look identical

The count added a moment ago measures how many files a node creates between
losing the directory and losing it again. On its own that number cannot be
trusted, and an outside review of the design said so before any of it ran.

The generation counter moves every time the node gives the directory up —
including when it takes it straight back. So a count of one means either "the
directory went all the way round thirty-two nodes between these two files" or
"the grant flickered and never actually left". Those are opposite findings, and
only the first is the contention being hunted.

- `xfs/xfs_inode.h`, `xfs/xfs_inode.c`: the tenure line now also carries the
  wait between the last file of the old tenure and the first of the new. Near
  a full trip around the cluster means a real handover; a millisecond or two
  means the directory never went anywhere and the time is being spent
  somewhere other than waiting in a queue.

The same review found two things wrong with how the earlier measurements were
being read, both recorded against the defect rather than fixed in code: the
clients are closed-loop, so raising the files per node lengthens the contention
rather than deepening the queue — the earlier claim that cost "rises with
outstanding work" was simply wrong; and the largest run was cut short by its
own guard, so its average is a lower bound, not an average. The verification
chain now runs its sweep forwards and then backwards over the same filesystem,
because a sweep that only ever goes one way cannot tell the parameter apart
from the time it takes to get there.

## 0.69.1 (sess483) — 2026-09-04 — a zero that could not have been anything else is not a measurement

The unmount-window counters added earlier today ran on thirty-two nodes and
came back zero on all eight — no allocation-group metadata and no inode
clusters written or read after the node published its groups as free, on a
workload that deliberately churned four hundred files per node first and left
every node still holding a group at unmount.

That is a useful answer only if a non-zero was reachable. It might not have
been: if nothing at all is submitted in that stretch of unmount, or if the
counting point is simply never reached there, all eight counters read zero for
reasons that have nothing to do with the question.

- `xfs/xfs_mount.h`, `pal/linux/xfs_buf.c`, `pal/linux/xfs_super.c`: the window
  now also counts *every* submission it sees, of any type, and reports it
  alongside the eight. A non-zero there beside eight zeros is a live instrument
  reporting a real absence. Zero there means the run proves nothing, and the
  per-unmount line says so in its own text rather than leaving the reader to
  work it out.

The verification harness scores it the same way: with the control at zero it
refuses to record a bound, instead of reporting the run as a clean negative.

## 0.69.0 (sess483) — 2026-09-04 — how many files does one node create before it has to hand the directory back?

Creating files into a single directory shared by thirty-two nodes is slow, and
this release does not fix that.  It measures the one number that says why.

The cost was assumed to be a fixed admission charge paid once per node and then
amortised.  A ladder run this session says otherwise: holding the node count at
thirty-two and raising the files each node creates from eight to a hundred and
twenty-eight, the average cost of a single create goes 193, 169, 550, 1558,
2151 milliseconds.  It gets *worse* per file the more files there are, which no
fixed cost can do — and two seconds to create one empty file is roughly three
hundred times what the local filesystem takes.

What can do that is the directory itself circulating faster.  A node has to own
the directory to add a name to it; the more nodes are queued behind it, the
sooner it has to give it up, and in the limit each file costs a full trip of
the directory around the cluster — which is about a second and a half here, and
is the right size for the numbers above.

That is a testable claim, and it needs one count: how many files a node manages
to create between acquiring the directory and losing it.  The generation
counter that already tracks losing it gives that for free.

- `xfs/xfs_inode.h`, `xfs/xfs_inode.c`: three fields on the directory inode and
  a short accounting step at the end of a successful create, under the lock the
  inode already has.  When the generation moves — which is exactly when the
  directory was handed away — the closed-out tally is printed:
  `P483-DIRTENURE` with the directory, how many files it took, their total and
  mean wall, and the line number of the code that ended the tenure.

  Counted always rather than behind a switch: output is bounded by handovers,
  not by files, so it costs nothing to leave on — and a switch is only ever off
  during the run that mattered.  One sample is dropped per directory by
  construction, the last one, since a tally is printed by the first create of
  the following tenure.

The prediction is specific: if this is the mechanism, files-per-tenure falls
toward one as the load rises, and the cost of a file tracks one trip divided by
that count.  If instead the count stays flat while the cost climbs, the trips
are getting slower rather than more frequent, and that is a different bug in a
different place.

## 0.68.1 (sess483) — 2026-09-04 — count the inodes in that window too

The counters added a moment ago watch allocation-group metadata, which is what
the group lock covers.  They do not watch inode clusters, which are covered by
the per-inode locks instead — and the unmount writes those in the same window,
from `xfs_unmount_flush_inodes`, with the same destroyed lock context.

That is worth counting on its own.  An inode cluster written without authority
is an open defect in its own right, and the corruption this whole line of work
is chasing includes an inode left chained in a group's unlinked list with its
mode and generation zeroed — which is an inode-cluster write, not a
group-metadata one.

- `pal/linux/xfs_buf.c`, `xfs/xfs_mount.h`, `pal/linux/xfs_super.c`: the same
  window now counts inode-cluster buffers separately from group metadata, with
  the same read/write and lock-context-alive/gone splits, and the per-unmount
  line reports all eight numbers.  The printed probe tag names which kind it
  was.

The verification harness had to be corrected for a trap it created for itself:
the buffer probe's format string now chooses its own tag at runtime, so the tag
does not appear in the built module at all, and the check that refuses to run
the fleet unless the module carries the probe would have refused a module that
carries it.

## 0.68.0 (sess483) — 2026-09-04 — the unmount hands the allocation groups away, and then keeps using them

A node that is unmounting publishes every allocation-group grant it still
holds — telling the rest of the cluster those groups are free to take — and it
does that about a hundred lines above the call that actually finishes the
filesystem's work.

What comes after the handover is not cleanup.  It is `xfs_unmountfs`, and its
first act, in upstream XFS's own words, is to "perform all on-disk metadata
updates required to inactivate inodes that the VFS evicted earlier in the
unmount process" — freeing inodes, which changes the inode allocation btrees
and the AGI.  Then it flushes the remaining inodes, and pushes the whole log
tail to disk.  Both of those write allocation-group metadata, or the inode
clusters beside it, for groups this node no longer owns — and the log-tail push
takes no lock at all, so it does not even need the broken acquire below to be
a problem.

The inode-free path does ask for the group lock: `xfs_inactive_ifree` takes it
around the entire free transaction, deliberately and with a comment saying so.
By then it cannot get it.  Sixteen lines after the grants are published the
mount's cluster-lock context is destroyed, and the acquire function opens with
a check that returns *success* when there is no context — which is right for a
single-node mount, where there is nothing to coordinate with, and which here
means every one of those transactions is told it holds a lock that no longer
exists.

None of this is measured.  There is a platter-reading audit at the release
itself, but it looks at the state one instant before the handover and nothing
after it.  So this release adds the instruments and changes no behaviour:

- `xfs/xfs_mount.h`, `pal/linux/xfs_buf.c`: the departure accounting now marks
  the moment the grants are published, and the buffer submission path counts
  every allocation-group metadata buffer that crosses it — split by direction,
  because a stale read poisons what is built on it while a write publishes this
  node's image over a peer's, and split again by whether the cluster-lock
  context still existed.  That second split matters: the earlier half of the
  window can still re-acquire, so only the later half is unambiguous.  The
  first eight of each kind print their block, buffer type and calling task.
- `xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c`: the acquire path now separates "this mount never needed
  cluster locking" from "this clustered mount's lock context is already gone",
  which had been the same silent success.  The second case is counted and its
